James Thomas Fraser
Grand Master 1937-1938

The seventy-first Grand Master of Masons in California was genial,
lovable Tom Fraser, who was born at Smithfield, Guysboro county, Nova
Scotia, August 28, 1868, and who received his education as he says, "in
the great outdoors," although he did take a course in English at the
University of California. Like many sturdy men, he was thrown on his
own resources at an early age, but always with a determination to be
true to himself and to his friends, and to make the best of his opportunities.
He is of Scotch ancestry, of the numerous and respectable clan Fraser,
and on his mother's side of the clan Mcintosh. His father died when
Tom was but eight years of age, and his formal schooling ended at the
age of thirteen, since which time he has been "on his own."
He located at Eureka, California, in 1889, where he has resided
cdntinu.ously ever since. He is an attorney at law, having been admitted
to the bar on March 12, 1917. Our Tom was always of a friendly disposition, albeit of strong convictions, and during his temporary absence
from California he was elected a member of the Eureka School Board,
serving four years, and was re-elected and served four more years as
President of the Board. He filled the office of Justice of the Peace for
sixteen years, · and at the date of this writing he is finishing his second
four-year term as District Attorney of Humboldt county. He has the
enviable record of never prosecuting a criminal case unless he was firmly
convinced of the guilt of the defendant, and his convictions have rated
the highest percentage of any prosecuting officer in the United Stateseighty percent.
His Masonic record is as follows:
Humboldt Lodge No. 79. Initiated June 9, passed June 27, raised
July 11, 1903; Master 1912.
Humboldt Chapter No. 52 R. A. M. Exalted May 25, 1931; High
Priest 1936.
Pacific Council No. 37, Eureka, February 16, 1932. Illustrious Master
1934.
Eureka Commandery No. 35. Knighted October 5, 1931. Commander
1935.
Oakland Consistory, 32 dei'I'ee, Scottish Rite.
Aahmes Temple, A, A. 0. N. M. S.
Eureka Pyramid No. 20 Sciots, Past Toparch.
Camellia Chapter No. 63, 0. E. S. Patron 1907.
In Grand Lodge: Inspector 1919 to 1931; Grand Orator 1932; Junior
Grand Warden 1934; Senior Grand War-Oen 1935; Deputy Grand Master
1936; Grand Master 1937.
His domestic life is a happy one. On July 31, 1897 he was united
in marriage to Dora Bessie Zerlang, a native of Eureka. To this union
there have been born two boys and one girl, all now .g rown to maturity
and all reflecting credit on their parents and to their legion of friends.
JAMES THOMAS FRASER
Grand Master

of the universe. The stars shall not shine forever, nor the fires of the sun
forever b.urn; the mountains shall not forever stand on · their granite
bases, nor the oceans forever roll. The glory of empires, monarchy and
republics shall not continue forever, nor the learning and eloquence of
man;· but the great things of the soul, Faith, Hope and Love, shall abide
forever.
Because of that fact may I invite the attention of the members of the
Grand Lodge to consider ·with me three lines of thought suggested in the
text, "And now abideth Faith, Hope and Love."
· We read in the Holy Writ, "Faith is the substance of things hoped for,
the evidence of things .not seen." In other words, faith substan ~iates or
gives to the bbjects of hope and is in itself an argument for that reality.
F aith, according to Locke, "is a reception of a proposition as true while · it
has not yet so been proven." Definitions are so often unnecessary, for we
know better what they mean through their natural use than we do by definitions. We know what it means to have faith in man, but very few of us realize
the importance of faith to man.
It .is by fai th that man's worlds are kept together, for man creates
worlds, If men were to lose confidence in their fellowmen, the world
which they have formed would soon fall to pieces. If the merchants
should lose faith in them with whom he has business, their relation would
soon be affected. There could be no commercial world without faith of
merchants in his fellow merchants.·
'
w:
If we as Masons should lose faith in one another, if . we should los.e
faith in our leaders, how long would our great fraternity last?
If brother should lose confidence in brother, friend in .friend, neighbor
in neighbor-if such a thing should happen here on this earth it would
make God repent that He placed man on it. Faith keeps the world of
commerce, of brotherhood, of family, of society; without Faith they would
fall to pieces.
It is by faith that all scientific truth is realized a nd it is by faith all
advancement is attained, and it is by faith that immortality becomes real
to the soul.
Of what value is faith to man? Every door through which the soul
must enter, in attempts to advance, are closed to the man devoid of faith.
But to the man of faith, all doors are open, and to him all paths are
accessible that lead to the betterment of the human race ; that lead to the
advancement of scientific research, that lead to truth.
Hope! What would this world be without hope? It seems to me that
without hope we would lie down and perish. Hope is the coming of
spring into the soul, chasing away the winter of disappointments and
gloom. It is a good angel which our Divine Maker has put with us to
inspire, to cheer us when we are faint and when our souls are discouraged
in the battle of life.
It is hope that keeps the soul steadfast in life's trials when the
storms of life overtake us, when we are buffeted about. Hope is the
anchor that holds man true to his ideals, true to his brothers, true to
·
his country and true to his God.
Faith, Hope and Love. Love is an attribute of the Godhead, and
because of that fact it is greater than faith or hope. God is not Faith or
Hope, but God is Love. As God, He has no need of faith or hope and
they cannot exist in His nature. No surprises come to Him, and His desired
ends are not experiments, for His very nature is love.
Man may have faith and hope; they belong to him, but lo ve is not

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
Urethren of the Grand Lodge:

,,.

In obedience to the demands of our Constitution I will endeavor to
set forth in this message a full report of my official acts during the Masonic
year now drawing to a close, and will, in a brief manner, try and give you
a report of the condition of Masonry in general throughout the jurisdiction,
and also place before you those recommendations which seem to me advisable for the best interest of our Institution.
Condition of Masonry Within the Jurisdiction
So rapidly has the Masonic year flown that it seems but yesterday
that we parted after the close of Grand Lodge, yet there have been long
hottrs of thought and some worry. The fault-findings were very, very
few compared to the one hundred and twenty-eight thousand Masons in
the grand jurisdiction of California. In my visits to the different districts
the brotherhood has shown me every possible kindness that could be desired, and I am forced to say that while I am ready to give an account
of my stewardship and lay the burden down, it is with the regret that
I could not have done more to stir the hearts and minds of my brethren
to a greater realization of the wonder-working power of our fraternity
and the sublime satisfaction we receive in the performance of our duty as
Masons and as loyal American citizens.
It is amazing that there is so little to complain of. It proves that the
individual Lodges are in the hands of good and faithful men and brethren,
and that the spirit of Masonry is lifting mankind to a higher plane of
living.
The complaints that have been brought to our door are not serious,
and yet there are some that deserve our attention
The most flagrant disregard for the principles of Masonry and the
good name of our Institution is to be found in the so-called Masonic publications. Complaints have come to us from businessmen of their agents
soliciting advertising under the name and influence of the craft and then
disregarding their pledged word to such an extent that" it almost amounts
to fraud, while others hold themselves out to the world as Liberal Free
Masons, opening their sewers of false doctrines to the utter disgust of
every right thinking person, both as members of the craft and as true,
loyal American citizens. There was published in the San Francisco daily
papers an item saying that the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California received $250.00 from the city and county of San
Francisco for advertising purposes, and an investigation showed that the
money was paid to two such publications and divided between them.
This should be stopped, and I recommend that a section be added to
our Constitution requiring that if there is such a publication, that it be
under the direct supervision of Grand Lodge, and that anyone using the
name of Mason, Masonic, Masonry or any other title that would lead the
public to believe our Institution was responsible for or interested in such
publication, without permissioft of Grand Lodge, that the publication
ther.eof shall be prima facie evidence of guilt and sufficient to subject the
publisher or publishers to expulsion, and he or they shall be expelled by
the order of the Grand Master.

Mascnic Homes
The great majority of our members little realize t he grandure and
magnitude of the work in which we are all engaged.
Our Homes are first in Importance. It is necessary to come in contact with the life and· management of t he Homes ·before we can fully comprehend the magnitude and glory of the work. The old folks at Decoto
are spending their declining years in peace and comfort, enjoying life
without a thought of the morrow so far as their maintenance is concerned.
At Covina the rising sun of life's morning is ever present. Our children radiate the joy and hope of childhood. They are taught a rever ence for
sacred things, a desire to obey and uphold our laws, and to reflect credit
on our Home and the fraternity in general. I t is pleasing to know that it
is said of them that ·in comparison with other children in the public schools
they stand above them all in obedience, in physical and intellectual attainments, and all those virtues and gifts which alone can raise mankind to
the elevated station which God intended him to occupy. This noble work is
that in which we are all engaged, and if you could all visit the Homes just
to feel the heart-throbs you would leave there with a sigh of adoration
to the Almighty lingering on your lips for the opportunity given to all of
us to participate in this glorious work. Our t hanks to t he Homes Board
for the faithful performance of this important trus t.
Boards of Relief
The next in importance, to my mind, is our Boards of Relief. It is
exceedingly difficult to fully understand the amount of labor and selfsacrifice exerted by the different Board members to ease the grief and give
relief to thousands, yes, thousands of our less fortunate fellow creatures
to whom we are bound by t he ties of brotherly love and affection. No employment can be more sacred than that in which the brethren, comprising
the different Boards of Relief, are engaged. To feed the hungry, cloth the
naked, bind up the wounds of the afflicted, and to find employment for
those wanting work in order that their loved ones may be fed, is enlisting
in the service of the Master and in the hour in which they shall stand before
the Tribunal Bar of our Supreme Grand Master may they hear t he final
judgment : "Well done, thou good and fait hful servant, enter thou into
the joy of thy Lord."
Endowment Board
Following closely in our noble work is the Homes Endowment Board,
with its indefatigable chairman. We have no brother within our ranks
that gives more to this grand jurisdiction in work well done and service
rendered than our honorable brother Frank M. Smith, chairman of our
Homes Endowment Board. To him and his faithful fellow w ork~rs our
sincerP. thanks are due and most respectfully t endered.

There is stored in the archives of memory many precious volumes in
which are recorded all the happy scenes, the kind and friendly acts, and
all those tender and brotherly services heaped upon the Grand Master during the year's visitations.
It would be useless for me to attempt to place before you the grandeur
of all your Grand Master's visits in the different parts of this grand jurisdiction, but to my mind my visits with the brethren in the Mother Lode
section was the most impressive, because -0f the memor\es it awakened.
Those old Lodges and their precincts have become sacred from the footsteps of heroes; men who laid the foundations upon which has been erected
the glories of Masonry and the magnificent structure we call California.
Our visit to the brethren in the Hawaiian Islands will long be remembered for the efforts they put forth to administer to, and anticipate, our
every desire. They are a happy and contented people and their joy found
expression in the wonderful entertainment provided for us while among
them.

15

I know that I have not visited as many Lodges as I would have liked
to, and yet I have covered a remarkable portion of this grand jurisdiction
and my joy has been full to find the Lodges prosperous and the member~
of the Craft happy in the work of the fraternity.
A Bouquet
The work of t he Grand Master is pleasing but difficult and were it
not for the solid r ock of Freemasonry upon whi~h all Grand Masters have
relied, namely, our Very Worshipful Brother John Whicher, our dearly
beloved Grand Secretary, there would be more mistakes and less harmony
among us. I cannot express in words my appreciation for all the kindly
advice he has given, not only to myself, but to the thousands who appeal
to hi~. Whe.n dear old John lays down the Grand Secretary's mantle
he will be missed more than any other man in the history of California
Masonry.

Visit to Halifax
My visit to the city of Halifax, Nova Scotia, to attend the bicentenary
of the establishment of Freemasonry in Nova Scotia and in all Canada was
filled with the glories that come to us from mingling with brethren from
all lands where Masonry abounds and prospers. In June, 1738, Henry
Price, Grand Master of Massachusetts, sent Major Erasmus James Phillips
to Nova Scotia with a warrant appointing Phillips Grand Master of Nova
Scotia. On his arrival ' in Nova Scotia he immediately organized a Lodge
at Annapolis Royal. From this beginning Freemasonry spread over the
entire Dominion of Canada. In Canada there are today nine Grand Lodges;
1402 Blue Lodges and 171,600 members. This does not include Newfoundland, which has a Scotch District Grand Lodge with six Lodges, and an
English District Grand Lodge with eleven Lodges.
Delegations fr om the Grand Lodges of Scotland, Ireland, England,
Newfoundland and twenty-one Grand Lodges in the U nited States, as
well as from all the Grand Lodges in Canada, were in attendance. Nova
Scotia will long remember that wonderful gathering of Freemasons of
which she may well be proud.
On July 10th, at 3 p. m. there was a service in St. Paul's church. This
church was built in 1750 by the British Crown and is the oldest Protestant church in Canada.
On July 11 the different delegations were received by the Grand Lodge
of Nova Scotia. At 11 :30 a. m. the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts held a
. special communication in St. Paul's cemetery for the purpose of dedicating
a monument to Right Worshipful Erasmus James PhiHip. The ceremony
of dedication was beautifully carried out, with all the dignity· befitting the
occasion.
On Tuesday, July 12th, we motored to the Masonic H ome at Windsor,
the only Masonic Home in Canada. From there we journeyed to Grand Pre,
the home of Longfellow's "Evangeline." The old well from which she
drank and the old church in which she worshipped are t oday as they were
when she lived iri that beautiful land. Farther down the valley, at Fort
Ann, formerly Annapolis Royal, Sir Francis J. Davies, Deputy Grand
Master of the United Grand Lodge of England, unveiled a tablet marking
the. place where the first Masonic Lodge was organized on Canadian soil.
Leaving this historic spot we drove down the Annapolis Valley to "The

Special Communications of Grand Lodge
Grand Lodge was convened on several occasions for the purpose of
laying corner stones and for the dedication of Temples. The laying of
corner stones in concrete buildings has become difficult to perform at the
proper time, and the ceremony is becoming such that I have hesitated to
take part therein. I feel that if the cerem ony cannot be properly per forme d
t hat 1t should not be done at all. O thers may not share this opinion with
me, but if we are to continue to place a slab of stone in a niche in a concrete wall and call it a corner stone we should at least change the wording
of the ceremony to conform to the occasion.
World's Fair at San Francisco
It has been called to my attention that we are going to have a World's
Fair in this city during the coming year and that it might be the desire of
the Grand Lodge to maintain an information bureau on Treasure Island
for. the . benefit of yisiting Masons ; a place where our visiting brethren,
~heir w1~es· and ch1!dren ca? go when in search -0f friends o r any other
mformation they might desire. I believe the matter should be discussed
and decided at the present time.
Necrology
During the year we have lost ·by death quite a large ·number of our
brethren, some of whom were prominent both in the a"anks of our
order and in public affairs; others were known by their gifts not only to
the fraternity, but also to the poor and needy who were n~t connected
with our Institution. In death they are all equal. It is dangerous to draw
comparisons of individuals, because no one save God alone can · tell of the
power stored in the mind of man or of t he struggle and hardships one may
have endured. to gain the small 3:PPearing gift, either in service or money,
he has contributed to any certam cause. When I think of those things
the past rises before me like a dream and I can see the'.-Great Teache;
as he "sat over against the treasury, an d beheld how the people cast in
mu~h. And the.re came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites,
which make a farthing. And he called unto him his disciples, and saith

.unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more
in; than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast
in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had,
even all her living." Our departed brethren will receive their just reward
wh.e n -they stand before the High Court of Heaven ; there will be no lawyers
there nor jurymen; one Judge will judge them all. Later in our proceedings
suitable services will be held and the usual and appropriate eulogies delivered
in order that our records may tell future generations of their worth.
Mourn not the dead
That in the cool earth lieDust unto dust-The calm, sweet earth
That mothers all who die,
As all men must.
But rather mourn
The apathetic throngThe cowed and meekWho see the world's
Great anguish and its wrong,
And dare not speak.
Chief Glory of California
Finally, my brethren, California with its thousand miles of sea coast.
its beautiful cities by the sea, noted for their wealth and magnificence; its
vine clad hills and orange groves; its fertile valleys, rivalling those of ancient Egypt and the Euphrates; its snow-capped mountains, down whose
sides the torrent runs out through the canyons, carrying within its bosom
the sediment that enriches the lands through which it flows; and its forest
of giant trees that have stood the earthquake shock, as well as the storms
and the blast of ages; all this makes California an inheritance of which,
as citizens we may well be proud. But while we rejoice in its wealth and
splendor, let us not forget, my brethren, that the chief glory of California
and of the United States of America lies in our free institutions and in
the Constitution of our country upon which they rest. Let the organized
mob destroy the constitutional right to hold private property, and American
liberty is lost. We have thousands among us whose minds have never seen
the rays of light from the torch of American liberty and whose hearts and
minds are incapable of grasping the fundamental principle that you cannot
destroy the constitutional rights of your neighbor without pulling down
and overthrowing y,our own.
·
When we look upon the school houses and other educational institutions
which adorn every avenue through which the rising generation must pass,
it is unbelievable, that at this hour in our country's history, we should
tolerate among us those who would tear down the structure of American
freedom, the foundation of which was laid by the forefathers and anoi~ted
with their bl.ood and tears, that you and I and all of us might enjoy the
fruits of their labor. Are we sleeping at our post? Are we worthy of
Masonry? If we are we will go forth from this Grand Lodge with a determination to uphold and maintain the Constitution and laws of our
country.
·
Dictators may scoff at democracy, but so long as we are true to those
principles laid down by our fathers and to our fathers' God America cannot fail. Deny men the right .to worship God according to 'the dictates of
their own conscience; destroy the rig.~t of free speech, and all of human lib-

GRAND LODG'E OF CALIFORNIA

1/

erty is lost. It shall not be, because we are going to buckle on the armour of
Masonry and go forth into every walk of life bearing aloft the standard of
our Institution and the banner of our country as a notice to all mankind
that we are drinking from the same fountain of thought from which our
fathers drank; that we are worshipping the same God our fathers worshipped, · and by His grace and power America will forever he the land
of the free.
May God give us strength to do our duty as Masons and as American
citizens, and may we so act that we will have His support through all the
generations to come.
Cordially and Fraternally,

J. T. FRASER,
Grand Master.

It may be of interest to note the numerical strength of our Lodges: One
Lodge has more than 1,000 members; 55 Lodges have 500 or more members;
72 Lodges have 300 or more members; 304 Lodges have each a membership of
100 and not to exceed 299 members; 119 Lodges have a membership of 50 and

a membership of 13.

Masonic Day at Exposition
The management of the Golden Gate International Exposition has set aside
Wednesday, April 19, 1939, as Masonic Day. That day will mark the beginning of the ninetieth year since the formation of the Grand Lodge of California.
I recommend that the Grand Master appoint a special committee to make arrangements for a proper remembrance of the day.

Social Security and Unemployment Tax
The subject of taxes levied upon Lodges by the F ederal Soda! Security
Act and of Unemployment Reserves Commission of California has occasioned

20

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

much correspondence and many complaints, and I will attempt to clarify the
matter by relating some of the efforts that have been made to secure a reversal
of the rulings holding Lodges to be liable.
At the February 23rd session of the conference of Grand Masters at
Washington, D. C., a resolution was adopted, reading as follows:
"Whereas, this conference of Grand Masters has no authority to bind any
Grand Lodge by its action, but meets for mutual helpfulness; and
"Whereas, the application of the Social Security Act to the fraternity has
been variously interpreted by different government officials ; now therefore,
"Be it resolved, that the chairman of this conference be authorized to
appoint a committee to study the entire subject of the Social Security Act as
applied to the Masonic fraternity and to report its findings and suggestions to
each of the grand jurisdictions."
The chairman of the committee so provided for is M.".W.".Joseph Earl
Perry, Grand Master of Massachusetts. His committee has not as yet succeeded
in getting a reversal of the ruling of the Internal Revenue Commissioner that
Masonic Lodges are not exempt from the operation of the Act. His committee's
argument is, in brief, that the entire fraternity, both Grand Lodges and subordinate Lodges, fall within the terms of both Federal and State statutes
exempting certain non-profit organizations operating exclusively for religious,
charitable, and educational purposes. Further, as to the unemployment provisions, both State and Feder-al, that no local Lodge in the United States has as
many as eight, or even four, individuals who are employes within the meaning
of the statutes; that is, individuals as to whom there exists an employer-employe,
or master-servant relationship, nor are their ritualistic officers employes within
the meaning of the provision construing corporate officers as employes; and that
therefore every Lodge is outside the scope of the unemployment provisions of
both Federal and State statutes.
As is stated above, no action has been taken by the Internal Revenue Commission.
The Unemployment Reserves Commission of California predicates its rulings as to the interpretation of the law upon the rulings of the Federal commission. And even if it should reverse its ruling that requires the payment of
the unemployment tax to the State of California, it would not relieve our
Lodges one whit, for in that event we would be required to pay the tax ·directly
to the Internal Revenue Collector. The total tax under the California Unemployment Reserves Act is 3.7 per cent; the Federal tax-now paid to the State
of California-is 3 per cent. Our saving would be seven mills only.
It is apparent that, until the Federal law is amended, or the rulings of the
Internal Revenue Commissioner are reversed, we must continue to observe the
law as interpreted.

The scope of our examination included a verification of total cash funds re"
ceived during the fiscal year ended July 31, 1938, from the annual returns covering the fiscal year 1936-37. Sundry funds received in advance and prior to July
31, 1938, in respect to annual returns for 1937-38 in amount $4,969.65 and carried in suspense are not taken into account, in our report.
.
Total receipts due from subordinate Lodges as per individual annual returns
were found to be in proof by total number of membership, classification of
source of revenue, and total amount of gross revenue received-as evidenced by
the recapitulation record of subordinate Lodges. Total of all receipts were
found accounted for and the cash received therefrom deposited in bank accounts. Bank accounts were reconciled and verified, and sufficient examination
of detailed expense vouchers was made as to satisfy ourselves as to the correctness of the accounting.

Referred to the Committee on Finance.

To the M:.w:.Gralld Lodge of California:
Another year has passed and again it becomes my pleasure, as well as
my duty, under the provisions of the constitution, to make a report of my
activities during that time.
·
I had the pleasure -0f installing the officers of more than thirty of our
Lodges. I attended meetings of Masters' and Wardens' Associations as
well as Lodge function& of various nature and have enjoyed the splendid
spirit -0f fellowship manifested on all occasions.
I was called upon by the Grand Master to present fifty year l>uttons
to two veteran members and on another occasion, I was asked to present
a Past Masters jewel to a retiring Inspector, as a token of esteem and
brotherly love from the district, over which he presided for many years.
Corner-Stone Ceremonies
By direction of the Most Worshipful Grand Master, I convened Grand
Lodge in the city of Colusa on March fifth and proceeded to lay the cornerstone of the new Postoffice building of that city. On March twenty-sixth,
I convened Grand Lodge in the city of Lodi for the purpose of laying the
corner-stone of their new Masonic Temple and on April thirtieth I again
convened Grand Lodge in the city of Davis for the purpose of laying the
corner-stone of the new City Hall. These ceremonies were all well attended
by the brethren and the citizenry at large.
Assistant Grand Lecturers
Following the custom of the past four years, the Ritual Committee
held four two-day meetings in San Francisco, for the purpose of reviewing
the ritual and considering such other matters as have been brought befor·e it.
Early in the year, Brother Lloyd E. Wilson, Assistant Grand Lecturer
for the Bay district, was called to New York on an important mission;
where he remained for approximately six months. This vacancy was filled
immediately by Worshipful Walter Leonard, Inspector of the 42nd District,
who generously agreed to carry on as Acting Assistant Grand Lecturer
until Brother Wilson's return. We are deeply appreciative to Brother
Leonard for this splendid co-operation, and realize that, without his help,
it would have been difficult to carry ritualistic instruction to the Inspectors
of that district.
Ritual
Lodges of Instruction have been held throughout the jurisdiction,
where the Inspectors were given the opportunity to confer the degrees,
under the guidance and supervision of the Assistant Grand Lecturers.
Where it was deemed necessary, as many as six such meetings were held
for the same group of Inspectors. The attendance records turned in by the
Inspectors, show that they have held Lodges of Instruction for the officers
of their districts at regular intervals.
Attention has been given, not only to perfection in the wording of
the ritual, but also to expression and emphasis. The ritual can be just
so many words, without meaning; but, with proper emphasis and inflection,
may be made to tell an inspiring story, never to be forgotten by the candidare. Individuality on the part of officers is encouraged. No two men
think or act exactly alike and where a gesture of the hand may be natural
to one, it would be decidedly awkward to another. Officers are enc-0uraged

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

to lend themselves wholeheartedly to the work and attempt to live the
part they are exemplifying.
The Ritual Committee has speDt many hours endeavoring to . correctly
interpret the ritual, and is passing these suggestions on to the Inspectors
and officers, in the hope that our work may be raised above the level of
monotony and become a living, beautiful and inspiring performance.
Without fear of contradiction, I make the statement that the Inspectors,
as a group, are highly proficient and that the ritual is being taught more
uniformly and intelligently in this jurisdiction than ever before.

received the degr.ees, they find nothing but degree w-0rk going on in the
Lodge_. and are given no opportunity to enjoy that, which they believed to
be an important part of. our meetings, they soon get in the habit of staying
a~~Y· ~he rule by which we are taught to divide our time as Masons is
d1v1ded mto three parts; one part, equally as important as the others is for
ref~eshment and repose. Failure to make use of this time, is to o~erlook
or ignore .o ne of the important phases of our work.
!he 1:1aster is. told at his installation that he is supposed to commumca.te ligh~ and m.s~ruction . to the brethren of his . Lodge, and he should

th.e member on t_he side lines is entitled to instruction and fellowship along
with the ~onferrmg of degrees, and if not provided by the Lodge, he will
soon l-0se mterest.
In some sections of the jurisdiction, clubs have been organized to study
th.~ _symbols of Masonry; their meaning, how they are supposed to have
ongmated and why they are used in the ritualistic work. The ritual contains many secrets which these clubs are attempting to reveal and when
their findings are given to the Lodges in the form of short talk~, they have
proven not only interesting but instructive. I commend these brethren for
their efforts to learn more of Masonry and recommend that others follow
their example. It has been proven that, if the members are given something worth while at the meetings, the side lines will be well filled.

32.

Condition of Lodges
It is pleasing to note from the various reports, that, generally speaking,
the Lodges of the jurisdiction are functioning smoothly and harmoniously.
Petitions have been plentiful in many of the Lodges and this has, of course,
caused greater activity. A great number of the Lodges, however, have
not been so favored and we constantly hear the complaint, "we have no
work." When a .Lodge officer talks about work, he usually means the
conferring of degrees, and when there is no candidate to confer the degrees
upon, he believes there is nothing else of importance to do, and the Lodge
room remains dark.
The ritual is the foundation upon which Masonry stands and without
it the fraternity would be as an empty shell, devoid of its strength and
beauty and entirely incapable of teaching to its followers the arts and
sciences of the craft. Perfection of the ritual and proper rendition thereof
is a subject, worthy of much time and effort on the part of any Mason.
It is unquestionably the most beautiful part of our work and perhaps the
most important, but if a Lodge expects to remain useful to i~s members
and the community in which it exists, it must also interest itself in other
things of importance. To expect the' ritual to carry the entire load is t-0
place a burden upon it that it cannot bear.
Many suggestions have come from this Grand Lodge for education
along lines of Masonic thought, and no doubt if put into practice by all
the Lodges, would pay dividends in greater Lodge interest and attendance.
Naturally a knowledge of what Masonry stands for and is tryin.g to do,
leads to better attendance on the part of the members, and if it were pos- .
sible to instill this knowledge in the hearts and minds of all, our Lodges
would be filled to overflowing at every meeting. Unfortunately, this is no
easy matter and no method has yet been found to bring it about successfully. The problem still rests with the individual Lodge and must be
worked out by the Master and his officers. No man should presume to
occupy the East unless he has definite knowledge of this responsibility and
feels that .he is qualified to discharge the duties impose? upon him in that
high position.
I have talked with many Masters who could lay claim to success
during their year in the East, and have found that ~ach had ~aref~lly
planned the meetings of their Lodges, not only to thet~ own sa~1sfact~on
but that of the membership as well. They have taken mto cons1deratton
the fact . that while the officers may be intensely interested in the ritualistic wo~k b~cause it is a part of their jobs, the members on the side lines
are not satisfied to see the same performance over and over again without
some deviation.
Some Masters are overlooking the need of.refreshment-the hour when
the brethren are given needed instruction or the opportunity to mingle and
enjoy the fellowship of their brothers. After all, this is one of the reas~ns
why many, men present their petitions to Mas.o nic Lodges. If, after havmg

33

Use of Slides, Pictures and Charts
F-0r many years, it has been the custom of some Lodges to use stereopticon slides and charts in conjunction with t'he lectures of the degrees believing that it helps the candidates to more easily understand the rituaiistic
work as it is imparted to them. To my knowledge, no objection to their
use has ever come from this Grand Lodge and naturally the practice continues.
During the past two years several Lodges have purchased new slides
and in one instance a Lodge sought approval of a motion picture. At the
request of the Grand Master, this picture was shown before the Ritual
Committee, into whose hands the matter had been placed, and it was found
that the entire second section of the third degn:e was portrayed.
We are bound by our · obligations and the laws of the fraternity to
conceal and not to reveal the secrets of our work, and while I believe these
brethren intended only to add interest to the degree w-0rk through the use
of these pictures, I am reminded that there is a limit, beyond which no
Mason should allow his enthusiasm to carry him.
To keep inviolate the secret parts of the degrees, I made the following
ruling, which was sent to the Inspectors, asking their co--0peration in seeing
that it was complied within their respective districts.
"Any slide, map, chart or picture of any nature, showing in part
or in whole, the secret work of the three degrees of Masonry, is
contrary to the laws of the fraternity and in violation of the obligations of the order, and no Lodge in this jurisdiction shall use
such equipment in any way, nor shall it or any Mason be in possession thereof."
Conclusion
In closing this report, I acknowledge my appreciation to the Most
Worshipful Grand Master and the Very Worshipful Grand Secretary for

ANNUAL ORATION

By WARREN E. LIBBY, Grand Orator
Our Responsibility
Brethren of tht Grand Lodge:
Whatever I say to you today is merely giving back to Masonry a very
small part of what Masonry has given to me. If I am led to impart to you
something of inspiration, something that will invigorate your thought, I am
only reftecting meagerly the inspiration that this Grand Lodge, and you, the
members of it, have been to me year after year. Each time I have returned
I have counted it a privilege, fdr the associations I have acquired 'and the
riches that have ftowed from them will never be estimated in any other way
than in heart responding to heart. And so, in the spirit of sincerest humility
I stand before you today blessed with the greatest honor of my life, that of
addressing you as your Grand Orator. May this occasion be to our mutual
benefit.
Our heritage in Masonry is indeed grand. But by the use we make of it
shall we be judged, and justified or condemned. Because the wisdom taught
by its glorious past has been imparted to us, we have a resi>onsibility. It is
of that responsibility I would speak to you today.
Have you ever asked yourself why it is that Freemasonry is so closely
woven around King Solomon's Temple? In Masonry, everything is a symqol
and every symbol teaches a lesson. No more perfect symbol of Masonry as an
institution could be chosen than that of Solomon's Temple. It manifested the
realization of a nation's purpose and the culmination of a righteous desire entertained for centuries. We get little or no inspiration from the material structure. For real inspiration we must soar into the realm of mind. We must
look above and bey-0nd the symbol. In contemplating the temple from that
viewpoint, we find it to be the outward expression of the unified thought of
a people, generated, protected and developed over many generations.
The Israelites had their beginnings in nomadic tribes with all their possessions in flocks and herds which furnished their own transportation whenever the wanderings of their owners required, Like us, they could best reach
the mental through some emblem or symbol, and thus it wa~ that they adopted
as their reminder of deity, the Ark of the Covenant. This was just as movable a thing as the rest of their possessions. It was housed in a tent and carried on the shoulders of men in the forefront of battle or upon the march, as
a constant reminder that they worshipped a single God and not idols or
gods many. This people it was who persevered through centuries of journeyings, in and out of captivity, over seas and rivers, through deserts and the
wilderness until they finally came to their goal-.,.the union for the first and
only time of the twelve tribes under one king, which is our symbol of democracy, and the erection of a permanent . temple for the worship ·Of their
God and for the housing of their Ark of the Covenant.
What more perfect symbol could there ever be for any institution
or body of men than such a reminder that rewards are the fruits of
constancy, fortitude and perseverance? Just as it took them centuries to
attain, s·o it has taken centuries for Masonry to bring about the present
freedom of thought. Later centuries have furnished no more perfect
example of such attainment through unselfishness of purpose and the

But, you say, I am talking of the problems and saying nothing about
the remedy. I am talking about the problems because every last one of
the~n contains ~ promise. How is that? you say. Every problem of a precedmg generation has been solved. That is why each one is a promise
that we can solve our problems today. The application of the same principle by consecrated, unselfish thinking will bring us safely through. But,
a little folding of the hands, even a ·s hort nap, might mean bloodshed.
Eternal vigila.nce is indeed the price of liberty! It has been necessary to
look at our history long enough to clarify our vision, to determine where
we are headed, and what our responsibility really is. Then, in the words
of an old hymn, let us be up and be doing, dare all and prevail.
That immortal Mason, Abraham Lincoln, wisely said that our nation
was "conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are
created equal." It was in seeking that liberty that men first settled. on
American shores. It was in the search for a greater freedom and the ·
avoidance of the irksomeness of even a liberal government that they
pushed the frontier farther and farther · out until they reach;d our own·
fair state. Recognizing in the first instance that the land was all taken up
and handed down from generation to generation without opportunity for
oth~rs to acquire it, men set forth in small schooners. In the second instanc«;,
feelmg that even the recently settled land was too hard to acquire they
set forth in prairie schooners. But who were the ones to ret.ain th~ new
possessions? Were they either acquired or retained without a struggle?
Were they ret.ained by those who started at the top of the ladder and went
down by immediately mortgaging them for all or more than they were
worth, or immediately gambling them away? Or were they retained by
those who appreciated their value and were temperate enough to make
sacrifices to retain them?
From the tall redwoods and the eternal snows of the north to the balmy
sunshine of our southland it was frugality, hardship and self-denial that
retained advantages once secured. The opportunity today is no different.
A rich heritage has been given to us from the past and yet we complain
of how hard · it is to retain it. Some have always had more than others
throughout history and it ever will be so because some work harder than
others, some are brighter than others, and some practice more temperance
than others. Some are more contented with less and that is the reason
they are richer than the avaricious. Because one man has a house, that is
no reason why another should seek to tear it down, but rather is it a
promise that by the practice of equal energy that other man may acquire a
house of his own. The rule is just as true as between youth and age as it
is between men of the same generation.
·
Modern inventions and appliances indicate that we shall never go
back to the inconveniences of former years but nothing can insure us
prosperity save the exercise of our mental faculties and the practice of the
age-old social and moral virtues. Only the development and use of those
qualities of character taught by our Masonic symbols and lectures will
ever bring us · peace and contentment. If they are of value, do not desert
them, but put them into use daily and hourly. Remember the promise
contained in each accomplishment of the past.
·
Our country may seem large and our influence may seem small. But
if the Colonial Masons proved that a righteous minority can govern we
can prove it today. Their sheer force of character actuated by the principles
we love, accomplished then and can accomplish today. If they could bring
order out of chaos, surely we can retain that order _g iven us as our heritage;
and not squander it, and leave to our children the task of regaining it.
It is for us to become militant in spreading throughout all society the prac~

tice of those great moral virtues of temperance, fortitude, prudence and
justice.
Samuel Adams was the prime instigator and the most prolific contributing member of the Committee on Correspondence at a time when
there were few newspapers, and the methods of communication were fewer
and slow. But that one activity led directly to the Declaration of Independence. It was merely a process of education. That is all our task is todaya process of education, a process we ourselves have too long neglected.
We can be forceful, we can re-arm, we can be militant in the spread of
Masonic education to the point that it permeates society. We need not d_o
it as Masons but as citizens. We need not do it by force of arms but by
force of reason. Reason is on our side and it will outweigh all the lies that
can ever be arrayed against it. Have faith; have hope; yes, have charity,
for those who, ignorantly or wilfully, betray the truth. Don't wait for the
other fellow to do it. We ourselves must do it now. The power of reason
is still ours. Masonry has stood for our rights as individuals. Then exercise
those fights and make our thought felt by all about us, Preach, but above
all, by our conduct be examples. In this way the whole mass will be
finally leavened by>the minority. Then will political freedom and individual
liberty again predominate.
Ours is a delicately balanced democracy in which the citizen is both
governor and ' governed, ruler, ruled and beneficiary. It is at the s~me
time inefficient and for that reason demands more and constant attention.
It will perish as quickly in an attempt to do a right thing in a wrong way as
it will in doing the wrong thing. Ours is the responsibility. This is our government-we are this government; this is our country-we are this country.
Then let us exercise that prerogative and see that our neighbor does the
same. Thus is the change accomplished by education, ever ~tward and
upward, broader and higher.
If the people are to govern, they must be alert enough to see their
government encompassed in their right thinking. They must detect deceit
in whatever guise it presents itself. That candidate for office who takes for
granted that his friends will believe and trust him no matter what comfort
he gives a su•bversive group by statements in behalf of· its cause, in orde.r
to get votes, is just as much a charletan and a demagogue as the devil
himself and should be blackballed on the ballot just as quickly as any other
traitor to the truth. Watch everything that has even a tendency to subvert
the peace and good order of society. Smash all spy syst_ems. Do not be
guilty of simply making another ruling ciass as Russia has done, but try
the spirits to see if they measure up to Masonic standards.
The greatest mistake is adherence to the wrong standard. If material
wealth and fame, if social preferment and glory, if ·worldly ·advancement
and prestige continue as the goal to be attained, then just so long will the
world remain awry. Until unselfish service, honest labor, just wages, fair
returns to capital become the foremost desire of the national thought,
discontent, dishonesty. distrust, privilege, graft and rackets will remain
the order of the day and .the passions of men will continue to be roused
and appealed to according to those dictates. Because graft exists and ra·ckets
sometimes rule the affairs of men, business and governments, the temptation is to try to accomplish something with the same weapons instead ~£­
first destroying the potency and effect of those weapons and excommunicating those who use them. Only as we adhere to the teachings of Freemasonry and declare that honesty, unselfishness and justice ·sh~ll reign
in the affairs of men can we hope to succeed. When those ancient and
homely virtues are ph1.ced fc:iremost . and uppermost, then,_ and: only then,

Patiently await the issue! Be mindful that as landscape painters

Eleven residents immediately made application to the Board of Supervisors
of Alameda County in the form provided. Although they were otherwise fully
qualified, the applications were denied on the grounds covered by an opinion
given by the Attorney General. Appeals were taken to the State Department
of Social Welfare; and on a hearing there the appeals were dismissed and
State aid denied.

It is our understaQ<!ing that aid was denied in consonance with the views
of the Attorney General as set forth in the following excerpt from an opinion
by him rendered :
"We do not believe the residents are entitled to aid under the Old Age
Security Law in. those cases where the old age residents have turned over
property of value to the institution, or· signed an agreement to turn over to
the institution any funds or property of which they may become possessed in
the future, or where the inmates are members of a fraternal organizatiOn suppcrting the institution and have paid an annual per capita tax or made other
contributions to its support. The fact that there is no written contract is imm~terial, the question is whether there is a legal obligation on the part of the
institution to care for the resident. Under the present statement of facts, there
is a continuous contractual obligation, express or implied, on the part of such
institution to care for such residents, which would be enforceable ·in a · court of
law."
The assumption that there exists between Masonic Homes of California
and the residents of the Home a contractual obligation enforceable in a Court
of law is startling to say the least; and is diametrically opposed to the theory
of Masonic relie.f which has prevailed from time immemorial. Furthermore,
we believe it is evident from the very language of the Act that it was intended
to provide State aid for those otherwise qualified who were being cared for in
institutions such as ours. And that seems to be the consensus of those who
are conversant with. the proceedings resulting in the enactment of the legislation. There were however many reasons unnecessary we believe to be here
stated which we felt precluded us from further pursuing the matter-and especially as we understand there will be an amendment proposed at the next
session of the Legislature which would relieve the situation of all doubt.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Disposition of Graduates
Under present economic and industrial conditions, the placement of our
graduates from the Covina Home ·is a serious problem. Young people graduating from high schools, from colleges, even from vocational schools, find
themselves in a world where apparently they are not wanted. Under these
circumstances it is doubly necessary that our boys and girls as they step from
our threshold, deprived as they are of normal parental support and backing,
shall be given a chance to make their living.
. During the year sixteen of our young folks have graduated from the
Covina High School. In the graduating class of that school, numbering 135,
one of our boys stood first in scholarship. He was awarded a scholarship by
the University of California at Los Angeles; he will enter that institution
this fall. The other fifteen are now, three months after graduation, distributed
as follows:
1 boy, to University of California with funds of relatives.
4 girls, to business college, with Masonic aid.
1 gi~l. to business college, with aid of mother.
2 boys, to C. C. C. Camps.
3 boys, jobs in business houses or manufacturing plants.
1 girl, keeping house for employed brothers.
2 boys; 1 girl, looking for jobs.
In spite of the fact that employment conditions are extremely difficult at
present, a survey of our 75 graduates of the past five years (28 boys and 47
girls), indicates that they have demonstrated a high degree of ability to secure
!mployment and make their own way in the world. Nineteen of the 47 girls
have married.
During the -past year also we have discharged prior. to graduation three
boys and one girl to their relatives on request, their ability to care for them
'laving improved; one girl to mother on account of ill health; two boy! to
relatives on account of conduct detrimental to others in the Home.
When the Past Commander's A~sociation of Knights Templar of Southern
California came to us recentJy and,. declared their willingness and their wish to
~elp the Home in whatever way was desired, we told them the greatest service
they could render would be to help the boys and girls leaving the Home to
~et a start in employment. We stated also that in many cases this would
.nvolve helping them to get short vocational training courses, since they leave
us with only a high school education. We are pleased to report that this organization of Past Commanders has responded enthusiastically to this suggestion; and .
today as a result of their activity, four of our 1938 graduates are attending a
business college in Los Angeles. We are assured that their interest in this
1-roject -will be a permanent one, and we desire to commend the service which
they are rendering, as of most essential value. ·
:.•. Sponsoring Lodge.s have also 'in a number of instances shown a genuine
interest in working out the after-graduation problems of their particular wards.
The most notable case of that this year is Fullerton Lodge No. 339, whose ward
had.·the qualifications that pointed toward college education; this Lodge matched
the $300.00 appropriation from the Masonic Home Scholarship Fund, and thus
made it possible for this promising young man to enter college. Other Lodges
in a number of cases showed a genuine interest and really helped their wards.
You will find as part .of this report, the reports of the Superintendents of
the two Hom~s . In these reports will be found a detailed statement of the
opera.tions of the Homes. It is hoped the qrethren generally will read them.

Report of Auditors
To the Board of Trustees, Masonic Homes of California:
In accordance with the authorization of the Finance Committee, we have
made a general audit and examination of the books of account of the Masonic
Homes of California, giving particular attention to a verification of the balance
sheet, or financial condition, as at July 31, 1938. Sufficient examination and
testing of detailed revenue and expense accounts was made as to satisfy ourselves as to the general correctness of the accounting.
Our examinat;on is based upon the main office .records at San Francisco,
and monthly operating reports mailed in from Decoto and Covina with paid
invoices and cancelled checks attached. Detailed distributions or segregations
between expense accounts are made at the Homes and are accepted as classified
in monthly reports.
We present herew:th the following statements :

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home
In August of this year Brother Hartman, Superintendent of the Home for
adults at Decoto, was stricken with appendicitis, and the resultant operation
kept him confined to the hospital for a considerable time. There were some
oomplfoations which retarded his full recovery, but we are pleased to announce
that the probabilities are that he will soon be again in vigorous health and able
to attend to his duties.
Brother Hartman has occupied the responsible and exacting position o:f
Superintendent of the Home since December 1, 1909; and in all the years since
he has until now never missed a day of service. He keenly regrets that he cannot at this time present his usual annual report.

tations to the Covina Home by Lodges and other organizations. Half of
these visitations occurred in the two months of May and June, as many as
four Lodges visiting in one day. We welcome visitations, but could take
care of them in a better way if they were better distributed. Large numbers
of people going through the Home at one time necessarily change the homelike atmosphere which we try to maintain.
On the other hand, we welcome visitors because of the good effect they
have upon the children. Older children are delegated to show visitors about
the Home; these contacts are valuable to the children as training in the art of
meeting and talking with people. They are also valuable in another way, because through them the boys and girls get an appreciation of the Masonic fraternity and its ideals, and are made to feel that they are "wanted" and cherished
by a great body of fine people. This is invaluable in building up their self.
respect, and their ambition to live worthily and amount to something in the
world.
We believe· that Officers' Associations particularly should be urged to visit
the Home, because their members are in a position to report and interpret to
the membership at large the work of the Home and its significance. Recently
we were asked to visit a Lodge located only a few miles from the Home and
speak to their membership. Only one-third of the Masons present had visited
the Home; the Master had never seen it. By a personal visit, which would
have taken scarcely more time than their attendance at this meeting, they could
have learned ten times as much about the Home as we were able to tell them.
During the past year we have on invitation sent representatives to a considerable number of Lodges to speak about the Home. Usually we have sent
one member of our staff and two children, a boy and a girl. This practice has
some desirable features, perhaps the main one being the value of the experience
for the youngsters. They gain practice in appearing in public, and also are
always iinpressed by the hospitality and kindliness with which they are received.

Report of Superintendent-Covina
To the T1"11stees of the Maso11ic Homes of California :
In reviewing the activities of the Covina Home during the past year, I
cannot but be thankful to have had the privilege of being associated in a work
so well worthwhile and so productive of 'good.
Visitations to Covina Home--During the year there were 42 group visi-

As a Boy Sees the Home--The view that a child in the Home has of its
life and activities, if one can truly get that view, is important. Last spring we
were asked to send speakers to a Masonic ga1hering in Los Angeles to tell
them of the life in the Home. One was a boy of thirteen, who spoke as
follows:
"I'm a member of the eighth grade. I have lived in the Home for eight
years. I am speaking to you as a younger member.
"Doubtless many of you have visited our Home. Probably passing through
it you see us as members of a group, and maybe to you we all look pretty much
alike. Yet there is much difference between any two of us, even between my
brother and · me. For instance, I am interested in stamp collecting, and he is
not. I have been carrying on that hobby for four years, and have gained what
I call a really fine collection.
"We have a great Scout Troop. I've been a member of this for more than
a year and now hold an office in it. Other boys don't care much for either
stamp collecting or Scouting, but have pets. There are two dogs that are cared
for by their master.s, and enjoyed by everyone else. Two other boys are raising
baby goats. They seem to get a lot of fun out of this though I don't know why.
The girls seem to care more for cats-( they would).
"Another interest a few of us have is to go down to the dairy sometimes and
help the milker milk the cows. I spend several afternoons a month around the
cows. Perhaps if I had to do this all the time I wouldn't think it was so much
fun.
"Some of the boys and more of the g irls take part in the school plays and
musical entertainment. Of course, you understand we attend public schools.

Others are interested in athletics, and each year our boys who go to the Covina
high school get their share of letters and sweaters.
A fad now in the Home is the keeping of baby turtles; you can get a turtle
for so many cereal box tops. The turtle raisers visit the 'cook in large numbers
and make his life a burden asking for cereal box tops.
"Some of the boys are fond of tinkering with motors, radios, and watches.
One boy has a lot of old watches and puts in all his time tinkering with them,
and once in a while he gets one to run !
"Perhaps when you have visited the Home you thought your guide had
learned a speech and said it exactly as he had been instructed to. He had not
been coached on what to say. He showed you the Home in his own manner, and
probably spent the most time showing you what he was interested in.
"Once I was showing a group of men around. I was talking away, as I am
quite a talker anyway. One of them called me to one side and said, 'You've given
us a very nice speech, but come on now and give us the lowdown. Is it all as
nice as you have made it seem? How about it?' Rather puzzled that anyone
would ask such a question, I answered: 'Why, I've not been hiding anything.
Why should I? Of course, we have our ups and downs; you can't have a bed
of roses without a thorn once in a while, but we are happy here.'
"Another question that I have sometimes been asked is, 'Is there trouble
with runaways?' Runaways! The trouble here is not to get out, but to get inand stay in. Nobody has run away from the Home while I have been there.
Alumni often come back to spend a week-end or several days with us; to them
it's like corning back home.
"I was glad to come to speak to you today. It has been my privilege to
·belong to the Home because my dad was a Mason. It is my home and I am
glad to try to tell you something about it. I've grown up in it, have learned
something (I hope), and have had my share of fun. It is a real Home Sweet
Home.''
Donations and Contributions-In the course of a year many people turn
their thoughts generously toward the children in the Covina Home, and the
past year has been no exception. A list of these contributions is appended
herewith. Special mention should be made of some. First, our Christmas
and Entertainment Fund this year reecived from Lodges, other organizations.
and from individuals cash contributions totaling $4,001.68. We rely upon
this fund not only at Christmas, but throughout the year, to supply to the
children entertainments and recreations. The greatest of these is the
summer camp at ·Balboa. All of the expenses of this camp are defrayed
from this fund.
One man whom we have never met, and who is not a Mason, sends us
$10.00 on the occasion of every holiday; these donations totaled $80.00 for the
last year.
The Grand Council, R. & S. M., which years ago built our Girls' Domestic
Science Cottage, has had a continuing interest in keeping this house and its
furnishings in good condition. During the past year they gave it a new electric
refrigerator, furniture and rugs; and paint to paint it inside and out; and in
addition a cash gift of $300.00. This cottage, a complete domestic establishment
resembling a small private home, has through many years proved itself as one·
of the most effective means of training girls in the art of home-making.
Another donor showing a long-continued and substantial interest in the
children is San Pasqual Lodge No. 452, which for many years has defrayed
the cost of graduation rings for all our graduates, numbering from twelve to
eighteen annually.
The Westerner's Club, made up of Masonic employes of the Twentieth

Home vs. Institution-The chief difference between an "institution" and
a home is that in an institution all the children are handled in approximately the
same. way, by ma~s methods, while in a home each receives individual understandmg and special treatment suited to his particular needs. It is our aim and
constant effort to make the Masonic Home a home in this sense. Therefore the
story of our Home is the sum of the individual stories of many children their
'
problems, and what is done in each case to help them.
. Phys~c~l ~are ai;id ~ec~eation-Many important things can be done for
children hvmg m an mstitut1onat grnup which it is not feasible to do for those

80

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

living separately and privately. First of all, they can be given better physical
care. Their diet can be scientifically managed. They can receive more adequate and systematic medical attention. In the Covina Home there has been
developed a preventive medical program which has greatly reduced the amount
of illness and has done wonders in building up children of frail physique.
Children in an institutional group enjoy better recreational facilities; modern educators hold that the right kind of recreations are powerful influences in
character development. Among their special advantages are trained recreation
leaders, greater opportunity for group play and activities, joyous holiday festivities, summer camps, well-equipped playgrounds and recreation rooms.
Trained Parents---The business of bringing up children is a task that requires skill. The person who undertakes it should have education, understanding
of child psychology, acquaintance with modern educational trends, knowledge
of problems of children's health and recreation. In the institution we can secure
as houseparents persons who have special training and preparation in these respects.
Good institutional houseparents have a deep and abiding devotion to the
human service which it is their privilege to render, but they take care to keep
away from sentimental relationships with individual children. An intense emotional relationship between the adult and the child does not conduce to wise
handling of the child. Parents blinded by affection often make critical mistakes
in operating upon their own children's behavior difficulties. The fact that institutional houseparents maintain an objective attitude toward the ch:Idren does
not mean that they are cold or indifferent; it does mean that they can approach
their task with better judgment and solve their problems with common sense.
The Feeling of Security-Much has been said, and with good reason,
about the feeling of security as one of the natural rights of childhood. That
child who is a member of a well-organized and well-supported institutional
home enjoys a sense of security much greater than that of the child in the
home bereft of even one parent.
Ordered Living-Children need not only to be made to feel safe and
secure, but. they equally need to be loaded with responsibilities commensurate with their growing strength; they need to be held to definite duties;
they need to be required to submit to regular schedules of ordered living;
they need to be controlled from without until they learn to control themselves from within. The routines of institutional life meet these needs
better tha~ is done in the majority of private homes.
·
Learning to Mix-Children in an institutional group exert a very important developmental influence upon each other. They learn of necessity the art
of "mixing" and of entering into all sorts of group activities. They ;tre made
to realize the weight of public opinion. As thew grow older they learn to
assume leadership and to carry civic responsibility. In the high school which
they attend our children constitute only seven percent of the student body, yet
at the last election of student officers half of the elective officers, including the
student body president, were filled from their number. Generally speaking they
have more than their numerical share of participation in various school activities.
Masonic Heritage-Children· in Masonic institutions enjoy another
advantage in their connection with Masonry. They come to realize something of what Masonry stands for in the life of the state and nation. Its
ideals become a part of their heritage; they feel the challenge to live up to
the hopes and expectations of the fraternity which has fathered them within
the walls of its institutional home.
JoHN M. DOWNEN, Superi11te11rlent.

REPORT OF MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
To the M.".W.".Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board herewith presents its sixth annual report, being for the
period between July 31, 1937 and July 31, 1938.
The Board is now constituted as follows :

Death of Brother Halcott B. Thomas
Another year has passed; another year has written its achievements
-its joys and accomplishments, its heartaches and sorrows, in to the annals
of the fraternity.
Prefacing the annual report of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund
for the year of 1938, the Board, with little heart for the task, must record
with deep sorrow the passing on of one of its members. The name of
Halcott B. Thomas, Past Master of James A. Garfield Lodge No. 566 of
Los Angeles, Past Chairman of the Masonic Board of Relief, and member for
several years of the Masonic Homes E ndowment Board, is but a memory
enshrined in the hearts of those who knew and loved him, but the memory
shall be ever green because of the concrete evidence of good deeds he left
behind; because of the faith he had in mankind, and because of the love and
protecting care he showered on those left in our care by a Divine Provi·
dence to the membership of the Board, to the brethren of his Lodge, to the
entire jurisdiction, the loss of Brother Thomas seems an irreparable one;
and yet his life in following so closely a pattern of understanding and
conscio~s Masonry, offers to all of us by way of emulation, a splendid mea.ns
of carrying on in his stead. The Board shall miss Brother Thomas's wise
counsel, his eager desire to serve, his constant consideration for those at
Decoto and Covina. We shall miss his cordial, friendly personality. To
the Great Architect we commend his soul.
Educational Program
The report of the Masonic Homes E ndowment Board presents for the
period just closed a document, interesting in that it contains both a pes~i­
mistic as well as an optimistic note. Optimistic in that it shows a defimte
increase of interest among brethren throughout the jurisdiction, yet pessimistic because of the still small per capita interest and small percentage
of members contributing in comparison with the potentialities of the mass
membership of the jurisdiction.
The program this year was carried out on the same educational plane
put into effect two years ago and repeated during the work of last year.

94

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Board still holds to its belief in the merits of the "non-quota" request
for fu.nds among the members, but believes that a great deal more cooperatI~n between the Board, constituent Lodges, and the membership, must
be obtained before results will prove worthy of the great trust imposed in us
by the Homes.

W~ believe the chain must be strengthened between Lodges and every
one of its members, and that, when this is effected, the burden will prove
less heavy upon those Lodges and those individuals who year after year
have met, with smiling faces and true benevolence, the ~alls made upon
them. We look forward to the day when every craftsman will be Homesminded and will view as unthinkable the passage of a year that does not
see ?is name recorded as a donor (however small the amount) to the
charity represented by the Homes program.
. We look f?rward eagerly to the time when every constituent Lodge
will m.ake charity the first order of business in every month of every year
and will see to it that its name is graven high on the benevolent scroll of the
Homes.

Literature and Correspondence
In vie:" of t~e continued stringency of the times with its unemployment and industrial unease, the Board found it undesirable to bring upon
the brethren anything that could be remotely referred to as a campaign
drive for funds. Instead, it contented itself with disseminating as much
information as possible among the membership and allowing them the
privilege of acceptance or rejection as they saw fit, or as their respective
financial condition would permit. In this sphere of activity the Board
circulated more than 215,000 pieces of literature in the form of pamphlets
and brochures.
The pamphlets were, in the main, prepared by Board members and by
officers of Grand Lodge, to whom the Board desires to extend the thanks
not only of the Board but of Grand Lodge as well. This wealth of printed
material circulated among the brethren throughout the jurisdiction we
feel assured did a great deal to bring the message of the Home clos~r to
the hearts of the craft.
The Board, with limited funds at hand, sought in as economical a
manner as possible, the complete coverage of the membership with informative material bearing on the Homes. In this, Masters, Secretaries and
Endowment Chairmen were called upon to pass the Homes data on to the
brethren without waste, but at the same time not witholding from a single
craftsman the opportunity of learning more about the Homes and of
answering the appeals carried in the printed folders.
