Financial Report
In presenting the financial report, the Board asks that due cognizance
be given prevailing depression conditions, and to ;b ear in mind that response
to appeals of charity may npt be measured altogether in terms of figures,
but must be considered in terms of sacrifice and of individual ability to
respond. Many donations, small in amount, represent great .sacrifice on
the part of the donor, and, considered on this splendid basis, should be

76.70

As of September 1st, total cash received from individuals and transmitted
through Lodges was $19,040.85, representing 4600 individual contributo~s, and
of which said number forty gave $20 or more; two hundred and twenty-six gave
$10, eight hundred and fifty gave $5, two thousand and ten gave $2 and one
thousand and fifty-four gave $1 or less.
The percentage of entire membership contributing was 3.61 % while the
average per capita contribution was 15 cents.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

During the latter part of the fiscal year the Board caused to be printed a
comparative chart of receipts from Lodges for the years 1936, 1937 and part of
1938. This pamphlet was distributed among the various lodges for the purpose
of bringing to the attention of interested brethren the vital facts and figures
concerning the Homes program.
The figures contained therein told a strange tale. They told us that out
of a total membership of 127,304 only 3000 brethren contributed in 1936 while
in 1937, althoug~ showing a considerable increase over the previous ye~r, the
number of contributors (5,800) constituted but a small percentage of the entire
membership. Such percentage in 1936 was 2.4 per cent, and in 1937 4.5 per
cent. The average per capita contribution for 1937 was 22 cents plus. This
year's.per capita of 15 cents shows a downward trend and is far from representative of the average possibilities of the jurisdiction.
When one considers how few of the brethren have, from year to ye,ar,
borne the burden of maintaining the Homes program, while the vast majority
seemed content, apparently, to have it so, one is filled, not only with deep admiration for those who uncomplainingly carried on, but also with the hope that
their splendid example will inspire the entire jurisdiction to the imperative need
of concerted action among ALL the brethren-not just a few.
·
The comparativt! chart brought to light the sad. fact that in 1936, 165 Lodges
saw fit to defer the privilege of giving and to allow the year to pass without
contributing a single cent to the magnificent program of the Homes. . One cannot, certainly, here, plead to depression or unemployment among the brethren
as a reason for not contributing even as low a sum as $5.00 for an entire Lodge,
because such a plea would assume the ridiculous. Here, apparently, was a clear
case of forgetfulness, or of procrastination, either of them hurtful to the program that would certainly have suffered had it not been for the generosity of
other Lodges which did not forget. In 1937, forty-six of these Lodges made
contributions, thereby cutting down the total of forgetful Lodges to a total of
119, still a number that required considerable concern to the Board as to the
proper method of bringing the vital message of the Homes to such Lodges.
The total number of forgetful Lodges this year, while less high, continues to
show a condition that .makes renewed effort imperative on the part of Masters
and Secretaries in bringing about a personal realization among the brethren
that the Homes ideal is theirs as well as all the rest in the jurisdiction.

generosity, for their consistent remembrance of the program, and for their
sacrifices to our program of charity and brotherly love. May their shining
example be a guide for us all to follow.

96

Hawaiian Lodges
Your Board cannot complete the story of the figures contained in the comparative chart without paying great and deserved tribute to our Island brethren
for their splendid support of the Homes program. Though thousands of miles
removed from the mainland, without any opportunity for their individual members to visit the Homes, save and except their representatives to Grand Lodge
carrying the Homes message back to Lodges in the Islands, the eight Hawaiian
Lodges have consistently and with great generosity presented an outstanding
example to other Lodges in the jurisdiction in the manner and amount of their
feelings for the Decato and Covina institutions. During the year 1937 the
eight constituent Lodges, with a combined membership of 1,713, contributed
to the Endowment Fund the amazing total of $2,633.00, which amount represents almost $2.00 per capita for each of our Island brethren. Should such a
per ·capita amount pertain throughout the jurisdiction, a sum in excess of
$250,000 would be forthcoming annually to the Homes program. For the current
year, records to date show Hawaiian Lodges have maintained their splendid
attitude of concern for those dependent on their benevolence and are leading
again in numerical and per capita contributions. The Board feels that proper
acknowledgment should be officially paid to Hawaiian Lodges for their great

97

Leadership of Grand Master
To our Grand Master, James T. Fraser, the Board takes this opportunity
of expressing its deep appreciation for the splendid cooperation rendered
throughout the year. Without his ever-ready courtsel, his heartfelt interest in
the program, in addition to many trips and addresses made in the interest of
our Home guests, the work would have been infinitely harder, the accomplishments less great. To our Grand Master goes our gratitude as well as that of
our wards at Decato and Covina.
Program for Coming Year
The Board recommends for the coming year a continuation of the educational program with an adequate appropriation to maintain the same, and urges
all Masters and Secretaries to co-operate to the fullest with the Board in disseminating printed material to the membership and lending all aid possible in
order that every craftsman may be informed about the part he is entitled to play
in the program for the ensuing year.
The Board suggests the continuation in service of the Endowment Chairmen
of the constituent Lodges, wherever possible, and further suggests that a member of the legal profession be placed on the committee in order that wills and
bequests to the Homes may be handled with greater expediency and with necessary legal safeguards, both for recipient and donor.
The Board again calls attention to the year-round necessity of the Homes
and urges that Lodges keep the program alive throughout the year by messages
in the Lodge bulletins, by talks before the membership, and by the formation
of a committee well grounded on factual information concerning the Homes and
which will make it a definite point to contact every craftsman in the confines
of his Lodge on the urgencies and necessities of the program.
Home Visitations
The Board again urges visitations and pilgrimages to the Homes at Decato
and Covina. Between the craftsmen who have visited the Homes, and the Home
guests, there is a cordial spirit of friendliness and regard, beneficial to both.
The child at Covina looks upon the Mason as his benefactor, his friend and
counsellor, while the elder at Decato longingly looks forward to friendly visits
from members of the fraternity and regards them as red-letter days on the
rapidly diminishing calendar of his life. The Board urges a more personalized
association between Craft and Home. The warmth and nearness of Home associations is a part of Masonic tradition that removes the Decato and Covina
Homes from the cold and distant atmosphere found in the usual charitable institution.
In a letter written this year to a brother Mason, a member. of the Decato
Home poured out his heart when he said, "The greatest hunger at the Home is
not that of the body, but that of the heart."
Those of us, outside the Home, surrounded by family and friends, cannot
know, cannot imagine the sheer joy and thankfulness that wells from the hearts
of our Home guests when "company from home" arrives. Have you forgotten
that brother or that child YOUR Lodge caused to be admitted to the Home?
Have you made the small sacrifice the trip entails in order to talk with the boy
or girl, or to clasp the hands of our elders at Decato? Have yon heeded the

98

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

appeal from our Home guests that something nobler, something warmer than
mere creature comfort is needed to make their lives happier?
Visit the Homes and bring to our guests the soul-satisfying response that
rests in your heart as a functioning Mason, ever ready to clasp the hand of the
lonely, ever ready to comfort the fatherless and motherless child, who looks to
us for protection and guidance.
·
Let's be dreamers-dreamers of others. Let's help humanity. Let's make
this a better world in which to live. Let us give, not with trumpets and noise,
but quietly, and deep from the heart. Let's maintain the haven of refuge for
our tired and workburdened elders; let's give the promise of life and future to
our eager children.
Let us avow anew the tenets of Masonry and pledge renewed faith and
continued concern for the institutions that represent our charity and our trust.
Let's build for that glorious future when complete endowment of our institutions has been attained, and when every craftsman has rendered his offering,
no matter what it may.be, on the altar made sacred by his service and his sacrifice. Let's speed that day!! ! !
Fraternally submitted,
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

To the Endowment Fund Co1mnittee, Masonic Homes of California:
In accordance with the authorization of the Finance Committee, we have.
audited the accounts of the Permanent Endowment Fund of the Masonic Homes .
of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1938. The following statements
are presented herewith :
Exhibit A: Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements (other than
Luckenbach Fund-Exhibit (C) Fiscal Year ended July 31;
1938.
Exhibit B: Summary Statement of Endowment Fund Assets as at July
31, 1938.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON NINETEENTH ANNUAL
OBSERVANCE OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
To the M:.W.'.Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of Californ4a:

STATEMENT OF ENDOWMENT INCOME AND CAPITAL ACCOUNTS

~he rep~rt was adopted with the .exception of that portion
re_latmg to finances, which was referred to the . Committee on
Finance.

The success of the Nineteenth Annual Observance of Public Schools
Week throughout the state is fairly indicated by the following excerpt from
a newspaper report of a local observance:
"The 'S. R. O.' sign was out early at the Public School Program
held in the auditorium of
Union High School on Friday
night. Despite falling rain the auditorium was filled to capacity
half an hour before the program was scheduled to start. By eight
o'clock the main floor aqd balcony were filled and extra chairs were
being placed. But still late comers were left standing."
What was said of the observance in that particular locality might
have been said of the observance in general-and not only with respect to
the large attendance at the public meetings, but also in the reference to the
weather. It would appear that this year t'he weather iri many parts of
California, in the north as well as in the south, was unusual. Not only is
there frequent mention in the reports of heavy and unexpected rains
affecting the attendance, but it appears that there were several districts
where high water or snow rendered the roads not only inconvenient for
travel, but in some instances absolutely impassable. And that Lodges were
able to report successful observances under such adverse conditions evidences intense public interest.
In this connection were we not precluded by custom, we should certainly mention the name of one of our brethren to whom our attention
has been caHed by the Inspector of his district. He is the secretary of his
Lodge and for several years has been chairman of the committee of arrangements in his community. He lives in an adjoining town and to attend the
exercises walked fourteen miles over a snow blocked road; and it took him
from 6 :30 in the morning until 2 :30 in the afternoon to make the trip, It
is certain that there was no other person anywhere who displayed more
interest, loyalty, zeal and fortitude in the observance of Public Schools
Week than did this faithful brother.
It is that sort of loyalty and zeal which accounts for the success which
has been achieved. It suggests the thought that although the observance
has become a community affair, it is more than likely that in the smaller
communities at least the high standing of the annual observance in public
favor would not be long maintained without the active aid and assistance
of our Lodge·s. And we think it may be said with becoming modesty that
the way in which Public Schools Week is observed in practically every
town and hamlet in California, as well as in the cities, is very largely due
to the direction and support by Grand Lodge. And in saying this we do
not in the slightest degree depreciate the splendid co-operation of the

Again this year forum and panel discussions were outstanding features
of many programs. In some instances the panel consisted of both school
people and faymen; and at many of the forums anyone in the audience
was privileged to ask a question. A novel and interesting panel described
in one of the reports was that ·in which five pupils by questions and

These forum and panel discussi.o ns were not only extremely interesting
·a nd entertaining, but were likewise, of course, very informative and instructive. In one where the panel consisted of six persons-four of whom
were laymen and two school people-there was a comparison of the
philosophy' and practices· of what is termed "the new education" with t~~t
of the so-called "traditional" education. Among other aspects there discussed, was the relationship between the teacher and the pupil in the contrasted philosophies of education. It was said that in the old school the
teacher was an authority. He poured out his knowledge to the learner
and then tested to see how much the learner could reproduce. There
was generally only· one answer-the one the teacher had. In the new
education the teacher is merely the leader of a group in a search for the
solutions to problems. The learners are allowed to discover the truth
for themselves and to test their theories by actual experiment if possible.
It is commonly known as the scientific method-theory, experiment and
evaluation with additional experimentation and a revision of theories.

It would be of incalculable benefit if the information acquired through
discussions such as these could be disseminated among the parents and
patrons of all our schools. There would then be less confusion in the lay
mind with respect to "progressives," "fundamentalists" and "essentialists."
It is extremely unfortunate that in the educational world as elsewhere it
is the label thiJ-t attracts or repels public approval and support. Too frequently an idea well worth while fails of support because of the nature of
the publicity attendant upon it. As was said by a distinguished educator
with respect to a particular movement: "Its sound and substantial elements
were ignored while the fantastic, spectacular and the marginal aspects were
played upon by both the friends and the enemies of the movement. Finally
the public unable to separate the sound ideas from the chaff of sensationalism and plain bally-hoo discredited the whole idea."
The most popular, apparently, of the special features this year was
the old-fashioned "spelling bee." This took various forms. In some instances there was a contest between teams representing, respectively,
pupils and parents. In others the contest was between a team selected from
the members of a service club and one representing the high school in
the community. One of the contests reported was county-wide. Each
school in the county had held an elimination contest to select a boy and
a girl to represent the school, and there were sixty thus selected who lined
up in the "bee" held during Public Schools Week. The boy and girl who
spelled down all the others were adjudged to be the best boy and girl
spellers in the county and received silver trophy cups by the local Lodge.
We regret that we are compelled to report that the returns from all
our Lodges were not made as promptly this year as they should have been.
Indeed from a few there was no report at all received. We are wondering
if there attaches to this the same significance that was attributed to a
similar condition in Montana by the Chairman of the Correspondence
Committee of another jurisdiction. The committee on Public Schools
Week in its report to the Grand Lodge of Montana had stated that there
were fifty-one Lodges which had made no report, but that it was assumed
that one-half of that number had held a meeting of which the committee
had no record. With respect to this the commentator said:
"The committee thinks half of the fifty-one put on the observance. Our guess based on some knowledge of human nature under
such circumstances is that this is much too high. If they put on
the observance usually they want to write in and brag about it. If
they did not, they are ashamed to write in and confess it."
It is not within the province of our committee to criticize any Master;
nor are we disposed to do so. It is inevitable that each year among the
five hundred and eighty Masters of our Lodges there will ·b e some who
do not sense the importance to both our public schools and to the fraternity
of our annual observance, and who will ·be remiss in a greater or less
degree in the discharge of their duties. That they are few in · number is
evidenced by the growth and development of Public Schools Week; because, as has been repeatedly pointed out in these reports, it is the Masters
of our Lodges who are entitled to the fraternity's share of the credit for
the success of the annual observance.
Again this year, as they always have been, the newspapers and broadcasting stations were of inestimable value in arousing and maintaining
public interest in the observance; and not only was fine publicity thus
obtained for scheduled events, but through contributed articles and radio
addresses authoritative information with respect to the schools and concerning modern education was made available to interested readers and
listeners. And there can be no doubt that there are many more people

today than ever before who are giving serious thought to the real objectives
of public education.
There are many parents and other patrons of our sch?°~s anxiou~ly
seeking the truth who find themselves bewildered by confhctmg theon.es
apparently held by educators, and particularly with respect to the social
studies which loom so large in the curriculum of the modern school. They
want to know whether it is the province of our public schools to mer~ly
inculcate a love of the good life in the individual, and P.erhaps p~epare him
to make a living, or if the schools "must t~ke the le.ad m spre~dmg among
the people an understanding of their national soc1al-econom1c goals and
in creating an active public opinion for their support." If the latter be the

MORNING SESSION
Wednesday, October 12, 1938.
. Grand L9dge was called on at 9 :30 o'clock, the Grand Master
presiding.
The minutes of yesterday's sessions were read and approved.
Distinguished Visitor
M. W. Arthur Smith, Past Grand Master of Utah.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History feels that the past year has been
one of substantial progress in gathering and preserving the history of the
Grand Lodge of California. New and important discoveries have been
added to our files, while continued research has clarified many doubtful
questions. Old records are being classified gradually with reference to other
material, and comprehensive indexes are being prepared to facilitate their
further use and study. Such work is necessarily slow, and particularly so,
when it must be done by voluntary workers who can afford to donate spare
time only without financial appropriations. Some very valuable assistance
has been given by brethren who are not on our committee. Inspectors
and subordinate Lodge officers have been generous with their help. From
our Grand Master -d own to some of our newly obligated brethren there has
been a fine spirit of cooperation throughout the jurisdiction. Success is
largely due to the contributions of willing helpers, and we are deeply
grateful to them.
Last year, during the week of Grand Lodge sessions, through the help
of the Activities Committee, we introduced entertainment consisting of a
talk which was illustrated by stereopticon views of a historical nature.
This feature proved to be so popular that we have been unable to comply
with all of the requests to present it before Lodges throughout the State.
Approximately six thousand Masons have attended meetings where these
pictures were shown. We are happy to report that various gifts from
Lodges and from individuals have made it possible for us to add to the
collection of lantern slides from time to time, thereby giving broader interest to this form of educational entertainment. As time progresses we
hope to make this particular feature more available and still more important.
There is widespread desire on the part of brethren to know more of our
history. Thousand Oaks Lodge No. 478, of Berkeley, has a committee
which presents lectures which alternate on matters of history and jurisprudence. Their officers assure us that this has stimulated attendance at
stated meetings and has caused interesting discussions among the members.
We commend this plan to other Lodges.
As in the past, members of your committee and others have continued
to respond to the requests of Lodges for talks before their gatherings, and
have participated in a number of programs of a historical nature.
Among various anniversary observances throughout the year a few will

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

129

be mentioned: California Lodge No. 1 sponsored an event in April to observe the eighty-eighth anniversary of the founding of the Grand Lodge of
California. To it they had invited Western Star Lodge No. 2, Tehama
Lodge No. 3, and Benicia Lodge No. 5, as those Lodges had participated in
the formation of our Grand Lodge in 1850. On May 7th, San Diego Lodge
No. 35 observed its eighty-fifth anniversary with a historical program
which dramatized events which had occurred since its founding. Harmony
Lodge No. 164 noted its seventy-fifth year of existence. Diamond jubilee
celebrations were appropriately observed by Redwood City Lodge No. 168
and by Mission Lodge No. 169. In connection with the latter, a member
of our committee assumed the responsibility of editing the history which
was published by the Lodge.
Seventy-fifth anniversaries are to be noted during the coming year by
Excelsior Lodge No. 166, Alameda Lodge No. 167, and by Elk Grove Lodge
No. 173. It was in Elk Grove Lodge where it was discovered that one of
their affiliate brethren was of doubtful Masonic standing because of peculiar
circumstances. He had been regularly initiated, passed and raised in a
legally chartered Lodge of an eastern jurisdiction. That parti.cular Lodge
required that a newly raised brother be elected to membership before he
actually became a full fledged member. For some reason the brother was
never thus elected, but he applied for affiliation with Elk Grove where he
was elected and served as a faithful member for several years. It was not
until 1890 that it was discovered that he had never completed membership in
his original Lodge. The matter was properly cleared by our Grand Master.
Struggles of early Lodges continually come to our attention. At ~ne
time the Master of Woodbridge Lodge No. 131 announced that the election
of Treasurer and Secretary, and the appointment of standing committees
would be postponed until the membership of the Lodge could be increased.
Ione Lodge No. 80 had not received its charter and was still working
under dispensation, when Lodge minutes very carefully and correctly note
that the Lodge was opened in due form for the transaction of business.
Then, the minutes simply record that "after considering the case of brethren
who were delinquent with dues the Lodge was closed in due form as there
was no further business." It seems that some of the early members did not
intend to pay dues until they knew the Lodge to be successfully organized.
Western Star Lodge No. 2 once found itself without funds for another
reason. The Secretary was short in his accounts. Apparently he possessed
nothing with which to make up the shortage except some . "greenback~"
· which were then a debased currency. The Lodge helped him out of his
difficulty by voting to accept the greenbacks at par, and remitted the
balance of the deficiency. In another instance a Lodge voted to "donate
to the Secretary the sum of $244.65 (the amount of his delinquency)."
Would such Masonic charity now prevail? Of course, we must remember
that those early Secretaries had no modern banking facilities, and they
had to mingle Lodge funds with their own. In those pioneer times men
often lost everything that they had in their possession.
In contrast to Lodges which were short of funds, San Jose Lodge No.
10 seems to have been affluent in 1879. At that time they ordered their
Treasurer to loan $800.00 to a San Jose bank for one year. The same Lodge
also paid a brother $20.00 a month to lecture candidates. It is suspected
that the brother was in need, but that the Lodge did not want it to appear
that he was an object of charity.
Early charities often reached staggering figures. Brother Winn of
Sacramento was generous in the money that he advanced through the
Masons of that city to bury the dead and care for the sick. Later, when

130

l'J{QCEEDINGS OF THE

efforts were beipg made to get some reim~ursement from the State ior
charities outside the fraternity, a committee reported that they were convinced that General Winn had advanced no less than $19, 140.24 for which
he had received no return. It was this same brother who presented a
large acreage of land for an Orphans Home and school at the first session
of Grand Lodge, in 1850, but there were no funds with which to build upon
the property. The land was located in the City of New Jerusalem, near
Sacramento, but was lost later because of difficulty in clearing the title.
The minutes of some of our older Lodges frequently show that "the
Lodge was convened upon the center." For the benefit of those who might
be puzzled by such an expression, this meant that the Lodge had been
opened in the third degree. According to old English rituals a Lodge was
said to be "convened upon the center" when all present were Master
Masons 1 and therefore equally near that imaginary point within a circle
which d enotes equality. In a Lodge of Entered Apprentices or a Lodge of
Fellowcrafts not all present were of equal rank and were therefore at
various distances from the central point. Hence, a Lodge of Master Masons
was said by our older brethren to have been "convened upon the center."
Minutes of San Diego Lodge No. 35 for the year 1852 reveal that when
the Grand Master, B . D. Hyam, visited the Lodge he inspected the records
and struck out various items which he thought to be wrong. He paid particular attention to all indirect references to .the fact that he had personally
conferred degrees upon men whose petitions had been rejected by different
Lodges. Possibly it was because of such alertness on his part that we
know so little of the story of that Grand Master, who asserted a prerogative to overrule the ballots of Lodges, initiate rejected candidates into the
fraternity, and to appropriate the fees unto himself. Shall we conclude that
Grand Masters of the present time fail to personally inspect minutes because the task would be too great with so many Lodges? Or, is it because
they consider their acts so far above reproach that they fear not what
Secretaries may do unto them?
It is observed that no Lodge of this jurisdiction bears the number
"606", and that thls number was purposely skipped in our roster. The Lodge
which normally would have been designated as "605" had several doctors
on its roll of charter members. That number had a peculiar significance
to them. They were willing to give "606" to certain of their patients,
but did not like to take it themselves as a Lodge number. Hence the number "606" has been deemed a numeral of darkness in the Lodges of California.
Woodbridge Lodge No. 131 had considerable discuss:on in 1872 over
an installation banquet. Some thought that those who attended should
pay for their own meal. Others thought that the expense should be borne
by the Lodge. There were those who argued that the latter plan favored
those who attended the banquet at the expense of those who were unable
to be present. The matter was settled by adoption a motion that the Lodge
would give each member two free tickets. but that those who did not
attend would be entitled to a credit of $1.50.
The old one story Lodge building at Hornitos has been officially designated as one of California's pioneer landmarks. It is revered by nonMasons as well as by those of the craft. During the past year a heavy
windstorm threatened to tear the roof from the building. A townsman who
was not a Mason, rushed into the Chinese restaurant in ~he adjoining two
story building and appealed to some CCC boy.s to help him place roc~s on
the roof of the Temple to save it from destruction. As the boys and Chinese
cook h;ft their meal, the roof of the two sto~y building was lifted by the

GRAND L ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

131

storm and the brick walls crumbled and buried their recently vacated
seats. Undoubtedly, the five men saved th eir lives because of their willingness to save our old Temple.
The foregoing stories ·will give some idea of the entertainment which
is to be found scattered throughout the more serious phases of our history.
We. are frequently asked when the material will be ready for publication.
I t would be ppssible to go ahead at once, but we do not believe it to be
advisable at this particular time. T he work which we are now doing will
guarantee a more complete and enjoyable history at a later date, and will
undoubtedly effect economies which we would not enjoy if we· were to
rush into print now.
Again and again we are impressed with the fac't that valuable records
and many relics have been lost by fire or scattered to the winds. In a recent fire, Turlock Lodge No. 395 lost its charter and other records. This
reminds us that Lodges in modern cities with supposedly adequate fire
protection are not immune to the dangers of conflagration. We regret to
note that some Lodges still have no places of safety for their records.
Others are partially protected against ordinary hazards. A comparative few
have excellent facilities for storage and safety of their records. We particulaTly commend large vaults which have been completed during the year
by Henry Clay Lodge No. 95 at Sutt er Creek and by Georgetown No.
25 at Georgetown. Mariposa Lodge No. 24 has also installed an excellent
1
safe cabinet of fireproof construction.
Our work suffered an irreparable loss in the death of Past Masttr John
A. Fisher shortly afte·r the last session of Grand Lodge. He had been a
Mason for more than sixty-seven years, and had served as an officer in
Hiram Lodge No. 43 for all of that time except for one year. He was a
man of wonderful memory, mentally alert to the last. It was Brother
Fisher who gave members of your· committee the fi»rst insight into the vast
store of human interest stories with w hich the Masonry of the Mother
Lode of California abouncl,s. He directed our steps into realms of research
and discovery, and caused much to be saved in the stirring Masonic history
of California. Brother John Fisher will be deeply missed.
For several years your committee has worked without any appropriation from Grand Lodge. Sundry expenses have been met by members of
the committee, and donations have been received from other s who were
interested in the work. However, we feel at this time that it would be
advisable fo.r us to have an appropriation to meet such items and to assist
in carrying out our plans. Much of our material is of such fragile nature
that it cannot be han dled without considerable risk of damage. The labor
required to put it into better shape will be donated if we can furnish the
necessary supplies from time to time. We therefore ask for a n appropriation of $250.00 and recommend that the work of the committee be continued.
LEON 0. WHITSELL

Committee.

Report was adopted.

To the M.".W.".Grand Lodge of California:
At the annual communication of Grand Lodge, held in October, 1937,
your committee submitted a Lodge System of Masonic Education. (See
1937 Proceedings, page 468-470). Grand Lodge approved the system and
directed the committee to write a Manual to be used as a source of material
for the instruction of candidates for degrees. The sum of $1200 was approved to cover the expenses of the publication and distribution of the
Manual.
· During the past Masonic year the Manual on Masonic Education was
written. The manuscript was submitted to the Most Worshipful James
T. Fraser, Grand Master, for approval. Upon receiving his approval the
Manual was printed and distributed.
The Manual consists of 147 pages covering many aspects of Masonry,
includ:ng its history, symbolism and interpretation of the ritual, as well as
a n explanation of the function ing of Grand Lodge and of the, constituent
Lodges of this jurisdiction. Nearly 2500 copies of the Manual were sent to
Grand Lodge officers, committeemen and Inspectors and to the three principal officers of each Lodge.
The response to the publication and distribution of the Manual has
been most encourag:ng. In addition to the 2500 copies distributed free of
charge, we have sold over 15CO copies, at twen ty-five cents each. O ne
Inspector ordered SO copies for the use of the officers of the Lodges of his
district. One Secretary of a Lodge of 162 members writes that the
"Manual is selling like ho t-cakes ; have ordered eighteen copies and have
started another dozen." A Mason; nearly eighty years of age, informs the
committee: "I have read almost haH of the Manual on Masonic Education,
and it is most instructive. I wish I had read the Manual when or before
I became a Mason." We have received a number of orders for the Manual
from officers of other grand jurisdictions.
Ten thousand copies of the Manual have been printed and nearly 4,000
copies distributed. This leaves almost 6000 copies on hand. If one copy is
given to each candidate, the supply on hand will be exhausted in a little
over a year. With this thought in mind, arrangemen ts have been made
with the printer to keep the type, or slugs, intact until now at no cost to
Grand Lodge. Shall the type now be destroyed or shall we pay a rt~n tal of
$ 15 to keep the type intact for an additional year so as to be available for
the printing of a second edition, with certain changes?
The appropriation to our committee was $ 1200. We spent $ 1 20~ in the
production and distribution of the Manual. But the work shoulcl now be
seif-sustaining as the money reecived from sales should pay all necessary
expenses during the ensuing Masonic year.
Your committee is of the opinion that the next task is to put the
Lodge System of Masonic Education into practical operation. This cannot
be done by your committee. It can only be done thro ugh the cooperation
of all the officers of Grand Lodge and the officers of the several constituent
Lodges. The Grand Secretary of an Eastern jurisdiction writes our committee : " I am waiting with keen interest the functioning of your educational program. My experience clearly indicates that what we need most
is the zealous cooperation of the officers of the L odges." .This statement
clearly states the work immediately before us. If you brethren an d other
officers of your Lodges will cooperate with our committee, our Lodge System of Masonic Education will be a success ; otherwise it will fa il.

136

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Assume that you own a factory. The machinery of the factory is all
set up. There is plenty of raw material on hand. There is a marked demand
for the finished product. Would you not do what you could to produce
that finished product?
You are the Master of a Masonic Lodge. The machinery is all set
up for instruction in Masonry. A number of candidates will be available
for "further light in Masonry." There is a demand that they become, not
mere members of your Lodge, but real Masons. Will you not do what
you can to make real Masons of these candidates?
In the production of the Manual, your committee has had the able
assistance of certain individual Masons of Riverside, California, who did
certain necessary researc·h work, checked the manuscript and read the
proof. In this regard, we express our appreciation to Brothers Loyal C.
Kelley, Henry D . French, James H . Jordan, Roy Haglund, Rufus Jones,
Richard Steves, Glen Bannister and to Willard C. Babcock, Inspector of
the 106th Inspection District.
Based upon the foregoing, your committee makes the following recommendations:
I. That the Committee on Masonic Education be continued next year;
its members to be appointed by the incoming Grand Master.
2. That the use of the Lodge System of Masonic Education be continued.
3. That arrangements be made to keep the type of the Manual intact
during the coming Masonic year.
4. That the sum of $300 be appropriated for the incidental expenses
of the committee in the furtherance of the work.

A. HEBER WINDER, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Returns has made a study of the consolidated
returns of the Lodges of this jurisdiction and makes the following report.
The years of depression are still with us. Last year we thought the
end was in sight and that this year we would show a small gain in membership.
Our net membership for July 31, 1938 is 127,122, a net loss from last
year of 182 members.
The past six years have levied a heavy toll of losses.
In 1933 we lost 3942 mem bers.
In 1934 we lost 4363 members.
In 193S we lost 300S members.
In 1936 we lost 1S98 members.
In 1937 we lost 422 members.
In 1938 we lost 182 mem bers.
We now conclude we have reached the end of annual losses.
It is noted that during these years we raised 18,7SO members and suffered losses by suspension, for non-payment of dues, 22,333 and by death
13,901. During the same period we remitted the dues of 40,290, about twice
the losE>es by suspension. Had we saved 10 percent of the suspensions we
should have a material gain.
We also note the group of Lodges up to number 400, considered as
old Lodges, lost 728 members, while the Lodges from 401 up gained 546,
leaving a net loss of 182 members. The older Lodges suspended 1288
members while the younger Lodges suspended 76S.
Your committee believes greater care should be made in the history of
m embers liable to suspension, that this loss be greatly reduced, and recommends that the several Inspectors give the matter due consideration when
visiting the Lodges of their districts.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS
To the M:. w:. Gra11d Lodge of California :

Your Committee on Accounts has met on the last Saturday of each
· month and in accordance with Constit utional requirements audited such
bills, claims or demands that were presented, and approved th ose that were
found in order.
In order that Grand Lodge may be advised of the handicap arising
from the lack of understanding of the provisions of Section 30 (Committee
on Accounts) by those who have a claim or reimbursement from funds of
this Grand Lodge, and once and for all to settle the matter of procedure,
this committee presents for your consideration a review of the legislation
as adopted by .this Grand Lodge as it refers to Section 30 and an amendment to the Constitution which, if adopted, will clarify the work of future
Committees on Accounts.
In 1924 when the present Constitution was adopted, Section 30, which
was in previous Constitutions, was adopted. In addition thereto the 1924
Constitution contained the following :
Section 220. All former written Constitutions of this Grand Lodge are
hereby repealed, as are also all Regulations, or parts thereof, which are
repugnant to or inconsistent with this Constitution; and no regulation shall
hereafter be adopted which shall be in violation of, or inconsistent with,
any of its provisions."
In 1929 (Page 659) Decision 6, the J urisprudence Committee reported
that Section 30 called for the audit a nd approval before the payment of
bills, claims or demands payable from appropriations made by Grand Lodge
for the work of specified committees. This report was adopted by Grand
Lodge.
In 1937 Grand Lodge committed itself to a policy, but did not pass
the necessary laws to enforce the same.
The foregoing with the exception of the 1937 reference is the standard
by which the approval of disbursements should be handled and in order
to permit this question to be discussed on its merits, the following resolution is offered and submitted for your approval:
Resolved : Any provisions of this Constitution and any Regulation
thereof insofar as it relates to the provisions of Section 30, ( Committee on
Accounts) adopted since October, 1924 which are in violation of or inconsistent with the provisions of Section 220 are hereby rescinded and repealed.
PAUL NATHAN
ANDREW B URKE
HENRY

D. O LIPH ANT

P AUL R. BJICK
OTTO G. FREYERM UTH
JOHN B . CONNOLLY
R o Y EMERY

Committee.

The report was adopted as read with the exception of the
proposed resolution which was referred to the Committees on
Policy and General Purposes and Jurisprudence.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws reports that twenty-five Lodges have
considered and adopted amendments to their by-laws during the past year.
The amendments of twenty-four of the Lodges have been carefully examined by the committee. They have also been approved by the Grand Master
and we recommend their approval by Grand Lodge·
One Lodge increased its fees, nine decreased their fees, two increased
dues, four decreased dues, and one eliminated its affiliatio? fee. The other
amendments had to do with the time and place of the ,meetings. All amendments showed study on the part of the Lodge officers of Grand Lodge
legislation and were well worded.
Russian River Lodge No. 181 desires approval o~ an amendment ~o add
to Article 4 of their by-laws to be known as Section 2A and reading as
follows:
"If a brother w'ho has received either the Entered Apprentice
or the Fellow Craft degree does not qualify himself to receive the
higher degree within a period of one year thereafter, the fee sl1all
be forfeited and the brother shall be dropped from the rolls of the
Lodge, unl~ss the Lodge shall•otherwise direct. It shall be t?e
duty of t'he Secretary to notify the brother of these facts,
registered mail, at the brother's last given address, at least thirty days
before the expiration date.."
Section 2 of the Uniform Code of By-Laws reads as follows:
"Sec. 2. If an applicant, elected to receive the degrees in this
Lodge, does not come forward ~o be initiated within three months
thereafter, the fee shall be forfeited, unless the Lodge shall o.therwise direct."
It will be noted that the limitation refers only to the Entere.d Apprentice degree after election. Therefore, under the ptsent law the amendment
cannot be approved. If a time limitation as to taking the Fe~low. Craft and
Master Mason degrees is desired, it is our ~pinion that leg1~lat1011 should
be introduced to amend sub-section 2 of Article 4 of the Umform Code of
Hy-Laws.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
Organ Solo: ''Traumerei".............._........................................................ Schumann
Invocation: Grand Chaplain. .

Most Worshipfld Grand Master and Brethren:
"Man comes and tills the soil and lies beneath."
There, in one short line, the poet Wordsworth told the story of life
and death, and short indeed is our allotted span in this world. We, the
living, who · are gathered here today know that "a time will come, and the
wisest know not how soon, when all distinction save that of goodness shall
cease, and death, the mighty leveler of human greatness, reduce us to the
same state."
So we take notice of those who have gone before, and in our memorial
service pay homage to those craftsmen who have finished their labors.
The Grand Lodge of Masons of California is an Institution, but those
who compose it are mortal, and one by one, year after year, these mortals
must obey the solemn summons and depart to the realms beyond the skies,
while other workmen from the quarries come forward to take their places
and to carry on their works.
"They are passing away, these dear old friends.
Like leaves on the current cast;
With never a break in the rapid flow,
We watch them as one by one they go
Into the solemn past."
The Secretaries of the subordinate Lodges -0f this jurisdiction have

numbers of their Lodges are includecl in this report, as follows:

Special eulogies are given in this memorial service for Brothers Frank
G. Watson, Charles H. Victor, Joseph E. Block, and Erle G. Spafford. If
time permitted special mention could be made of eaC'h of the others, as each
had his particular merits and each did his work well as a man and as a
Mason. We call particular attention to the death last October, jus•t !lfter the
annual communication of Grand Lodge, of that fine old man, Brother John
Adolphus Fisher of Hiram Lodge No. 43. For sixty-seven years he was
a Mason, and during all but one of those years he was an officer of his
Lodge, serving twenty-three years as its Worshipful Master.
While we miss all these brothers, and weep at their passing, we know
that they are happy in their Father's house. It is we who are left behind
who suffer from their absence, but we have been taught that wJ will meet
again in that blissful Lodge which no time can close, and have been
admonished that purity of life and conduct will gain us admission thereto.
Our greatest tribute to our dead, then, is to go forward zealously with
the work they have begun, and to exert the talents wherewith God has
blessed us for His glory and the welfare of mankind.
·
And so of the missing brothers we say :
"Weep not that their toils are over,
Weep not that their race is run;
God grant that we may rest as calmly
When our work, like theirs, is done."
Respectfully submitted,
ALBERT F. Ross
Roy H. PARKINSON
WALTER D. ADRIANCE
LEONARD L. WILCOX

In Memoriam
FRANK G. WATSON
by WILLIAM A. SHERMAN, Past Grand Master

To the M:.W.' .Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
For seventeen years Brother Frank George Watson guarded the outer
door of this Grand Lodge. His term of service in that capacity ceased by
Divine Summons on January 9, 1938 after failing health of considerable
duration. During his long term of office, he made friends with every grand
officer, representative and visitor who came to the communications of this
Grand Body. He was always mindful. of the dignity, duties and responsibilities of his office and insisted upon their strict observance. At times
brethren smiled at his frankness in disapproval of some carelessness or inattention but their respect and affection for him increased by reaso:1 of the
nature of the criticism which carried no sting nor word of reproach. His
fine personality radiated a character best summed up in the phase that he
was "a man and a Ma'Son."
Frank George Watson was born at Searsport, Maine, May I, 1858,
being in his eightieth year at the time of his demise. His public school years
were few. L'.ke many boys of his time in New England, the sea had a great
attraction for him. At the age of seven teen he started his career as a seaman. He served in all capacities on the deck from ordinary seaman to
captain. His captain's unlimited license, which he always kept renewed,
carried the coveted statement, "to sail any ship, any tonnage, any ocean."
Often when in reminiscent mood he would say, "I was a sailor when the
ships were made af wood and the men of iron. Now the siiips are made of
iron and- the men of wood." The fact that at the required intervals he had
his license or "ticket", as he called it, renewed, proved his unfailing interest
in maritime affairs which lasted throughout his life.
Brother Watson was married in Searsport, Maine, the place of his
birth, on April 5th, 1889. It was to please his wife that he gave up "going
to sea" and came to San Francisco to iive. She passed away some years
ago. There were no children.
·
Masonically, Frank George Watson was initiated in Mariners Lodge
No. 68 at Searsport. Maine, March 10, 1883, was passed the same date and
raised April 11, 1883. He was a Master Mason nearly fifty-five years.
Upon the formation of Presidio Lodge No. 354 in January, 1903 he became
one of its charter members and its first Junior Warden. He was elected
Master in December, 1904. He served the Lodge faithfully and well, impressing his fine traits of character upon all who came within his influence.
He was appointed Tiler of the Lodge in 1907 and continued in that position
until his death. He was also a member and Sentinel of San Francisco
Chapter No. 1, R. A. M., California Council No. 2, R. & S. M., and the
California Bodies of the Scottish Rite. He was also a member of Islam
Temple, A. A . N. 0. M. S. He was a Past President and Titer of the
Past Masters Association of San Francisco. He was appointed Grand Tiler
of the Grand Lodge in April, 1920, succeeding the late George Perrin Adams
who had held the office for twenty-two years.
Frank George Watson lived and loved Masonry. In living Masonry he
helped in the organization of several Lodges, teaching ritual, encouraging
young officers, insisting upon paraphernalia being kept spic and span and
a "punctual attention to all the duties of Masonry." It is in his love of
Masonry that his true character portrayed itself. Known to few, which wa~

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

159

in keeping with his kindly, humble, self-denying character, he gave more
than generously of his earnings to various Masonic charities, no.tably the
Masonic Homes Grand Lodge and his own Lodge. Though childless he
loved children a's evidenced b; his gifts to our Covina Home. These included the furnishing of a room, an automobile, gold watches for awards
for efficiency iii studies, in addition to regular contributions to the Christmas fund. These are but a few of his beneficences, sufficient, however, to
describe the benevolent and unselfish character of this "man and Mason."
In the passing of Brother Frank Watson, I, personally, lost a close
friend and adviser, one who taught me my first lessons in Masonry. It was
he who gave me my first appointment to Masonic office. To him I owe
my utmost gratitude for early teachings and inspirations which have served
Pie well in my Masonic activities. Since my election as Junior Grand
Warden I have conducted the annual installation ceremonies of Presidio
Lodge which, of course, always included Brother Frank .Watson as Tiler.
After the installation last December he came to me stating that he knew
that he was about to be called from his earthly labors and that he wanted
me to conduct his funeral services. Although knowhig that he was not a
well man and that he was nearing his eightieth birthday anniversary, nevertheless I assured him that l was certain he would serve Grand Lodge and
Presidio Lodge for many years to come. In keeping with that definiteness
of character and purpose which was so pronounced in him, he insisted that
his hour was fast approaching. Reluctantly I told him to state his wishes
to Worshipful Brother Clinton M. Smith, newly installed Master, and that
they would be observed. This he did to the smallest detail.
Death came to Brother Frank Watson on January 9, 1938 and in accordance with his wishes I conducted hi~ funeral on January 11th. The
eulogy was pronounced by Worshipful Brother Hugh K. McKevitt, also
a Past Master of Presidio Lodge. As written in the Masonic World, of
which magazine Brother Watson was a regular c~ntributor, ''!he~e we~e
no vain platitudes in the words there spoken. A friend was te!1mg m plam
phrase of the excellencies and high qualities of one he loved. Regard thus
deeply based must discard ~he superficialities of. spee.ch and . rea~h to th~
language of the heart. So briefly, yet eloquently, chd this one bid his brothet
the farewell that must be spoken in all mortal relationships."
The spacious Templar room in the Masonic Temple was filll d w:th
sorrowing friends and brothers for this man's gentle courtesy and kindly
deeds reached far beyond the fraternity. And so with the ritual of the Craft,
wherein Faith and Hope bring comfort to Grief and with soft music th~t
is of the sunset hour that which was mortal of our beloved brother parted
from his brothers.
"There is no death I
What seems so is transition;
This life of mortal breath
Is but a suburb of the life Elysian,
Whose portals we call death."
Song: "The Good Shepherd" (a musical setting of Van de Water, the
23r0 Psalm.)

In Memoriam

JOSEPH E. BLOCK
by WARREN WILLIAMS, Master of Marin Lodge No. 191

To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Supreme Grand Master in His infinite wisdom has called our beloved Brother Joseph E. Block to the Celestial Lodge above.
With the passing of our esteemed brother on June 18, 1938, the Masonic fraternity and the community have sustained a severe loss.
Brother Block was born in the city of Cincinnati, State of Ohio, on
January 12, 1875. He was made a Master Mason in Marin Lodge No. 191
F. & A. M. on June 2, 1917. He was elected Master of Marin Lodge, and
served in that capacity during the year 1925. He was a member of Marin
Chapter No. 102 Royal Arch Masons, a member of the Scottish Rite bodies,
a member of Islam Temple A. A. 0. N. M. S. of San Francisco, and an
active member of the Masonic Club of San Fr~ncisco.
For many years Brother Block served on various important committees
of the Grand Lodge of the State of California and because of his contact
with the Grand Lodge, he was of inestimable assistance to the successive
Masters and officers of Marin Lodge. Through his close association with
the late Brother Thomas Baker, Grand Lecturer of the Grand Lodge, he
was enabled to maintain a high standard of ritualistic efficiency in Marin
Lodge. We have no place to turn for his equal in our work.
During the construction of our Masonic Temple in San Rafael, Brother
Block was an active member of the building committee, and through his
untiring efforts and his wise counsel, this edifice was completed to the
satisfaction of his Masonic brethren. In addition to his Masonic interests,
Brother Block took an active part in civic affairs. During the World War,
he gave unsparingly of his time in raising funds for the American Red Cross
and was also a member of the campaign committee on the various Liberty
bond drives, and participated on innumerable committees assisting the
United States government during that distressing period.
Our brother was keenly interested in the Boy Scouts, Camp Fire Girls,
The Order of DeMolay and everything that tended to improve and develop
the welfare of the youth of our community. As a member of the Public
Relations Committee, which was organized for the purpose of promoting
the welfare of the Public Schools System in San Rafael, Brother Block
gave valuable advice and assistance during the various bond campaigns for
the erection of new school buildings, and he took special interest in the
programs arranged by this committee for Public Schools Week. He also
took a very important part in promoting and establishing the Marin Junior
College and served for several years as a member of its Board of Trustees
up to the time of his passing.
Brother Block was devoted to his family and his home; he loved to
commune with nature; he was happy in his garden with his many flowers;
he gave unstintingly of his time and his energy to every deserving cause.
He was in the highest sense a good citizen and practiced those truly Masonic virtues brotherly love, relief and truth.
"May the earliest buds of spring unfold their beauties o'er his resting
place, and there may the sweetness of the summer's last rose linger longest!
Though the cold blasts of autumn may lay them in the dust, and for a time
destroy the loveliness of their existence, yet the destruction is not final,

.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOJl.NIA

161

and ·in the springtime they shall surely bloom again. So, in the bright
~orning of the world's resurrection, though thy mortal frame be now laid
~n the dust, thy ~pirit shall spring into newness of life, and expand, in
immortal beauty, m realms beyond the skies.
And so, my brethren, may the spirit and the memory of Brother Joseph
E. Block long live on in Masonry.

ERLE G. SPAFFORD

In Memoriam
CHARLES H. VICTOR

by ]AMES B. NORTON, Master South West Lodge No. 283

by EzaA DECOTo, Past Master of Live Oak Lodge No. 61

To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:

To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:

It is a distinct honor for me as Master of South West Lodge to he priviledged to address this body of Master Masons in memory of the life and
service of a distinguished member of our fraternity.
For many years it has been the custom of Brother Erle <?· Spaffor?,
a Past Master of South West Lodge, to attend the annual meetmgs of this
body. He is not with us on this occasion. Neither will he be with us hereafter. On June 23rd, 1938, he departed for that undiscovered count~y from
whose bourne no traveler returns. We who knew him and loved him cannot find it in our hearts to hopelessly mourn his departure. Rather we feel
a sense of pride and satisfaction in the record of this brother who so successfully practiced among us the virtues of Freemasonry. ·
Broth~r Erle was initiated on October 11th, passed on October 23rd
and raised on November 12th, all in the year 1919. In 1928 he served as
Master of South West Lodge No. 283 and since 1932 he was Inspector of
the llOth Masonic district.
In our community Brother Erle devoted himself unsparingly to the
service of two .g reat institutions: the pu.blic schools and the ~asonic fraternity. In these two lines of endeavor he found the opportumty to se~ve
his fellow man which engaged his time and talents to t·he full and which
brought him his greatest joy.
.
As a grand school-master qe drew design~ on the trestle bo~rd of hfe
for the guidance of the youth of our commumty who, as symbolic entered
apprentices, were engaged in laying the foun~ations for the Te.mples of
their lives. These foundations now solidly set m stones of moral~ty, truth
and brotherly love are living testimonials of the immortality of this m:ist~r
craftsman. The lives of literally hundreds of our young people will m
years to come show to all men the results of his handiwork.
No member of our South West Lodge has more seriously lived ac~o~d­
ing to the teachings of Freemasonry. No member has ever been so w1llmg
to whisper words of brotherly counsel in the ear of a wayward brother.
No member has ever more ably directed the feet of young Masons along
highways trod by countless thousands of our brethren for !ol these .many
years! No member has ever more. thor?ughly devoted himself, without
stint or limit, to the welfare of our 1llustr1ous order.
Surely, the life of Brother Erle is a lasting testii;nony of the g~eatness
of our cause. Surely, we who must serve yet a little longer will draw
strength and encouragement from his example.
.
.
The hope of immortality is the reward of all .of us ~ho. practice out~1de
the Lodge the virtues inculcated in it. A ~ubhme faith m the . certamty
of this reward glowed like a steady flame m the heart of Brother E~le.
we who knew him so well have faith this day that ~e now finds et.ernal JOY
in the service of the Supreme Architect of the Umverse..For th1.s reason
we find satisfaction rather than sorrow in our hearts on. this occ'.1s1on. No
prouder titles are borne by living men than those which have been well
earned by our departed brother.
·
Brother Erle we salute you as master teacher and as Master Mason.

Youth is the season of friendships, when we are prodigal with our
affections, and thus it happens that of all those bonds so thoughtlessly
formed, some endure. It is an instinct of the heart that provides a store
for the winter of life. Some say the youth of friends hip is better than its
old age, but sometimes friendships ripen and mature and, like golden fruit,
mellow with age.
Charles Harris Victor, then a young 'man, affiliated with Live Oak
Lodge in Oakland, May 7, 1907. I , a young lawyer just appointed prosecuting attorney of the city of Oakland, had joined Live Oak the year before. We were both appointed to the floor team and then, through the succeeding years, we were appointed and elected to the successive offices of
the Lodge. I, being one office ahead of Charley, became the Master in 1916,
and Charley became the Master in 1917. As we worked through the chairs
of our Lodge, just one station apart, we grew closer and closer to each
other. I found his counsel in all things to be sound and well thought out.
His views were always broad and tolerant. He maintained throughout his
life a healthy, wholesome outlook. While he was deeply religious, no one
enjoyed the good things of life more than he. H is point of view was never
narrow or prejudiced, and at all times he thought and acted upon the square.
His interest in Masonry continued throughout his life. He was Grand
Orator in 1917 and 1918, and during all his life he was actively interested
in the affairs of his own Lodge, the Grand Lodge and the Masonic Club of
San Francisco. H is lecture upon "Masonry and the Bible" has been the
inspiration for a deeper faith in those Masons who heard it.
He was a devoted son, husband and father, and extremely interested
in the welfare of every member of his family. He has left with his mother
and his chlidren a dear memory of thoughtfulness, love and devotion.
Those of us who were so fortunate as to know Charley Victor valued
him as a friend. He was just as comfortable as an old shoe, and I know
no higher compliment to pay any friend. You all know the comfort of
such a friend, the inexpressible comfort of feeling safe with him, having
neither to weigh thoughts or measure words-but pouring them L'Ut, just
as ~ey are, chaff and grain togeth;r, certain that a faithfu l hand will sift
them, keep what is worth keeping-and with the breath of kindness, blow
the rest away.
Whatever the number of a man's friends, there will be times in his
life when he has too few. As we grow older, we value more and more the
friends who have remained true throughout the years, and regretfully we
see the number grow smaller and smaller. Believe me, in this world which
is ever slipping from under our feet, it is the prerogative of friendship to
grow old with one's friends. Charley Victor is gone, but those of us who
knew him still have with us the warmth of his friendship. He was a true
friend, and every true friend is a glimpse of God.

The minutes of yesterday's session were read and approved.
REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Control is pleased to submit the report of its activities
during the Masonic year.
·
We have received the hearty cooperation of the Grand officers and
particularly Grand Secretary Whicher and his Assistant, Frank Hobbs.
The Boards of Relief and indiv.idual Lodges have given to us their usual
hearty co-operation.
Notwithstanding that real justified relief has been in no way curtailed,
the calls for refunds from the Grand Lodge have become negligible. This
is due to the careful analysis and systema_tic handling of relief cases by
Boards of Relief and Lodges.
As mentioned last year "Our work however has grown in the direction
of consultations and advice on many problems that arise during the year,
and we believe the results are the avoidance of errors in policy and growth
in uniformity of the work of the Boards of Relief and Lodges."
Meetings
We held one business meeting of the Board during the year; also a
general meeting of the Board of Control and represent.atives of the various
Boards of Relief and Employment was held the evemng of October 12th.
Many problems were discussed, and the consensus of opinion v:as that
the meeting was highly educational and should be repeated durmg the
next session of the Grand Lodge.

•

Recoveries
There has been recovered for the Grand Lodge $623.00.
Reimbursements
In submitting our report on relief reimbursements we are again happy
to announce a slight decrease from the amount _requested !~st year. . The
effect of the various governmental relief agencies has agam made itself
felt in lessening the burden of our Fraternity. The very fine work on the
part of the Secretaries of our various B~ards of Relief _in arranging for use
of these agencies in cases where possible and practical cannot be commended too highly.
However small the requests for reimbursement may appear, we are
convinced that the glorious work of relieving th~ distress of our less fortunate brothers and their families is being earned on by our Boards of
Relief in a truly Masonic spirit.

Employment Service
The Masonic Employment Service in this jurisdiction continues to
increase in value and importance to the Craft. It affords an opportunity
for the practical application of the principles of Masonry found in no other
channel. The brethren engaged in the work and those directly benefited
are becoming enthusiastic.
In the year just ended 10,386 Masons and their dependents were placed
in jobs that gave them courage and security for the fu ture, and at no cost
to them or to the employer. In addition to the six established offices in
the- State, Boards of Relief in the smaller cit-ies are finding jobs for deserving brethren and at least one Board, Fresno, is extending its service
this year to include a definite Employment Service program.
The Board of Control has under considerat ion a suggested plan for
circularizing all Lodges of the jurisdiction with information and advice
concerning employment as well as a further plan for the clearance of requests for employes to fill positions in any place where local applicants are
not available.
The agreement of employers with employes in some localities to fill
all positions only through hiring halls is having a direct effect upon our
service and is a factor that must be definitely borne in mind in this great
work.
Your Board of Control commends the management of the several Employment Services of this State for their efforts and accomplishments this
past year.
Appropriations
For years Grand Lodge has appropriated a cons·i derable sum of money
toward the support of this Employment work. The local Boards of Relief
spend generously of their own time and funds in this connection. At this
time we recommend to the Finance Committee the following appropriations for 1938-1939:

REPORT OF MASONIC CLUB, U. C., LOS ANGELES
To the M:. w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Directors of the Masonic Club of the University of
California at Los Angeles fraternally submit their report for the year
ending September 30, 1938.
Last year we suffered a severe loss, as did this Grand Lodge and the
State of California in the passing of our esteemed Brother, Ira F. Thompson.
Shortly after our last communication, we suffered another severe loss in
the passing of Brother Wm. S. McFadden, Past MaS'ter of University
Lodge No. 394, one of the most valued members of our Board. He had
served as chairman of our Building Committee from the time he became a
Director in 1928 until his passing, and the usefulness, beauty and stability
of our Club House are largely due to his efficient and untiring work.
These two vacancies were filled by our Grand Master by the appointment of Brothers Oscar Lawler, Past Grand Master, and K. R. Bradley,
Past Master of Southgate Lodge No. 320. Needless to say these two
brethren are most welcome on the Board and their services are much
appreciated.
Once again the enrollment at the University exceeds any previous
year and your Club House continues to stand as a beac'O n light in the
lives of hundreds of young men and women.
Those of us who contact the students from time to time find them
very warm in their praise a,nd grateful for what is being done and has
been done for them, many coming back time and time again after their
graduations. A spirit of informality prevails, the atmosphere is pleasant
and friendly, with the result that the Club House is gradually acquiring
some w-0rthwhile traditions.
The study room has been dedicated to Brother Thompson and designated as Thompson Hall. It is well patronized and provides facilities
much appreciated by our young people.
Our Masonic Affiliate Council which supervises the activities of the
Club House has functioned efficiently and is well organized for the new
school year. Meetings are held twice monthly and the students who make
up this governing body are always careful to maintain the dignity of our
order. The Areme group, composed of fifty young women, made it possible for four underprivileged children to enjoy a mountain camp this
summer.
One thousand persons were present the evening we were privileged
to receive Most Worshipful Grand Mast er Fraser, together with a number
of his officers and their wives. The reception of the Grand Master is the

179

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

outstanding event of the year and one which all look forward to with
great pleasure and enthusiasm.
With respect to the budget for the coming year, our estimate is as
follows:

GENERAL REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To the M." .w: .Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Finance begs leave to submit the following report:
Audit of Accounts
Your committee has again employed Brother Floyd F. Webb of the
firm of Ruckstell, Burrows and Webb, certified public accountants, to
examine the books and records of the Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary, the Masonic Homes of California and the Endowment Fund. The
reports of Brother Webb's examination of these records have been filed
with your committee and have had its consideration. These reports are
now on file with the records of Grand Lodge. They indicate that all records
are correct and in proper shape and all receipts properly accounted for and
all expenditures properly made.
Your committee is again mindful of the debt it owes Brother Webb
for the personal interest he has shown in making the various audits. He
has devoted considerable time to the affairs of Grand Lodge, for which
he is asking no remuneration, and for which your committee is duly appreciative.
The amount asked for the complete audit is the same as it was for
last year, that is the sum of $700.00. Of this sum $550.00 is paid by the
Trustees of the Homes and only $150.00 paid out of Grand Lodge Funds.
Grand Lodge Week Activities
The Committee on Grand Lodge Week Activities has furnished your
committee with an estimate of the cost of the entertainment which it has
provided for the members who are attending this session of Grand Lodge.
Necessarily the best that the committee can do at this time is to furnish
this committee with an estimate, as it is very difficult to determine the
exact amount of expenditures until all activities are over and the bills
actually presented.
For the purpose of' the entertainment of this Grand Lodge the Finance
Committee of last year budgeted $2,000.00. The estimate presented indicates that this sum will be exceeded by about $1,200.00. Most of this
overage is due to ·the expense incurred by the committee in transporting
the members to and from the Home at Decoto.
Your committee is in accord with the representatives being afforded
entertainment and also of their visit to the Masonic Home. It also believes
that the Activities Committee has done a good job and has incurred a
minimum of expense in presenting the entertainment and doing the other
things it has for the delegates and is, therefore, anxious not to seem that
it is criticizing the committee or any part of its work. Your Finance
Committee is, however, reluctant to see an established budget exceeded
for any purpose.
It is also to be noted that Tuesday evening's entertainment cost per
member $3.21. Of this amount $1.50 was contributed by each member
who attended and the balance is being paid out of the funds of Grand
Lodge. This per member cost appears large.
For the purpose of carrying the Grand Lodge Activities for this
coming year, your committee is budgeting $2,500.00. This is $500.00 more
than was budgeted for the year just closing, but $700.00 less than the sum
actually expended. The Finance Committee feels that it must request the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

181

committee for the coming year to keep within the budget allowance. Your
committee therefore offers the following resolution and recommends its
adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $1,200, in addition to the budget of $2,000,
or s.o much thereof as may be necessary to pay the expenses incurred
b; the Grand Lodge Week Activities Committee, be and the same. is
hereby appropriated out of the funds of Grand Lodge, and that the same
be allocated to the payment of the expenses incurred in the entertainment
of officers and members during this session.
Masonic Education
Your committe to which has been referred that portion of the report
of the Committee on Masonic Education relating to expense incurred in the
publication and distribution of a pamphlet for the Masonic instruction of
candidates, begs leave to report as follows:
It has looked over the report with considerable interest and the information compiled has been examined. It would seem to this committee
that the ,Committee on Education has started a movement that is worthy
of a complete trial and has done it at a minimum of expense. It is in accord
with the wish of the committee to follow-up on the plan towards accomplishing its thorough trial.
The Educational Committee has requested that it be permitted to use
$300.00 ~f the funds being received fro.m the sale of the pamphlet, that
it may continue to follow-up on its efforts. While your committee is in
accord with the wish of the Educational Committee, yet it believes that all
funds received from the sale of the pamphlet should be paid directly to
the Grand Secretary and funds expended should ·be from funds appropriated
for that purpose. Your committee therefore offers the following resolution
and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $300.00 be appropriated from the funds of
Grand Lodge to defray the expenses of the Education Committee in further
promoting its educational plan.
Masonic History
The members of your Committee on Masonic History have appeared
before this committee and discussed the work they have been doing and
the need for some funds to properly compile and prepare some of .the
history and material already in their hands. It appears to your Committee
on Finance that this committee has been doing a very able and extensive
piece of' work and has been mos t modest in its request for help from
Grand Lodge to defray its expenses. The H istory Committee feels,
however, that this year ·it should have $250.00 to help out on its expenses.
We are thoroughly in accord with its request, and therefore offer the .following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $250.00 be appropriated from the fund of
this Grand Lodge and be paid to the chairman of the History Committee
to defray additional expenses which may be incurred by the committee
in compiling ·and preparing additional information gathered on the history
of Masonry in California.

attached thereto. We . are con,vinc.ed that the greatest of care is being
