Masonic Homes
Your Committee on Finance to which was referred that portion of
the report of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes, relating to the
finances of said homes, begs leave to report as follows:
Your committee has carefully studied the report and conclusions of
the certified public accountants, and is of the opinion that the financial
affairs of both Masonic Homes were not only fully and correctly reported
by the Trustees, but also that they reflect efficient and fraternal management in keeping with the high purposes of the homes.
We note with pleasure that from the funds allocated to them the
Trustees paid on their Endowment Fund note the sum of $50,000.00,
leaving at the end of the fiscal year a balance of only $25,000.00 on the
original obligation of approximately $250,000.00 which was incurred in 1930
for building purposes. While it is not shown in the report, we are happy
to learn that this balance has been paid since the beginning of this fiscal
year and the Homes are now free from obligations other than for maintenance and upkeep. We realize that during the years this obligation has
been pressing, the Board of Trustees, repairs and replacements have been
kept at an absolute minimum · and that in the future it will be necessary to
expend a larger sum for this purpose. Approximately $14,000.00 was spent
last year for this purpose at Covina which accounted for an increased daily
cost of twenty-four cents per resident. The daily per capita at the Decoto
Home also increased from eighty-eight to ninety-four cents. We believe,
however, that this is not out of line with the necessities of the situation
and that it reflects good management on the part of the Board of Trustees.
We note that the cost of outside relief for both Homes has again been
decreased for the third successive year, and that during that three year
period it has been reduced from $43,208.00 to $31,037.00, in the case of the ·

GRAND LODGF; OF CALIFORNIA

183

Decato Home and from $4,196.00 to $2,875.00 in the case of the Covina
Home. We believe that the Board of Trustees should be commended for
this result and encouraged to further reduce this item of expense until
such time as the Homes are operating to capacity, which is not the case
at the present time.
We have discussed the necessities of the Homes for the coming year
with the chairman of the Board of Trustees and have concluded with his
approval that it will be possible to reduce the special home maintenance
per capita tax from fifty cents to forty cents. We, therefore, offer the
following resolution:
Resolved, that the special per capita tax for the maintenance of the
Masonic Homes be set at forty cents.
. Masonic Homes Endowment Board
Your Committee on Finance has considered very carefully the sixth
annual report rendered by the Masonic Homes Endowment Board. As
you have already learned from this report, the Board has followed the
policy adopted several years ago of educating the membership concerning
the Homes, stressing the advisability of building up a Ptrmanent Endowment Fund but refraining from making " quota" drives in the membership.
During the past year the Permanent Fund has been increased by about
$98,000.00 to a total of about $1,100,000.00. Of the increase, about $68,000.00
came from be.q uests, $21,000.00 from donations through the Lodges and
about $9,000.00 from profits or adjustments in book values through the
sales of securities. It is noted also that the contributions through the
Lodges came from 4600 individuals, a very small proportion of our entire
membership.
While your committee wishes fervently that some means could be
devised by which the entire membership could be aroused to a sense of
their responsibility to the Homes, we agree thoroughly with the decision
of the Board to refrain from any action which might be interpreted as a
drive on the membership for funds. We believe that the apathy of the
members can best be overcome by quiet educational methods rather than
by spectacular drives.
While a net increase of $98,000.00 does not appear to be large from
the standpoint of our needs, we must remember that we would not have
had that if we had not organized the Endowment Board. In other words,
we are just making a start on this project, and while a fund of $1,100,000.00
seems quite substantial, it can and will be increased only by a concerted
effort on the part of a continually increasing number of interested Masons.
We believe that Grand Lodge owes a great debt of gratitude to the
members of the Board and especially to the chairman, Brother Frank M.
Smith, for their untiring efforts on behalf of a more substantial Endowment Fund, and we trust that their efforts will be rewarded by a more
generous response on the part of the Masons of California during the
coming year.
For several years Grand Lodge has appropriated $6,000.00 for the
use of the Endowment Board. We believe that this money has been spent
very wisely and that it should be continued.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, that the Masonic Homes Endowment Board be commended

for its efforts on behalf of the Endowment Fund and that the sum of
$6,000.00 be and is appropriated from the general funds of Grand Lodge
for the use of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board during the present
fiscal year.

Additional Traveling Expenses of Retiring Grand Master
Your Committee on Finance has discussed with the Grand Master the
Master the sum necessary for his traveling expenses during the coming year.
He has already received innumerable invitations to visit Lodges, and
hopes not only to accept these but also to visit extensively in all parts of
the jurisdiction throughout the year. After consulting with the present
Grand Master, he is of the opinion that the sum of $4,500.00 will be required for that purpose.
Believing that such visitations should be encouraged, and realizing
that our incoming Grand Master, with his great knowledge of Masonic
history is peculiarly fitted for this task, we agree with his conclusion and
offer the following resolution:
Resolved, that the sum of $4,500.00 be appropriated from the funds
of Grand Lodge for the traveling expenses of the Grand Master.
Portrait of Grand Master
For many years it has ·been the policy of Grand Lodge to request the
retiring Grand Master to have his portrait painted that it might be included
in the gallery of portraits of Past Grand Masters. The expense to be paid
by Grand Lodge. Your committee is sure that Grand Lodge will wish to
continue this custom and have the portrait of our present retiring Grand
Master included in this gallery, Your committee, therefore, recommends
that our retiring Grand Master, James Thomas Fraser, have his portrait
painted and present the bill to the Grand Secretary in an amount not to
exceed $250.00, who is authorized to pay same, and when the portrait is
finished to be hung in the gallery of Past Grand Masters.
Portraits of Preceding Grand Masters
Last year's report of this committee called attention to the lack of
presence of portraits of Past Grand Masters William Rhodes Hervey,

Grand Lodge Per Capita
The Constitution provides for the levying of a per capita of fifty cents
to provide for the expenses of Grand Lodge and its various committees. In
addition to the sum provided for by this per capita levy there is an additional sum coming into Grand Lodge for degrees conferred and from
income on investments derived from surplus accumulated in prior years of
about $20,000.00. There is some further revenue derived from the sale of
supplies and surety bonds covering Lodge officers but which revenue cannot be taken into consideration in the budget, because it is offset by items
of disbursements which are also eliminated from the budget.
This income is not sufficient to pay the operating expenses of Grand
Lodge during the coming year and to care for the various appropriations
that are being made in this report. In reports by this committee for the
years 1936 and 1937, attention was called to the continually increasing
deficit and of its firm conviction that the time was at hand when the income
of Grand Lodge must at least equal its out-go. This was practically accomplished this last year. In order to accomplish this an additional per capita
levy was made last year of fifteen cents.
It is apparent to your committee that the income from the sources above
mentioned will be somewhat less for the coming year than it was for the
past year.
It will also be noticed by this report that the appropriations have been
somewhat increased. The committee has done its best to keep these
appropriations to the minimum, but in spite of all efforts, we have not been
able to do this. Therefore, in order to cover these additional appropriations,
as well as to overcome the decrease in revenue, it becomes necessary to
increase the per capita levy from fifteen cents to twenty-five cents.
This does not mean, however, that there is to be any increase in the
total per capita levy, for in going over the budget with the Trustees O·f the
Homes, it appears to this committee, which conclusion is concurred in
by the Trustees, that instead of a fifty cent per capita levy to provide for
maintenance of the Homes, as was provided for last year, they can get
by with a ten cent decrease, or in other words a forty cent per capita levy.
Your committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and recommends
its adoption:
Resolved, that a per capita levy of forty cents per member be levied
and when paid, shall be paid by the Grand Secretary to the Trustees of
the Homes for the operation and maintenance expenses of the Homes,
and be it further
Resolved, that a per capita levy of twenty-five cents per member be
levied for the payment of Grand Lodge expenses and for its various
Masonic activities.
Budget

receipts and disbursements for the year ending July 31, 1938 discloses that
the major items of the 1937-38 budget have been approximately adhered
to. Mentioned elsewhere in this report, under separate captions, unavoidable excess has been commented upon, as has the matter of deficits
of prior years.

realized, and your committee is pleased that such has been the case. The
current ·budget contemplates a like result, and your committee urges
those agencies of Grand Lodge who are charged with the disbursal of

Your Committee on Charters presents the following report:
On October 3, 1938, the Grand Master issued a dispensation to Dos
Palos Lodge, located at Dos Palos, Merced county. Your committee is
advised that the members of Dos Palos Lodge did not present a petition
for a charter at this communication, for the reason that they desire to
avail themselves of the opportunity to demonstrate, during the coming
year, their worth as a Masonic Lodge, to the end that one year hence they
may merit favorable consideration. This attitude on the part of the members of Dos Palos Lodge is to be highly commended.
Your committee has received from Veteran Lodge No. 373, located in
West Los Angeles, an application requesting your approval of a resolution
read at the stated meeting of Veteran Lodge, held on September 7, 1938,
and, thereafter, duly adopted at the stated meeting of said Lodge on
October 5, 1938. All proceedings had by Veteran Lodge in connection with
said resolution are duly certified by th-e Master and the Secretary and bear
the seal of the Lodge.
In the resolution thus adopted, it is proposed to change the name of
Veteran Lodge to West Los Angeles Lodge. Request is also made for
the retention of the number 373.
Before passing upon this application, your committee held a formal
hearing at which hearing there were present officers and representatives
of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42, the Master of Veteran Lodge No. 373, and the
Inspectors of the two Lodges named. We are indebted to these brethren
for an able presentation of the facts.
We learned that Veteran Lodge was apparently conceived and perfected by men who were, without doubt, prompted in their efforts by that
spirit which the word "Veteran" so aptly implies. We also learned that
Veteran Lodge has enjoyed an honorable and uninterrupted existence over
a period of thirty-two years.
Your committee recognizes the right of any Lodge to propose a
change of name. We feel, however, that in the instant case those reasons
advanced for the preservation, intact, of Veteran Lodge in that name and
that spirit in which the Lodge was conceived more than offset the reasons
presented in support of the contemplated change.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution:
Resolved, that the resolution of Veteran Lodge No. 373, wherein it is
proposed to change the name of said Lodge to West Los Angeles Lodge,
be not approved.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
CLANDESTINE MASONRY
To the M.". W.' .Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonic Activity begs leave to report as
follows:
The several Negro, Filipino, Mexican and Co-Masonic Grand bodies are
still in existence, as previously reported. We find, however, that the activity of some of them has greatly diminished, although in the case of others
it has accelerated, and new subordinate bodies have been organized.
Generally speaking, the same men and women whom we have previously reported as being in official charge are still directing the affairs
of these bodies.
The M. W. Prince Hall Grand Lodge:
The Prince Hall group of negro Masons are apparently enjoying better
financial circumstances. Their Grand Lodge met July 7, 1938 at Riverside
and Theodore Moss of San Jose was elected Grand Master. In Fresno,
one of the local Lodges held its annual meeting and installed Douglas
Houston as Worshipful Master. On March 15, 1938 this local Lodge
sponsored a dinner, the proceeds of which were to be used for a building
program. On October 31, 1937 they held a grand public ceremony known
as "Lodge of the Sorrow." We understand that this Grand Lodge has
purchased property on the highway near the town of Tulare and are developing plans for the construction of an Old People's Home.
The local Fresno Lodge purchased property in that town where they
intend to construct a temple for their own use. The only Lodge of this
rite in the Imperial Valley is located in the town of Imperial and R. J.
Burley is Master. Another of the Lodges is the San Diego Lodge, with
Milton Warner as Master.
M. W. Hiram of Tyre Grand Lodge, A. F. & A. M.:
This Negro Grand Lodge also seems to be entering upon a period of
better financial conditions. They held an Annual Communication on June
20 to 23, 1938, in Watts, near Los Angeles and L. P. Lea of 1378 East
108th Street, Los Angeles, was elected Grand Master .. J. S. Meadows of
Fresno was elected District Deputy and Grand Tiler. The subordinate
Lodge in Fresno held its annual meeting last December and installed
Timothy Williams as Master. Of this local Lodge four members hold
Grand Lodge positions. They seem to meet regularly on the first and third
Tuesdays of each month in Garibaldi Hall, Fresno, and for some time
conducted a publication entitled "The Ancient Traveler"; this, however,
has been discontinued recently.
We are recently informed of the existence of a body known as the
Lauaan Lodge No. 21 at San Francisco, operating under this rite.
Also Mt. Moriah Lodge of Los Angeles, whose Secretary is Howard
Ervin, living at 1011 East 43rd Place, Los Angeles. We have the complete roster and list of officers of this Lodge.
We are informed that the Negro Grand Lodge Hiram of Tyre is
warranted by and operating under a Charter from a national group of
negro masons, known as the General Grand Masonic Congress of Masters.
The head of this national organization is Nelson N. Boozer, with headquarters at 302 Lincoln Theatre Building, Houston, Texas.
A list of these Grand Lodges is attached hereto.

Information comes to us of the existence of Makeling Lodge No. 24

A subordinate Lodge of thi~ rite is located in El Centro with thirty

Legionarios del Trabajo:
.
This Grand body held a Grand Convention December 3, 4, and 5, 1937,
m the Ambassador Hotel, Los Angeles. We understand there were twentyfive Lodges and triangles (whatever that may mean) present; a list of
these Lodges is in the hands of your committee. We are informed that
this is a semi-labor organization, having been organized by an enthusiastic
Mason who was also an active union labor worker. An address presented
to this body by Manuel L. Quezon, President of the Philippine Commonwealth, who is an honorary president of this fraternal organization, was
read at this Grand Convention, and in it Mr. Quezon states:
"The Fraternity Legionarios de! Trabajo is· firmly convinced
that the Philippines is capable of managing its own future. Consequently, this Fraternity shall work for the national independence
of the Philippines through peaceful and legal means.
"This fraternity shall further work for the implantation in
this country of social justice; the equalizing of all before the law;
the abolition of any kind of privileges and discriminations, and the

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RITUAL
To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Ritual, to which was referred a resoluton authorizing
the preparation of such additional ritual to the funeral service as in our
judgment might be appropriate and useful, reports as foll ows :
The purpose of the resolution is set forth in its preamble.
"Whereas, it is believed that the funeral service could be improved
upon by adding thereto a supplemental and complete committal service
for use at a crematorium or a cemetery, in addition to the present funeral
service now used at undertaking parlors."
Your committee has carefully considered this in relation to the present
funeral service. We call attention to the fact that the present funeral
service is so arranged that it may be used in the Lodge room, church, home,
undertaking parlor or any other appropriate place, and if it is desired to use
it in part at the place designated for the service and in part at the place
designated for burial or other disposition, we call attention specifically to
paragraph two on page four of the present service, which reads as follows :
"The service is then resumed down to but not including the paragraph
beginning, 'Soft and safe,' etc. indicating the part to be used at the place
of service."
We also call attention to the last sentence of the last paragraph on page
four:
"After the casket is placed and the mourners ilre in their carriages,
the procession disbands and the officers and members return to the hall,
the Master and such members as can, going to the place of sepulture,
where the ritual is completed, followed by the benediction," indicating the
part to be used at the place of sepulture.
We regard the present service as both suitable and adequate for any
and all occasions and we believe that its language can scarcely be improved
upon.
Since the resolution authorized the committee "to prepare such additional ritual as in their judgment may be appropriate and useful for such
committal service," and since in our judgment there is no need for any
change, we do not present any such additional ritual at this time.
We recommend that the resolution be not adopted.

L. E. Woon,
SIDNEY K. LEHMAN,

LLOYD E. WTLSON,
G. c. DEFOREST,
CHESTER WARLOW,

Ritual Committee.

Report adopted.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
To your Committee on Appeals and Grievances there have been referred a total of twenty-four records. Five of these records are petitions
for restoration and will be treated in separate reports to be later given to
you. Out of the remaining nineteen records, there have been two appeals
from the determination of the trial Lodges and these two matters will
likewise be separately reported.
Of the remaining seventeen matters, all which are covered by this
report, fifteen are proceedings under Section 192 of our Constitution
dealing with automatic expulsion following conviction in the courts of the
land of crimes classified as a felony and imprisonment pursuant thereto.

land.
In none of these seventeen matters reported to you herewith has there
been an appeal by either the accuser or the accused. In each of them the
penalty has been fixed at expulsion.
Your committee has carefully reviewed each and all of these seven teen
records and finds therein no irregularities of any consequence whatsoever.
We feel that in each instance substantial justice in accordance with the
precepts of Masonic law has been accomplished. We, therefore, feel and
recommend to this Grand Lodge that the determination of the several
Lodges in each of these matters should be affirmed.

REPORTS OF COMMITTE ON
. POLICY AND GENERAL PURPOSES
To the M.".W.".Gmnd Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered the
recommendations and resolutions and other matters presented to the Grand
Lodge and referred to your committee, and it respectfully reports thereon,
as follows:
Recommendations of the Grand Master:
The Grand Master again directed the attention of the Grand Lodge
to complaints of flagrant disregard for the principles of Masonry of certain
so-called Masonic publications. Such suggestions have heretofore been
made by Grand Masters, and stern warnings have been given, both by
Grand Masters and this committee, in order to enable the publishers of
Masonic papers to mend their ways, else to be the objects of drastic action
by this Grand Lodge. The Grand Master recommends that a section be
added to our Constitution requiring that if there is such an offending publication, that it be under the direct supervision of Grand Lodge.
It is the opinion of your committee that Grand Lodge should not
undertake t~e supervision of any Masonic or so-called Masonic publication,
nor should 1t be responsible in any way for the objectionable practices of
the publisher, nor for any part of the contents of any such publication.
All of these publications are commercial enterprises conducted for profit
and constitute no part of the activities in this Grand Lodge. Such abuses
as have arisen are properly chargeabie to the Mason or Masons engaged
in publishing or contributing to a purported Masonic periodical. In any
case of unmasonic conduct on the part of a Mason, there is now in our law
ample provisions for trial and punishment ; but for persons who are not
Masons, offending through the publication of purported Masonic periodicals,
there is no recourse in Masonic Law. If the abuses complained of are
continued it ma y become necessary. to prohibit Masons from engaging in
the publication of so-called Masonic periodicals, or it may be neces·s ary
to forbid any Mason to use the word "Masonic" in connection with a
periodical.
Until a furthe r investigation. of this matter ;;nd the examination ·of
specific instances of abuses which may be brought to our .attention, w'e
find ourselves unab le to make a recommendation ;tt this time for the
amendment of the Constitution as suggested by the: ·Grand Master.

Adopted.

Exemption from Dues
Harry Bobbitt, Master of San Jose Lodge No. 10, and Arthur Jones
·Miner, Master of Friendship Lodge No. 210, proposed a resolution which
is concurred in by the Masters by ten other Lodges to amend Section 128
of the Constitution by providing that any member who shall have been a
member in good standing in this jurisdiction for fifty years or more shall
he exempt from the further payment of dues and shall receive a special
life membership certificate from his Lodge. They also pl'opose amendments to Section 41 of the Constitution and Section I of Article 9 of the
Uniform Code of By-Laws to bring them in harmony with the amendment
to Section 128. This subject matter came before Grand Lodge at its annual
communication in 1932 and was referred to your committee on Policy and
General Purposes, which reported thereon as follows:
"It is the opinion of your committee, and has been the policy of this
Grand Lodge during all the years of its existence, that every member
should contribute to the support of Masonry unless his dues, in proper
cases, were remitted. This duty of contributing to the Lodge for its
support and that of the charities and other activities of Masonry is not
affected by the matter of years or of service, but is inherent in the charac.ter of a Mason. Money is required to carry on our works and without
money our institution as ·an organization would come to a standstill and
the usefulness of Masonry would be seriously impaired if not destroyed.
The burden of providing sufficient funds for Masonic purposes should be
evenly distributed on the membership and ho one should be allowed to
shift his obligation onto his brethren, for lightening the load of one
by exemption increases that of the other members. Many of our brethren
of mature years are better able to contribute to Masonry than many of
the younger brethren, because age does not necessarily indicate the extent
of a man's resources or ability to pay. Whether a brother be old or young,
his dues should be, and will be, remitted by the Lodge when the circumstances of each · individual case requires such action.
· "The Grand Lodge instituted the custom of presenting fifty-year buttons in order to honor and distinguish those certain brethren who have for
half a century been faithful craftsmen. It was a graceful and fraternal
recognition of long years of Masonic · service, but it was not intended as,

Seating Capacity of Grand Lodge
Charles A. Watson, Master o.f Carmel Lodge No. 680, offers a resolution that Grand Lodge take suitable action to reserve one seat for the
duly elected or accredited representative of each chartered Lodge in the
jurisdiction, and that such seat he held for the sole use of such representative for the entire period of the communication.
The reason for the proposal by Brother Watson is readily understanda·ble by every person in Grand Lodge. We will agree that the present
situation is deplorable. His suggestion of one seat being reserved for
each Lodge would not meet with general approval, because many Lodges
are represented by more than one person, and the representative.9 therefrom would find a single seat more uncomfortable than Grand Lodge
finds the restricted capacity of Grand Lodge hall. There may be ways
found to remedy the present conditions and, therefore, the proposal should
not be rejected but should be referred to the incoming Grand Master and
Grand Secretary; that it may induce them to give serious consideration to
the situation the proposal is intended to remedy, and your committee
recommends that the resolution be so referred.

Adopted.
Grand Lecturer
Clarence S. Cole of Whittier Lodge No. 223; George M. Rodecker,
Master of Azusa Lodge No. 305, have presented resolutions recently passed
by their respective Lodges disapproving the present system of the teaching
of the ritual by the Grand Lecturer and his Assistant Grand Lecturers
and recommending that Grand Lodge revert to the system of the full time
Grand Lecturer.
Since the death of the late lamented Thomas J. Baker, the supervision
of the ritualistic work in this Grand Jurisdiction has been intrusted to
the Grand Lecturer and several Assistant Grand Lecturers. This committee has ascertained that some of the members prefer what is known as
"the Tom Baker System'', \Vhile other members prefer the system now
being practiced. Your committee, itself, is divided in the opinion on the
subject and feels that the method of teaching a ritual should be decided by
Grand Lodge where the representatives of the Lodges who are constantly
dealing with the subject may have a voice in the decision of the question.
That the matter may be brought properly before Grand Lod.ge for discussion and decision and not as an expression of the unanimous opinion
of your committee on Policy and General Purposes, the committee recommends that the resolutions changing from the present system to the socalled "Tom Baker System", be not adopted.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPR'uDENCE
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:

__ Yo_u r_ Cqmrniilee- .<m-· Jat'tsprudence has ·had- tinder consideration the
resolution set forth in the report of the Committee on Accounts relating
to the provisions of Section 30 and Section 220 of the Constitution.
It is obvious that the framers of this resolution misconstrue the wording of Section 220, which reads as follows:
"All former written Constitutions of this Grand Lodge are hereby
repealed, as are also all Regulations, or parts thereof, which are repugnant
to or inconsistent with this Constitution; and no regulation shall hereafter
be adopted which shall be in violation of, or inconsistent with, any of
its provisions."
Section 228 defines a regulation as follows : "By a regulation of the
Grand Lodge is meant any resolution, edict, law, or ordinance of any kind
whatever, other than the Constitution, which it may adopt."
The resolution presented is an apparent attack on the provisions of
Sec. 37e and 37k of the Constitution, as being violative of the prohibition
regarding regulation contained in Section 220.
These Sections 37e and 37k are as much a part of the Constitution as
is Section 220, and the latter section was not intended to prohibit Constitutional provisions thereafter to be enacted which might be in conflict
with the Constitution as originally adopted.
The effect of this resolution would be to attempt to rescind or repeal
unmentioned and undescribed sections of the Constitution. It does not
attempt to specify what provisions of the Constitution are in violation of
or inconsistent with the provisions of Section 220, and its adoption would
not accomplish the desired result but would create more confusion than
can possibly exist under the present circumstances.
Furthermore, the resolution does not purport to be an amendment to
·the Constitution, and an amendment to the organic law cannot be accomplished by a mere resolution.
We recommend that .the resolution be not adopted.
Report adopted.

and in lieu thereof the words "applications whether for degrees or affiliation
or both" be inserted; that the words "application" "applicant" and "applicants" be subst:tuted for the words "petition" " petitioner" amt "petitioners" respectively where sa_id latter words appea r in said section;

REPORT OF ACTIVITIES COMMITTEE
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grand Lodge Week Activities respectfolly reports as.
follows:
• Your committee is charged with the duty of attending to all entertainment
during Grand Lodge week, and it has proceeded with the thought that recreation and entertainment are an essential part of the Grand Lodge communication. With this in mind, we have endeavored to produce clean and wholesome
recreation and entertainment.
The major events of the week provided by the cvmmittee were the Good
Fellowship Dinner and the trip to Treasure Island and the Home at Decoto.
At the dinner approximately a thousand of the brethren availed themselves
of the affair, and the trip to Treasure Island and the Home was patronized
by over a thousand of the brethren and their ladies.
A full accounting of the costs of the committee has been made to the
Finance Committee.
We trust that the brethren and their families have been pleased with the
social events of the week. If it has met with your approbation, the committee
has performed its duty.
ARTHUR JOEL,
THOMAS ANDERSON,
ANDREW B URl<E,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ANNUAL ELECTION OF OFFICERS
The annual election of officers was now held, the result
being as follows :

The R:. w:. Leon 0. Whitsell of Orange Grove Lodge
No. 293 was elected Grand Master.
The R. ·. W. ·. William H. Waste of Durant Lodge No. 268
was elected Deputy Grand Master.
The R:. w:. William B. Ogden of Hollywood Lodge No. 355
was elected Senior Grand Warden.
The w:. Lloyd E. Wilson of Ingleside Lodge No. 630 was
elected Junior Grand Warden.
The v:. w:. William P . Filmer of King Solomon's Lodge
No. 260 was re-elected Grand Treasurer.
The v:. w:. John Whicher of King David's Lodge No. 2(f)
was re-elected Grand Secretary.
The v:. W:. Leslie E. Wood of Provident Lodge No. 6ff)
was re-elected Grand Lecturer.
The Grand Master-elect caused to be read the names of the
appointive officers, as follows :
Grand Chaplain, Richard R. Perkins of Durant Lodge No. 268.
Grand Orator, Ellsworth Meyer of Liberal Arts Lodge No.
677.
Assistant Grand Secretary, Frank G. Hobbs of Alexandria
·
Lodge No. 531.
Grand Marshal, Charles Goff of Parnassus Lodge No. 388.
Grand Standard Bearer, Chas. A. Shepherd of Kilauea Lodge
No. 330.
Grand Sword Bearer, Fred A. Kelsey of Mount Olive Lodge
No. 506.
Grand Bible Bearer, Jeremiah Ames Vaughn of Forbestown
Lodge No. 50.
Senior Grand Deacon, George M. Duntley of Highland Park
Lodge No. 382.
Junior Grand Deacon, Leo V. Youngworth of Hollenbeck
Lodge No. 319.
Senior Grand Steward, Lem. F. Harvey of Santa Ana Lodge
No. 241.
Junior Grand Steward, Otto Liersch of Olivet Lodge No. 205.
Grand Pursuivant, Harry W. Beatty of Taft Lodge No. 516.
Grand Organist, Charles E . Anderson of J ewe! Lodge No.
374.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

247

Grand Tiler, Ralph K. Marshall of Occidental Lodge No. 22.
He also announced the appointment of Chas. M. Wollenberg
to be a member of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes
of California, vice self, term expired.
The M:. w:. Dana R. Weller was appointed Master of
Ceremonies and the officers-elect and appointed were installed
by the retiring Grand Master in due and ancient form.
The newly installed Grand Master then invested his predecessor with a Past Grand Master's lapel button, in which was
set a beautiful diamond; and also invested him with the apron of
a Past Grand Master. The Chas. Albert Adams insignia was
transferred from the retiring to the incumbent Grand Master,
and the other chair officers exchanged the Arthur S . .Crites lapel
pins.
John Gries, Past Master of Ferndale Lodge No. 193, in behalf
of Grand Lodge, presented to the retiring Grand Master a set
of flat silver.
Augustus H. Allen, Inspector of the one hundredth district,
then presented to the Grand Master, in behalf of the officers of
the Lodges of his district, a beautiful gavel, bearing all the
emblems of Masonry embellished with gold, with a diamond in
the end of the handle.
At 1 :45 o'clock, all business being completed, Grand Lodge
was closed in Ample Form.
LEON 0. WHITSELL,
Grand Master.
JOHN WHICHER,
Grand Secretary.

October, 1938
By JESSE M. WHITED
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
For the fifteenth annual period in a service of seventeen years as
Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence, herewith is presented its
Report. As in former years, the same is the work of the Chairman and
the views expressed under the various topics are, of course, his own. In
compiling the same the Proceedings of over 60 Grand Lodges have been
summarized, with a view of giving the reader briefly the thought and action
of the various Jurisdictions. There is no dearth of material and the problem is to select and confine within the pages allotted interest and instructive
information.
We find ourselves in perhaps the position as the Radio Announcer the
other night, who in broadcasting the reception to "Wrong Way Corrigan"
in New York, stated he was in a difficult situation in endeavoring to condense nine yards of press copy, particularly as what had taken place might
in future be history.
In general there have been no outstanding matters that have not been
before the Fraternity in former years. We still find opinion or action
divided on the same lines as in our National life of today, to-wit, "Conservative" or "Progressive." Whichever course followed is taken or suggested for what appears to be the best interests of the Fraternity, viewed
in the light of existing national or local conditions.
WHO'S WHO IN CHINA: Peace and tranquility Masonically again
prevail. In our Report last year we noted the breach in fraternal relations
between the Grand Lodges of England, Massachusetts, Scotland and Ireland with the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands. This was based upon
the establishment of lodges in China by the latter Grand Lodge. We arc
glad to report that after negotiations a satisfactory agreement governing
the operations of the various Grand Lodges in the territory in question has
been signed. Fraternal intercourse and the exchange of Representatives by
the Jurisdictions to the Pact have now been resumed.
We were privileged a few weeks ago to meet the R. W. H. C. Mei,
District Grand Master for the District Grand Lodge of China under the
Philippine Constitution, and Dr. Elbert Chung, Past Master of Westlake
Lodge No. 113, Hang Chow, China. These brethren are outstanding men,
and from other sources we were informed that they are representative of
the Craft in China. With such leaders the Fraternity in China would appear to be in good hands.
THE FIRST STONE OF THE BUILDING: A number of Grand
Masters report officiating at the laying of Corner Stones for various classes
of public and other buildings. The Grand Lodge of Louisiana has a rule
that they will not lay a Cornerstone unles it bears on .the exposed face the
figures of the year and the words "Laid by the Grand Lodge of the State
of Louisiana, Free and Accepted Masons." The propriety of this might
be questioned. As one Reviewer remarked, it smacks of perpetual advertising for Masonry.
The following criticism by Brother Allen, Chairman of the Correspondence Committee of North Carolina, is typical as to what generally goes
into Corner Stones ; "One would judge by the record that everybody

about Fort Smith took advantage of that occasion to get his history into
a place of preservation in the Corner Stone of the Ft. Smith, Arkansas,
Court House. There were laid away in that cornerstone-box about a
hundred of such 'brief histories'; histories of the banks; histories of all

R. P. Strozier. Perhaps the most valuable item of the lot was the 'Assortment of Present Day Coins.'"
ORDER OF DE MOLA Y: While the Order of DeMolay uses every
effort to impress upon its members that the organization is not a junior
Masonic organization and has no connection with Masonry, a survey of
some of the Jurisdictions shows that a large percentage of the younger
members have formerly been members with this Organization. This percentage is higher in the Jurisdictions that have been responsive to the work
of DeMolay and groups of a like character. This is the day of the
young man, and the difference between them and the older generation is
best expressed in the following sentiment:
"Youth lives; we exist.
They feel; we think.
They come; we go.
They play; we fumble.
They dream; we dream asleep.
They sleep; we toss.''
While the older generation cannot be as they are, the recognition of
this difference should not be hard to reconcile. Some Grand Lodges have
taken definite action along this line, others are hostile and the remainder
are passive or marking time. Approximately 25 pages of the Proceedings
reviewed are devoted to this question.
"LET THERE BE LIGHT": The efforts of Grand Lodges to sponsor
or assist in programs for the Education of their members appears to occupy
less attention than heretofore. Where this work is being sericmsly undertaken, the Lodge Course as developed by the Grand Lodge of New York and
other Jurisdictions, seems to have met with the greatest success. The Chairman of the Correspondence Committee of North Carolina, who we believe can speak, as an expert not only from the Masonic standpoint, but also
from that of the School Teacher, as that is his profession, presents the
matter in a sensible light.
First, the term "Masonic Education" is not an inspiring one. Masons
are not by it intrigued to attend meetings, but the opposite. If we can forget
that we have heard the term "Masonic Education", and start something
with a more attracting name, we shall do well. It may not be far distant
in goals and procedures, but in name it must be quite remote. Second, we
must remember that what we have in Masonry, while it is not perfect, yet
seems to have stood fairly well the test of time. Included in what we have
is a reasonable amount of rote memory. To some of us the rote memory
scheme of teaching seems very childish and elementary; but right here we
tried the other scheme which was expected to be much more successful and
isn't. SO WHAT? Well, the answer to that slang question is not an easy
one. One says that we are urging a return to the old traditional system.
Maybe we are-by inference. Maybe we are urging a combination of this
and some good reading. We rather think we are doing this last. Our ideal ·
would be to have available some exce1lent books and to get some of them
read-not the same selection for each and every candidate; but we should

283

let the candidate browse, as is the best ~aY. with all libraries, and then
with a little intelligent suggestion, take his pick. We have got too. many
Masons in these United States that don't know how to read; aI!d this condition is getting worse rather than better. Our folks are getting so lazy
that they refuse to read, but run off to the cinema for entertainment, where
they can sit back and look at the picture and learn the story of som~ great
book with effortless ease. The cinema is penetrating the schools-is. e~en
supplanting the schools. We Masons can well remembe~ the great ~ussion
which William Preston ascribed to Masonry, and use it as a medium of
"return to good books on Masonry."

The Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia has created what is
known as a "Fidelity Medal." It is awarded only to those in good standing
of Masonic Lodges in that Jurisdiction, and presented only to the member
in each Lodge having the longest period of Masonic good standing and to
a member in the entire Jurisdiction who has the longest such period'. He is
enti~led to we~r it only while a. m.e~ber in good standing, must sign a
receipt and written agreement stipulating that upon his death or the loss
of his Lodge membership the Medal shall be promptly returned to the
Grand Se~retary. The presentation is made in open Lodge. If two or more
?ret!tren m the same Lodge have the same period of membership, the medal
1s given only to the brother who is oldest in point of years.
Th~re may be, and of c~urse is, some objection to the awarding of any
dec~ration ~ased upon noth~n~ more than membership for only a specific

penod. It 1s a matter of op1ruon. As we are taught that it is the internal
and not the external qualifications, perhaps the unwritten law of England
and some Grand Lodges of its Dominion that it is not good form to wear
Masonic jewelry of any kind except in the Lodge Room or on strictly Masonic occasions, has some merit.
THE CITADEL OF OUR LIBERTIES: As imitation is the sincerest form of Battery, the Public Schools Week, as inaugurated by our
Grand Lodge, is being adopted in other Jurisdictions. Montana and Georgia
have followed it and other Jurisdictions are treating it sympathetically.
With all of the isms and organized destructive forces at work now among
the children and youth of our country an effective antidote is needed.
We believe the bulwark of our Nation is our Public Schools System.
As eternal vigilance is the price of liberty, Masonry can do nothing more
helpful than to keep that understanding before the citizens by a militant and
continuous campaign on behalf of the boys and girls. Our School Books
should be just as vital and symbolic to us as the Flag of our Country or
the Great Light of Masonry.
"TELLING THEM WHERE TO HEAD IN": In line with the
above here's an example of COURAGE. The pastoral letter of the archbishop and bishops of the metropolitan see of Cebu, in which the Catholics
of the Philippines are enjoined to send their children only to Catholic
schools by way of counteracting the Government's refusal to teach religion
in its schools, has drawn the following censure from President Manuel
L. Quezon:
"I am amazed at the boldness of the Metropolitan Archbishop and Suffragan Bishops of the Ecclesiastical Province of Cebu in taking up at an
episcopal conference a matter concerning the constitutional duties and prerogatives of the officials and branches of the government of the Commonwealth.
"I had so far ignored charges made to the effect that the hierarchy of
the Catholic Church in the Philippines had instigated and was behind the
movement for the enactment of the bill regarding religious instruction in
the Philippines. But the pastoral letter signed by the Metropolitan Archbishop of Cebu and the Suffragan Bishops of that ecclesiastical province
is an incontrovertible evidence that we did face at the last session of the
legislature, and we do face now, one of the most menacing evils that can
confront the government and people of the Philippines, namely, the interference of the Church in the affairs of the State. It seems that the Archbishop and Bishops who have written this pastoral letter are blind to the
lessons of history including our own during the Spanish regime. Being
myself a Catholic, I am no less interested in preserving the independence

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

285

of the Church from the State than I am in preserving the independence of
the Government from the Church.
"It should be unn,.cessary to remind the ecclesiastical authorities in
the Philippines that the separation of Church and State in this country is
a reality and not a mere theory, and that as far as our people are concerned, it is forever settled that this separation shall be maintained as one
of the cardinal tenets of our government. The ecclesiastical authorities
should realize, therefore, that any attempts on their part to interfere with
matters that are within the province of the government will not be tolerated.
If the said ecclesiastical authorities desire to have the government respect
their rights and afford them every kind of protection in the free exercise
of their religion, they must not only abide by the laws and lawful orders of
the government, but they must also acknowledge and respect the principle
of the separation of Church and State.
"On matters purely ecclesiastical, the Catholic bishops may speak for
the Filipino Catholics; but when it comes to expressing the will of the
Filipino people as a · political entity on any matter concerning legislation
or governmental measures, the Catholic bishops, some of whom are not
Filipinos, are assuming too much when they pretend to speak for our
people, as they do in the pastoral letter, when they say that the majority
of the Filipino people are demanding the enactment of the bill which I
have vetoed. The fact that the majority of the National Assembly voted for
the said bill does not necessarily prove that the majority of the people
are for it. It only proves that a majority of the members of the National
Assembly were for the bill.
"If I were inclined to interfere in the affairs of the Church, as the
Catholic bishops are attempting to do with the affairs of the State, I would
tell the Archbishop and the Bishops of the ecclesiastical province of Cebu
that the lack of Sunday schools and catequists to teach the Catholic religion
is mainly responsible for the d.e plorable ignorance of their own religion that
is found amongst the Catholic youth. Everybody knows that there are
many towns in the Philippines where parochial schools do not exist and
where there is not even one single Catholic priest. It seems that the high
authorities of the Catholic Church would blame the government for the
negligence or inability of the ecclesiastical authorities to perform their duty
to teach the doctrine of their faith. The words of our Lord Jesus Christ
cited in the pastoral letter 'Teach ye all nations. . . . teaching them to
observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you' are not addressed
to Kings or Presidents but to the Apostles and their successor&--the
bishops.
"A very unfair campaign has been launched against the government,
making it appear that we are not complying with the provisions of the
Constitution regarding optional teaching of religious instruction. The
truth is the opposite, as evidenced by the fact that while the enrollment
in classes in religious instruction during the academic year 1932-1933 was
only 29,996, this had increased to 187,089 in the academic year 1937-1938.
During this last school year in the 817 schools where religious instruction
was given, more than one-half of the children enrolled in said schools
received religious instruction.
"Moreover. if the desire is to have hours exclu~ively devoted to religious
instruction in the public schools, so that the regular school activities may
not interfere with said instruction, I am placing Saturdays and Sundays at
the disposal of all the ministers of all the religions existing in the Philippines. On Saturdays and Sundays, the public schools are not being used
for school purposes and, therefore, they may be used for religious instruction if it is so requested. What is prohibited in the existing legislation and

by the Constitution, and which, therefore, I may not allow, is that any

"It is my earnest conviction that the Filipino people will not heed the

In bringing this Introduction to a close we quote from an original
piece by the Chairman of Correspondence of Wyoming. He has served
in that capacity for a number of years, and, like him, we hope that this
effort will show we still retain our "pep."
"I am just a little older than I was a year ago,
Older only in the number of the years I have to show.
There may be added wrinkles and a few more aches and pains;
There may be dimmer vision and a slowing up of brains;
There may be tougher chewing on old vacated gums,
A little more of rheumatiz, with fingers much like thumbs;
There may be more lumbago to make me growl and swear,
A little more of baldness, a little less of hair.
But these are minor matters and if you will watch my step
You'll find I still am functioning and haven't lost my pep."
Yours sincerely and fraternally,
JESSE M. WHITED, Chairman.

The lack of attendance still continues to be a problem. Masonry today
must compete with the moving picture, the automobile, the radio and many
other forms of amusement .and profit to the individual. The problems of
today are different than those of a generation ago. Many no longer attend
Lodge or have a desire to witness degree work or the constant repetition
of principles or platitudes which they have heard many times.
A man's religion, his business, his politics or his morals are covered
by certain general rules, the non-observance of which brings their own
penalty. The thing in which Masonry, or any other organization may
specialize is activity in social contacts. Along this line are ever increasing
demands on the time of the members and what we do must be well worth
the time spent. The promotion of acquaintanceship and fellowship, either
in Lodge or the ante-room, is a field which if actively and intelligently cultivated will produce a bumper crop. The principles of A. A. A. need not
apply there.
Ohio (1937):
(G,.and M aste,.) : I earnestly recommend that you open your Lodge on time
and that you do not make the meetings too long. Strive for perfection in
the Ritual. Have good educational programs. Ask each member present to
bring another Mason with him to the next meeting. Get your Brethren in the
habit of coming. Let us show a little more interest in our members than we
have in the past. See to it that the new members are given every consideration. We devote our time to conferring the degrees upon a candidate and then, all
too often, immediately proceed to forget him. Let some older member see that
the newly raised candidate comes to Lodge at the very next meeting. Introduce
him to all whom he does not know. Make him feel that he is really a part
of this great Fraternity and that his continued presence at our meetings is
desirfd. There is much more to Masonry than the conferring of degrees and
• making members. Radiate good fellowship, friendliness, and brotherly love
at all of your meetings, make them interesting and worth while, and the attendance, I am sure, will take care of itself.

Western Australia (1937):
(Chai,.man Cor,.espondence Committee) : The need for greater and more
regular lodge attendance is being urged in many Jurisdictions. Quite an
elaborate list of "ways" is suggested in various quarters. Grand Mastersespecially in the United States-discuss it in their annual addresses. Grand
Lecturers seem to have what is called in those States "another think coming"
when they consider absentee brethren and "how they grow." s.uggestions
everywhere. Varieties of "Nights" almost as numerous : as the quills on the
fretful porcupine, radio meetings, lectures, debates, elocutionary :co~tests, question boxes and so forth and so on. But the regularity and contmmty of lodge
attendance' are as elusive as if they were the Scarlet Pimpernel. Dispensations
to wear regalia at church are supposed to encourage interest. A delegation of
white-hooded brethren of the notorious Ku Klux Klan to present a cheque
to the minister of the church to mark the Klan's appreciation of his worth as
a clergyman and a Mason did not seem to me, when I witnessed it, to be capable of stimulating lodge interest.
Regularity and continuity of lodge attendance constitu!es a pr.oblem as great
as the regularity and continuity of church members attendmg their. churches. So
far as the churches are concerned, it has always seemed to the writer that they
themselves were to some extent responsible owing to the almost superhuman
efforts to procure "full houses" by "stunt" services. Services for football clubs

(church decorated in football colors) and such-like supposed attractions;
sensational methods of inducing large congregations by picture shows, whistling
concerts, procuring distinguished persons to deliver addresses ; one was a
. divorce court judge who entertained the congregation for half an hour with
his court anecdotes. An interlude of singing in the church with the lights
switched off and the conductor wielding an electrically illuminated baton.
These I have witnessed in American churches, and while they did induce large
attendances on those occasions, the attendance exhibited a relapse when such
inducements were absent. Methods-although not similar, but with the same
object-in connection with Masonry may induce large gatherings when they are
used, but have no lasting effect. To endeavor to promote lodge attendance by
spectacular stunts does not convey a right conception of the Craft, but creates
an impression unfavorable to the objective sought.

AS THE TWIG IS BENT
Masonry should be a select organization, with more safeguards thtown
around it to produce these results.
Fundamentally the quality of new members depends upon the work of
the Investigating Committee. Too often this most important duty is
neglected, as witnessed by the Reports of Grievances and Appeals Committees. Again in a number of cases there is a tendency to resolve any
question of doubt in favor of the applicant, rather than for the benefit of
the individual Lodge or the Institution. .
Some Jurisdictions and Lodges have established a semi-official investigation Committee, composed of some of the Officers, Past Masters and
others qualified. They interview the petitioner and his sponsors, and pass
upon him before the petition is actually presented to the Lodge. Again a
waiting period between each degree of a reasonable length of time, with
opportunity for the candidate to become familiar with Masonry and his
obligations, could not help but improve not only the individual but the •
Lodge.
Opening the doors, as occurred during war time hysteria, or as again
may happen by reason of the dearth of candidates or the financial condition
of Lodges, that have been affected by "depression" and "recession," cannot
lead to any other result than "MASONIC INDIGESTION."
District of Columbia (1937):

(Chairman Co rrespondence Commitlee): A brother who held a certificate
from a lodge in Germany, but was unable to get in communication with his
lodge, was permitted to petition in one grand jurisdiction, but a similar case in
another grand jurisdiction was turned down. Both these grand jurisdictions
were in amity with the Masonic bodies in Germany prior to the present regime
in that country, but the two Grand Masters involved took different views of
the situation. The first Grand Master held that since the applicant's Grand
Lodge in Germany had been in amity with the Grand Lodge of his own state,
the German brother's petition for affiliation might be accepted. The second
Grand Master held that since the Grand Lodges of Germany had been interdicted
by the Government, no German lodge was recognizable in the United States.

Kentucky (1936):

. (~rand Master}: A real ~ason is dependa·ble. His simple word is as good as
his Bible oath and he does a little more than he promises. He is just as honest in
his own room in the dark as he is in public.. A real Mason does not want something for nothing, nor does he want pulls, tips, favors; he wants work and
honest wages. He treats his fellowmen as he would have them treat him.
A real Mason is loyal to his friends and guards their reputation as his own.
A real Mason honors a woman, any woman. He cannot hurt a woman physically
or morally. A real Mason minds his own business. He does not judge other
people or speak unkindly of them. He. always has excuses for others never
for himself. He is patient and charitable to them. To himself he is' strict.
A real Mason is glad to live and not afraid to die. He is a real man the finest
best, noblest thing on all the green earth, unless it is a real wom;n. If yo~
are a Mason such as this, my brethren, you will receive all the wages of
Masonry.

. . (Chairman Corresp~ndence Commit!ee) : The Grand Secretary (West Virginia) made an unofficial recommendation that contains a great deal of merit.

Says he, "I have thought for many years past that in addition to the moral and
intellectual qualifications of a candidate and the recognition of duty to a brother
in distress, there should be the further qualification of ability to pay his dues and
other legitimate calls upon him as a member of the Craft." Not only should an
applicant be able to pay his dues but if he has dependents they should be protected by life insurance. No man has the moral right to join the Fraternity and
knowingly throw on it the responsibility of looking after his dependents should
such an occasion arise.

We are not entirely in sympathy with Brother Rice's ( Washington) talk
but we do intone a fervent amen to the latter portion of his remarks. In this
he voices a protest over the haste with which we rush the candidate through
the three degrees·. Behold, says he, the milling throng stampedes through
King Solomon's Temple-not halting on the ground floor long enough to learn
the simple code of ethics and moral philosophy there taught. The guards at
the outer and inner doors are pushed aside and the untutored throng dashes into
the middle chamber after taking the winding stairs on a high lope and three
steps at a time. The furniture and decorations of the Middle Chamber, the net
product of ages of civilization are devoid of interest to the undisciplined band
of candidates. To them the books are "dry," the art incomprehensible and the
sciences and philosophies meaningless jumbles of words. Only he who spends
years in climbing those stairs of learning will find pleasure and profit in a sojourn in the Middle Chamber.
Our disappointed brothers finding nothing to interest them in the Middle
Chamber, next pass on and crash the gates of the Holy of Holies. In this

A number of years ago a noted California ex-Secretary of the Interior,
Franklin K. Lane, spoke in words which have become a classic regarding
the Flag. In a parallel column it is worth while to embody the words of
Lucia Ramsey Maxwell regarding the Constitution of the United States.
I AM THE CONSTITUTION of the United States of America, your
title deed to f~eedom. I am the Magna Charta of the rights of the Republic,
the rights of States, and the inalienable rights of the people. I was ordained
and established by the people, for the purpose of securing for you and your
posterity the blessings of unity, justice; tranquility, the common defense, the
general welfare, and the perpetuity of liberty.
I am a government of law,· a superior, paramount law, changeable only
by those by whom I was founded and enacted-the people. My principles are
fundamental, and were designed to be permanent.

MORE WAYS THAN ONE
While there are some who claim that all of Masonry is embodied in
the three degrees, we are "progressive" enough to believe that while they
are the basis of the Masonic System, they can be a stepping stone to further
enlightenment.
Our educational system has the Public Schools, followed by the
Univer.sity. If Masonry could be considered along the same lines there
would be a better understanding and a larger field for practical Masonry.
The co_-ordlnate bodies through their form of organization are privileged
to engage in a work denied the Blue Lodge by tradition and practice. In
some of the Jurisdictions the Grand Masters have established a working
agreement between the Grand Lodge and the Representatives of the socalled higher bodies, with a view of stabilization and an increase of Masonic
efficiency. This leads to a better understanding, greater results and less
cause for criticism.
While the so-called "playgrounds of Masonry" have at times given to
the general public a false impression an awakened Masonic opinion and
legislation are minimizing and eradicating the evils complained of.
In some Jurisdictions time limitations upon the individual have been
abolished and movements are on foot in others to repeal them.

ANCHORS TO WINDWARD
Twenty-five c_enturies ago Diogenes said, "Education is the basis of
the Greek State." This is as true of America today as it was of Greece
then. The commencement of our Public Schools system in the early
history of our country was in a large measure due to the active work of
Masons, such as George Washington, Benjamin Franklin and DeWitt
Clinton. This is a heritage handed down to us to maintain, protect and
guide, not only as Masons but as Citizens. We have no patience with the
argument that any program or activity of Masonry to improve and perpetuate the Public Schools is directly or indirectly engaging in politics.

"The news that the Masons of South Carolina will cooperate with the
civil authorities for increased regular school attendance is revelatory of. how
social work is developing in a changing world. From a movement dominated
largely by motives, it has developed into a movement in which motives compete
for dominance with intellectual conviction.

driving power is a conception of social welfare in all its phases. Its conception
is not only. of the material lack of nourishment and shelter, but of mental and
cultural lacks. As meaningful, too, is the extension oi the agencies, the organizations and activities through which the supplying of such lacks has spread.

unable to attend without the assistance which Masonic Lodges might give
· through the attendance teachers and other school authorities.

A DISTINCTION AND A DIFFERENCE
The home of the Mother Grand Lodge is remarkable in more ways than
one, not only from its magnificence but also the method of financing. It
was built by voluntary contributions which in itself is a record. ,
The establishment and operation of its Institutions for Charity also
operate along the same line. When we read their history and record we
are impressed by the fact that our English brethren are like their nation,
"safe, sane and conservative."

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Charity is an important feature
of the English Masonic fraternity.
The Royal Masonic Institution for Girls: This is the oldest of the charitable institutions, established in 1788, and having throughout many years the
King and Queen as its Royal Patron and Patroness. The King is now listed as
Royal Patron. President of the Institution is the Grand Master, the Duke of
Connaught. It is maintained for the purpose of clothing and educating the
daughters of Freemasons. Girls are admitted into the junior school at Weybridge at the age of seven, and at 10 or 11 are admitted to the senior school at
Rickmansworth where they remain until 16 or 17 years of age, when, if showing
promise, they are assisted to further their education. Fathers must have been
members of lodges under the English Constitution for seven years, except in
case of death. The Anniversary Festival is held in May of each year and the
brethren are very generous in their support of this institution.
The Royal Masonic Institution for Boys was incorporated by Royal Charter;
it was established in 1798. The King is also Patron of this institution. President of the Board, the same as that of the Girls' Institution, is the Duke of
Connaught, Grand Master. Boys of all religious faith, are accepted. From 6
to 8 they are maintained as near tlie residence of their parents as possible; at
the latter age they are entered in the school at Bushey where they remain until
16, when, if they show promise, they are given opportunity for higher education.
The Annual Festival is in June of each year.
The Royal Masonic Benevolent Institution is for aged members of the
fraternity, their wives or widows. Again the King is Royal Patron. The fund
was founded in 1842; the Grand Master is President. The qualifications for admission to the fund are particularly interesting. An applicant must be at least
60 years of age, and a subscribing member of a lodge under the English Constitution for at least twenty years preceding the filing of his petition. During
this time he must have paid dues for fifteen of these years. His income must
not exceed $275.00 per annum from all sources. The annuity is now $340.00
per annum to a married brother; $320.00 to an unmarried brother and $280.00
to a widow or spinster daughter of a deceased annuitant. No home is maintained for the aged. An Annual Festival is held in February of each year .
The Royal Masonic H ospitaf is one of the finest and best equipped hospitals
in England. The Grand Master is President of the institution which is conducted on nursing home lines and is available for members of the craft, their
wives and children. It is intended priwarily for patients who are unable t,
afford nursing home or hospital charges. The minimum charge is about $15 a
week, with a small payment, according to ability, towards surgical charges.
The hospital was opened July 12, 1933, by His Majesty King George V. It
provides accommodation foi: 200 beds, including wards for small children.

{Chairman Correspondence Committee): Freemasonry has not been unaware of the evil effects of this vice. A manuscript in the ' archives of the

District of Columbia (1937):

{Chairman Correspondence Committee): Grand Master Anderson (Canada) had some troubles about lotteries, but it seems to this writer that if a
Mason wants to bet on a horse race he has the same right to do so that anybody else has. There seems to be a lot of confusion about lotteries run by
Masons for Masonic purposes and just ordinary lotteries. But in the long run
human nature will take its course, even if it does not produce a flock of gondolas.
The lottery racket invaded (Alberta) from another grand jurisdiction, but
was promptly suppressed. He said: "Canadian and American authorities cause
these tickets to be seized whenever discovered. Yet members of Parliament have
been known to rise in their seats in the House of Commons with lottery tickets
in their pockets, and Masons far and near are regular purchasers. So long as
men buy, there will be men to sell."
It seems to this writer that we are not so much concerned with gambling
as we are concerned with whether or not it is done under Masonic auspices. So
long as human nature dominates man's activities we may reasonably presume
that a natural born gambler, Mason or profane, will continue to follow his bent.
But let us not give him the chance to gamble under Masonic auspices.
New York (1937):
(Grand Master): This edict which the Grand Master felt constrained to
issue has received a sympathetic response, and seems to have been scrupulously
observed. Let it be understood that it was not in the heart of the Grand Master
to take any legitimate joy out of the lives of Masons. Nor was it his intention
to meddle in any respect with legitimate pleasures. The purpose of the edict
was to remind the Craft that Freemasonry is a law-abiding institution, and
that what is forbidden by law must not be indulged in by Freemasons.
It would have been a sorry thing if a Masonic Lodge had been raided on
the pretext that at the time it was engaged in an unlawful gambling or lottery
enterprise. The tragedy of such an occurrence has victimized other organizations. It was the determination of the Grand Master that no such experience
should be shared by the Masonic Fraternity if it were in his power to prevent
it. We may rejoice that we have escaped the shame of contact with the law
enforcing authorities.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Here is another Grand Master
(Connecticut) who has seen trouble on account of the raffle-and-lottery craze,
now running wild- in this country.
I recommend that Chapter XLVI, Section 17, of our Grand Lodge Rules
and Regulations be amended by adding the words: "and the Grand Master shall ·
suspend for unmasonic conduct all persons who shall promote, or assist in the
promotion of, such lotteries, raffling or games of chance for the purpose of
raising money for Masonic purposes or for any of the organizations known
to be affiliated with Masonry."
This is the best thing we have seen. The trouble has been that promoters
of these things have reasoned that after the Grand Master has gotten through
telling them they must stop them, he has not the authority to kick them out
of Masonry as a punishment, but must depend on action by some lodge having
personal jurisdiction over an offender; and the said offender has got as good
a chance before the lodge as he would have before a dumb jury with a smart
jury lawyer at his side. So there has been a feeling of justified security in
the hearts of these lottery and raffle promoters, which he proposes to dispel.

THE OLD, OLD STORY
Grand Lodge Sessions continue generally to be purely routine matters,
perhaps monotonous to the brethren and the Reviewer. There have been a
few flare-ups here and there, but have been handled along Masonic lines,
without serious result to the Jurisdictions wherein they occur. The administration of the usual Grand Lodge functions by a Board of General Purposes, such as practiced in England, Ireland, Scotland and a number of
Canadian and'Australian Jurisdictions eliminates a large part of this, including the high cost of printing Proceedings, with rosters, detailed financial
statements, auditor's reports, etc. In these Jurisdictions the reports are
therefore brief, but in the final analysis the results are there.

THEIR PLACE IN LIFE AND LEGEND
The messages, addresses, visitations, activities and "what have you"
that pertain to the office of Grand Master have changed very little with

307

the passing year. A large proportion of their time is evidently devoted to
answering questions, wise and otherwise, that could easily be solved by
reference to the printed law or decision of the Jurisdiction.
Here and there was found a Grand Master who refused to issue dispensations, rendered no decisions, made his annual message a concise and
business-like one, without embodying the usual Masonic platitudes and
omits all of his official correspondence during the year, statistics, visitations,
etc. They, however, are generally an exception and are an oasis in a vast
desert of nothing but words.
Georgia (1937):
(Committee on Jurisprudmce): The Grand Master ruled that he did not
have the authority to make a Mason at sight. There is much confusion as to
what is meant by making a Mason at sight. According to some authorities
this merely means issuing a dispensation for six additional Masons to assemble
as a Lodge U. D., with the Grand Master to confer a degree. Others, however, underst;md this to mean that the Grand Master may confer all three
degrees upon a candidate at one session, even though such candidate has been
rejected by a subordinate Lodge.
Mackey, it is true, gives as one of. the landmarks that the Grand Master
can make a Mason at sight. H is landmarks were published in a private manual
by the late John W. Akin, but this manual was never adopted by this Grand
Lodge, which definitely ruled that this manual was not the Masonic law of
this State.
Other authorities differ with Mackey and as a result some of the jurisdictions of the United States declare that the Grand Master has the right
and others deny it. One of our regulations more ancient than Mackey is that
no Mason can be made in a regular Lodge without due notice and previous
inquiry. Our by-laws expressly provide that the three degrees cannot be conferred at one session, and Mackey, in his "Jurisprudence of Freemasonry," page
Ill, states as an ancient custom of the body that time shall elapse between
conferring of the degrees that proficiency may be attained. We have held that
the Grand Master cannot grant a dispensation violating this by-law.
No two writers en Masonry agree as to what are the ancient landmarks
of the Craft and your Chairman of this committee is reminded of a query made
of an old darky on the coast some years ago as to whether he believed in signs ·
he answered: "Boss, I sho' does, and a sign will never fool you, but wheneve;
you sees a sign, if you look close, you'll gen'ly see another sign what nullifies
that 'first sign."
Louisana (1936):
(Grand Master): At the beginning of my term of office, I made up my
mind that I would try to have some money left in the Grand Master's account
for the purpose of donating it to the Home at Alexandria. I felt that its use
in the purchase of food and clothes for our nearly one hundred children was
much more important than for me to pack a full dress suit and ornamented
aoron around Louisiana and other states and go through the formal ceremonies
of reception and a lot of talk that would have been forgotten five minutes after
I left. I do not mean to say that a Grand Master should not make visits and
deliver talks. I believe that I covered more than three-fourths of the territory
of the State of Louisiana by the simple expediency of attempting to arrange
to have as many nearby lodges represented through their officers and some
members as was possible every time I visited a lodge.

North Carolina (1938):
(Chairman Correspo11de1ice Committee) : Then there is one innovation in
the book which we like. It is the Inaugural Address by Grand Master D. Burns
Douglass (Indiana) incoming. It is not one of these pop-up things but a real
address of some seven pages. We have often wondered why this was 1;1ot the
"vogue" among Masonic presiding officers. Well, when one comes to think
about it, it is a perfectly natural thing. No Grand Master's election is a surprise to him unless in Kansas or Iowa. When he is elected, he is almost always
called upon for some remark of acceptance. It would be a fine thing for him
to have a heart-to-heart talk with his members at the outset of his term, so
that they may know what he has in mind and he may enlist their assistance.
The fact is, that if a Grand Master has any recommendations to make that are
of any importance, he ought to make these and get their adoption as he begins
his "year"; for of all persons, he is the one who will do the best job of putting
into execution what he thinks is worth while and what happens to be new.

their own cars at the rate of 3c a mile. This certainly does not allow for extras
but it will practically cover actual expenses.
Western Australia (1937):
(Chairman CorreJpondeiice Committee): A . matter brought before Grand
Lodge of Nebraska might, perhaps, suggest the title "How to Have a New Car
with a New Grand Master." An opinion was expressed that it was quite unfair to expect a Grand Master to drive his own car because he was not only
giving his time without remuneration, but as he would be using his car, his
wife and family were deprived of it. Also, a car thus used had a tendency to
contract premature senile decay, and its value when traded in could only be
represented by the mathematical sign for the unknown. An alternative to
using. the Grand Master's own particular car was to purchase a low-priced
one-the names were given, but the reviewer is unwilling to advertise thembut it was suggested that in the low priced 'car, the Grand Master and Grand
Officers could travel to the Masonic here, there, and everywhere on Masonic
business more cheaply than by public transportation services, and when it became necessary to please a new Grand Master with a new car, the twelvemonths-old one would not have undergone such an amount of premature decadence as to render it unfit to be traded in at a better value. This remarkably
joyful plan of supplementing joy in a new Grand Master with joy in a new
car went before the Finance Committee, which wrestled with it with · almost
agonizing care, deciding to defer the matter for a twelve-month in experimenting with the amount of. joy to be derived from hiring a car from a garage ·
on a milage basis, for the use of the Grand Master and his Grand Officers.

In some Grand Lodge Proceedings the monotony is broken by finding
here and there a spark of humor, or perhaps a poetic gem. Some are well
worth passing along, so for that reason we embody a few that are not perhaps of too ancient a vintage.
It seemed theer was a discussion between St. Pe~er and St. Nick because
their two crowds were intermingling, and they decided to put a fence between
their domains, and St. Nick says, "You have all the carpenters so you build
the fence and I will pay my half of it." They built the fence and after it was
completed St. Nick met St. Peter and St. Peter said: "I am ready for my
half of the money," and he said, "I have decided not to pay anything." St. Peter
said, "If you don't I'll sue you." He said, "Just see how far you will get;
I have got all the attorneys."
