FROM STORES OF MEMORY
On a par with the question of "How old is Ann?" or "Who Hit Billy
Patterson" and other stock quotations of bygone days, Masonry still continues to ask "What is a Landmark?" There are as many different answers
as there are Jurisdictions with various sorts of legislation upon the subject.
It does, however, furnish arguments which while they might not be vital.

311

South Australia (1937) :
(Grand L ecturer) : Taking for his text Proverbs 22-28, which read :"Remove not the ancient landmark which thy fathers have set," V . W. Bro.
Kiek said that in ancient times, and even at present in Palestine and other
Oriental lands, it was customary to mark with a pillar or a heap of stones the
boundary of a field or farm.
In an agricultural community, t he maintenance of such landmarks was
naturally of great importance. Unscrupulous persons sometimes removed these
landmarks with a view of extending their own property at the expense of an
ignorant or helpless neighbor. Public opinion, however, regarded such ·conduct
as an offense against religion as well as an offense against social morality.
In the Deuteronomic Code, a solemn curse was pronounced on the man
who removed his neighbor's landmark (vide Deuteronomy 19-13 and 27-17).
The practice was again condemned in the Book of Proverbs (22-28 and 23-10).
The Book of Job had a scathing denunciation of this form of wickedness (24-2).
Even among the heathen, the ancient landmarks were regarded as under
the protection of Heaven. The Greeks had a god named Leus Horios, who
watched the ancient landmarks, and avenged their violation. The Romans also
had a god named Terminus, whose functions were similar.
In modern usage, the term, landmark, had come to mean a custom or
moral principle handed down from the past and regarded as settled and established. Such landmarks were found in the realm of jurisprudence.
The doctrine that an alleged offender was entitled to trial by his peers
was a landmark of British law, which dated back to the time of Magna Charta.
The doctrine, that no person should be deprived of his liberty without legal
warrant, dated back to the Petition of Right and the Habeas Corpus Act in
the 17th Century. The doctrine, that a slave setting foot on British soil automatically became free, dated from Lord Mansfield's decision in Somerset's
case, in 1774. In fact, our whole legal system was intensified to define and defend the ancient landmarks established by venerable usage. That was why the
poet spoke of "freedom broadening slowly down from precedent to precedent.''
Even more important were the landmarks which defined the boundaries of
good and evil in the realm of morality. The Ten Commandments and the Golden
Rule were obvious examples. Those landmarks, and many others were clearly
defined in the Volume of the Sacred Law. Right-minded people had always
recognized the sacredness of those landmarks. Assuredly, they could be justified on grounds of reason and social expediency, but for the most part we did
not argue about them. They were taken for granted. They belonged to a realm
of what Kant called "the moral imperative.'' Kant regarded such ancient landmarks as belonging to the fundamental order of the universe ; they sprang from
the will of God Himself. No doubt there was a sense in which much of their
morality might be described as "customary", but that was not to deny its sacredness or undermine its authority. It was "customary" in the sense that it represented the accumulated experience of the race and the verdict of. good men of
every age.
,
The maintenance of the ancient landmarks was necessary unless life was
to become disrupted and chaotic. Any society which cut itself off from history
was doomed to insta,bility. True progress presupposed true conservatism. The
Ancient Landmarks of Freemasonry, so far as he (V.".W.".Bro. Kiek) was
aware, were not written down. Rather did they belong to the tradition of the
Craft. They assured its continuity, and the preservation of its organic character.

313

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

One could mention a few of them-belief in the G.".A.'.O.".T.'.U.'., the exclu·sion o-f women, the prohibition of political and sectarian controversy, the ethical
code of Brother Love, Relief and Truth. Freemasonry did not debate these
things; it assumed them. Without them the Craft would cease to be.
Every Freemason, from the humblest Entered Apprentice to the Gr.and
Master, was pledged to the maintenance of the ancient landmarks. But the
obligation was particularly stringent on those who were called to be rulers in
the Craft. Grand Lodge existed, among other things, for the purpose of guarding private lodges against any unintentional deviations. In so doing it was, of
course, essential to distinguish between what were really "ancient landmarks"
and what were merely non-essential customs and traditions, for they must never
forget that Freemasonry was a progressive science, and the details of their
practice must be open to modification to meet new situations and new needs.
It was for Grand Lodge to define how far they might go in that direction.
Nor should they abandon the ancient idea of God as the ultimate Guardian
of the ancient landmarks. He had set for them the boundaries of good and evil
and assuredly punished any transgression thereof. Men and nations who departed from the ancient landmarks did so at their own peril. History was full
of instances. of the Divine judgment on corrupt men and corrupt societies.
So also was it full of instances of the judgment which had overtaken those
who had recklessly sought to overthrow the principles of piety and morality,
who had subverted by violence the foundations of social order. The ancient
landmarks were the protection of the poor against exploiters and oppresors.
The same was true in these modern days. Many seemed to be arguing that
might was right and that any restraints on their imperious lusts may be scorned
and disregarded. Religion and law, morality and patriotism, were scoffed at as
mere archaic survivals. To all must be proclaimed the Divine veto, "Remove
not the ancient landmark which thy fathers have set."

THERE OUGHT TO BE A LAW
Someone aptly said that the present is "The Reign of Legal Terror."
When it comes to legislation Masonry is not immune. The United States
Government issues a publication known as the _FEDERAL REGISTER,
which is distributed daily Tuesday through Saturday. It contains the official texts of all current Presidential proclamations, Executive orders, and
all other 'orders, regulations, certificates, codes, licenses, notices, or similar
documents having general applicability and legal effect, issued or prescribed by the President of the United States, Executive Departments and
other Agencies of the Executive Branch of the Government.
The Federal Register Act provides that no such document becomes
valid as against persons without actual notice thereof until filed with the
Federal Regiitter Division and made available for public inspection. The
contents of the Federal Register are required by law to be judicially noticed and may be cited by volume and page number. The hour and date of
filing appear with each published document.
The fotaf documents published for the·past two years and four months
total 9,256. With this amount of law already in existence, and daily being
added to, the rule that "Ignorance of the Law is no excuse" would seem to
be obsolete.'
In addition to the abov~· we find the following in a legal publication: ·
"Moses was prel!ented_with only Ten Commandments and Woodrow Wilson delivered 14 points to the Versailles Peace Conference, but Legislatures
of 43 American States in· regular sessions last year enacted 18,483 new laws.
The record is a' tribute to the ingenuity of the Senators and Representatives

ON THE WATER WAGON
The remarks under gambling are also applicable to the liquor situation
from the Masonic standpoint. Some of the legislation, as well as its interpretation or decision by Grand Masters produces strange and startling

314

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

results. A Reviewer stated sometime ago, "Nobody has got down to it
yet, but if it keeps up we may soon find that to watch a brewery truck
unload will be a Masonic offense."
In Jurisdictions where the matter is left entirely to the judgment of
the individual Lodge, there is of course no extended treatment of the
question. Other Jurisdictions find themselves in the same predicament
by having repealed their Regulations on the subject during the prohibition
era and up -to the present have failed to reenact the same. This vexing
matter will undoubtedly continue to demand consideration in some form or
other until far into the future.
Colorado (1936):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): It seems to be universal that the
use of liquors, even light beer, at lodge communications is prohibited, and the
occupation of a portion of lodge buildings even by druggists who dispense
liquors is forbidden.
In many cases, as in Colorado, the question both of initiation and of retention of membership of those engaged in any way in the liquor trade is left
largely to the good judgment of the members of subordinate lodges. A twothirds majority can discipline any member, and one only can prevent any one
from being initiated. We really, as in cases of crime and other offenses against
common decency, need no specific legislation upon the question. Any member
who so conducts his business as to bring discredit upon the Craft is and always
has been subject to charges of unmasonic conduct, whether that business is the
sale of liquor, the handling of securities, or even the practice of law.
We don't want the low-down type of saloon keeper wearing our emblem
behind his bar, but we are loath to part with one of our members who may
be only a small stockholder in one of the large national drug companies. Let
him who wishes to deal with the question by definite legislation draw the line.
Your Chairman can't.
Illinois (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Comm~ttee): Whenever the liquor question or
the traffic in intoxicating liquor has been discussed, the undeniable soundness of·
the views expressed by Most Worshipful Brother Grover C. Niemeyer of our
own grand lodge, is admitted. From a Masonic standpoint this traffic involves
more than a mere legal question. A question of good morals and good citizei,.
ship is also involved. It is not enough that the vendor obeys the Federal, State
and Municipal laws, sufficiently at least to avoid criminal prosecution; the business itself is degrading, debasing, debauching and demoralizing both to the one
who for profit sells the stuff, and to the unfortunate victim who buys and drinks
it. It has been a long time since running a saloon in this country has been classed
among such legitimate businesses as selling dry goods, hardware, groceries or
other such merchandise. The business is hedged about by all sorts of restricting laws in the hope, not of destroying its evil influence, but in the hope so far
as possible of minimizing the injurious results. It is a very proper subject for
police control.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A careful reading of these may

were the Mason members of the Legislature in enacting this law? How about

sell, many buy, and all profit. If the arguments of this Grand Master are .carried to a logical conclusion, Iowa and North Carolina Masons are in a sad
situation.

North Carolina (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): New Mexico has got the simplest
situation with respect to liquor legislation, that we have found in any Grand
Lodge. We find that years ago there were on the books some laws about liquor,
but the Amendment to the United States Constitution was passed prohibiting
its sale and so forth, and later in the new Constitution of the Grand Lodge of
New Mexico the subject was omitted entirely and there is no law about it in
the books of this Grand Lodge at all. Perhaps this is the only American Grand
Lodge whose law is silent about liquor. Well, the Grand Master gets the matter
before the Committee on Jurisprudence, with the result that that committee
declares that it "has always been the inherent right of the constituent lodge to
pass on the moral standards of its members and the qualifications of its petitioners and we, therefore, recommend that this inherent right remain with the
lodges; and there it remains. What fault can you find with that philosophy.''
Ohio (1937):
(Grand Master): On April 26, 1937, my attention was called to the fact
that beer was being used in some of the Masonic Temples of this State by certain
Lodges, Chapters, Commanderies, ·and by organizations which base their membership upon Symbolic Masonry. I learned upon reliable authority that noisy,

316

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

hilarious, and boisterous revelry was at times indulged in to such an extent that
the disturbance could be heard on the street; that Masons occasionally went
home from our Temples in an intoxicated condition, and that there were, at
that time, 3,600 bottles of beer stored in the basement of one of our Masonic
Temples ready to be used at a ceremonial the following Saturday night. The
fact that some of the beer used may have been what is commonly known as 3.2
per c~nt beer seemed to me to be no excuse for this intolerable condition.
Tke important fact is that 3.2 beer is intoxicating to some persons and it is
immaterial that some courts hold that it is not. Furthermore, if 3.2 per cent
beer is permitted to be used in our Temples at all, then it is an easy matter to
substitute beer of higher alcoholic content. We do not serve beer in our
churches, and I do not think that beer of any alcoholic content whatsoever has
any place in a Masonic Temple. It is difficult to avoid excess when the .crowd
is drinking and the beverages are free, and such conditions are conducive to that
intemperance which impairs the faculties and debases the dignity of our profession.
·
Our Fraternity is different in many respects from all others and we must
continue zealously to guard the high standing and reputation of the Order. To
preserve unsullied that reputation ought to be our constant care. Our actions
as individuals, should be-and as Masons, must be, above reproach. ·Therein lies
the real strength of the Masonic Fraternity and accounts for the fact that
it has ~ontinued to survive and to prosper throughout the vicissitudes of time.
Believing that these abuses should no longer be tolerated in Masonic
Temples, I made the following decisions on April 28, 1937, and sent them to
·
each of the Lodges :
1. No spirituous, malt, vinous or fermented liquors or beverages having
an alcoholic content of more than one-half of one per cent by weight can be
used for beverage purposes (except ceremonial) in any Masonic Lodge room,
anteroom, banqueting room, or adjacent room in such Masonic Temple within
this Grand Jurisdiction. This also applies to gatherings in Masonic Temples of
organizations whose membership is predicated on Blue Lodge Masonry.
2. No Lodge or Masonic Temple Company may rent or lease any portion
of its building where the same is to be used for selling or dealing in intoxi-·
eating liq1mrs for beverage purposes.
3. It shall neither be deemed a violation of Section 58 of the Code nor a
Masonic offense to sell 3.2 per cent beer, or any other beverage that has been
legally determined to be non-intoxicating, but no such beverage can either be
sold or drunk in or about a Mas9nic Temple in this State.
4. Ohio Masons are at all times subject to Masonic discipline for unmasonic conduct in this State due to the excessive use of intoxicating liquor
wherever obtained or used.

(Grand Master): During the year, I have been asked repeatedly if men engaged in various branches of the liquor business were eiigible for membership
in the Masonic Fraternity. To this, I have replied that the only prohibition in
our Code concerning liquor is against those who operate or tend bar in a
liquor saloon, and then call attention to the provision of the Code defining a
liquor saloon as "a place where the main business conducted is the sale of
intoxicating liqµors to l:ie consumed or drunk on the premises where sold."
The difficulty in inteq1retating this law is to define or determine what is
meant by "main business." There should be no difficulty with respect to new
material. Any man who is working in or operating a place conecrning which
there is any question should not be admitted into the Fraternity. Masonry
cannot afford to play along the border line, and every doubt should be resolved
in favor of the Fraternity.
With those, however, who are in the Fraternity and selling liquor, a different situation exists. If charges are preferred, it is difficult to secure evidence. It is difficult for trial commissions to determine just what is meant by
"main business" or whether or not the main business of the member is the sale of
intoxicating liquor. Under these conditions, trial commissions do not feel justified in convicting members, and members and lodges are reluctant to file
chargts.
The result is there are Masons operating or working in places within the
state which, if not saloons within the strict interpretation of the law, at least
their business is of no credit to Masonry and causes Masonry to be criticized
and held up to ridicule and scorn.
This is a problem which should have some intensive study.

Washington (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): On the liquor question some
Grand Lodges have dodged the question and have endeavored to temper its laws
with prevailing tendencies. We admire the position taken by the Grand Lodge
of Michigan in basing its legislation on the morality of the question rather than
on the legality of it. Freemasonry has always frowned on liquor in any form,
and should all of our Grand Lodges consistently base their actions on such
traditional beliefs much discussion and oratory would be suppressed.

they meant the United States, as no other place counted. When American
brethren speak of Freemasonry do they only mean the United States, and that
Freemasonry elsewhere does not count? It is perfectly true that all the United
States have gone dry since Prohibition, but prior to that, there were some
Jurisdictions in the Repubilc that were not in that class. Moreover, even at the
present time one reads of Grand Masters who are members of the Ancient

Arabic Order, Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, a body predicating its membership

V.S.L. does. There are non-alcoholic Masonic lodges in Australia-the writer,

never dream of attributing to Freemasonry, as a whole, the capacity to frown

IT'S FINE WHEN YOU KNOW THE RULES
While the benefits and privileges as well as the responsibilities of a
Mason are embodied in the charges of the Three Degrees, they have been
summaried in the following concise manner, which is effective by reason
of its brevity:
1. FAITH IN GOD. .
"On him, this comer-stone we build
On him, this edifice erect
And still, until this work's fulfilled
May he the workman's ways direct."
2. FAITH IN OUR COUNTRY.
"Love thou thy land, with love far-brought
From out the storied past, and used
Within the present, but transfused
Thru future time by power of thought."
3. FAITH IN OUR NEIGHBOR.
"I see from my house by the side of the road
By the side of the highway .of life,
The men who press with the ardor of hope
The men who are faint with the strife.
'But I turn not away from their smiles nor their tears,
Both parts of an Infinite Plan.
Let me live in a house by the side of the road
And be a friend to Man."
4. FAITH IN OURSELVES.
"We are all blind until we see
That in the human plan
Nothing is worth the making if
It does not make the Man.
Why build these cities glorious
If Man unbuilded goes?
In vain we build the world unless
The Builder also grows."

District of Columbia (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Speaking of discussions in lodges
by way of making the communications interesting when there was no degree
work, the New York Grand Master said:
"In our Lodge Room there can be no verdict. As said, Masonry does not
take mass action. It invites its members to educate themselves on every subject
which will help them to be loyal, intelligent citizens, but they must act as
individuals solely-never as a Masonic Group."
This is sound Masonic Doctrine, and in these present days, when there
seems to be a disposition on the part of some to try to make Masonry as such
take a part in public affairs, it is particularly timely.
Minnesota (1936):
(Grand Lodge): The Grand Orator delivered a fine address, while rather
lengthy, still very much worth while. His seven major points in our opinion
are the sum total of the present world condition. We take pleasure in quoting
them:
1. Policies without principles, the win at any price idea.
2. Wealth without work, something we are all looking for.
3. Pleasure without conscience, I am not my brother's keeper.
4. Knowledge without character, accomplished crooks.
5. Business without morality, every man for himself.
6. Science without humanity, exemplified in modern instruments of war.
7. Worship without sacrifice, or mere lip service.

of the supposed freedom-loving people. Let us make uniformly active warfare

and become dyspeptics. Let us teach our members, "where to head-in" as citizens,
real Americans and Masons, and tell them the truth of the insidious assaults
which are gradually going on and on to destroy our liberties. Then will
Masonry become a real vital force and her three million votaries in our land
will truly worship at her shrine, and Americans will pay great honor to our
accomplishments.

THE MESSAGE OF THE FIGURES
The summary from the pen of Bro. J. Warren Allen, Chairman of the
Correspondence Committee of North Carolina, is the . opinion of an Expert.
For a number of years he has compiled and published Masonic statistics
that are the admiration of the Masonic world.
If in the coming decade we could be assured of Quality in our members
we might look with little regret on the loss in Quantity. So many factors,
not only from a fraternal standpoint but in every other walk of life, will
influence the result that one guess is as good as another as to what will
happen. Perhaps we can only "Watch and Pray."
North Carolina (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): _We have be.en writing Masonic .
Reviews since 1923, and have been <;ompiling statistics for just about the same
period. Those fifteen years have seen many changes. In 1923, we were reporting
net gains in membership running up into almost unbelievable figures. Suspensions
for nonpayment of dues were unknown or negligible. The keywo_rd was "Masonic Education"-everybody believed that every Mason needed, and wanted
to be educated Masonically. Then came a day of reckoning. Masonic educational programs went up in thin smoke. Huge number of ·raisings and vast net
gains dwindled. Here and there a net. loss in membership reared its head, and
ere long all of the Grand Lodges were reporting net losses. Then ten years of
this sort of change has come over .us, and heri;with we show in a special tabulation, the effect of these ten years. Note it. In eleven years, our membership
in the United States has dropped from 3,233,757 to 2,587,212. Simple arithmetic
tells us that the difference is 646,540 Master Masons fewer today than eleven
years ago. But this has come about while the lodges were still at work. Six
hundred sixty-one thousand men have been raised to the sublime degree of
Master Mason in that time, and in spite of this work, still we look those six
hundred forty-six thousand of Masons "gone with the wind" in the face. What
is the reason? The answer is easy to see. Nine hundred twenty-six thousand_
Master Masons have been suspended, dropped, excluded, erased, or what have
you, in those ten years-not to mention four hundred thi'rty-three thousand
who passed into the Great Beyond. These figures do not look extremely roseate.
To have worked diligently for eleven years and while doing so, to have seen
the ·results of one's labors, and more, slip through one's fingers, is not at all
heartening-and that is what we have seen going on during the decade ; slipping
back from three and a quarter million to a bare few over two and a half
million. This brings our membership back to where it was in the year 1920.
So we learn our lesson of over-expansion in the days following the World War.
We sowed the wind and we reaped the whirlwind.
Or, we might look at the whole picture from another way.' Our loss over
the period of eleven years is less than twenty per cent. Compared with the
losses ·in the organizations whose membership is based on Masonry, this is
small. It is smaller than the losses have been in any of the dependent organizations. The Shriners have lost nearly forty per cent of their membership of
576,539 of 1928, but they are now vigorous and are probably in better condition
in some ways than they were ten years ago. Their minimum dues of twelve
dollars per year made their loss rate very high. The Grotto started out with
144,835 members and at the end of that decade had lost more than half of
these. They had seen a mushroom-like growth, which collapsed the more com·
pletely because it was such.
Among the older organizations, all lost in about equally great percentage.
The Royal Arch Masons dropped forty per cent of their membership, about
the same as the losses of the Templars; the Royal and Select Masters lost

321

nearly forty-three per cent, and the Seottish Rite lost nearly twenty-six per
cent. Of all of the larger organizations related to Mason,ry, the Eastern Star
came out best; in fact, this Order fared even better than the lodges themselves;
for, beginning the decade with 1,821,792, they lost only 222,869, or twelve and
a quarter per cent, of their membership. ·

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Perhaps some day or other, there

the Grand Master's arms." And as if this was not enough for fame, it was
· said to have once belonged to Oliver Cromwell, and it appears there was some
ground for accepting the statement. In 1838 it escaped with its life from a fire
but was so mutilated that the hilt, the scabbard, and a small portion of the point
were missing. A cutler restored the blade, and a new hilt and scabbard were
supplied. But it has again disappeared, and search is now being made for the
"Lost Sword," and the entire Craft of South Carolina is expected to take part
in ascertaining the whereabouts of the wandering weapon.

THE STATUS OF THE NEGRO
In the early history of Masonry in the Colonies, some English Military
Lodges admitted Negroes. In the development of the Craft there sprung
from it what is now generaly known as the Prince Hall Grand Lodge,
composed exclusively of Negroes. While there is a question as to their
legitimacy, they are generally termed "irregular" rather than "clandestine."
They maintain a separate organization, along the same forms as ours. The
Grand Lodge of England by reason of its far flung Dominions does not
recognize the color line; consequently Negroes belonging to Lodges of
that Jurisdiction are, regular.
In the United States the only regular Lodge composed exclusively
of Negroes is under the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of New Jersey.
Its history, is therefore both interesting and authentic.
New Jersey (1937):
The Masonic Fraternity in New Jersey has been fortunate in l'he peace and
harmony that has, as a rule, prevailed within its jurisdiction.
There was, however, one matter· that for a time threatened that peace and
harmony, not only within the Grand Lodge and its members, but also the fraternal relations existing between it and other Grand Lodges.
That was the existence of a lodge in this State that permitted colored
persons to become members of it.
It has often been asked how it is that the Grand Lodge of New Jersey has
~nder its jurisdiction a regular and duly constituted lodge the membership of
which consists entirely of men of the negro race.
This Grand Lodge never authorized the establishment of a lodge for colored
men and two petitions for such a warrant were negatived by it; nevertheless, it
is q~ite true that New Jersey is the only Gra!ld Jurisdiction in the United ~tat~s
where a lodge of colored Masons is constituent to a Grand Lodge which 1s
fully recognized and in fraternal relations with all regular Masonic Bodies
throughout the world.
It was one of the outcomes of the Civil War. The abolition of slavery and
the recognition of the negroes as free citizens encouraged so.me of them who
belonged to the clandestine colored lodges to hope for social and fraternal
equality as well.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

325

There existed at that time what is known as Prince Hall Masonry. It was
one of the developments of the Revolutionary period and was started in Boston
in 1784 by a native of Barbadoes, named Prince Hal1; hence the name.
It has since established its lodges in most of the States, including New
Jersey, each with its own Grand Lodge.
The members of those lodges are looked upon and treated as clandestine
Masons, with whom the regular Masons can have no Masonic association or
intercourse.
Encouraged by the more tolerant attitude to.ward their race in the Northern
States, they sought fraternal recognition by the regular lodges in several of
them, but met with a prompt and emphatic refusal.
However, some of the more enthusiastic "Abolitionists" in Newark, who
were members of regular lodges, determined to do what they could to provide
an opportunity for the local colored Masons to establish themselves as regular
Masons.
Accordingly, a petition was presented by one of them to the Grand Lodie
of New Jersey at the Annual Communication held on January 19, 1870, from
some of the colored Masons in Newark, asking for recognition and connection
by granting them a warrant for a lodge to be known as Cushite Lodge.
This petition was rejected on the recommendation of the committee, on
account of "its being irregular in form, and for other reasons satisfactory to
them . .. But the committee deemed it consistent with the duty assigned them
to intimate to the petitioners that there is one, and but one, regular way in
which their .affiliation with the Grand Lodge can be realized, and that is by
pursuing the same process to which a11 profanes are subjected."
Apparently in anticipation of the above report, made to the Grand Lodge
on January 18, 1871, another petition was presented by their sympathizers for
a warrant for a new lodge in Newark to be ca11ed Alpha Lodge, which was
granted, after rumors as to their intention to admit colored men to membership
in it had been denied by the officers-elect.
In spite of those denials, the new lodge received and proceeded to act upon
petitions from the colored men in whose name the first petition was presented.
This created quite an excitement amongst the Fraternity and the subject
became a matter of discussion in the Public Press, charges of "deceit and misrepresentation" being made against the officers of the lodge.
By order of the Grand Master, the warrant was arrested and while his
action was. approved by the vote of the Grand Lodge on Janu;ry 16, 1872, at
the same time the Grand Lodge by a sma11 majority ordered the return of the
warrant. The lodge proceeded at once to carry out the original intention by
conferring the three degrees on the colored applicants, and trained them in the
official work of the lodge.
As regular Masons the colored members of Alpha Lodge dimitted from it
and presented another petition for a warrant for a lodge to be known as
Surgam Lodge, supported by the recommendation of the white members of
Alpha Lodge.
·
This petition was also rejected by the Grand Lodge, which put itself on
record that while it would not grant a warrant for a lodge for colored Masons,
it did not intend to interfere with the action of any individual lodge as to the
material it might choose to select as members, so long as they possessed the
required qualifications. ·
This attitude was re-affirmed by the Committee on Jurisprudence in 1900
in these words : "This Grand Lodge does and always has recognized the eli~
gibility of any man to be made a Mason who possessed the proper qualifications
without regard to his race or color."
'

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Those colored Masons re-affiliated with Alpha Lodge No. 116, and in the
course of time all the white members thereof severed their connection with it,
leaving it entirely in the hands of the colored ·Masons.
Thus it came about that the only regular lodge of colored Masons in the
United States was formed in New Jersey.
Up to the beginning of the twentieth century, the membership .of; Alpha
Lodge seldom exceeded thirty in good standing, and during the first thirty
years of its existence it raised only thirty-seven Masons.
Since the World War there has-been a marked increase in the membership,
the latest returns showing ninety on the membership roll.

"AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?"
As the Fraternity is composed of individuals of every sort it is, therefore, human. Consequently some of their actions are subject to Masonic
judgment in the form of trials.
Masonry is generally judged by the action of its individual members
which become public and our standing, naturally is measured by them.
A possible preventive of this is a stricter investigation and taking advance notice of such actions on the part of the individual which in the end
might bring disrepute upon the Fraternity.
Nevada has a system which in a measure could well be followed. The
Cognizance Committee is a standing Committee in each constituent Lodge.
When by general knowledge or special charges it is found that a Mason
is "straying from the straight and narrow path," he is summoned before it.
Opportunity is given to remove the cause for complaint, but if persisted in,
charges are preferred and a trial had. This in a large measure accounts for
the absence of Masonic trials in that Jurisdiction.
Canada (1937):
(Grand Master): During this last year an anonymous letter was sent to
many of the members of the Board 0£ General Purposes compla,ining of certain
matters affecting the administration of Grand Lodge Such 'communications
always carry a sting with them and leave unpleasant feelings · with those who
receive them or with those who may be meanly criticized by them. Only a
coward, or putting it a little more mildly, only one who lacks the courage of
his convictions (if the statements in such letters may be called convictions)
will stoop or resort to such underhand, unmanly and unfair methods of making
an objection or offering a criticism. Most persons on receiving such letters consign them to the flames that no other person may be troubled with seeing or
reading them. I would not mention this incident had such a letter been received
by any one person only, but it was sent to several and created a very unpleasant
sensation. The writer of the letter is evidently a Mason with somewhat intimate acquaintance with the affairs of Grand Lodge, and I am surprised that
one of our Order, who has been privileged to know the details of official and
financial matters of Grand Lodge, has so far lost his sense of self respect, his
manhood, and forgotten so completely his obligation of fidelity, as to write a
scurrilous letter about a brother Mason or our Order, and be so weak, spineless
and unworthy as to write and mail it unsigned. It is serpentine in its nature.
I hope the writer of that letter may read this, and cause him to repent his unmasonic and contemptible conduct. To those brethren who received the communication referred to, I would say destroy it if you have not already done so.
If there is anything in that letter that should be discussed let it be brought forward properly, without reference to this anonymous epistle, and have it considered in the open, sponsored by a brother who is courageou!!" and conscientious

Nevada (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Review of Nevada is written
by our good friend and Brother Lloyd C. Henning, our Nevada Representative.
As to your question about the Cognizance Committee. Each constituent Lodge
must appoint a Cognizance Committee of Three (usually Past Masters). All
complaints of un-Masonic conduct coming to a Worshipful Master are referred
to this commitee. Usually a personal appearance of the erring Brother before
the committee acts as a reprimand or at least makes him think. It would surprise you the number of cases that are straightened out. If in their judgment,
a trial should be had, such is their recommendation to the J. W. of the Lodge.

"I READ IN THE PAPER"
From a Masonic standpoint this may be considered under two headings
-General and Masonic. Under the heading of General too much of the
Fraternity and its doings have been given to the world through the secular
press. It has even included the Radio. In our early .history the Craft was
shrouded in secrecy, which necessarily had an attraction. Then it could
be well said that we were judged by the work we did and the known ideals
of the Craft. ·With this ·removed we have perhaps become just another
Fraternity.
T~ Masonic publicity ~vailab~e ~nly to members, through recognized
Masonic sources, or Masonic pubhcations read generally only by the Craft,
there can be little objection.
R,~v. Joseph Johnson, P.M., P.A.G. Chaplain (England), very truly
says: It should be understood that Freemasonry never encourages brethren
to disclose their membership of this Fraternity to all and sundry whom
they may meet in the walks of life. To parade it'is undignified and often
leads to a brother's motive being misunderstood, if not misconstrued. It is
better that brethren talk less about Freemasonry, and apply more of their
energy to the demonstration of its ideals and principles in their conduct.
Freemasonry has nothing to gain by its members publishing on the housetops that they have been received into its fold, but it will gain immensely
if they will let it be seen that, having been brought face to face with its
great ideals and teaching, their own lives have been enriched and ennobled. This is what the world wants to see."

Maso!1i".. pu~lications which was a distinct loss to the Fraternity. Perhaps
the ehm1nat1on of some of the less readable or dependable, in a small measure, compensates for their suspension.

and those honors, privileges and rights not be parcelled out through political
intrigue within its ranks. Am I a brother, or am I?

Others use the more subtle method of haviQg their photograph taken while
conspicuously wearing a Masonic emblem or their Shrine or Grotto fez, and
having these photographs inserted in their political advertising.
I call upon the editors of all the Masonic, Shrine, and Grotto papers and
magazines published in this State, and each one of you, to co-operate with me
in doing whatever is possible to discourage this unmasonic practice. Candidates
must no longer be permitted to use Masonry to further their political ambitions.
Help us to keep Masonry out of politics and to keep·politics out of Masonry.
There may possibly be a few localities in the State of Ohio where open
installations are proper and serve some useful purpose, ·but my opinion is that
the objections to them far outweigh their value, and I believe that they should
be absolutely prohibited. The public is then invited to enter. Many come simply
out of curiosity, and are quite interested to see what a Lodge looks like when
opened on the Master Mason Degree. Some Mason tries to read the installation
ceremony. In only rare instances is it ever committed to memory. He mispronounces many of the words, and the general effect is no particular credit
to the Fraternity.
Often members thoughtlessly give Masonic signs in full view of the public.
The room is full of women and children and men who are not Masons. The
Master then and there is made to violate one of the ancient charges at the very
time he is being installed. The andience is thereupon informed of the duties
of the various officers, which, after all, are none of the public's concern. The
public is permitted to see a Lodge of Master Masons called from labor to refreshment before being dismissed from the Lodge.
But more serious than all these objections is the situation that sometimes
arises and did arise last fall in one of our districts.
It was an open installation and a large crowd was present, including men,
women, and children. The presiding officer read: "If any Brother is apprised
of any just or Masonic reason why any of these officers should not be installed,
let him speak now, or forever after be silent." A Mason thereupon made an
objection to one of the officers. What followed can well be imagined.

District of Columbia (1937):
(Grand Master): Early in the year various brethren took occasion to ex~
press to me regret that our Sunday newpapers had failed for several years to
carry a column of Masonic news, and call to my attention the fact tli.at the
ptlblication of the Trestle-board showing, in advance, the schedule of work and
activities of our constituent Lodges for the ensuing week, had been discontinued
entirely.
Most of our brethren receive the Lodge bulletins of only those Lodges in
which they hold membership. Situated as we are here at the seat of the Federal
Government, with so many sojourning brethren constantly and more or less permanently within our midst, we have here a large number of Masons who have
no readily accessible home Lodge. Many of them are desirous of being advised
of the meetings which our Lodges hold. Not alone that, but I feel that the public generally, may, within certain restrictions, with entire propriety be informed
that our Lodges are working and active and that their meetings are interesting
and elevating, as they are ; otherwise color may be given to the false conception
that some persons seemingly have that Masonry is an antiquated institution
in which progres is stifled and restrained ·by limitations and customs themselves
antiquated, and not the dominant, forceful and inspiring organization we know
it to be.
I accordingly requested the Grand Pursuivant, to collect the Masonic news
and to see that such news was carried in a Masonic column in our newspapers
each Sunday. With the assistance given him by the Masters Association of 1937,
he has ·been able to have published not only the Trestleboard showing the entire
work of our Lodges for the ensuing week, but more than 450 Masonic news
items. I am convinced that this has in a measure stimulated Lodge attendance,
particularly at the series of Grand Visitations.

Western Australia (1937):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Sixteen dispensations were granted
to lodges (Rhode Island) to attend Divine service in regalia. Whon one remembers that the United States possesses besides Freemasons what is probably
the largest and most varied list of fraternal associations, quite enough of them
with animal names to stock a zoological gardens, and all more or less bedight
with medals, sashes, and what an old-time Australian legislator, long deceased,
described as "the gews, the gaws, the gauds, the fal-de-rals, and whigmaleeries
of life," it is not difficult to picture what would be the appearance of a church
interior in which possibly a dozen societies of the "gews," etc., brand worshipped with the lodge with such ostentation.

Now my next reference is wholly and solely the Philippine Islands' affair,
but if I were a Mason of that enterprising community, I would register undiluted horror of Masonic broadcasts. To the ear attuned to the songs of birds,
radio, accompanied by noises called statics, is about level with a combination
of crooning and jazz sounds mistakenly called music. To adapt broadcasting
to the profanation of Masonic talks "for the purpose of enlightening the general
public on the character, aims, and ideals of the Masonic Fraternity and counteract propaganda carried on by our enemies" may seem as "delicious" as
Damascus was to Mohammed. But if I lived in the Philippines, I should feel
myself a most improper gander if I listened to broadcasting of that description.
The Grand Master's (Quebec) visitations were numerous, but not so his
rulings. In reference to a question concerning holding military nights and
military church services he gave rulings which are worth quoting. He saw no
objection to a lodge holding a military night where their members wore their
military medals. But as regards the holding of a military church service with
medals, he held it would be entirely inconsistent with the regulations of the
Order. The wearing of medals or jewels of a Masonic nature, he said, was
not and never had been considered in good taste, let alone additional military
decorations. From some· points of view, these decisions seem inconsistent, or,
at· any rate, to raise a curious question, not of mere propriety, but of wearing
complete official Masonic regalia ·at military church services. All lodge officers
wear official jewels as part of their official regalia of their respective offices.
If the wearing of jewels' of a Masonic nature is not considered good taste at a
military church service, what are the officers to do when they attend not only
as military men but also as lodge officers ? It is quite possible to conceive that
to wear military medals and lodge medals or jewels other than official may not
be in good taste. Indeed, I question whether Masonic medals can be worn with
military medals on any occasion, whether a church service or otherwise. I know
that in Australia some, if not all, military lodges do not favor the wearing of
Masonic presentation jewels by their brethren even when attending lodges in
mufti, and much less when attending lodge in uniform. But I have never heard
of their objecting to wear official office jewels when attending lodge in uniform.
In fact (until I lent it to i brother now deceased) I had a portrait of R. W.
Bro. Lord Kitchener, wheri District Grand Master of the Punjab, in uniform
and wearing the District Grand Master's regalia with the appropriate pendant
jewel. But- and this is' important, as supporting M.W. Bro. Campbell's view
iri part-Lord Kitchener wore no military medals when the portrait was taken.

For an increase and perhaps betterment of our membership, we might
consider the parable of the Lost Sheep. As we are prohibited both by
written and unwritten law from solicitation for new members, our numerical
strength must necessarily depend upon retaining those who are already on
our rolls, and continuing to interest those who become members from time
to time. There is, however, a good field for an increase in the Reinstatement of those who severed their connections through only financial or ·other
conditions over which they had no control. An intelligent, active solicitation of former members of this character might materially increase and
strengthen the Lodge from which they were forced to withdraw.
Arkansas (1937):
(Grand Master): We lost during the past few years by suspension for
non-payment of dues and withdrawals, more than 13,000 members. This report
to me was teeming with tragedy. It was filled with facts that sting and was
bristling with suggestions that challenge consideration and should compel action
on the part of the powers that be in Masonry.
A review of this staggering fact prompted the question, "What has been
lost?" Certainly the more than 13,000 men, who once proudly affirmed that they
were Master Masons, had lost rights, lights, and benefits beyond compute. Any
attempt to enumerate or estimate their loss, however sincere the undertaking,
must, perforce, be feeble at the best.
With the knowledge that there were thousands of worthy men, who in the
past had been members of the Fraternity and, because of conditions over which
they had no control, had been forced to drop their membership, I adopted as my
program of the year, "Re-instatement of worthy men who had been suspended."
Letters were sent to all the Lodges calling their attention to the condition
existing and requesting that they make an earnest effort to get these worthy
men back into the Lodge.
In order to make it more interesting I offered awards to the Lodges that
made the best showing in this work. The Lodges were divided into groups,
according to the number of men they had suspended during the past five years,
and the number reinstated.
The response to this program has been very gratifying to your Grand
Master as many of the lodges entered into the work and I am sure that the
returns will show a large increase in reinstatements over suspensions.
District of Columbia (1937):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : A suspended member petitioned
for reinstatement inclosing a check for $18 to cover his delinquency and two
years advance dues. The check was returned marked "no funds," and the question arose as to whether or not the brother was in good standing. The Grand
Master decided that inasmuch as there had been delay in depositing the check,
assuming it had been good when accepted, and the brother had been regularly
reinstated, .the lodge could not question the validity of the transaction, and that
in order to void it they would need to prove that the brother intended to be
dishonest when he presented the check.

ROUTINE AND IDEALS
In "the horse and buggy days" Relief of the distressed was an incidental activity .of Masonry. It was largely voluntary, and entailed some
financial sacrifice upon a Lodge or individual member and was, therefore,
made in keeping with the ideals of our organization. With passing of time,
Charity instead of being a Virtue not only in Masonry but in other lines,
has become an Industry. Perhaps Masonic charity will be greatly lessened
through Social Security, Old Age Pensions, Unemployment Insurance and
what might be a possibility, $30.00 every Thursday.

the Home. This the old folks refused to do.
Arizona (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Arizona has a splendid and valuable property as its Masonic Home. It is large, roomy and ideally situated in
a year-round climate. Yet in this jurisdiction we have found thus far that the
most satisfactory and least expensive system of dispensing Masonic charity and
relief, is to maintain our needy folk in their own homes and among their own
kindred by the payment of monthly sums for that purpose. Perhaps this system
might not work in Alabama, but we submit the thought fo,r what it is worth.

North Dakota (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): This year a situation developed
which show how necessary it is for lodges when authorizing Masonic funerals
to be specific as to the amount of financial responsibility. During the year a
Past Master of one of our lodges died in California. A Masonic funeral was
requested and authorized; later a bill in excess of $100 was rendered to this
lodge but the lodge was unable to meet such expense and neither did it feel
that the situation warranted it in view of the evident ability of members of the
family to meet such expense. Nevertheless the funeral was held and the expense was incurred. The question involved was "Shall California pay funeral
expenses of North Dakota Masons?" It was the feeling of your. Relief Committee that ours was the moral if not legal responsibility in this case and so
after some correspondence with the Chairman of the California Grand Lodge
Board of Control, a warrant for $100.00 was sent to discharge this obligation.
Your Committee wishes to emphasize tlie importance of definite commitments
clearly indicating what and how much expense is authorized and preferably
the handling of all such ·Interstate Relief matters through this Committee and
the Grand Secretary's office.

Western Australia (1938):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): In California there is (or rather,
was when I was there) a boarding-house which proudly notified on a tablet that
it was "for temporary domiciliarians." Generally, persons of that character are
called "transients" in the United States and Canada, but the Californian place
wanted something different, and apparently got it. Too often, these "temporary·
domiciliarians" are a nuisance to the Masonic boards of relief, as they claim
assistance on the score of being Masons. The Grand Master gave an instance
of how one of the Canadian boards tested the reliability of claimants. The president of that ·board happens to be the Chief of Police, and the secretary, when
applied to for relief, if not satisfied, tells the applicant to see the president
whom he will find in the City Buildings. "Just ask for the Chief of Police," he
is told. If the man is genuine, he goes, but if not, he still goes, but not to the
City Buildings. "We have saved considerable money thereby," the secretary
states.

Missouri (1937):
(Grand Lodge): Rabbi Samuel Thurman presented one of the best statements on what is the matter with Church and Masonry that it has been our
pleasure to read. In part he said :
"I have often asked myself, are there any good reasons why our fraternity
has suffered deflections in membership, and are there any good reasons why our
fraternity does not increase in membership in proportionment to its distincton,
to its past achievements, and to its significance as a great community of men
within a state. I feel that the Masonic fraternity is passing through the same
kind of a transition period which the church and the synagogue have been suffering this past quarter of a century. What is the matter with the church?
Every now and then you read reports in the newspaper that the church is weakening. Every now and then we are reminded, or at least it is pointed out to
us by some one who writes a pert, though not pertinent article, that the church
is weakening and serious honest leaders in the church are sensitive to the forces
which make for the weakening of the great religious bodies of the land. But
the church is weakening for reasons, not from without, but from within. There
have been certain restrictions, certain associations within the church which have
meant; perhaps, the dying out of the old faithful ones, without the replacement
of them by new faithful ones. I do not believe the same conditions · may be
applied to the Masonic fraternity. There is something that Masonry has lost
in recent years due to the general trend. Some of you will be surprised when
I say this, but I believe it is due to the general trend of competing with other
community forces, and when I say competing I use a mild word. The church
has been guilty of trying to take the place of the moving picture theatres, or
the dance halls, or even sometimes the gambling club. When these distractions
came into the community and deflected membership from the church, it was
said, 'Well, what is the church giving its membership? They want entertainment, they want good fellowship, they want friendly approach and address, and
unless you give these things to the members cif the church and the synagogue,
they will go elsewhere, or at any rate, they will not come to church.' As a
matter of fact, when we try to compete with the other attractions of the community, we are not raising the standards of the church but we are lowering it.
That is self-evident, it hardly needs any argument, and yet there is an argument
on the part of those who try to introduce the spirit of fellowship and friendship in the church. It is true that for many years and still, in some parts of the
country, the church is not the warmest place, nor the friendliest place, nor the
most interesting place. The same may be true of the Masonic fraternity. Has

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

339

any Mason ever taken an oath as an Entered Ap'prentice, as a Fellow Craft, or a
Master Mason, with the thought that he was going to get something out of
Freemasonry outside of his spiritual wages? Were that true, you know that
would ·be the very first condition for rejecting such a candidate for membership
in our fraternity. Yet, my friends, that is exactly the spirit under which we
have been laboring. It has been a kindly spirit and a human spirit, but it has
been the kindly and human spirit that is very childish and child-like. It has
been groping in the dark."

him he borrowed ten cents from it for his carfare home.

Indiana (1937) :

(Grand Lectzirer) : It has been reported to me that innovations, novelties
or changes have been injected into the degree work by a few Lodges. I say reported, because, naturally, such innovations, novelties or changes would not be
perpetrated in my presence.
A report has reached me from a reliable source that one of our large city
Lodges recently violated our official ritual before a large audience, composed
of officers and members of several Lodges, by introducing a certain "soliloquy"
into the ceremony of the Master Mason Degree. This innovation is a direct
violation of Masonic law. I refer you to the annual Proceedings of 1936, which
shows that this Grand Lodge adopted a resolution prohibiting the use of this
"soliloquy."
Such ·a practice as this, particularly when perpetrated by one of our larger
Lodges should be discontinued, not only because it is a violation of Masonic
Law but for the more important reason that it might tempt others to add
further innovations to our work and thus seriously mar our beautiful and
impressive ceremonies. Evidence of such practice brought to the attention of
the Most Worshipful Grand Master, no doubt, would cause severe penalties to
be inflicted.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Washington Grand Lecturer
has always been opposed to the substitution of the Key for the mouth to ear
mode of instruction and in his talk on the matter said he shudders when he
contemplates the danger he had passed through during the past year, for, says
he, if something had happened to him and had strict search 'been made of his
body he feared a key of work would have been found. This would have
been a terrible catastrophe, especially when at the present time a complete word
for word, with all the signs and passes, expose of the work of the Jurisdictions
of the United States can be purchased in any large city.
To our way of thinking Ritualistic Proficiency is a very fine thing and each
Master should be familiar with the Ritual in its entirety. It can, however, be
stressed to the point where it overshadows a more important requirement in a
Master. We refer to leadership and ability to transact the ·business of the Lodge
and make its meeting interesting. We have in our own experience met Masters
who were good ritualists, knowing perfectly every word and in addition abundantly able to present its work with full dramatic effect, yet they were entirely
devoid of that certain something called leadership and as Masters of Lodges
were perfect failures. A good Ritualist with histrionic ability is usually at heart
an artist and devoid to a considerable extent of business acumen. It is good,
hard headed business men with ideas that we need as Masters of our Lodges.
Western Australia (1937):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Before Grand Lodge closed, the
Pro Grand Master called attention to the doubt which existed as to whether it
was still right and proper on Masonic occasions to drink the toast of"The King
and the Craft." The fact that the King was a Mason ought not to stop them
from drinking a toast which was a concrete evidence of the loyalty of the Craft.
It is curious how these doubts arise on almost every occasion when a new
monarch ascends the throne of England. These doubts are not confined to the
Mother Country. They arise, apparently, everywhere in the British Commonwealth of Nations. Yet, over and over again, it has been pointed out in unmistakable terms by Masonic authority that the association of the Sovereign with
the Craft in the form of a toast is one of the inherited customs of the Craft,
and that it has the sanction in Masonic precedent, and that in associating the two
-the monarch and the Craft-when proposing and honoring the toast, Masons

343

are pledging their loyalty to both. It is a Masonic custom, sanctioned and supported by records of lengthy usage, and there should be no departure from so
ancient and excellent a custom.

••••
In the United States most Masters of lodges scrupulously observe the fashion of wearing a hat while ·presiding at a lodge meeting. It is claimed that
Masonic tradition requires that the Master of a lodge must remain covered.
The same rule obtained in England both before and after the Great Revival, and
gave rise to the question and answer: "Where does the Master hang his hat?"
"On his head." Before Hitler proscribed· Freemasonry in Germany the same
fashion was observed in German lodges, and many years ago I saw a portrait
of the celebrated Italian patriot, Mazzini-who was not only a Mason, but
served as Master in his lodge-wearing a hat while presiding. Be-hatted
Masters were not unknown in Ireland before its Masonry became wholly
speculative. Curiously enough, there are brethren in the United States who
regard this custom as entirely American both in origin and practice, and deny
its traditional character. Indeed, they go further, and question whether it is a
custom in that country.
Wyoming (1937):

(Grand Master): Our Masonic Clubs have proved to be a wonderful help
in developing interest among the brethren. They serve a most useful purpose
in providing a standard of perfection in the ritualistic work. If the competitive
feature is included in the meetings, which I ·believe is a good idea, there is very
little opportunity for social contacts. I would suggest that where it is possible
for lodges to exchange visits they should do so and arrange the work so tpat
there will be ample time for the brethren to visit and become better acquainted.
It is often the personal touch which keeps the brethren interested in our
Masonic work, and causes a lodge to stand out as a good lodge.

"COMPARISONS ARE ODIOUS"
Perhaps no better example of a difference between English Masonry
and that as practiced in the United States can be observed in the Peace
Memorial in London and the George Washington Masonic Memorial.
How soon the latter will be finish~d one one seems able to tell. Like Topsy,
the demand for additional funds just .continues to grow and grow. Some
of the Grand Lodges who never joined the movement or participated in the
initial collection of $1.00 per tl'ember (afterwards increased to $1.75 per
member), are now being criticized as are those who paid the $1.00 assessment, but believe that they are under no moral or legal obligation to pay
the increase. Perhaps it might be possible to interest the Government,
through the P.W.A., W.B.A. or some other alphabetical agency to assist.
Such work might be more worthwhile than some projects on which public
funds have been wasted.

(Grand Master): A Lodge should not rent its hall to a labor union, if
there are members of the Lodge affiliated with rival labor unions ; to do so
may possibly lead to unpleasant relations between members of the Lodge. The
dignity and honor of the Fraternity demands that the sanctity of the Lodge,
and respect for its members, be the constant care of the Brethren. (Approved).

District of Columbia (1937):
(Grand Lodge): In 1922 Grand Lodge purchased the property known as
Temple Heights for the purpose of erecting a Masonic Temple on the site. The
ground cost $900,000 and estimates of the cost of a building amounted to
$2,320,000. Out of a total of $1,436,452.51 in pledges, $829,902,25 had been paid
to November 1936, and no substantial financial progress had been made for the
past seven or eight years. Although more than $1,200,000 had been spent on the
project, only $554,000 had been paid on the property, the balance largely representing interest and taxes. Convinced that the Mason.s of the District of
Columbia cannot build or maintain such a structure as was proposed or would
do justice to the site, the Grand Master recommended that the project be discontinued and the property sold. The Masonic Temple Committee recommended
that 160,000 square feet of the ground which was necessary for the Temple
buildings be set aside and the remainder amounting to 232-931 square feet be
''
sold, and Grand Lodge approved the recommendation.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Masonic Lodge Rooms are at
the disposal of chapters of De Molay. The Grand Master of Texas learned that
the chairman of the State Executive Committee was a profane and that he and
others after attaining their majority were permitted to attend De Molay meetings in Masonic Lodge Rooms. He gave orders that if this practice of permitting these men to hold high office and to attend meetings after feaching their
majority continued, he would deem it necessary to deny the order the use of
Masonic Lodge Rooms in the future. He did recommend that the law be
changed to forbid such usage but the committee to which it was referred did
not coincide with him in his views. He also felt that attention should be given
to the Order of Rainbow for Girls, which admits members whose fathers are not
Masons.
This writer feels that Grand Master Weatherred has been a wonderful
executive and rendered inestimable service during his term of office. We, however, do not see eye to eye with him in the matter of the use of our Lodge
rooms. We do not feel that the space enclosed by four inanimate walls, even
though we~ by certain acts and words, dedicate it to certain purposes, is a holy
place, which a young girl in all her innocent purity would profane by entering.
If Masonry means service, what greater service can it perform than to provide
for the younger set a place to meet in, that will imbue them with a feeling of
respect for the things their elders hold in respect. Far better that we provide
them with such meeting places, than by so not doing, we discourage and disrupt
their organization. I would far rather have a son or daughter of mine meet
in such surroundings and imbibe the teachings there proclaimed than have them
parked in an auto, or in a booth in a roadhouse, and imbibe teachings not nearly
so wholesome. Let us not as Masons bow down so low to this inanimate Temple
made of brick and mortar lest in doing so we take our eyes off the Temple
contained in our own hearts and minds .

GO OFTEN TO THE HOUSE OF THY FRIENDS
The practice of visitations between Jurisdictions is increasing. There
is no doubt it is beneficial to all concerned. Rev. Joseph Fort Newton said
one of the tragedies of the human race was that Men were Strangers, and
Charles Lamb also stated that you can't hate a man that you know.
Visits between Lodges in California and Nevada are matters of common occurrence and are more general between these Jurisdictions than in
others.
District of Columbia (1937):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : This writer has often thought
that Worshipful Masters frequently fail to use discretion in the appointment
of committees for the examination of visiting brethren, whether it ·be a temporary committee for the occasion or a standing committee. In too many cases
the committee is composed of expert ritualists, to whom failure on the part of
the visitor to cross every "T" and dot every "I" is a cause for suspicion.
It is often the case that a brother who has never served as an officer will forget
some of the finer details of the lectures, yet retain all the essential details of the
degrees.
We remember an occasion shortly after having received the degrees, applying for admission as a visitor to an Illinois lodge. The dean of the Past
Masters, whom we had known very well in former years, was chairman of
the committee. His first question was one from the M. M. degree, which we
answered correctly, because it was fresh in ourr-mind. Much to our surprise,
chagrin, and confusion, he said: "Brother, if you can't answer the first question
in the catechism, you can't travel here." When he was reminded that the question was from the M. M. and not from the E. A., he apologized, and admission
was gained without further difficulty. But it was embarrassing for the visitor.
On another occasion, in Nova Scotia, after having sat on a hot spot for about
an hour, the writer was informed: "Brother, we knew you were all right all
the time. We just wanted to find out what kind of Masons you make in the
District of Columbia."
We do not mean to imply that admission to lodges should be made too easy
for visitors. But we do not believe "catch" questions should be indulged in.
Neither should hints be given nor corrections made. Nearly every brother can
give a fairly comprehensive story of what occurred during the progress of the
degrees, while he might make poor answers to a series of set questions. To this
writer the idea would seem to be to decide from general results rather than
technicalities, whether or not a visitor should be admitted.
Western Australia (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master of the D. of
C. ideas on visiting are interesting, as the following quotation will indicate:
"Whilst a M. M. is privileged to attend as a visitor the meeting of any other
lodge, that privilege does not extend to the Festive Board. Invitations to the
Festive Board are within the power of the W.M. of the lodge, and unless such
invitation is given generally in the lodge or specially by a member with the
W.M.'s approval, the visiting brother as a matter of etiquette should refrain
from being present. There is not one of us who would dream of asking ourselves to dinner in another person's home, and the Festive Board ·of a lodge
is to all intents and purposes that lodge's dinner table. I do not think that

WE, TOO, ARE THE PEOPLE
Not only for the good of our Country in general but Masonry in particular the value of an active interest in the young man of today should be
self-evident. Perhaps no better argument for such a course can be given
than the following which now describes what is a Boy:
He is a person who is going to carry on what you have started.
He is to sit right where you are sitting and attend to those things you
think are important, when you are gone.
He will have control of your cities, states and nations.
He is going to move in and take over the courts, prisons, churches,
schools, universities and corporations.
You may adopt all the policies you please, but how they will be carried out depends upon him.
He is going to sit at your desk in the senate, and occupy your place
on the supreme bench.
All your work is for him, and the fate of the nation, of humanity is
in his hands.
·
The social, civic and economic questions of our present day civilization will be solved by him.
So it might be worth while to pay him our serious attention.
Arizona (1936):
(Grand Orator): Grand Orator Taylor delivered an address on Youth,
of which we reproduce part:
A generation that is already crowding us close to hold our place. What
are we doing to ·lead the way?
A few years ago some of our far-sighted brethren organized the order of
DeMolay, a wonderful work, pushed along by a handful of our members who
give of their time to the guidance of the boys who will be doing our work tomorrow. The Boy Scouts, another great institution which takes boys at an
early age, and endeavors to build character into them. Some of us serve by
giving our money to such work, some by giving our time and ourselves, some
by doing both, and more are needed.
The boy is a natural hero-worshipper. Are we going to leave him to
pattern after the gangster and the racketeer whose nanie he sees screaming from
the headlines of the paper, or are we going to give him a neighbor to look up
to and follow as a scout leader or a DeMolay councilor, a man who is looked
up to in the com1mmity and of whom his fellows speak well? The scout leader
teaches his followers the value of good health, a strong, clean body, a good
deed toward someone else, how to read Nature and to take advantage of the
knowledge. Further along the DeMolay Councilor teaches his group the histories and beauties of the symbolism of the ancient arts and sciences. The
youth is only going to take interest in the man who takes an interest in him,
and youth is keen in its eyesight.

Michigan (1937):
(Grand Master): In pursuance of the instruction given by the Grand Lodge
at its last Annual Communication, and the request of the Grand Master, about
fifty percent of the Lodges, so far as reports have been received appointed a
committee of the Lodge to study into and advise the Master df the Lodge
res~cting the Lodge's contact with the youth of their several communities.
This c?ntact has been requested to be made only along lines recognized by
Masonic precedent, and for the dual purpose of benefiting the moral standards
of the youth of the community, and obtaining a heartier spirit of appreciation
among the younger members of communities of the good work of Masonry and
the likelihood for membership therein.
'
New Jersey (1935):
(Grand Master): Consequently, I take the opportunity of expressing the
hope that each and every one of us will stand up and be unafraid to join with
all other constructive forces in an endeavor to help stem the tide of all unAmerican trends, so that, after we have laid down the working tools of this life
'
it may be truly said of us that we did our 1'est to keep America American.
I have always felt that no great good is ever accomplished by impeding
handicapping or stifling any youth movement. The old adage "Youth will b~
served" is to me quite true. Throughout the history of civili~ation, youth has
always surged upward and on·vard towards its goals, dreams and ambitions and
to my mind, the same spirit dominates the youth of our own day. Youth wili
continue to be an irresistible force which will be able to overcome all obstacles
by its own tremendous power, and it seems to me insofar as it is possible for
us to exert an?' influence over the youth of our day, whether '.boys or girls, we
should not hesitate to try to guide them into paths of true and loyal Americans.
West Virginia (1936):
(Grand Master): The West Virginia division of the American Legion held
the first session of the Boy's State at Jackson's Mill which had for its purpose
the assembling of high school boys from all over the state with the objective of
teaching them good citizenship. The Department Commander requested permission for the various Masonic Bodies to participate in this laudable movement.
He said that our Bodies had been selected because of the fact that their membership is entirely American in their every thought and action. After consultation and reflection, it was held that the Grand Master was unable without a
vote of the Grand Lodge to authorize any direct official participation.
Quoting from a Grand Master of the distant past we stated as follows:
"Free~asonry is. not a political institutio.n. It knows nothing of kingdoms or
republics or empires or states. It deals with men only as children of a Common
Father and has. nothing to do with political controversies that distract nations.
It labors to relieve the suffering of the living and give decent sepulture to the
dead."
North Carolina (1938):
(Chainnan Correspondence Committee): Also, the Grand Master gives the
Order of DeMolay a place in the proceedings of the Grand Lodge. He makes a
statement which is to us absolutely startling. In these days when we discover
that the average age of our membership is getting higher every year and that
we are not receiving young candidates in -any great numbers it is discovered
that in Ohio, 82.5 per cent of all Masons 21 to 25 years of age were former
DeMolays; two-thirds of all Masons 21 to 30 years old were former DeMolays ·
and 43 per cent of all Masons of all ages were former DeMolays. We do not
know whether the DeMolay order is the final solution of the problem, nor do

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

349

we think that, whatever the final solution is, it is in a proselyting agency as
such; but the fact is, that the age at which the most powerful impressions are
made is before twenty-one years; that other organizations recognize this; and
there is a definite need for some force connected with Freemasonry which can
make an impact upon youth in America.
This country is appalled by the conspicuous place which youth has in the
present records of crime. Many explanations have been offered, none of which
in itself is satisfactory. The public schools are censured-unjustly, we feel
quite sure, except insofar as their as legal limitations and prohibitions are responsible. The American home is censured; and it is, after all, not nearly as
much worse than it was forty years ago as we find it pictured. American life
has become more complex and American youth needs and must have, special
consideration and treatment which is acutely necessary now as it has not been
in past generations; and we firmly believe that youth organizations of the right
sort go far toward helping in the solution of the problem.
"BOUQUETS AND BRICKBATS"
The Proceedings of our Grand Lodge, its officers, activities in connection therewith, as well as other Masonic events taking place in California
continue to find mention in the Reports of the various Reviewers, who are
Experts and generally qualified to speak from experiences. Of course,
there are necessarily differencs of opinion between them, but generally
Masonry in California as viewed by them meets with general approval.
87th Annual Communication, Grand Lodge, F. & A. M.
San Francisco, California, October 13-16, 1936
Earl Warren, Grand Master
Canada-:
A fine array of 20 Past Grand Masters and 1,602 Officers and Representatives were present.
The Grand Master's message was a worthy one.
Among the Grand Master's many decisions, some will be remembered, as
he is a lawyer of distinction.
Delaware:
An interesting Oration was delivered at the Communication held the second
day by W. Brother Albert F. Ross, Grand Orator.
A feature of this Grand Lodge is the report of the Committee on the
Observance of Public School Week. Several pages are devoted to this report.
Iowa:
The spirit of the session. as the Proceedings disclose, was strictly business.
Practically everything of importance is included in the address of the Grand
Master. While his biography does not appear, and 'there is no advice on his
avocation or occupation, it is manifest that he must be either a Lawyer or an
Auctioneer. His message is long, prolix, and reiterative. All Masonic speakers
and writers have an obsession for poetry.
According to the Grand Master, the State of California is idyllic. Let his
words tell of it.
Then with satisfaction he moralizes on the ideal situation.
With good judgment he urges the reestablishment of the Correspondence
Committee so that his Craft may be better advised on doings elsewhere.
If the Past Masters' pictures are of the class and character of many hung
