in our lodge rooms, he should welcome placing them in a burglar-proof safe and
suggest that the combination be lost.
Observation on life membership is sensible.
For one activity California Masons cannot be too greatly commended, and
that is in urging the fullest support to the Public School. It cannot be better
said than in the words of this Grand Master.
The report of the Grand Treasurer is short, complete, and so set up as to
be wholly understandable to the layman.
The report of the veteran Grand Secretary, John Whicher, is well set up,
properly subdivided, concrete as to fact, and clear in expression.
The collections for the Masonic Homes have been large, as have been the
expenses for conduct and maintenance. The Homes have been well supported,
have been well managed, are performing a fine service, and wholly deserve the
pride the Craft has in them.
The Grand Lecturer makes a long report and a good one.
The annual oration was delivered by Brother Albert F . Ross. It was a
good sensible talk, with no attempt at the ornate, but replete with sound advice
and homely illustration. .
The reports on the Homes are in full detail and cover many pages of the
Proceedings. They are well worth reading but do not lend for quotation.
For seventeen years California Masons have observed Public Schools Week.
The committee in charge submits. a long report, intensely interesting. To disclose the scope and effectiveness of the work, only a close reading of the report
will suffice. To all who are interested this is emphatically recommended.
The report of the Committee on Necrology is fittingly written in good
taste.
There is no report on Fraternal Correspondence. They believe that the
money it would cost can be better used. The Grand Master does not a~ree.

The committee also discovered "the only difference between the new saloon and
the old. saloon is that men sometimes find difficulty in getting a place at the
bar because of the women customers." Reviewer Warner (Calif.) has hopes
that the good sense of our membership will take care of the liquor question and
that while we do not desire the low-down type of saloon keeper, we are loath
to part with one of our members who may be a small stockholder in a national
drug company.
Imprisonment, in pursuance of a conviction of felony, subjects a member
to automatic expulsion in California; such a law has been found to be most
useful in saving of time, energy and expense. Masonic lodges in that jurisdiction are not empowered to act as trustees since such service entails expenditure
of considerable time, without compensation, and might be unfair and onerous.
The Grand Master further disapproved the use of the title "W. M. Emeritus."
California departed from its established practice of having a full-time paid
Grand Lecturer and delegated the work to a part-time Grand Lecturer with
four unpaid assistants. There seems to be a question as to whether this system
is working satisfactorily and the subject was the basis of a questionnaire issued
by the Grand Master.
In 1938, the Grand Lodge of Arkansas will publish its history, commemorating its Centennial Year.
California has a committee on Masonic History whose business seems to
be to hunt up old Masonic relics, books and charters and to inspire the various
lodges of that jurisdktion in printing their own histories. One thing which
appeals to us is an attempt to secure the written story of the personal and
Masonic activities of those venerable brethren who have received the fifty-year
button. The committee is also attempting to get information as to the naming
nf the various lodges. An attempt to print the history of the Grand Lodge of
California, by securing 2,000 volunteer subscriptions, has apparently failed.
The most interesting report of clandestine Masonry comes from the Grand
Lodge of California, which apparently has more of these organizations to deal
with than the rest of the country combined.

Missouri:
California's Grand Master decided that cocktail lounges, taverns, buffets,
etc., were in fact saloons and came within the California law. He also thought
that when there was doubt as to the eligibility of an applicant, the doubt should
be resolved in favor of the Craft. A committee referring to the passage of the
18th amendment, said it was passed "in the disappointed thought that the U . S.
Government would have more power in regulating liquor than Masonry had."

Oregon :
Gambling in California has made the problem of eradicating it from other
Jurisdictions a more difficult one. It has thrived in California because in several
instances Grand Masters have had their wish bones where their back bones
should have been.
The observance of Public School Week under the auspices of the Masonic
Lodges has an ever widening influence.

In their proceedings is found much of keen· interest to Masons the world

.
The Committee on Segregation speaks a grateful word for their very W orshipf ul Grand Secretary, John Whicher, who for thirty-one years by faithful
service is not only honored and praised throughout the Grand Jurisdiction of
California, but is so known and respected by Masons everywhere.
·
The Grand Orator, Brother William B. Ogden, in an able and eloquent
oration urges all Masons to cherish their Masonic heritage and to avoid becoming indifferent to many important things which may not immediately and
directly affect their purse or their person.
The Masonic Homes of California are doing a mighty fine piece of work
for their youth and for their aged.
The Committee on Public School Week is exerting an earnest effort and
encouragement in the cause of Public Schools and popular education, but not
without some criticism of political activity at school elections.
The Sesquicente.nnial of the Constitution ot the United States was observed by an address by Brother Lloyd E. Wilson, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Brother Wilson spoke fittingly and eloquently that as citizens and Masons we
need to uphold and revere the constitution of our country.
In October, 1937, it was my great pleasure to visit the neighboring Jurisdiction of California on the occasion of its Eighty-eighth Annual Communication. Approximately eighteen hundred representatives of Lodges were present
I was impressed with the pomp, yet dignity, of their opening ceremony, the
formal dress of the Officers, the reception of the flag of our country. I was
accorded every kindness and consideration, and gleaned much of interest. P.G.M.
Charles M.· Wollenberg, a former Arizonian, took me in special charge and his
fraternal courtesies will ever be remembered. The address of the Grand Orator\
Brother William B. Ogden, was especially noteworthy.

353

The observance of Public School Week and its connection with Masonry
in California has been criticized in some circles. Let those who object note this
statement regarding the present situation. "Although the observance has become, as it should be, a community affair and net a Masonic event, and although
the civic organizations of the community and the school people should be represented on the committee of arrangements, the Lodge should be the nucleus
of the organization created for the observance which is fostered and supported
by the Fraternity."
District of Columbia:
Brother Jesse M. Whited furnished an excellent topical review, which is
well indexed for the benefit of his readers. He finds our Grand Master had
something interesting to say in regard to Masonry's connection with religion
and gave his readers the benefit by quoting it. He also felt that the part of
this writer's report concerning the matter of Grand Lodges sponsoring outside
organizations was worth repeating, as well as part of our comment on the
liquor question.
Maine :
California has always stressed the observance of Public School Week and

report, which makes interesting reading and outlines some of the difficulties
which have confronted the committee in the earlier years. To this Maine
reviewer it seems a commendable activity for the brethren of every community,
for upon our Public Schools rests the perpetuity of our country and its institutions. Eight pages of interesting reading constitute the illuminating report
of this Committee.
A scholarly address on the Constitution, covering seven full pages, was
delivered by Bro. Lloyd E. Wilson and contains much of interest as touching
the part played by our earlier brethren in the framing of that hallowed docu·
ment.
The report of the Committee on Correspondence is of the topical variety
and as usual written by M. W. Bro. Jesse M. Whited.

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are generaity known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly speaking,
they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish Rite, for the
· one catted York is peculiar in its organized proceedings only to the United
States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitutar, the Cryptic
and the Templar Degrees.
The Symbolic Degree·s are conferred in a Lodge an!f are the Entered
Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They are catted
Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is by symbols.
The Capitular Degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the Mark
Master, the Past Master, the Most Excettent Master and the Royal Arch.
The supplemental and honorary degree of High Priesthood is conferred
in a Council of High Priests upon those who have been regularly elected
to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They are catted Capitular
because they are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning
"done in a Chl!-pter."
The Cryptic Degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the Royal
Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excettent Master. They are
catted "Cryptic" because the word "crypt" means a secret vault or underground passage.
The Templar Degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are th;e
Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight Templar comes
from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the temple at Jerusalem
from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the 33rd; inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States (which includes
att territory south of the Ohio River and west of the Mississippi River)
the ·organization of the different Bodies, and the degrees conferred by
them, are: Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix,
15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh, 19° to 30°; Consistory, 31° to 32°; Supreme
Council, 33°.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes att states north of the
Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River) the degrees conferred are:
Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14•, inclusive; Council Princes of Jeru1alem, 15•
and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and 18°; Consistory, 19° to 32"; Supreme
Council, 33 •.

MEMBERSHIP STATISTICS, UNITED STATES
AND CANADA
Grand Lodge of Iowa, A.F.~A.M. _"Bulletin" .
The figures below represent the annual compilation of Masonic membership statistics, as derived from figures submitted by the various Grand
Secretaries, or taken from the official publications of Grand Lodges. It
will 'be noted that of the fifty Grand Jurisdictions of the United States,
forty-four suffered a loss in membership, while six showed a..gain during
the past year, namely, Alabama, District of Columbia, Mississippi, ' Ne~
Mexico, Philippine Islands and South Carolina. However, the loss was, m
most instances, less than previous years, and the net loss was 24,039 less
than last year.
In the Canadian Grand Jurisdictions all lost membership during the
past year, with the exception of New Brunswick.

Leon 0. Whitsell
Grand Master 1938-1939

Our seventy-second Grand Master of Masons in California was the
dynamic, energetic, genial Hawkeye, Leon 0. Whitsell, who entered this
world on the 10th of July, 1876, at Centerville Iowa, his parents being
George W. and Elizabeth Smith Whitsell. His .g randparents were among
the pioneer settlers of Iowa, ·coming to that State from Ohio by ox-team.
Leon studied law in his native town in the office of the Honorable
Claude R. Porter, who was recently a member of the Interstate Commerce
Commission. He passed the bar examination in the spring of 1900 and
very soon thereafter began the practice of his profession in Idaho.
Abandoning the law for a time, in 1910 he filed a claim on the TruckeeCarson project in Nevada and there engaged in farming until 1915, when
he with his family moved to Orange County, California, and engaged in
the raising of oranges and lemons. For three years he was a member of
the Board of Supervisors of Orange County. He was also President of
the Orange Community Chamber of Commerce, and President of Villa
Park Farm Bureau.
He entered a larger field when, on July 28, 1925, he was appointed by
Governor Friend W. Richardson to fill the unexpired term of Egerton
Shore on the California Railroad Commission. Was reappointed by
Governor Richardson on January 1, 1927, for a full term of six years. In
the year 1928 was elei:ted as President of the Commission. On January 1,
1933, Governor James Rolph reappointed him to the Commission, and from
August, 1934, to the end of his six years term again served as Pr.e sident.
In September, 1913, at Ottumwa, Iowa, he was joined in marriage with
Bessie McKaig. Two fine sons have :been born of this union. Mrs. Whitsell is a woman of rare mental attainment. She is a lecturer on California
history and a writer of California historical poems, many of them having
been published in California magazines and other publications.
MASONIC HISTORY: May 22, 1917, was initiated in Orange Grove
Lodge No. 293; passed June 5, and raised June 26, 1917. Junior Warden
1919; Senior Warden 1920; Master 1921. Member and Past High Priest
of Orange Chapter R. A. M.; member of Santa Ana Council R. and S. M.;
member of Santa Ana Commandery K. T.; member, 32d degree, of Los
Angeles Consistory No. 3, Scottish Rite; member San Gabriel Conclave
Order of Constantine; member of Al Malaikah Temple A. A. 0. N. M. S.
0

He has been an officer of Grand Lodge since 1928, when he was appointed Senior Grand Deacon. At that time he also was appointed a member
of our Committee on Masonic History, serving diligently and enthusiastically until his election to the office of Grand Master in October, 1938.

J,EON 0. 'V-HITSELL
GRAND MASTER

1938

Address-V." .R: .RICHARD V. PERKINS, Grand Chaplain
You, my Brethren, making rne your Chaplain, ask me in our assemblies
and now in our 90th Communication to do one of two things. I am to
encourage an agreeable atmosphere, using a fit and traditional vocabulary
and well-worn expressions, to invoke a vague approval of a very distant
Supreme Grand Master who rates a thin reverence but not too close
company. Or you wish me, for moments which might be a precious fraternal
and personal experience, to come directly at that central core of royalties
excited by the higher realms of Masonry. In this deliberately planned
interval there might appear a 'brilliantly illumined pathway, a spiritual
vista, a consciousness of our significance and positive dependence upon God
and our dependence upon each other which would really lift this entire
annual communication into something beyond the complete ken of mind
or spirit, yet perceived as fresh air in a crowded room, sunny warm.th
after chilly exposure or readiness for labor after rest and refreshment. We
might not perhaps make of this room a throne-room of Almighty God,
but we might with flashing reality know, together, that that bowing down
which we call reverence is the most uplifting experience of life, individual
and collective.
This I cannot do for you. It depends upon the last man here as to
whether, in any degree, I may do it with you.

stars and out of his mouth proceeded a sharp sword with a double edge
and his face shone like the sun in full strength. When I saw him I fell at

of good fortune runneth over. They that belong to thee go about with

Friendliness and good will are in their hearts. Thou carest for thy sick

Necrology
On Sunday, October 30th, 1938, Masonry in California suffered an
irreparable loss in the untimely passing of that 1beloved man and Mason,
Past Grand Master Benjamin F. Bledsoe. His entire life was characterized
by loving servi'ce, both as a citizen and as a Mason. He was a fearless
advocate of civic righteousness and was always in the front ranks~a
valiant fighter for what he conceived to be right. He made his lasting
mark upon the entire Sta-te and upon California Masonry, and his passing
leaves a vacancy not easily filled.
On May 22nd, DeRoy H. Gates, Inspector of the 107th Masonic District, passed away at his home in Banning. For seven years he effectively
s~rved his district in that capacity. He loved his fellowmen and by his
kmdly acts won the esteem and affection of all who came in contact with
him.
On August 2nd, that dearly belov:ed man and Mason, Charles K.
Tuttle, was called to his eternal reward. He served as Inspector of the
56th District for thirty-two years, faithfully and well. At the time of his
resignation, ·he was in point of years of service the dean of the Inspectors
in California. His life was gentle, his friends were legion, and his entire
career was a delightful benediction. At the request of his .family, I conducted his Masonic funeral at Cypress Lawn, San Mateo county, on August
4th. The R.'.W.'.Junior Grand Warden and many Inspectors together
with scores of the brethren, were present to pay their tribute of affection
to this splendid character.
. On August 7th, Brother Frank M. Wise was called from his earthly
labors. For approximately seventeen years he served as Inspector of the
87th District, and for more than ten years he was a member of the Board
of Control. In ·both official positions he exhibited an unusual capa·oity for
hard, faithful, constructive work. In his many years of service to the
Craft, he "put his consdence in his every endeavor" and established an
~nvia~le record: He was beloved by all his fellowmen in the community
m wh1ch he resided, and he numbered among his faithful friends thousands
of the best citizens of California.

Anniversaries
On May 16th, I was present at the 80th Anniversary of Pacific Lodge
No. 136. It was indeed a highly pleasurable occasion. This Lodge has
given to California Masonry some of its strong, virile characters and has
a history replete with interesting incidents.
On May 27th it was my pleasure to be present at the 75th anniversary
of Elk Grove Lodge, the membership of which has continued throughout
the many years of lits existence to materially contribute to the upbuilding of
their community, and has stood in the forefront of every movement in the
interest of .good government.
On June 10th, I attended the 75th anniversary of Harmony Lodge No.
164 at Sierra City. This Lodge with a membership of thirteen, is the
smallest Lod·g e in the State, but is strong in Masonry. Situated up in the
mountaiins, it has always had upon its roster men imbued with the true
Masonk spirit. It has miraculously survived the vicissitudes of time and
has militantly held high the banner of Masonry.
On August 7th, I .took part in the observance of the SOth anniversary
of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296 at San Diego. This Lodge has had a rather
colorful career, and its iinteresting hi~tory is now being prepared and will
shortly be published in pamphlet form.
On September 16th, I attended rhe 75th anniversary of Alameda Lodge
No. 167, at Centerville. This Lodge has, from the very beginning, been
exceedingly fortunate in the selection of its officers. They have been men
of unusual attainments and standing in the community. By the lives they
lived and by the Masonlic teachings t hey promulgated, they have inspired
the membership with a strong love for their Lodge and loyalty to the
Fraterni.t y.
On Septem:ber 23rd, I was present at the SC>th anniversary of Dunsmuir
Lodge No. '297. This Lodge is com.posed for the most part of railroad
employes and its history disdoses an enviable record of Masonic charity
and adherence to the best traditions of the Craft.

Research Lodges
Some of the grand jurisdictions have established research Lodges for
the purpose of engaging in Masonic research and giving to the Craft the
results of their extensive labors, in published form.
These research Lodges are granted charters and• meet at stated intervals to discuss and consider the results of their work T hey are the same
as other constituent Lodges, ex.c ept that they have no authority under
their charters to confer degrees. Their stated and special meetings are
less frequent than other Lodges.
Members belonging to a regular blue Lodge may become members
of a research Lodge. Therein they have dual membership.
I foel that the California Grand Lodge could materially contribute to
the cause of Masonic research by authorizing the establishment of one or
more such Lodges in the State. In my humble judgment, this matter is
of sufficient importance to merit the earnest consideration of Grand Lodge.
Therefore, I recommend that the in·com.ing Grand Master be empowered
to appoint a committee of three to investigate the advisability of the esta.bLishment of one or more Lodges of research in this State, and to report
their findings at our next annual communication.

I congratulate the Committee on P ublic Schools Week on their many
years of constructive public service in carrying on this .g ood work, under
the able chairmanship of Past Grand Master Chas. Albert Adams.
Masonry should be vitally interested in every phase of public education.
Masonry should at all times be vigilant in the interest of our free taxsupported public school system, and should ever stand in the forefront in
de.fense of that institution. Our public schools are vital to American Freemasonry. An enlightened and intelligent citizenry is Masonry's best guarantee of perpetuity.

Decisions
No. 1. I was asked if an application for degrees may be received from
a .young man using his stepfather's surname in his signature.
It appears that the applicant has used th is name for the past ten or
twelve years, is known by this name by all the people in the community,
and desires to continue the use of this name.
I held that under the circumstances of this case, it was perfectly
· proper, in applying for the degrees, for applicant to use the name he has
adopted.
The law permits a person to change his name at will so long as he
does not do it to defraud or injure others. This may be done by court
a'Ction, but such court action is not necessary.
No. 2. I was asked to lend my official sanction to the "giving as a door
prize an automobile" and to the "operation in connection with the bazaar
what is commonly termed a paddle wheel."
The above being for the purpose of paying the debts of a Mason.c
Temple Association, I held that the proposed activity was in violation of
section 319 of the California Penal Code and, hence, is prohibited by section
166a of our Masonic Constitution.
No. 3. I was asked if a Lodge room on the ground floor can be legally
used for Lodge purposes.
My answer was, yes, if the Lodge room can be properly tiled.
The method now in vogue in the building art has materially changed
the construction of Lodge temples and Lodge rooms and obviates the necessity of prohibiting Lodge rooms on what is commonly known as the ground
floor. T"he building of Lodge rooms wholly within a building; that is, a
box wi·thin a box, where there are no windows to the outside, the only
outlets from the Lodge room being two doors to the west that lead to the
anti-rooms and the air-cooling vents, makes such a Lodge room subject to
perfect tiling.

Service Committee
The many years' experience of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in
maintaining in each lodge of that grand jurisdiction of what is known as
a Service Committee, and several distressing ·cases in this State called to
my attention during the year, suggests the advisability of recommending
to the constituent Lodges the appointment in each Lodge of a committee
whose duty and function would be to consult with the de.pendents· of deceased Master Masons and to advise them as the circumstances of each
case may warrant.
At the death of a Master Mason, it is not an infrequent shuatfon for
dependents to be confused as to their future. Many widows, never having
had business experience and suddenly finding themselves in possession of
insurance money and other assets, too often become an easy prey to unscrupulous solicitors for get-rich-quick projects and other high-pressure
schemes.
If the Lod·g e provides a committee on friendly advice to whom she may
turn in the very initial stages of her ·c onfusion and grief, in' all probability
great as·sistance could be rendered and ill-advised action avoided.
I seriously recommend to the constituent Lodges the advisability of the
appoinhnent and maintenance of such committees.

Masonic Homes
The one Masonic act[vity to which we can unanimously point with
greatest pride is our Masonic Homes-those institutions where youth and
age are mainfained in such perfect security, where members of th~ Craft
and their dependents receive every reasonable care and support which the
affection .of our membership may dictate.
Masonry, a•s far back as history records, has been distinguished f~r
its thoughtful care of distressed, worthy brother Master Masons, their
widows and orphans. This fraternal function has endeared our Institution
to the membership and to the profane alike. J.t has clothed the unfortunate
with the mantle of security and has .given to our Masonic youth the chance
to develop mentally and physically. It has equipped them with an education sufficient to enable them to enter the battle of ma ture life with more
than a casual chance to succeed. This is good work - square work Masonic work.
The members of the Craft in California who have never embraced the
opportunity of vi•shing our Decato and our Covina Homes, have neglected
a rare privilege and one which would cause their hearts to swel! with
pride and satisfaction.
From my three years' experience on the Board of Trustees, I know and
appreciate the fine service performed for these Homes and the members
of the Fraternity by the four appointed members of the board. These
members have throughout the years g iven freely and unselfishly of their
time and their •talents to this great Masonic work, and they more than deserve the high regard and affection in which they are held by the Fraternity.
Endowment Board
I have been vitally interested in the Homes Endowment Fund Board
activities since its very inception under that much beloved and dynamic
personality, our late Brother Wm. P. Jeffries, who so materially contrib~ted
to its early success.
During the past several years, under the able leadership of Brother
Frank M. Smith as chairman, that board has carried on a · campaign of
educa•tion which has resulted in a greater Homes consciousness on the part
of the entire Craft throughout the State.
They have, in my judgment, wisely majored on the educational feature
1

0

381

as distinguished from a per capita contdbution on ·the part of our membership. I have for some time past doubted the propriety of each year embarking upon a drive or campaign of solicitation for a per capita contribution oo any specific sum. Let those who feel they can, contribute to this
worthy cause.
The desired objective will in time be attained through substantial bequests and gifts to this fund on the par·t of those abundantly able to contribute, without the embarrassment to the individual Lodge members
through continued yearly drives or campaigns.
Masonic Relief and Employment Service
In the year just passed, I had the pleasure of attending three outstanding breakfast meetings of the Masonic Relief Boards and Employment
Service; on February 4th, at Los Angeles; April 2nd, at Long Beach, and
May 14th at Berkeley.
These meetings stimulate a healthy interest in the constructive service
being .performed by these two agencies.
The large number attending from the lodges in the respe.ctive sections
and the enthusiasm displayed on •these occasions demonstrated that practical Masonry is very muoh alive in California.
This is some of the finest work in which we are engaged-the relieving
of distressed worthy Master Masons-the rehabilitation and salvaging of
willing workers out of employment through no particular fault of their
own. This is in the truest sense Masonry in action-Masonry at work.
W·hen you aid a brother Mason in obtainfog gainful employmentwhen you put him on a pay roll, you perform for him and his dependents
a service the value of which cannot be calculated in mere terms of dollars
and cents. You thus assist in raising his morale and, in sustaining his pride
and self respect, you restore his initiative and inspire him with an enduring
courage to carry on and endow him with hope for the future.
The constructive work being performed by the Masonic Employment
Service richly deserves the unstinted praise and gratitude of the entire
Fraternity.
Constitution Rearrangement
At the last communication of Grand Lodge, Past Grand Master ] ohn
Stewart Ross was requested to prepare an up-to-date edition of his Digest.
Preparatory to this work, he rearranged the sections of the Constitution
by consolidating into one section the provisions applying to a subject which
are now found in separatep sections of the Constitution, and, further, by
setting apart as ordinances those sections that are not a part of the fundamental organic law of Grand Lodge.
As soon as the rearrangement was completed, I submitted it to the
Committee on Jurisprudence and the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes for their consideration. This work and the arrangement of the
Digest to accord with it, is the result of many months of arduous and
painstaking work. It is a work that wdll be of great benefit to officers and
members of the Craft. I feel that the members of the Craft in this jurisdiction are under lasting o·bligations to Brother Ross for this monumental
work so long desired by all who have occasion to administer our Masonic
law. If Grand Lodge at this communication sees fit to adopt it, and I trust
that you will, I earnestly recommend that the Constitution and Regulations,
as prepared, be published under the name and to be known as Ross' Digest.

Masonic History
Our Grand Lodge committee on Masonic History, under t>he able leadership of Brother Mark A. Sawrie as chairman, has, during the year, performed yeoman service in the interest of California Masonry. The members of the committee have sought oU't the hidden places and, by their
patient and untiring research, uncovered and brought to light much -ya1uable mJaterial whi.ch has heretofore escaped the scrutiny of the Committee.
The history of ~any important and interesting Masonic characters
has been perfected and the tangled threads of Craft lore have been un·
raveled and now safely repose in Grand Lodge files.
This grand jurisdiction unquestionably has collected together the greatest mass of Masonic data ever assembled by any similar body in the United
States.
I authorized the publication of a pamphlet entitled "Years Past and
Minutes Gone," which was prepared by the chairman of this committee.
This booklet is in the main a resume of interesting inddents of the first
five years of our Masonic history. It contains some rather muminating
sidelights on the activities of Brother B. D. Hyam, our third Grand Master.
I commend this to the Craft as a well written and creditable piece of research work.
I urge upon Grand Lodge the necessity of continuing this Committee
for the coming year, and recommend that the modest appropriation desired by the History Committee be granted in furtherance of this most important and highly desirable research work.
Mother Lode Lodges
I would not he true to myself if I concluded this message without
brief reference to my first love in California Masonic history. Those old
Lodges on the Mother Lode from Mariposa county on the south to Sierra
county on the north-where Masonry in the early days was the most
potent factor in the lives of those hard-working and hard-playing pioneers.
Those old Lodges where Masonry is still found in all its original puritywhere Masonry is still a re1igion. Those old Lodges hoary with age, many
of them weak in numbers but strong and virile in the spirit of Masonry.
They form a real and definite link, joining the romantic and hectic past
with at times the all too prosaic present.
It is in this historic and happy environment that I can always recharge
my Masonic batteries and from which I gain and absorb an overflowing
measure of Masonic inspiration.
. My brethren, permit me to urge upon you t·he advisability of paying
this delightful section and its Lodges a visit. Visit the old Lodge rooms.
Get the smell of Masonry of the Fifties in your nostrils and you will come
back refresihed and renewed to carry on in emulation of those brethren
who in the early days impressed upon the Fraternity the strength of their
characters and their fidelity to the precepts and principles of our beloved
Craft.

Inspectors
Our law requires that Masters- and Wardens-elect be thoroughly proficient in those portions of the Constitution and Regu lations of the Grand
Lodge which relate to the governmerit of a Lodge. It has been held by thi3
Grand Lodge that an Inspector may require attendance of the officers of
his district to study and d·i scuss those things that every officer should know
to be qualified to govern the Lodge ·o ver which he has been or ma}· be
called to preside. I find that most of the Inspectors are holding Officers'
Association meetings for this purpose. Where these meetings are held
frequently throughout the year with proper leadership the results are
gratifying.
Some Inspectors, however, hold not more than one or two Officers'
Association meetings during the year and some devote no time to this work,
or, if any at all, it is in connection with and as a part of a school of instruction on ritual.
I seriously urge the importance of each Inspector requiring attendance
of the officers of all the Lodges in his district at frequent meetings through.
out the year for the study and discussion of matters relating to the government of a Lodge.
I am pleased to report that I have, without a single exception, received
the wholehearted co-operation of the Inspectors.
They have willingly and cheerfully rendered me every assistance possible.
I · feel that I owe them a lasting debt of gratitude for their kindness
and courtesy in arranging official receptions, attending to all of the infinite
details incident thereto, consulting my every wish and seeing that every
instruction given was scrupu'lously carried out.
I have, upon numerous occasions, enlisted their assistance in the investigation and the correct and satisfactory solution of many troublesome
problems arising in their respective districts. In each instance they have
ex·hibited a thorough knowledge of our laws and have abundantly proven
their a·bility to arrive at proper conclusions which in every case has obviated the necessity of action on the part of the Grand Master. I have
leaned heavily upon their competent shoulders, and I acknowledge my
indebtedness to them for their unselfish services to me and to this Grand
Lodge. I express to them individually and collectively my sincere appreciation.

man of California Masonry, that Grand Secreta.ry par excelience, our >wn

Valedictory
If Masonry in California is to reach its highest destiny and cause all
men to regard it with that measure of favor and admiration to wihich it is
justly entitled, the individual Masons must put into practice in their daily
lives and a-ctions those precepts and principles of which we so proudly
boast. They must practice what they preach, and thus, through the lives
they live before their fellowmen, glorify this Fraternity they profess to
love.
Masonry is judged by the conduct of its votaries, and justly so, because it is practically impossible to distinguish between the Masons as
individuals and the Institution. To the outside world, in your daily intercourse with your fellowmen, YOU ARE MASONRY.
To be accorded the ·privileges of Masonry is a sacred trust and respon9ibility-a responsibility not to be tightly appraised. Those who accept its favors should scrupulously avoid betraying it. Let it not be said,
my brethren, that you have in the slightest degree been Wlfaithful to your
~~

'

The past year has been one of happy work to me. It has been a joy
and a ·pleasure to serve the Craft as Grand Master. If I have in any way
succeeded in impressing, even a small part of the Craft, with the importance
of Masonry; with the duties and responsibilities incident to membership;
with the glorious history of our past, and with an ambition to further perfect themselves in Masonry, I will feel that my efforts have not been in
vain. When I surrender the gavel to my successor, it wit! be with a feeling
of appreciation and thanksgiving that such a high degree of harmony has
been evidenced during the year. This has lightened my burdens and ha·s
made my year as Grand Master to be remembered as one of the happiest
in my life.
In conclusion, my brethren, I now express to this Grand Lodge .ind
to the members of the Fraternity throughout the jurisdiction, my sincere
appreciation of the high honors conferred upon me and the many courtesies extended to me during the past four years.
I am particularly mindful and appreciative of the fine spirit of loyalty
and the support accorded me as Grand Master by the Past Crand Masters,
the line officers of Grand Lodge, the Inspectors, and officers of the constituent Lodges.
The acquaintanceships made and the friendships established will, I am
sure, remain strong and firm throughout the years and continually remind
me of the great debt I owe to those faithful brethren for their fidelity and
unselfish service to me.
I have given to the Craft as Grand Master during the past year the
best service of which I am capable. If I have failed in any respect, I trust
you will be charitable enough to consider it an error of mind, and not of
heart.

To the Finance Committee, Grand Lodge:
We have audited the books of account and records of the Grand Lodge
F. & A. M. of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1939, and present
herewith the following statements:
Exhibit A: Grand Secretary's accounts, statement of cash receipts and
disbursements-general fund-fiscal year ended July 31, 1939.
Exhj.bit B-1: Statement of per capita dues collected during 1933-39 for
Grand Lodge from 1937-38 annual returns.
Exhibit B-2: Statement of per capita dues and home tax collected during
1938-39 for Masonic Homes of California from 1937-38 annual returns and
three quarters $25.00 Home tax 1938-39.
Exhibit C: Grand Treasurer's accounts, statement of cash receipts and
disbursements-fiscal year ended July 31, 1939.
Exhibit D: Statement of assets, and capital account, as at July 31, 1939.
Comments-Sufficient revenue from per capita dues and other sources was
received during the year to cover all expenses and appropriations. As shown at
the bottom of Exhibit D, the revenue exceeded the total of expenses and appropriations by $3,771.76.
All dues payable during the current year, reported on the 1937-38 annual
returns, have been paid in full. Total receipts due from subordinate Lodges
as per individual annual returns were found to be correct by total number of
membership, classification of source of reve.nue, and total amount of gross
revenue received-as evidenced by our Exhibits B-1 and B-2 of this report.
The total of all receipts were accounted for and traced to proper depositaries. Disbursements were made by checks and supported by properly approved vouchers.
All bank balances were verified by correspondence. Certified lists of
stocks and bonds belonging to all funds, were received from the Anglo
California National Bank which holds said securities in trust.

WILLIAM P. FILMER, Grand Treasurer.

Referred to the Committee on Finance.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
It is with pleasure on my part that I make this, my fifth annual report
as your Grand Lecturer, and give an account of my activities during the
past year.

At the request of the Grand Master, I presented seven fifty-year buttons to veteran members. An amusing incident occurred at the presentation
of two butto11s at Guerneville, when one of the recipients made the remark
that he did not particularly care for the button as it was the prelude to a
Masonic funeral. After the meeting, Brother Mark Body, a member of
Santa Rosa Lodge, informed those assembled that he had worn his button
for nineteen years and considered himself far from dead.
Assistant Grand Lecturers
Following the custom, established five years ago, the Ritual Committee
held four two-day meetings during the year. These meetings were devoted
exclusively to the study of the ritual. The vacancy created in the committee
by the election of Worshipful Lloyd E.. Wilson to the station of Right
Worshipful Junior Grand Warden, was filled by the appointment of
Worshipful Walter Leonard, who at the time of his appointment was
Inspector of the 42nd district in San Francisco.
More than fifteen thousand miles have been traveled by the Assistant
Grand Lecturers, and Lodges of Instruction have been held for the benefit
of every Inspector in the jurisdiction. No set plan for holding these meetings in a particular district at a certain definite time has 1been established.
The present set-up for teaching the ritual has been in practice a sufficient
length of time to permit the Assistant Grand Lecturers to determine the
districts where the assistance is most needed, and in some cases several
meetings have been held for the same Inspectors. The ultimate hope and
ambition . of the committee is uniformity throughout the entire jurisdiction.
Condition of Lodges
Judging from the reports of the Inspectors and Assistant Grand
Lecturers, and from personal visitations to many of the Lodges, it appears
that Masonry in California is sailing on an even keel. True, there are a
few of the Lodges that have gone through the year without receiving any
petitions, but they are the exception rather than the rule. In a vast majority
of the Lodges enough petitions have come in to keep the officers proficient
in their work and it is gratifying to note the uniformity with which the
ritual is being rendered. I find that the officers are eager to learn the ritual
as it is being taught by the Grand Lodge. The Inspectors cannot be
praised too highly for their untiring efforts in teaching this work to the
officers and for the efficient manner in which they keep an ever watchful
eye over the Lodges of their respective districts. They are regarded by the
officers and ·members as contact inen with the Grand Lodge and their advice
and 'c ounsel is sought and given whenever needed. Truly, their work is a
labor of love for the Fraternity which they so ably and intelligently serve,
ofttimes without the proper recognition.

,,PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
~ ~istrict Officers' Associations

It has been ·brought to my attention, that in some districts the Officers'
Association meetings have been discontinued or are held so infrequently as
to ,!>.e, prji~tically o_f no value.
The experience of that past several years has demonstrated that these
Associations are a practical educational system for the preparation of officers and a splendid opportunity for an entire district to get together and
compare notes on problems confronting the Lodges and to derive a real
benefit from one another's experiences. I know of no better method to
school the officers in Masonic law and procedure.
I realize, of course, the difficulties encountered in some districts, where
tlie Lodges are widely scattered and the officers are cibliged to travel long
distances to attend, ·but I believe the benefits to be derived from these meetings .is worth the time and ·effort" expended. I recommend the continuance
of these Associations in . districts where they now exist and strongly urge
that they be formed in those districts that have not taken advantage of
them in the past. ·
·
Innovations in the Ritual
During the past year I hav~ received five requests from Lodges and
:Degree Teams that they be permitted to make various changes in the confer~·ing of the degrees, giving as a reason that it would create more interest ·
and attract more members to the meetings. One of these requests was
that they be permitted to use twelye fellow-crafts in the third degree and
another sought approval of robes for the officers. A degree team, evidently
having seen the work conferred by another jurisdiction, asked that they
be allowed to use some parts of that ritual, with which they were impressed,
omitting parts of our own.
. •. I can easily understand how such innovations might create a temporary
interest and for a time increase attendance, but fortunately for the ritual,
no one person has authority to sanction such changes and the ritual must
remain as it is until such time as Grand Lodge recognizes the need for
a_ change. .
To all of these requests I have replied that I have no authority in the
matter, except to see that the ritual as adopted by Grand Lodge be adhered
to by all Lodges and officers in the jurisdiction. In substantiation of this
I have quoted from Section 121 of the Constitution of Grand Lodge.
" . . .. The ritual now taught by the Grand Lecturer and recognized
by the Grand Lodge must be adhered to by all Lodges and Masons in the
jurisdiction. The Grand Lodge alone has power to authorize changes therein for the purpose of having it remain as it was handed down from time
immemorial. No' degree shall ·be conferred except in conformity therewith,
and all propositions looking to any change in the ritual will be denied
consideration in the Grand Lodge."
The section is so ~lainly worded that it leaves no doubt as to its meaning and certainly requires no explanation from me.
Masonic Funerals
Qnce before, in my report to this Grand Lodge I mentioned the matter
of funerals and made certain -suggestions, hoping that it would awaken the
Lodges to the fact, that in . some cases our appearance before the public is
not representative of Masonry. Lodges must be made to realize that

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:

The committee appointed to consider the message of the Most
Worshipful Grand Master, and the report of the Very Worshipful Grand
Secretary, respectfully submits the following:
The spirit of optimism perm,eating the Grand Master's message is
indeed heartening.
Your committee knows of no other Grand Master who has visited
every district in the jurisdiction during his term of office. Each district
has, received, from the Grand Master, a history of Masonry in California
known to few men. Masons who have heard him speak are amazed at the
wealth of material which he has accumulated, and which evidences years
of research and untiring effort.
We desire to direct particular attention to the Grand Master's admonition that we place a "watch at our .lips," when discussing Masonic
matters of a secret nature.
· We compliment the Grand Master on his visits to those jurisdictions
bordering upon our great State. We feel that they have done much to
strengthen the ties of friendship and good will with our neighboring
Grand Lodges.

ANNUAL ORATION

The world in which we live is crowded with organizations. ()ur .fellf)w·
men are banded together in innumerable. groups, Ord.en, clubs and. societies for·
the attainment of a myriad' of goals; In the :political field there ·are ·countless
precinct, municipal, state, and national · organizations. .Some are big •and little
Tammanies for personal aggrandizement, while i others are striving for the
common weal with the purest of motives, the highest ooncepfs o f civic duty and
statesmanship. The religious realm has seen the· rise of its · ratio of groups de-·
voted to missionary work at home and abroad, to the promotion· of religious
fellowship and the discharge of the duties of the laity. The social.-sphere .is
surfeited with societies for dancing, cards, and music•. The. worlds o.f ·commerce, industry, and the professions are overflowing with··bankers'. ins.titutes,
manufacturers' and trade associations, labor unions, inedicaLand bar associations.
So numerous the groups, so short the day,.that even the ancient custom of eating must have its accompaniment of organized effort, and· those oL a mind.
may open the day by attending a breakfast club, pause for a luncheon club and'
finish with a supper or dinner club. Gone, too, .is the time when .activity in an
organization was a concomitant of plenty· alone, for even those on relief now:
have their "Workers' Alliance" for the promotion o.f ·their programs and the:
attainment of their ends. Human activity hu become· so incubated that the,
hours for sleep alone remain unorganized :pending the formation of an institute
of insomniacs.
As we thread our daily course through this fabyrinth -of ·organized activities,'
as we endeavor to respond to the many demands for our time,· interest and effort,
well may we inquire the purpose, the necessity> for any given organization; It
behooves us who are assembled here to examine· the transactions of the past
year, to plan and legislate for the coming year, to intelligently inquire respecting the mission of ·Freemasonry in this modern, chaotic, yet over-organized·
world. Perhaps our explorations will lead us to the goal of our Quest.

By G. Ei.LsWORTH MEYER, Grand Orator
()CTOBER 10, 1939
The Quest

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
In the treasure house of Freemasonry are many gems of symbolism. They
have been gathered from the valleys of the Nile and Euphrates, the temples of
India, the Acropolis of Athens, from Persia, Mount Moriah and Calvary, from
the Rhineland and the banks of the Thames. There are pearls of faith, emeralds
of hope, amethysts of temperance, the bloodstones of fortitude, sapphires
of prudence, and rubies of justice. Gradual products of human evolution,
crystallized by experience, they have been cut and polished by forgotten
philosophic artisans. They all are of rare beauty, and in the light of contemplative thought glow with the eternal fire. They have captured and imprisoned
individual rays of the light divine.
Yet, there in our treasure chamber is to be found one jewel surpassing all
others, a diamond of majestic size and incomparable beauty from whose facets
are reflected all the prismatic hues. Viewed from any angle it presents a
thousand lights and shadows. Like a giant star heralding the dawn, it sparkles,
it glows, it bids us seek the light. It is The Quest, the search for the Lost Word,
the indagation of the infinite, the simultaneous journey to the past and to the
future-the mysterious, intriguing, eternal, compelling Quest.
Masonry is not alone in its apologue of a quest; the theme has been a
favorite of poets and minstrels in every age and clime. At the dawn of civilization they who dwelt by the Nile told of Isis searching for the body of ()siris.
The Greeks gave us the allegory of Jason, the Argonauts, and the Golden Fleece,
as well as Homer and his epic quests of the "Iliad" and "()dyssey." From the
epidemic fervor of the Crusades came the chivalric quests immortalized by
Malory in his "Morte D'Arthur," and by Tennyson when in the "Idylls of the
King" he recounted the stirring tales of King Arthur, Sir Galahad and the
Knights of the Round Table in quest of the Holy Grail. Wagner in masterful
style sent Sir Launfal in search of the Sacred Spear and the Grail in the opera
"Parsifal." Tennyson's Ulysses sailed uncharted seas to the Happy Isles, and
Maeterlinck followed Myltyl and Tyltyl through a child's fairyland of fancy
to find the Bluebird of Happiness.
These are but a. few examples of every age and people, according to their
own spirit, adventuring on symbolical quests. They are tales of perilous journeys
beset by dragons, ruffians and death, of heroic struggles to possess objects said
to confer supernatural powers. They show the animistic spirit of man endowing certain articles with spiritual associations, significance and power. They are
mythical chariots to the sun, imaginary ladders to the stars, built to satisfy
eternal aspirations. ()f the same character, though couched in less fanciful
terms, is our traditional story of the search for the Lost Word. To examine
that Quest and at least one of its implications shall be our present purpose.
There are some possible explanations of the word, the logos, with which we shall
not concern ourselves, not because of intrinsic defects, but merely that every
Mason having the right to see our symbols through his own eyes, we shall
exercise our prerogative to find in The Quest a symbol applicable to our present
lives and needs. ()f what then are we in search? To what noble deeds and high
adventure does this allegory call us ? Where can we each discover the Lost
Word?

4{)5

Are we then banded together for economic advancement? W ill we .l earn
the Lost Word in the market place? We would not even proffer this question
did we not know that, notwithstanding the fine sieve of investigation, there are
a few each year who slip through expecting to learn on the other ·side of the
preparation room door some sesame which they. hope will ·open the gate to
personai economic advantage. W e would not ask the question were it not true
that once in a long while some subordinate Lodge indicates the possible p'resence
of some confusion. Reduced to its simplest terms' the answer niay be stated in
the question, how could Masonry promote the financial advantage of one brother
over that of another when the latter may be, and most likely is, his business
competitor? How could the Fraternity engage in such preferences and remain
a brotherhood devoted to unselfishness and lofty principles? · Yet Masonry can,
and will, make these two better friends, better men, and give them a commcin
bond which they might otherwise never acquire. If Masonry h~d not been ab,c;ive
mundane business affairs, had economic or other con~roversial issues been permitted to obtrude into the Lodge room it would never have been possible for
President William McKinley, while a Union . o(Iicer, to receive the degrees at
the hands of Confederates. Masonry cannot enter the market place with its
barter and sale unless it is prepared to be .sold itself. If ever we turn from
our high purposes to enter our ()rder in the et:;onomic struggle, then will
Masonry be inventoried and price-tagged. Nay, we· must pass the . market place
·. ·
in our Quest for the Lost Word.
Can we then find it in the political arena? The answer is axiomatic. There
is substance, not shadow, supporting our maxim that no Lodge shall participate
in partisan politics. True there have been occasions when some action, some
resolution of this Grand Lodge, or of a subordinate Lodge, has seemed to some

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

brother to be clearly indicated. We know his intentions have been of the highest,
only his fervor has prevented for a time his seeing the wisdom, the necessity
of silence and inaction. Some of the sad experiences on the Continent have
demonstrated the salutary nature of a rigid, a complete ban on partisan political
action. The records of more than two hundred years avouch the wisdom of the
policy and admonish us to be zealous in its regard. Yet this wise policy does
not mean that we as individuals should be without opinions on controversial
political issues or neglect our civic duties. Quite the contrary, our Fraternity
has always taught that it is our bounden duty to thoroughly inform ourselves
on civic and world issues, to be alert, to separate the chaff from the wheat, the
goats from the sheep, to speak and act vigorously and courageously through
those means outside the Lodge room afforded for the expression and registration of our opinions. The Mason who neglects the ballot box for golf on
election day, since he knows and should remember his duty, is the worse slacker.
But that fine line of demarcation between proper conduct and that which is
forbidden is important and aptly illustrated in the career of our distinguished
brother, George Washington. His correspondence repeatedly demonstrated his
pride in and affection for the Fraternity. He was the Master of his Lodge and
served in other · Masonic connections. Few men ever enjoyed a measure of
personal and political confidence equal to that reposed in him by his brethren
and countrymen alike. He could have been King or President for as many
terms as he desired had he not unequivocally refused. Yet when he was called
to lead the struggling, ill-fed, ill-clothed, untrained militia, when the Continental
Congress sent him resolutions instead of food and arms, he did not call upon
any Lodge to support him. He never requested any Lodge to memorialize the
Congress. In his darkest, most trying hours he observed and preserved the
traditional policy of our Order. Later when called to the highest executive
post of the new nation, he never sought Masonic support for his political views
or policies. He never confused Washington the General, the President, with
Washington the Mason. Instead, Washington the commander-in-chief of army
and nation practiced in those offices the exemplary principles which Washington
the Mason had learned at our altars. This policy is another of his which we
may well emulate. Masonry cannot enter the political arena as a gladiator, a
champion of some partisan cause or candidate without sooner or later feeling
the heel of a new champion and receiving the thumbs-down of public opinion.
We must seek elsewhere for the Lost Word.
Masonry is unlike other organizations, and the greatest danger it faces in
this nation is the possibility that its membership may unwittingly tend to make
it a prototype of others. It is not alone its claim to great antiquity which commands respect. Antiquity is a liability to most groups. There is much beyond
age which in turn actually is responsible for its survival and great age. It cannot invite candidates; they must come of their own free will and accord, and
they continue to come because of certain factors which, though they may not
entirely understand before initiation, are attributable to its distinguishing
features, its high purposes and policies. If, then, they are attracted by a difference, how foolish to try to simulate other groups. The wise Master will bear
in mind those differences and plan his activities accordingly. He will then find
that attendance will not be a problem and that, while not every member can
participate in the conferring of degrees, every member can find inspiration,
noble thoughts and deeds within the Lodge and his own part therein. Within
the Lodge room is to be found the chart and compass which will guide his
footsteps in The Quest.
Like Galahad returning to Camelot, there within the Lodge in time will
come the realization that, though we may sail distant seas, traverse many lands,
joust and conquer, yet if we are ever to find that of which we are in search,

to attain Sangreal, we must find it within ourselves. Our Quest will end in
victory when we learn that the Lost Word is engraved upon our own hearts,
that we can pronounce it aloud to the world by the lives we live. There may be
Modreds to sneer and seek to destroy by contempt, by indifference, citadels they
dare not directly assault. There may be those who look upon personal ideals as
a sort of phosphorescent mist hovering over a marsh, bright and shiny, but
evidence of stagnation below. Yet as long as this world is more than one of
jitter-bugs and jelly fishes, the development of personal character will continue
to be of primal import.
"For we are all blind until we see
That in the human plan
Nothing is worth the making if
It does not make the man."
To those few unfortunates who can find in life no mystery to be solved,
to those blind eyes which cannot distinguish the light from darkness, to those
ears which can only hear the prescribed dogmas without curiosity, to those
poor, benighted souls who have never asked why, where, or when, our words
would be a hopeless jargon, Masonry a child's recitation with awkward gestures,
and The Quest a hollow, empty vessel. But to him who can see the stars and
hear the music of their motion, who can tell the day from the night, thrill to
the dawn, to him who can demand of the silent, black sky whence he came and
whither he is traveling, Masonry speaks. To these The Quest is life itself,
eternal, omnipotent.
Personally I doubt if there is any human ant so bm;y with the work of the
world, so engrossed in dragging a carcass into his hole, that he has never paused
to see the sunset's glow, the stars swinging in their orbits, nature and the
universe proceeding in response to the inexorable command of law and order.
Certain it is that if he has paused but for a moment, he has seen everything
within the range of his vision moving according to the silent but compelling
law. Can he then safely wager that he alone is not subject to the higher command? Is he not a fool if he persists in gambling his all upon being the exception? Is he less than the electron spinning about the nucleus of the atom,
or greater than the starry constellation navigating the sky to its rendezvous?
For centuries scientific men devoted their lives to the cataloguing of facts,
to proving their theorems. Each labored in his own place, the geologist among
the rocks, the archaeologist amid the ruins, the botanist among the plants, the
historian among the musty pages, the astronomer peering into the sky. Then
suddenly they looked at each other, they spoke, for each had discovered THE
law. They called it evolution-not a mere descent of men from monkeys, but
a grand march of the animate and inanimate from the simple to the complex,
a march from origin toward a goal, all nature on its Quest. The evidence which
the physical sciences have disclosed has reached the point where it preponderates
against superstitions, a point where cries of heresy and the repetition of dogmas
and creed are no longer availing, a point at which evolution, progress, has at
last been recognized as the divine plan, the story of the past, the process of the
present, the hope of the future, a living, thrilling Quest.
But evolution-progress-has not had to rely upon natural selection alone,
nor has it been confined to natural processes. Man has taken part of the plan
into his own hands and speeded it up. He has experimented with cross-breeding
of various plants and animals to develop superior species and bring desirable
characteristics to the fore. He has expanded his knowledge of parasites and
disease until he has stamped out many which were commonplace a short while
ago, and removed the menace of others not yet eradicated. In so doing he has
not only made life more comfortable, he has lengthened his own existence. He

407

has harnessed the lightning from Franklin's kite and made it provide light,
warmth, and carry his messages and voice over wires and through the air. He
has burrowed into the ground to find ores and petroleum and put them to .new
and greater usage. But his progress has not been confined to material things
alone. He has carved new empires from the dark shores of ignorance and gone
forward in seven-league boots on many paths. No longer are barbarous tortures
and punishments meted out for crime. The vulgarity prevailing in the lowest
niodern dive is approximately that which prevailed among the elite of the
Elizabethan era. We frequently hear cries of immorality against the modern
age; yet, on the whole, probably no age has equaled the morality which now
generally prevails. Yet with all the advan.ces made, there are yet new goals
to be reached higher standards to be established, and I for one am firmly convinced that the human race is capable of completing its Quest. There have
been serious reverses, lapses to barbarism, such as we are witnessing _in ~he
European conflict, but our horror of the holocaust of war, and our realization
of its utter futility, are themselves evidence of progress.
There are many indications that the human race is turning its attention
from material progress to spiritual values. Take not my word for the future,
but hearken to the words of scientists, industrial leaders, men of every walk
not given to sentimentalism or wishful thinking, who have declar.ed that our
generation will witness no new inventions like the telegraph, the mcandescent
lamp, the motion picture, or the radio, but t.hat w_e shall. see great moral,
social and spiritual gains, that control of the mtang1bles will be developed to
equal' existing controls of the material. Thes_e th~nking me~ have declared that
even now the survival of the fittest is evolvmg mto the higher concept of . the
struggle for others, just as self-preservation in our own lives can evolve mto
parental protection, just as the concept of the Creator has ~valved from a. God
of retribution to a God of love. Man has developed physically, grown mtellectually, and now pushes forward spiritually. ~e seeks the Lost Word that. he
may truly travel in foreign countries and be a bmlder of the temple of humanity.
For several moments we have been speaking in a sort of collectivistic sense,
but we have not forgotten that society is made up ?~ individuals, t~t the whole
is but the sum of its many parts, that no great edifice was ever bmlt but stone
by stone brick by brick, timber by timber. We have not forgotten that for the
shrine e~ch stone must be hewn true and square. s~, t?~· with lif.e. the tenor
of nations the progress of society, depends upon the md1v1duals which make up
the social ~rder. Man's long, hard struggle against tyrants, against intolerance,
has been the struggle for the emergence of the individual. W ~ hav~ grown
from the idea that the individual was .created for the state, to the higher 1deal~gy
that governments were created for the service of men_. True we a~e observmg
in some parts of the world what looks like an unravelmg of the ~nhre tapestry,
but every age has seen some human hesitation, some retrogression; yet, after
a short period of fever man has ceased acting as a. meas~ring wor!Jl a~d donned
his seven-league boots. He will agai~. . I~ ancient hr_n~s. only philosophers
speculated as to individual importance, md1v1dual respons1b11tty. Then gradually
the common man began to think of himself not as a slave to tyrants, the pup~>et
of hierarchies, but as an individual with in~lienable right~, and later as havmg
correlative duties. Masonry is very much m tune therewith. ~n fact there are
those who say it has kept alive that philosophy, and t?ey l?°mt to th~se who
would stamp out the Order because they fear that 1t will keep alive that
very song.
. . .
. .
The candidate who knocks at our door comes as an md1v1dual, he is ~n­
dividually received, all the lessons taught him, all ~he symbols used a_re applied
to him individually, to his individual conduct. He 1s. taught t? face his. Creator
individually, to pray for himself and not through an mtermed1ary. He 1s taught

to stand on his own feet, that he is individually responsible. It is any wonder
that collectivism and some so-called idealogies see in Masonry an antithetical
philosophy? Freemasonry teaches the candidate that spiritually, morally, he
must travel the rough and rugged road of life alone until he has faced the
ruffians of vice, avarice, and intolerance, until by experience he has conquered
the forces of evil, has proved himself true to those instincts which are within
him, until he can live daily and in every action in response to that small but
insistent voice within, until he has attained the light, found the Lost Word and
made it articulate in his life. No truer words were ever penned than the
admonition of Polonius to Laertes when, after summing up that which should
and should not be done, the father said: "But this above all-To thine ownself
be true; and it must follow as night the day, thou canst not then be false to
anyone." Yet the admonition to Laertes, "To thine ownself be true," is no
small command; it is a clarion call to a task supreme, a bugle call to the battle
of life.
"The bravest battle that was ever fought,
Shall I tell you where and when?
On the maps of the world you will find it not;
It was fought by the souls of men.
"No marshalling troop, no bivouac song,
No banners to gleam and wave,
And 0 ! that battle, it lasts so long
From the cradle to the grave." (Adapted)
There may be "no banners to gleam and wave," but there is an abiding
satisfaction to be gained which riches cannot buy, which poverty cannot deny,
which wordly honors cannot exact, from which pain cannot detract. Victory
in The Quest demands that we have faith in Divine Providence, faith in ourselves and our fellow men; it demands of us hope for the future; it demands
of us temperance of thought and deed; it requires of us that higher courage to
live, not to die; it requires of us that prudence which is reason. With victory
we cannot help but attain justice and charity toward all mankind, keeping alive
the flames of humanitarianism through the boundless realms of eternity, preserving to posterity that highest political concept, democracy. Victory will insure
an economic system in which life may be lived, not merely endured. It will be
conducive to a social order in which the tremendous possibilities of the future
may be realized. It will inevitably lead us to such knowledge and awareness
of the Infinite as is possible to finite minds.
In a world capable of peace, honor, tolerance and charity, but momentarily
confused and floundering, Masonry presents, in allegorical form, The Quest.
Let us then heed the clarion call of Ulysses:
"Come my friends,
'Tis not too late to seek a newer world,
Push off, and sitting in order smite
The sounding furrows ; for my purpose holds
To sail beyond the sunset and the baths
Of all the western stars, until I die.
It may be that the gulfs will wash us down;
It may be we shall touch the Happy Isles;
Though much is taken, much abides ;
That which we are, we are;
One equal temper of heroic hearts
Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will
To strive, To Seek, TO FIND, and not to yield."

412

.To the M.".

w:. Grand Ledge of California:

At the 1938 communication Brother Charles A. Watson presented a
resolution that Grand Lodge take suitable action to reserve one seat for
the duly ele.c ted or accredited representative of each Lodge in the jurisdiction, and that such seat be held for the sole use of such representative
for the entire period of the communication. This was referred to the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes, which committee reported
thereon as follows:
"The reason for the proposal by Brother Watson is readily
understood •by every person in Grand Lodge. We will agree that
the present situation is deplorable. His suggestion of one seat
being reserved for each Lodge would not meet with general approval, because many Lodges are represented by more than one
person, and the representatives therefrom would find a single seat
more uncomfortable than· Grand Lodge finds the restricted capacity of Grand Lodge hall. There may be ways found to remedy the
present condition, and therefore the proposal should not be rejected, 'but should be referred to the incoming Grand Master and
Grand Secretary, that it may. induce them to give serious consideration to the situation the proposal is intended to remedy, and
your committee recommends that the resolution be so referred."
This report was adopted.
We have given this matter serious consideration and have communicated with a nt!mber of other jurisdictions with a view of ascertaining
how the seating problem is handled by them.
New York has 1037 Lodges with an aggregate mem!bership of 269,000.
Its Grand Lodge hall has a seating capacity of 1500. Each Lodge is
entitled to one representative who must be a Master, Warden or Past
Master acting as proxy. In addition, it admits District Deputies (ranking
as our Inspectors), officers of Grand Lodge, members of committees, representatives of other jurisdictions, and distinguished visitors.
Ohio has 623 Lodges with a membership of 176,000. The Grand Lodge
is composed of officers of Grand Lodge, Past Grand Masters, District
Deputies, Masters and Wardens, making an approximate possible attendance of 1925. Attendance is usually not to exceed 1200. Past Masters are
not members of Grand Lodge.
Illinois has 998 Lodges with a membership of 210,000. Grand Lodge
always meets in Chicago, where there are many large halls suitable for
Grand Lodge purposes. The attendance last year was 1400. Past Masters
are admitted when there is room for them, but they are not entitled to
vote. There are one hundred districts in the jurisdiction and the representatives are seated by districts.
Texas has 900 Lodges with a membership of 95,000. The Grand Lodge
is composed very much the same as in California, where we include Past
Masters. Its auditorium seats 1500. At the 1938 annual communication
more than three hundred were denied admission because of lack of
sufficient room.
The registered attendance at our Grand Lodge in 1938 was 1498,
made up as follows: Masters, 334; Wardens, 494; Past Masters, 660. Of the
Past Masters, 288 registered from San Francisco and East Bay Lodges,

Past Masters are not inherently members of Grand Lodge, but by
Constitutional provision are permanent members of this body. We hesitate
to suggest any curtailment of these useful members of their privileges,
and leave that phase of the subject entirely in your hands.
This year we are trying out an experiment by placing loud speakers
in an adjoining room, where a considerable number of brethren may be
seated and listen to the words spoken before the microphone. It may
prove to be a satisfactory answer to the problem of adequate seating, but
we are not at all sanguine that it will.
In connection with this whole subject, and as a partial solution to the
problem, we submit for your consideration a resolution that failed of
adoption in 1936, largely we believe through a misunderstanding of its
full import. The resolution is as follows:
"Resolved, that section 22 of the Constitution be amended to
read as follows:
"Sec. 22. Each Lodge represented •by a Master, Warden, Past
Master, or Representative duly elected, shall be entitled to one
vote.
"That sections 21, 23, 24 and 25 be repealed."
This amendment, if adopted, would deprive officers of Grand Lodge
and Past Grand Masters, and Past Masters not representing Lodges, from
the privilege of voting, but would not deprive them of the right to speak.
Taking the subject by and large, we are of the opinion that the views
of Brother Watson would be accomplished by the adoption of the New
York plan of representation. We express this opinion with some trepidation, having in mind the great value of the presence of Past Masters.
We ask that this report be referred to the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes for earnest study and report.

ANNUAL REPORT OF TRUSTEES OF THE
MASONIC HOMES
To the M.".W.".Grand Lodge of Califoniia:

As required by the Constitution, we present herewith a report of the
property, condition and operation of the Homes for the year ended July 31,
1939, together with a roster of residents to and including August 31st.
Pursuant to section 35 of the Constitution the board organized immediately after the close of Grand Lodge in October, 1938, by electing Charles
M. Wollenberg (whose term expires 1942) as president, and James B. Gist
(term expires 1939), as vice president.
The other members of the board are the following:
Samuel E. Burke (term expires 1940).
Chas. Albert Adams (term expires 1941).
William H. Waste, Deputy Grand Master.
William B. Ogden, Senior Grand Warden.
Lloyd E. Wilson, Junior Grand Warden.
The first report of trustees of the Masonic Widows and Orphans
Home was presented to this Grand Lodge at the annual communication of
October, 1892. The total membership of the jurisdiction then was only
16,000. In that report there was included the rules for admission and conduct of beneficiaries. Section 6 provided that "It shall be expressly understood that all beneficiaries of the Home shall be employed, according to
their age and capacity, in such household work, or mechanical or agricultural employment as may ·be required for the success and comfort of the
Home, it being rather a home than a hospital or an asylum."
All successive boards of trustees have adhered to that rule in the belief
that the beneficiaries, adults and children alike, should assist in making the
institution a real home, and that all should assume some share of the physical work required. A few-happily a very few-of the adult members of the
Home family object to performing physical labor, arguing that the Fraternity owes them a living. These few are unhappy and critical of the
management; whereas those who enter into the Home spirit are passing
their sunset days in serene contentment.
Profit and Loss on Bond Transactions
It is interesting to note from the report on the Endowment Funds

that all amortization of loss on bonds purchased is charged against the
income of the Home, but all profit on bonds sold is credited to the Endowment Fund. This, in the opinion of some of us, should be corrected.
While, generally speaking, it has not caused any financial distress to
the Homes, there are occasions when such a transaction might be of
moment to the particular fund involved. We call attention to schedule B-2, ·
Students' Loan Fund, wherein there was a loss on $5,000 Sugar Pine Lumber Company bonds of $2316.93, approximately 5 per cent of the total
amount of the fund.
We believe that if the Home funds absorb the loss, the Home fund
or general fund of the Home should also have the benefit of the profit.
