PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Improvements at Decoto Home
In April last we entered into a contract with Jones & King of Hayward to grade and surface the roads at the Decoto Home -at a cost of
$3,865.00. The work consisted of tearing up all the old roadways, including
the side ditches, bringing them to a uniform surface and resurfacing with
three courses of crushed rock and screenings and emulsified asphalt. Now,
instead of the dusty, rough old macadam roads, we have a modern, safe
and comfortable road from the State highway to the Home buildings.
The laundry machinery at Decoto, which had been in constant use for
many years, was partly replaced by _one 24x36 Troy minute man washer,
one 30-inch Hoffman Vorclone, and two ,30x36 Tumblers with double
steam coils.

Power Plant-Decoto
For several years we have endeavored · to obtain a lower rate for
electric power from the public service corporation serving our Home at
Decoto but without success, and this, notwithstanding that they give a
much lower rate to Mills College, only a short distance away.
It is our intention to remodel our existing boilers, · install a turbine
generator and as a by-product of our steam system, produce electricity.
In addition we will have to install a Diesel unit as a standby and to be used
in hot weather. We feel that a few years' operation of this system will
pay for itself,
Medical Care--Decoto
For many years the residents of Decoto were served by Dr. Elon A.
Ormsby, a resident . of the town of Centerville, who was very faithful in
his attendance on the Home. On March 24, 1939, he passed away.
He has been replaced by Dr. W. L. McWhirter, also a resident of
Centerville, a member of Alameda Lodge of that town.
We have arranged with our doctor for tri-weekly clinics, for a daily
attendance in the hospital and for such emergencies as from time to time
might arise, either by visitations to the Home or by visitations of our .
patient to his office. We feel that adequate service from the medical standpoint will be given our family at Decoto.
Old Age Security
Ever since the adoption of the Old Age Security law, the question of
the right of an inmate or resident of a Home such as ours to benefit by it
has been a moot subject. Two years ago we reported in detail the
situation under which fraternal homes were regarded by the State Department of Social Welfare. This year the law was amended and we hope
that no longer will members of the Masonic Fraternity and other similar
organizations be excluded from the benefit of this pension, if residing in a
Home such as ours.
·
There is considerable difference of opinion among members of the
Fraternity as to whether or not we should encourage the residents of our
Home who purpose remaining there to apply for old age security from the
State. There is some slight difference of opinion even among the members
oi our board of trustees. Some of us believe that it is inequitable and
unfair to aged dependents residing in fraternal institutions to be excluded
from any benefits to which they are entitled as citizens of our State. It is
our hope that this year will see the final solution of this problem.

GRAND LODGE OF CAI;IFORNIA

417

Value of Social Workers
Again we call attention to the value to the Homes in particular and the
Lodges generally, of our two social workers. They not only help and
advise with those who receive our grants but they carefully delve into all
avenues of government or family assistance that should be utilized before
making application for a grant from our funds.
Again we repeat that if you have any problems with your aged dependents that you wish us to help in solving, we will be glad to give you
the assistance of our investigators.
Repairs and Improvements at Covina Home
About a year ago, being faced with the necessity for certain improvements in our mechanical equipment at Covina, we authorized the superintendent to retain the part-time services of a consulting engineer to advise
in these matters. His report indicated that the first need was a •better
supply of domestic water. When the Home was built there were but few
people living between our institution and the source of supply in the wells
of the San Dimas Domestic Water Company. As the region settled up,
increasing demands were made upon the pipe line, until at certain periods
of the day there was no water to be had.
At our request the State Railroad Commission made a survey of the
situation and advised that the four-inch pipe be replaced with a six-inch
pipe; and on their recommendation we loaned the water company $3,501.00
to build this line, the water company crediting our monthly bills against the
loan and paying interest on the obligation. The result is a very much improved supply of water.
It also appeared in this connection that the layout of the water lines
within our property could be much improved with regard to fire protection.
Consultations were had with the Los Angeles County Fire Warden, and
with the Covina Fire Department. On their recommendations we installed
several fire hydrants; and we now have an arrangement with the Covina
Fire Department to answer any alarm from the Home property, a service
not heretofore available.
The County Fire Warden found that our wiring and switches required
certain changes in the interest of safety, and his recommendations have
been complied with. Our switchboards are now all dead-front; much open
cord wiring has been replaced with the safer metal mold.
A water-softening plant was installed to furnish soft water for steam
boilers, laundry, and dishwashing machine. The boilers have been thoroughly cleaned, furnaces relined, steam piping and valves overhauled or
renewed. Other minor changes too numerous to list have been made, each
one in the interest of safety, better service, or .greater economy. On the
whole, the mechanical plant is in better condition than ever before.
Also at Covina during most of the past year an extra painter has been
employed. Many dingy interiors have been repainted, and much of the
furniture has been repaired and refinished. On the whole the buildings are
in better condition than for many years past.
Sale of Dairy
During the year the Los Angeles County Health Department inspected
our dairy plant and found that it had fallen behind the times, and that an
expenditure of $3,000.00 or more would be required to remodel it to comply
with present standards. We found that we can buy good milk as cheap or
cheaper than we can produce it, e:xcclusive of the cost of rebuilding the plant.

We found also that the dairy had no special training value for boys in the
Home. We accordingly authorized the sale of the cattle and the closing
of this department of the Home's activities.

Education of the Children
It has been the policy in the Home from its inauguration to educate its
children in the public schools. Most of our children complete their high
school course. Each year for the past five or six years we have had an
average of sixteen boys and girls graduating from the high school. Beginning more than a year before their graduation, a careful study is made
of their attainment in school, and their proclivities as to a trade or occupation. We find it necessary for those who do not go directly into trade or
industry, that their high school program 'be supplemented with some vocational training. This we are a-ble to do through gifts that have been
made to our scholarship fund from time to time by generous individuals.
Real Children
It has ·been the aim of the Home since its foundation to be a home in
reality and not merely in name. We want our boys and girls to be real
boys and girls and not merely well-behaved little automatons. With this
in mind we think you will be interested in getting the portrait of one boy
a5 he picture~ himself in his application to be reappointed for another year,
as all o?r ch1.ldren. must do after the age of fifteen. He is not a model boy,
but he 1s seemg himself pretty clearly. This is the picture of a boy living
his own life, and not a life on an institutional pattern.
Let us quote first what his housefather says about him:
"He is a most likeable chap, pleasing personality, and rates
very high with his mates. He is not doing the best he can in school
studies; his school work is about average. He is somewhat disorderly in the •building and is inclined to rough-housing. ·when corrected shows his displeasure. We feel that in the next year he will
show considerable improvement because he realizes his faults. With
patience and guidance he should be among our best citizens next
year." .
Now here is what the boy says about himself:
"I believe that my conduct is characteristic of any boy going
through his adolescent stage. At times I have been corrected for
rowdyish conduct, 'but as Mr. Downen puts it himself, it was only
natural for me to be like that. I have been guilty of ·being one of a
party of four that stole a chicken from the pens at the farm; also
convicted of being A. W. 0 . L. about four times. My temperament
at times is far from agreeable; during these moody periods I am
not susceptible to correction without becoming disagreeable and
sometimes very stubborn. However, I realize that such a condition can be corrected by conscientiously applying myself to abandon these moods. On the other hand I am told that I am usually
a very likea.ble person and one easy to make friends.
"I class myself as a fair worker with better abilities than I
usually put forth. My earnings have 'been only 74 per cent of those
of the average working boy in my building. I blame this partly to
too many outside interests; during football season my mind is on
the gridiron, the same with basketball, track, and baseball. My
school work is average; I know I can do well over this but I ·have
a difficult time applying myself to my studies. I want to attend

The Freedom of the Home
Two girls, eleven and fourteen, recently were discharged to their
father, he having remarried and re-established the home which had been
broken years ago by the death of the children's mother. After her death
the father had the children in the care of various persons, including housekeepers and boarding homes, until finally they were accepted by your
trustees. After their recent discharge to their father an aunt wrote as
follows:
" I want to thank you and the housemothers for your interest
in my two nieces. T he Masonic Home gave those girls the only
physical, mental, and spiritual security they have had since they
lost their mother. They were so happy there. The older one
wanted to learn to do something so she could stay on there after
she graduated from high school. They are thinking about you all
every day, and are homesick for the freedom of the Home."
Of course we hope that they will find an even better home with their
father, but we are glad to believe that we were able to serve usefully in
the development of their lives when they were in need.
An Appreciative Graduate
Los Angeles, June 3, 1939.
To the Trustees of the Masonic HomeDear Friends:

Report of the Superintendent-Decoto Home
To the Board of Trustees:
Illness prevented my personal attention to the Home Report of 1938,
but I am pleased to present my statement for the year ending August 31
1939.
'
T•his constitutes my thirtieth annual report, rendering to you a complete review of Home service and progress during the past fiscal year.
It would be both a delight and an accomplishment to record all the
wonders of the Home. I have endeavored to impress upon each member
of the family individual responsibility, thereby creating a personal interest
in the enforcement and observance of most liberal and lenient rules and
regulations in the government of the Home.
There were enrolled at the beginning of the fiscal year, 345. There
were admitted from September 1, 1938, to August 31, 1939, 53, making a
total of 398. Passed a way during the year, 47. Voluntary departures, 2,
leaving a total of 349 residents, men and v. omen. There are 27 married
couples.
The man·y operating departments include janito!' and maid service
throughout all buildings. Members of the Home family are required to
service their own rooms. However, a house maid gives their rooms a
thorough cleaning ea·c h week.

441

Dining rooms and kitchen are large and airy. Ventilation and cleanliness, vital necessities, are refreshing and healthful.
Regular employes, assisted by Home volunteers, prepare and serve
a well balanced bill of fare of inviting and substantial food. Diet tables
are provided for those whose physical condition require special food.
Laundry is equipped with latest modern machinery. With expert
laundrymen to direct, clean linen is returned weekly to the members of
the Home.
The sewing room is one of the most important and busy units of operation. Three very obliging and ·pleasing needle experts not only mend and
repair all Home linen, bed clothes, curtains, etc., but find time to darn,
patch and almost make new wearing apparel of every description.
Tonsorial service is an absolute essential to health. Our !barber shop
is indispensable. An efficient workman is on daily duty each morning,
except Friday and Saturday, .for men. Thursday is reserved for ladies.
The drug store is open twice daily, except Sunday. Here one finds
toilet articles, to·b acco, stationery, notions and many other miscellaneous
little things to complete his desire for physical and mental comforts.
All staple and standard remedies for minor complaints are dispensed.
Prescriptions are filled and delivered daily, by a reputable and dependable
pharmacy within close ·proximity to the Home.
Realizing that proper care of teeth and eyes is a most important factor
for prevention of many physical disorders, we stress the necessity of dental
and optical treatment. Appointments for this attention are made with the
best nearby practitioners in the profession, and transportation is furnished
for patients' visitation.
The Emporium at the Home is a very important shopping center. All
wearing apparel received by the Home, if not clean and in good repair is
sent to the cleaners and tailors for proper conditioning. Many suits, hats,
shoes, underwear, etc., are always available for members of the Home family. Everything left unclaimed by deceased members, and donations of
others is distributed through 'the Emporium.
One of the best equipped key shops possible, in charge of an expert
locksmith is one of the most useful mechanical departments. Carpenter
and paint shop, directed ·b y competent workmen keep the Home secure
and attractive.
The grounds are supervised by a regular gardener. However, many
of the residents have their own gardens whkh they •h ave beautified by the
planting of shrubs and flowers.
Regufar days are assigned for those who have business, optical, dental
or medical engagements in Oakland and San Francisco. Cars leave the
Home twice a week, returning in the afternoon in time for the evening
meal. All members must register out or in when absenting themselves
from the Home. Transportation is always cheerfully provided for special
trips, and morning and evening service to Niles, for railroa-d patrons.
Mail is received once a day, except Sunday, and is collected twice
daily. Very prompt and efficient service is rendered by those responsible
for its delivery.
Telephone hours are from 7:00 a. m . until 10 :00 p. m.
T•he Home hospital is situated in rear of the North Wing where noise
and other annoying features are eliminated, and where a corps of nurses
are in constant attendance day and night. Orders of the Home physician
are obeyed with sympathetic understanding and kindness.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The efficiency of the medical department is evidenced by the low
deat·h rate. There is no doubt that our hospital is one of the best equipped
fraternal institutions of like character to be found.
The general health and mental condition of the Home family seems
to be far above par when age is considered.
The best way to discover physical happiness or mental dissatisfaction
is by observation of the daily actions of those seeking relaxation and playful
pastimes. Amusements vary to suit the individual liking of those who participate.
·
The library, reading and club rooms are popular, where hundreds of
books and magazines furnish opportunity for restful moments and intellectual improvement.
Visitations of various Masonic organizations, Eastern Star Chapters,
Job's Daughters, Order of the Rainbow for Girls, Order of De Molay, etc.,
who present dramatic and musical programs are always greeted with large
and appreciative audiences. The silver screen is illuminated every Thursday
evening with the latest and 'best movies.
Lectures are enjoyed and largely attended. Our orchestra furnishes
dance music for our socials, and dances given in our Assembly Hall. Community singing is a delightful weekly affair. Cards, bridge, five hundred,
whist, and every other game are always open for an extra player.
Club rooms for men, where billiards, pool, cril>bage and solitaire are
principal diversions, are well patronized.
The visitors' dining room is situated in the basement of the South
Wing. Visiting delegations, large and small, find everything necessary
for indoor picnic parties. Exceptional equipment is arranged to supply
every culinary need.
A pleasing Sunday afternoon, nonsectarian, religious service is conducted in the large Assembly Hall. The Home choir is a group of splendid voices, and is a most enjoyable feature of Sabbath observance.
Special effort to produce sufficient poultry, fruit and vegetables for
the Home consumption is not attempted. However, a large percentage of
farm yard items served are home grown, wherelby a saving of no small
amount is recorded in our operating expenses. ·
T•h ere •has been no decrease in our water supply. Our reservoirs have
been kept full at all times and they have :been equal to all demands made
upon them for household, lawns and irrigating purposes.
The imposing and spacious Temple on the Home grounds stands for
what the members of the Craft have found in it. Meetings are frequent
when visiting Lodges exemplify the work, thereby bringing to the brethren
of the Home the opportunity of again going to Lodge and refreshing their
memories of the good old days when they participated in the making of
a Mason.
An intimate personal observance is always my objective in locating
and reconditioning those things which make the Home safe from any unforeseen happening which might result in serious accidental occurrence.
All driveways were resurfaced during the summer. New stairway from
boiler house to main building was installed. Two large illuminated signs in
blue and gold now invite the stranger who pass.es this way, to California's
Masonic Home.
The visitors' register shows very large increase) over former years,
and many are impressed with our perfertly appointed buildings, beautiful

grounds, gardens of splendor and color, and atmosphere of contentment.
They cannot refrain, when registering, from expressing with notation,
their tribute of praise for California's Home of Fraternal Blessedness.
The observance of special days is celebrated on National holidays.
Appropriate entertainment is offered on Christmas and New Year's Eve
and Day. Thanksgiving, Lincoln's and Washington's Birthday, Memorial
Day and Fourth of July. Christmas is the day of days. T1he Home family
wait for Santa Claus with childhood antidpation. Lodges, Eastern Star
Chapters and immediate friends are indeed mindful of t·h e opportunity to
shower gifts of love upon those whom years of faithful service deserv.e
more than a message of good cheer.
Officers of the Grand Lodge, the Board· of Trustees, members of
various Lodges, and Eastern Star Chapters have honored us with visitations during the year. We welcome your interest with true Masonic spirit.
This is your recognition of our usefulness, and we desire at all times your
outspoken praise or constructive criticism.
The past year has been uneventful of exceptional mention. We have
as in former years accepted conditions and situations with cautious investigation and sensible judgment. This year of service has proved a pleasant
task and a happy period for me. Harmony and good will have pervaded,
not only in the Home family, but throughout all departments. Employes
have been of great assistance, putting forth every effort in a keen understanding of the fulfillment of duty.
The matron and myself have endeavored to enforce a constructive program of popular co-operation. Some problems are very real, others seem
imaginary, yet all are particular and must be solved. We know our judgment has been accepted in most cases for the best.
The Home stands as a monument to the zeal, energy and la'bor of all
California Masons.
In conclusion, the Matron and myself extend our gratitude and thanks
for your confidence and favors bestowed. May our future actions, as
directors of your orders, in the operation of the Home continue with God's
guidance and blessed assistance.
For the welfare of all concerned, we should ever remember those precepts which unite us into one indissoluble band of friends and Brothers,
whose chief concern should ever be: "Who best can serve and best agree."

442

FRANK B. HARTMAN,

443

Superintendent.

Report of the Superintendent-Covina Home
To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:

Herewith I am presenting my thirteenth annual report as superintendent of the Covina Home. During the past year there were 20 admissions, (18 'boys and 2 girls); and 27 discharges, (12 :boys and 15 girls.)
In the admissions during the past three years, boys have outnumbered girls
by about two to one; and at the present time there are approximately twice
as many boys as gi.rls in t'he Home. This disproportion is to be regretted,
because an approximate balance as between boys and girls makes for a
more natural and wholesome social group.
The graduating class of this year was the largest in the history of the
Home, twenty. Of these, five are attending college, four are attending
vocational schools, eight are working, three are at home with relatives.
Of those who are going on for further schooling, two are obtaining aid
from the Masonic Home Scholarshi\> Fund; the seven others are working
their way or are ·being aided from other sources.
Special mention should ;be made of John Morgan of this year's class.
Among 165 graduates of the Covina High School Class of 1939 he ranked
first in scholarship. He was prominent in scho~l athletics, w;s president
of the Student Body of the High School. He has entered Harvard University this fall as the winner of a $900.00 scholarship, 'being one of twentyseven students in the United States to win such scholarships.
The Los Angeles Masonic Employment Service has taken an active
interest in placing our ·g raduates in jobs. One boy who .g raduated was a

Gustav White, a member of Arcadia Lodge ~o. 547, and a professional
vocational and personal counsellor. His services to them have been of
distinct value.
Alumni-The terms "alma mater" and "alumnus" are comm?nly used
to designate educational institutions and their. graduates. But smce . they
mean "foster mother" and "foster child" we thmk they apply appropnately
to the Home and its former children. We class as an alumnus any boy or
girl who formerly lived in our Home, whether graduated or not.
We endeavor to keep in touch wit>h these former members of the Ho~e.
They return frequently for visits. Every week-end some of them ~re with
us; in summer, visits from those living as far away as San Francisco are
frequent.
We issue once or twice a year an Alumni Newsletter, which is mailed
to all the alumni whose whereabouts we know. In this Newsletter are news
items about many individuals, also news of the Home. We get many expressioqs of appreciation and interest after each Newsletter.
During Grand Lodge week of each year the alumni living in the San
Francisco Bay area have a reunion dinner, always attended by fifty or
more alumni, their hus'bands and wives. Those living in the Los Ange.les
area have a homecoming at the Balboa Camp each summer, and a reunion
dinner at the Covina Home in February.
I have often said to a boy or a girl who thought I was too severe, ."I
am not so much concerned with what you think of us now as I am with
what you will think of us ten years from now." I believ.~ that almost
all of those who have lived here in former years look upon their alma mater
with loyalty and love. If they did not I think we should .stan~ j~stly
weighed and found wanting. We continually st~dy our alumm, then: Judgment of our work with them, and their progress m the world, to rectify our
course in the conduct of the Home.
Health-From a membership of 153 children we had during the year
an average number in the hospital of 1.76, or slightly more. t~an one per
cent the best health record in our history. We .feel that this is the result
of o~r thorough program of preventive medicine. Ea~h c~ild is . carefully
examined upon entrance, and periodically thereafter. V1tamm-bearmg products and endocrine preparations are prescribed in many cases.
The clinic of Drs. Magan, Norwood and Nethery, which has taken
care of our medical work for many years past, has recently greatly enlarged
its facilities, and these are at our disposal. In the dental line, Dr. D. H.
Wilkins has taken care of our children for the past fourteen years, most
efficiently. Eye examinations are given when there is indicati.on of defective vision; glasses have been supplied to about 30% of our children.
Psychological Point of View-It is a serious responsibility and a high
privilege to be concerned as we are with the developing lives of children.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

463

We are constantly striving to gain more insight into the hidden processes
of character development. More and more, we are finding out that desirable behavior on the part of children will come about naturally if their emotional life is well ordered. There is no such thing as a bad child; a so-called
bad child should rather be recognized as an injured or damaged chill:l.
Modern psychology does not accept the idea that children should be
brought up under a regime of blind obedience to authority. It holds that
it is essential that a community of feeling be established ·between the child
and the adult who is leading him, and that the child should participate
in every decision regarding him. Less and less do we depend upon "discipline" and punishment; more and more do we depend upon finding and
removing emotional disturbances that produce anti-social behavior.
The child who is always obedient and completely docile, while he serves
our convenience for the time being, is not serving the interests of his own
future welfare. A certain amount of struggle against the controls that are
imposed upon ·him is to be expected from the youngster who is getting
ready to take his part in the battle of life.
During part of the past year we have had the .p art time services of a
well-trained psychologist. His work has been effective in helping us to
unravel the tangles of disordered personalities. Through his contact with
our staff members they have gained a better understanding of the causes
of various types of children's behavior and how to modify that behavior
into more desira•ble patterns.
Summer Camp at Balboa-As usual du ring many years past, the children spent the major part of the summer at Camp Tucker on Balboa Island.
The camp was kept in operation for ten weeks, a longer period than in any
previous summer. While the location of the Camp has become less desirable than formerly on account of the fact t hat it is now in the midst of a
densely ·populated town, nevertheless it is still on salt water, with swimming, boating, fishing, picnicking, and California sunshine all abundant.
Aside from these the camp has a capital value in that it gives the children
a change of scene and a relief from monotony. Children can endure monotony less well than grown-ups; and a weakness of group living is that it
necessitates routine. We have not yet invented a way to get a long without
bells, signals and programs. After nine months of this the summer camp
is welcomed as a release; the children come home from camp recreated
and ready for school again.
Children are also allowed to spend as much as thirty days a year visiting friends or relatives if conditions are suitable. Summer is the season
for most of these visits, and the effect of them is generally beneficial.
Birthdays-In a child's life a birthday is important. He likes to have
notice taken of it. To him it is a milestone in his progress toward being
grown up.

In the Home our cook always makes a specially decorated birthday
cake for each child, with candles, and his name lettered on it. He may
invite his special friends to dinner at his table, with this cake as the feature
of the dinner. When candle~blowing time comes, everybody in the dining
room is waiting to see if he succeeds; but whether he does or not they all
clap their hands. Oftentimes his mother or some relative is here to celebrate with him. Little private birthday parties are often held in the children's buildings, with presents from relatives and from other children.
Altogether, birthdays are happy times for our children.

Boys and Girls Speak to Lodge&-The activities of the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board have led to numerous requests for us ~o send older
children 'to Lodge meetings, in order to bring the ~tory of th~ Hom~ to
their membership. While we do not approve of the idea of making trained
performers of our children, we have been glad to re~pond t~ these requests
whenever possible. We usually send a boy and a girl, of high school age,
and we try to send d.jfferent ones each time. Their presentations, informal
and unrehearsed have 1been well received, and have been of value to the
youngsters as ex'perience in meeting people, and in public speaking. Moreover, they have ibrought back to the other children a better understanding
of their relationship to Masons and Masonry.

Picture Shows-Through the year we have been able to give the children a weekly picture show on Saturday nights. Films for this purpose
have ·been supplied free of charge by a number of the leading film exchanges. We are indebted to Brother Bill Knotts, owner of the Covina
Theater, for contacting the various exchanges weekly and arranging with
them for the bookings of our pictures. We are also indebted to Masonic
employees of the Twentieth Century Fox Company for indispensable service in keeping our motion picture equipment in good working order. The
motion picture is preferred by our children to every other form of entertainment. There seems to be no limit to the number of pictures they want
to see.
Awards for Good Citizenship-The concept of public spirit and community service is not an entirely easy one for the adolescent to grasp.
Yet there is no idea which it is more desirable shall be inculcated in his
thought. Through the interest and generosity of Brother Robert T . West,
the Past Grand Comma·nders Association, Knights Templar of Southern
California, we were able to offer again this year two awards, each a gold
watch, to the boy and the girl who were deemed to have done the most in
the way of public spirited service for the Masonic H ome community. The
decision as to these awards was made by the older children themselves;
and in accord with the suggestion of Brother West they made their selections in a series of three ballots, three months apart. This voting, together
with the discussion that accompanied it, had a marked effect in bringing the
conception of good citizenship into focus in the children's consciousness.

REPORT OF MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California.:
Your board herewith presents its seventh annual report, being for the
period between July 31st, 1938, and July 31, 1939.
The board is now constituted as follows:

William P. Filmer, Treasurer

Reynold E. Blight, Secretary
The Harvest Season
This is the season of the harvest. This is the season when crops-if well
planted and diligently cared for-are ready for the hand of the reaper. Man
has, since his first knowledge of nature's seasonal bounty, observed the fall a~
the time for garnering the products of his toil against the barren months to
come. The results of his agricultural diligence are displayed in the ripe fields
and in the burdened vines of his tilled grounds and tended orchards. A great
joy fills the heart of the harvester and-since the dawn of history-his husbandry has been made the occasion for autumnal rites and ceremonies in keeping
with the joyousness and abundaoce of the season.
It is, therefore, felicitous and altogether conformable with established customs of husbandry that we gather here today, to examine in nature's harvest
time the harvest of our hearts ; to ascertain the yield of our stewardship in
the fields of love and charity; to learn whether the seeds we have sown over
the years have blossomed and ripened, to learn whether we have cultivated all
we possibly could; to find out whether our harvest is as great as we desire, or
as bountiful as we are entitled by our efforts and labors.
Program for Year

Work of Lodge Officials and Endowment Chairmen.
fo carrying out the work for the yea!"' just closed, the board, as in the past,
placed much dependence upon officials of constituent Lodges and upon the
shoulders of Endowment chairmen, who were, in many cases, l'.eappointed at the
request of the board and in line with the Masters' and Secretaries' desire to
place the affairs of the Homes Endowment Fund in thoroughly experienced
hands.
The early appointment of chairmen was urged by the board at the beginning of the fiscal year, in 'order that the work could be mapped out and prorated over the ensuing months with the purpose of bringing to each member
the opportunity and privilege of rendering his share, large or small, to the
program. It is interesting to note that Lodges making such early appointment of

480

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

481

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

chairmen, are now leading, almost without exception, in the parade of achievements for the year. It thus offers proof anew that the Homes Endowment
Fund program is an all-year-round program, requiring constant diligence and
effort on the part of informed officials in bringing to the brethren the privilege
of service. The sole reason for any constituent Lodge's failure to become
listed in the Endowment Fund's annual scroll of honor, is today, and has beeh
in the past, due altogether to either procrastination or forgetfulness. And,
inasmuch as no single Lodge, or group of Lodges, possesses a corner in generosity-all being equal by common Masonry-all that is needed is the contact
work of an active committee, to transform a pas.rfue concern into a wholehearted and active participation. This is guaranteed by the work of an experienced, capable committee, thoroughly informed on the many phases of the
Homes program, and anxious to perform personal contact service among the
brethren in the interest of our Home guests.
Correspondence and Literature
During the year, the board, adhering strictly to its policy of conducting an
educational program, rather than a drive-for-funds, inaugurated several plans
for furthering the work of the Homes among constituent Lodges and its members. Serving as a clearing house for new and meritorious ideas, the board was
enabled to exchange data with secretaries and chairmen in matters which had
proven worth while in other Lodges. Among those who submitted excellent
ideas for use by his colleagues of the jurisdiction was Brother Frank S. Templar
of Pentalpha Lodge No. 202, whose interest and concern met, not only the thanks
and approval of the board, but of those who shared his ideas as well. The
board welcomes a free exchange of plans which have proven their worth, and
urges a continuation of this brotherly phase of activity among Lodge officials
and chairmen.
The board caused to be printed and distributed a "Card of Remembrance,"
which was designed for display during Lodge sessions either on the Tiler's or
Secretary's desk, as a gentle but insistent reminder that within our home circle
were men, women and children, whose daily lives were wholly dependent. on the
care and solicitude evinced by the Craft. The board believes that the display
of the~e "Cards of Remembrance" served a valuable purpose throughout the
year and suggests they be utilized continuously during the coming months.

In keeping with the plan of co-operation with constituent Lodges in all
phases of the Fund program, the board, realizing the importance of the printed
word, prepared and distributed a number of Homes Endowment briefs for use
in Lodge bulletins. These briefs, prepared in sentence and paragraph form,
were released as an aid to the various bulletin staffs, and we were gratified to
observe their use in Lodge bulletins throughout the year.
During the year the board received about 1,000 pieces of correspondence
and sent out 18,780· pieces. In addition to regular monthly correspondence with
Masters and Secretaries, the board drafted letters to donors, to Lodges which
had made no contribution . for a period of two years, to the twelve Lodges
leading in contributions for 1938, to attorney members of the Craft regarding
wills and bequests, and a special Christmas letter to all Lodges during the holiday period of 1938.
Pamphlets to the number of 140,000 were mailed out during the year.
Many of these printed pieces represented compilations of previous years and
were requested as an aid to the program by secretaries and chairmen. Of the
new pamphlets, those under the titles of "Democracy of Masonry," "The
Helping Hand of Masonry," and "The Miracle of the Homes Endowment

Dollar," enjoyed a wide distribution and undoubtedly served to more fully acquaint the brethren with the idealism and benevolence of the Homes Endowment program.
Bindings containing all the pamphlets compiled to date were placed in the
hands of all Secretaries as a means of supplying source material on the Homes
and of providing a catalogue from which desired copies could readily be ordered
at any time the need arose.
Comparative charts showing the amounts accruing from all Lodges for a
prior period of two years were also sent to Secretaries in order to keep the
various Lodges informed as to the general response as well as the financial
status of the Homes.

In order that your board may function during the ensuing year, we offer
the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
"Resolved, that the sum of six thousand dollars be and is hereby appropriated from the funds of this Grand Lodge to be paid to the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board for its expenses for the year ending July 31st, 1940."
The board, in presenting the figure of $26,813.20 which was realized through
voluntary contributions from the membership during the fiscal year (as of
September 1), begs leave to comment on the prevailing retrogressive financial
conditions as well as the continued unemployment among our brethren. In
view of these conditions the total sum realized is of significant importance in
the accounting of our stewardship. In comparison with flush as well as lean
years, the aggregate discloses Masonic generosity in spite of unfavorable times,
but still does not reach the heights dictated by whole-hearted mass regard,
irrespective of times or conditions.
.
Reduced to individual figures, the board's meaning is clarified: With a
total membership in the jurisdiction of approximately 127,005, donors to the
Fund this year reached a total of 6,500, representing a percentage of 4.33 in
comparison with last year's percentage of 3.61. The average contribution' of
.21 represents an increase of 6 per cent over the average of 1938.
The 6,500 donors, listed as of September 1, 1939, represented individual
contributors from 414 Lodges out of 582, leaving a total of 168 Lodges yet to
make reports, or to pass up the privilege for the year of making a true investment in happiness. An interesting side light on the number of specified amounts

It is interesting to speculate on· the splendor, the complete possibilities of
the program, if such generous donors were multiplied by the total membership
of about 127,000 ! ! ! The heart and soul of the Fraternity is its charitable
activity and in making a donation toward the welfare of our beloved institutions,
brethren are assured not only of efficient administration and wise investment,
but of the soul-satisfying realization of duty well and permanently done, for
here, in the Grand Lodge, is a fund never to be decreased, but one that goes
on and on, multiplying in its donor's name the benevolent care and solicitude
that is the existence and purpose of a mighty Fraternity.
Testamentary Gifts
The fund for the year was swelled by the entrance of testamentary gifts to
the amount of $31,772.51. These wills and bequests, made possible largely
through the efforts of attorney members of the Craft, are destined to fulfill the
intent of the benefactor of supplying financial bulwarks and of guaranteeing
additional safeguards to the members of the home circle at Decoto and Covina.
Becoming a part of the Permanent Endowment Fund, these gifts, symbolizing
their legators' Masonic benevolence, are in truth, monuments in miniature, in
that they will everlastingly prorate over the years the kindness and generosity
that inspired them.
The board is deeply grateful to members of the legal profession throughout the State for their interest in bringing to their clients' attention the opportunities for providing happiness and the far-reaching good that accrues from a
Home investment by will or bequest. Such attorneys know that the Grand
Lodge has so judiciously invested its proceeds that despite the stringency of
the times not a single dollar has ever been lost from the Permanent Endowment
Fund; they know that in suggesting the Homes Fund as a beneficiary, that principal is never decreased and that returns are administered as wisely and as
economically as their clients would desire it.
There is a vast field for good, both for donor and recipient in Homes
Endowment wills and bequests, and in expressing sincere thanks to jurisdiction
attorneys for their past great work, the board urges their continued co-operation in this worth-while realm of Masonic charity.
Home Visitations
The board is pleased to report an increase of Homes-mindedness among the
brethren, with a corresponding increase of individual and group visitations to
the Homes at Decoto and Covina. During the year many brethren accepted
for the first time the standing invitation extended by the management for Home
visits and were much impressed by the efficient administration, the ideal home
atmo~phere, the peace and contentment of the elders, and the happy, life-loving
activities of the youngsters.

484

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The first time the visitor saw these things and, marveling, swelled with pride
at the thought that his fellowship with Masonry made him a partner in the
exalted reality of the Homes. He learned that the elders and children, while
happy and at peace in their surroundings, were made yet happier by his visit,
his interest in their welfare, and by the fact that he was welcomed both as an
individual and as a representative of his Lodge. He then realized that he had,
all unsuspectedly at the outset of his visit, drawn tighter the bond that united.
them with the Lodge that had asked for and received permission to place them
within the Home circle; he realized that the children and elders are equally
the wards of Lodges as they are of the Homes proper. He understood for
the first time that here was no one-sided contract, with the burden placed
entirely upon the Homes and others, but one in which he and his Lodge, which
had sought and received permission for their entrance, should participate freely
and equally, both in material and spiritual support.
He had learned the lesson that Masonry becomes more conscious through
human contact, and that in establishing personal relationship and responsibility
he had bettered not only himself, but the objects of his concern as well. The
board recommends to all Lodges-to all brethren-a visit to the Homes at
Decoto and Covina. It guarantees an object lesson in direct and personal
responsibility, and, in association with members of the Home family, it vouches
for the kindling of a new and keener cognizance of the great heart work of
the Fraternity.
Work of Grand Master and Officials
The report of the year would be incomplete if the board failed to properly
record its deep appreciation of the splendid work of our Grand Master, who,
throughout the year gave freely of his time and efforts in promoting a better
understanding between Lodges and the Homes. Brother Whitsell, learned in
Home affairs through long association, deeply interested in the welfare and
happiness of our Home guests, traveled throughout the length and breadth
o f the jurisdiction, giving unstintingly of his deep knowledge, and unquestionably
contributed greatly to the general increase of interest among brethren of the
jurisdiction. The board appreciates the great work performed by our Grand
Master, and it extends its sincere thanks to him for conducting a splendid
campaign of education among constituent Lodges, and for giving the brethren
an opportunity of learning infinitely more of our program of love and mercy.
To Masters, Secretaries, and chairmen of Endowment committees, the
board also expresses its gratitude for work consistently well done. Without
the sympathetic service of Lodge officials, working in accord with the idealistic
principles of the Homes Endowment Fund, the board would be powerless to
proceed with the work at hand. It must, of necessity, depend on the cooperation and assistance rendered by officers of the various Lodges, and past
experience has shown that in the main, such support has been readily and
whole-heartedly given. For this the board is indeed grateful.
In furthering the work for the coming year, the board earnestly solicits
of incoming Masters the early appointment of Endowment chairmen; the prorating of work over the entire year rather than a short period of intense work;
the consistent use of Lodge bulletins in portraying the various phases of the
Homes progra!TJ; the dissemination of informative pamphlets among the members of the Craft ; and the regular appearance of Homes Endowment speakers
at Lodge gatherings.
During the past year the board received a number of communications from
brethren who complained that the Homes Endowment matter had never been
brought to the attention of their respective Lodges. The incoming Masters'

485

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

only answer to such a charge is to institute and carry out the aforementioned
program in such a manner as to present ~o. ~~ery Craftsma? .an equal op~r­
tun,ity with others in sharing the respons1b1hties and. the pn~ileges of s~r~1ce
extended by the Homes. No member sh~uld be d_emed his nghtfu~ partmpation in the program dedicated to the idealism of his chosen Fraternity.

Report adopted as read, excepting that portion asking for an

To the M.". w:. c,.and Lodge F. & A. M. of Califo,.nia:
It has seemed to your committee that a report to Grand Lodge on the
Twentieth Annual Observance of Public Schools Week might be appropriately devoted to a review of the growth and development of what in its
inception was a purely Masonic undertaking. This will, of course, preclude a detailed report of our latest observance; and we must omit the
special mention which would be otherwise made of many notable programs
presented this year.
The nature of the observance in general might be well described as
was a loca·I observance by the County Superintendent of Schools who in a
letter said: "We took the school to the clubs and brought the people to
the school." In that terse and epigrammatic sentence there is implicit the
development of the ideal program designed to convey to the people information concerning their schools, and also the fine co-operation received
through the service clubs and other organized units of community life.
The only other reference that will be made to this year's observance will be
such as may be suggested by a review of the years of long ago.
There are many, of course, to whom the story of Public Schools Week
is an old one; but judging from the inquiries received each year it would
appear that even among the Masters and Wardens there are some who do
not seem to have a very intimate knowledge of the observance in which
they so actively participate. This wiJI not seem strange if we remember
that a very large proportion of the Craft in California today (and among
whom are the Masters and Wardens of recent years) became members of
the Fraternity since the time when Public Schools Week was first brought
to the attention of practically every Mason in this jurisdktion.
In our reference to the past it is our purpose "because now it can be
told" to make mention of some of the trials and tribulations of those early
years when success hung in the balance; and of the apathy and even seeming
opposition in certain quarters where encouragement and support instead
might well have been expected. And when convenient we shall include
excerpts from reports heretofore made to Grand Lodge--with the consciousness that no one will remember ever having heard or read them.
It will be remembered, of course, that Public Schools Week was instituted in 1920 because of the crisis with which the public school system
in America was · then confronted. Due to several causes, but principally to
the lure of high salaries elsewhere, there was such a scarcity of teachers
that more than 18,000 schools had been closed. Someone had wittily said
that there were so many resignations that it seemed as though the teaching
profession had become a procession-into other pursuits. Furthermore,
of the 600,000 teachers available, at least one-half had had no special training; one-third had had less than four years schooling :beyond the eighth
grade and one-fourth were under 21 years of age. There were more than
6000 teaching on temporary permits. Here in California, there was a
shortage of 12CO teachers and. 600 schools had been closed-mostly in
rural districts.
Certain remedial measures had been proposed, but apparently were
receiving little, if any, public attention. There was evident everywhere
an apathy which undoubtedly resulted from a lack of knowledge of the
real situation.

508

PROCEEDINGS OF . THE

Here was a great danger threatening an institution in which every
American citizen was vitally interested and which has always been the
especial concern of the Masonic Fraternity. That danger might be averted
if the people could be aroused from their apathy.
Now it happened that the Grand Master of Masons in California had
long been of the opinion that the professions we make as Masons .demand
that as citizens of the Commonwealth we take an active and intelligent
interest in all public questions, and especially in all matters affecting our
public schools. It therefore seemed to him eminently proper that the Craft
in California should be fully informed of the situation, and that an effort
should be made to awaken them to a realization of their duty as citizens.
He therefore concluded to set aside by Proclamation a week to be known
as "Public Schools Week" in the Masonic Lodges of this jurisdiction during which attention would be focused on the public schools. The time
originally set was the last week in May; ib ut after consultation with friends
of his among the school people it was changed to the week commencing
September 27th. In his proclamation the Grand Master requested. that during that week a meeting be held in every Lodge which would be open to
the friends and families of the members, and at which conditions affecting
the public schools should be discussed by qualified s.peakers.
Although the idea was a novel one, and to some revolutionary in character, there was an almost universal compliance with the request .made by
the Grand Master. Although the meetings were open to the public, and
were so a-dvertised, they were held in the Lodge rooms; and as would be
expected, the attendance was very largely confined to the members and
their families.
The State Superintendent of Public Instruction had expressed his willingness to aid in every way possible; and with the notices whi~h had been
sent out by him to the County Superintendents, no difficulty was experienced in securing their co-operation. The speakers at these meetings were,
very naturally, in great part school people; but there were also lay speakers
who had become conversant with the subjects to be discussed through literature which was sent to the Lodges with a "Bulletin of Suggestions"
and a tentative program.
One of the subjects which was .d iscussed was an amendment to the
State Constitution which had been proposed and was to be on the ballot
at the ensuing election. Incidentally it was adopted; and to this fact is
largely due the enviable position California now occupies in the educational world; because it established in the Constitution a fixed contri'bution
of state fonds for the public schools based on average daily pupil attendance
and which was thereby freed from political trade and barter.
In view of the criticism which in the early days of the movement came
from some of our sister jurisdictions to the effect that the Masons in California were engaging in politics, and particularly because of the reference
just made to the Constitutional amendment, it wiU be well, we think, to
here set out certain inhibitions imposed from the very beginning in connection with the observance.
·
The following excerpts are quoted from the Bulletin accompanying
the Proclamation establishing Public Schools Week and to which reference
has 1been already made:
·
"Masons should be reminded that as good citizens and because
of their professions as Masons it is their duty to inform themselves
regarding conditions . affecting the public schools in their several
communitie!'. . . .
·
·

509

"It will be at all times remembered, of course, that Masonry
is not a political organization and that the Fraternity and M~sons,
as such take no part in advancing the interests of any particular
candida~e for office; and that the purpose of these meetings is o~ly
to inform the members of existing conditions, and of the remedial
measures proposed so that they m~ as individuals discharge their
duty as citizens. There will be no im~ropriety, however,. in suggesting to those present that if they believe the measures discussed
deserve the support of all good citizens and are for the benefi~ of
the public school system an? .therefore, of cour~e, ?f the. Nation,
they may, and should as ind1v1duals do all that hes in their power
to secure their adoption.
"In this conneci'ion, however, it is to be particularly remembered that these discussions are not intended as propaganda for
the support of any part_icular ~easure-:--nation~I, state or. local.
They are intended to be informative and . instr~ctlve only, with .the
idea that there shall ·be a fair and full d1scuss1on of every subiect
presented. Any member present should not only b_e P.ermitted,. ~ut
encouraged, to express any views he may entertain in oppos1tion
to those presented by a speaker.
"Whatever may be the nature of the program ~opted there is. to
be ~io action of a11y sort taken at any of these meetings. No pending
legislation is to be endorsed or disapproved and there is to be no
resolution adopted concerning it."
This pioneer observance of Public Scho?ls W, eek was an unqualifi~d
success from every point of view. Informat10n with respect to the penis
confronting the schools was disseminated not onl.y. by th~ speakers at these
public meetings, ·but through the newspaper publicity which the ~bservance
attracted. And there was great rejoicing both within and without. the
Fraternity among all the friends of the p~blic schools. The Masons felt
that as traditional protagonists of the public school system they had been
given an opportunity to square their professions with their practices;. and
the school people were loud in their praise of wh~t had been accomplished
by the Masonic Fraternity in awakening the pub!1~ generally, no less than
the Craft itself, to a realization of existing conditions.
Although the immediate crisis which gave birth to the idea. h~d pass.e d,
each successive Grand Master continued the observance until 1t beca~e
a firmly established activity of Grand Lodge; but for a few years following
the first observance such obstacles were encountered as could not h~ve
been overcome had it not been for the loyalty, zeal and unselfish devotion
of those ardent friends of public education who sensed the value of the
movement and who persisted in their endeavors in the face of repeated
disappointments and discouragements which took various forms.
There had been always a little group in Grand Lodge (a very small o~e
it is true but an influential one) who were honestly doubtful of the wisdom of a' Masonic activity such as this ; and to whom it was an innova·tion
that should not be encouraged even if countenanced. No support could be
expected from them; nor was any received: There were others who, ~~­
thusiastic in the beginning, apparently believed that now tha;t the cns1s
had passed it was all wasted effort and that nothing wo;thwhile could be
accomplished by continuing the observance. T~ey .~ailed to . see. what
Grand Master Crites later pointed out when he said: The subject is not
one of passing importance. As a matter of f~ct it becomes with each yassing year of greater significance. There are influences that are consc10usly

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

antagonistic to popular education. There are others selfishly concerned
to deny to the schools that generous support that must be accorded if
they are to give the desired results. There are new facts to be considered;
new alignments of forces that must be estimated; political and economic
factors that require careful thought to properly measure. Then again the
interest already aroused must 'be maintained and intensified. The Fraternity in California cannot afford to rest on what may have been accomplished. It must press forward to new and greater achievements."

had not been provided or the proper method had not been followed to
secure the active co-operation of the civic organizations in the community.
The greatest difficulty experienced in those early years was in having
it generally understood that although instituted and fostered by the Fraternity, the observance of Public Schools Week was not merely a Masonic
event but a community affair in which the entire community should participate. Masters seemed to feel that they had done everything that was
required of them if they sent to the various organizations of the community
a special notice or perhaps an invitation; and this notwithstanding the fact
that it had lbeen repeatedly pointed out to them that just as every individual
is more interested in a movement in which he has a part than he is in one
in which he is merely an onlooker, so to secure the active co-operation of
the civic organizations in the community they should be given representation on the committee that they might realize that it was their observance
as well as ours.
As is generally known, the State organiaztions now co-operating in
the observance of Public Schools Week include the California Congress of
Parents and Teachers, California Teachers Association, California Department of American Legion, California Federation of Women's Clubs, California League of Women Voters, California Chamber of Commerce, State
Department of Education and State Farm Bureau Federation; and the
extent to which the civic organizations in some communities co-operate is
indicated by a report received a few years ago from a community in which
sixty-two different organizations were represented on the committee of
arrangements.
In view of the extent to which the observance has developed, it seems
incredible that there could ever have been any dou·bt of the success which
has been achieved. As has been intimated, however, the reports of the
early years recorded many discouraging experiences; and typical of the
situation in more than one community was a letter received from one of
our most earnest brethren which we quote :
"Weill This is the 'morning after' the Public Schools Week
observance meeting.
"We rented the Civic Auditorium, had a band, glee club, De
Molay for ushers, Will C. Wood for speaker, lots of publicity and
the cost about $75.00. Attendance-a mere handful (75 or 80) out
of a population of 8,500. And as usual, Masons only conspicuous
by their absence.
"I am wondering this morning if it is worthwhile? Possibly
it might be better not to have these meetings (and let the opposition 'b elieve that we are really interested in and protec·ting the free

make it pu'blicly known that we don't live up to our professions
or care a rap.
"This apathy and indifference upon the part of our own members make one almost heartsick.
"Sincerely trust that it is not so in other communities."

510

There were indeed antagonistic forces to be reckoned with; and they
were not voiceless. The burden of their complaint was that the "California
Masons were endeavoring to make the public schools their own peculiar
charge"-and that "neither newspaper editors nor legislators will make a
just appraisal of American school problems as long as this kind of thing
(Public Schools Week) is countenanced A secret society, the philosophy
of which is naturalism, sponsors a week of propaganda for schools the
religion of which is naturalism, for nowhere in such schools may the supernatural be recognized."
The force to be overcome, however, was not avowed antagonism to
our public schools, or even to this activity in their behalf; but rather an
apathy it was difficult to dispel and an opposition due to a misconception.
For instance, from the very start we had the earnest support and hearty
co-operation of the most prominent educators and school administrators
of the State; but in certain communities there was what appeared to be
almost opposition on the part of the local school trustees which of course
influenced the principals and the teachers. There was no avowed opposition even here; but there was evident an apathy where we felt we had a
right to encouragement. That apathy was undoubtedly due to the fact
that the worth and importance of Public Schools Week was not at once
sensed; and what appeared to be opposition may have been nothing more
than a hesitation, not all unreasonable or improper, to give official sanction
to an undertaking initiated by a fraternal organization. In any event when
it became evident that the institution of Public Schools Week was not for
the aggrandizement of the Masonic Fraternity, but solely in the interest
of the public school system of this State, that feeling gave way to the cordial, hearty and valuable co-operation of the school people which we na'w
everywhere enjoy and which with the support of the newspaper and broadcasting stations is largely responsible for the growth and .development of
Public Schools Week.
Much of the discouragement of the early days was due to the fact that
the observance was generally confined to public meetings and that attendance at these meetings held at first in the Lodge rooms, but afterward
in the school auditoriums, seemed to be the measuring stick by which was
gauged success or failure. Those arranging the meetings worked hard and
earnestly and were very naturally disappointed and discouraged when their
· efforts did not result in attracting the attendance for which they had hoped.
They lost sight of the fact that they were contending with a condition
which of itself militated against the probability of a large audience and that
the lack of attendance of which they complained was due primarily to that
same apathy which had tbrought about the conditions which gave birth to
the idea of Public Schools Week.
Each succeeding year, however, even at a time when the public meeting
continued to be the main, if not the only, feature of an observance, the
attendance increased; and after a few years it became evident from reports
made to the Grand Lodge Committee that where there was no great public
interest in any community it was because either the right sort of program

The success of the annual observance became assured with the realization on the part of the Masters that there is no city, town, nor hamlet in
the State of California in which there is a public school and where there
is located a Masonic Lodge in which a successful observance of Public
Schools Week cannot be held; and that it is largely, if not entirely, a question of "the man behind the gun," and of the zeal, industry and intelligence
with which the arrangements are made.
Mention hs been made of the passing of the crisis which brought about
Public Schools Week. . It should be rememtbered, however, that there was
another time some years later when, although for a different reason,
schools were again being closed or maintained with shortened terms. The
nation was in the throes of an acute social and economic disturbance; and
for lack of necessary funds educational service theretofore considered absolutely essential to a modern American school system-such as the maintenance of kindergartens, night schools and special classes for mentally
and physically handicapped children were being discontinued or materially
curtailed. And even at this v.e ry time there are many states, fortunately
California is not among them, where the school situation is not a reassuring one.
Whatever may be the reason and whether, as has been charged, most
of the school difficulties can be blamed upon the small unit of administration, or i·s the result of a faulty tax system, it is nevertheless a fact that
there are several states in which state aid for their schools was materially
cut this year. In New York, which has for many years headed the list in
ev'e ry educational rating, there was a cut of ten million dollars; and in
Michigan of nineteen million dollars. "Payless paydays for teachers" have
appeared in more than one state; and it is said that the situation is so bad
in Pennsylvania that 6000 teachers have received no salaries for as long
as ten months.
·

It is doubtful that there will ever ·be a time when those who administer
our public school system will not be faced with problems which go to its
very heart; and there will never cease to be need for an informed and intelligent public opinion. That opinion must necessarily be based on an understanding of modern educational methods and purposes; and as has been
repeatedly pointed out by educators here in California no better opportunity can be found for acquiring that understanding than is furnished by
the annual dbservance of Public Schools Week, through the type of programs now being presented.
It is a far cry from those first meetings in their Lodge rooms of Masons and their families to that week in April of this year when throughout
the entire State there was a literal outpouring of the patrons of our pU'blic
schools into the classrooms and auditoriums to witness, and in some instances as on the "Back to School" nights to take part in, programs designed to convey authoritative information as to just what the schools
are doing and how and why it is being done. Of course to describe, or
even to mention, all the different kinds of programs would be practically
impossible in a report of this character. All that can be said is .that they
included demonstrations of actual classroom procedure, and of the cultural,
vocational and home-making activities such as music, band and orchestra
work, with folk dancing, dramatics, pageantry and supervised play. There
were on display not only in the classrooms, but in some instances in store
windows and the lobbies of public buildings, school exhibits of all sorts
and kinds-many of them being the handiwork of the pupils in the shops
and special classes. There was a nota•ble increase in the number of forum
and panel ·d iscussions which made their first appearance a few years ago;

REPORT OF SPECIAL TAXATION COMMITTEE

Altogether this was another of those "bigger and better" observances
which each succeeding year has brought forth. We may now confidently
assert that there is hardly a community in the State, not even excepting
the very small ones represented by the one-room school at the crossroads
which does not now join in the observance of Pu•blic Schools Week. In:
deed taking the State as a whole and having in mind those little remote
communities, we think it is not too much to say that with the exception of
Independence Day, and of course Thanksgiving and Christmas, there is
probably not another anniversary which is so generally observed everywhere in California as is Public Schools Week. It has meant and of
course will continue to mean, the expenditure of considerable effort and
the incurring of trouble and bother, by the Masters of our Lodge~ and
those who carry on the work. There are, however, few things in this
world really worth while that do not involve some trouble and effort.
And no one who knows what is being accomplished doubts that Public
Schools Week is well worth while.
It is only proper of course that fitting acknowledgment should be made
of the co-operation that has been received; and if we do not as Masons
express gratitude therefor to those from whom it came, and who are not
of our number, it is only because it might imply that we believe that the
public schools are less their concern than they are ours. And 1 of course
this is not the fact .. The Grand Lodge of Masons in California is only th;
agency through which there is each year provided an opportunity for all
the champions of free, public education to join in bringing about that close
contact between the public and its schools that is so essential to a continuation of the friendship, faith and confidence upon which they necessarily
depend.
All of which is respectfully submitted,

To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
The Social Security and Unemployment Tax Committee was appointed
in November, 1938, by M:. w:. Leon 0. Whitsell, Grand Master, pursuant
to a resolution by the 89th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Members of the committee included:
Henry C. Clausen, chairman, Ingleside Lodge No. 630;
James E. Hammond, Park Boulevard Lodge No. 568;
R. P. Wisecarver, Thousand Oaks Lodge No. 478.
The committee commenced functioning in November, 1938. From that
time and down to date, numerous meetings have rbeen held. At these meetings all members of the committee were present.
To satisfy insistent requests from the subordinate Lodges in California
for prompt information, four written reports were made 'by the committee
to the Grand Master, three of which were printed and distributed to all
the subordinate Lodges. Copies of these reports are hereto attached.
A great deal of correspondence was exchanged .between the committee
and the subordinate Lodges in matters affecting their tax problems. Many
letters were exchanged with the California Tax Officials and other Fraternal
organizations who were guiding their course of conduct on our activities.
Communications were also exchanged with M.'. w:. Jo.'leph Earl
Perry, Grand Master of the Massachusetts jurisdiction and Chairman of
the Grand Masters' Committee on Social Security.
The Tax Problem of 1938
The problem that confronted the committee at its inception was twofold:
First, does the Masonic fraternity come within the scope of the exceptions to the Social Security Act, that is, is it a religious, charitable,
scientific, literary or educational institution, all of which are excluded from
its coverage?
The second issue had to do with the unemployment tax only and involved the definition of the term "employee." Both the federal and state
departments in charge of the administration of the acts had ruled with
respect to fraternal societies that all ritualistic officers were to be counted
as employees. The effect of this ruling was that all Lodges would be
declared to have more than the required minimum of eight employees under
the federal act and four employees under the state act, and hence ~ubject
to tax under both acts on the salaries actually paid.
In the opinion of the committee the Masonic Lodge should be exempt
from the payment of taxes with respect to both of these issues. It was
the committee's opinion that the Fraternity was exempted as such from
the operation of the act because it was a religious, charitable and educational
institution, and it was also the committee's opinion that the Department's
interpretation of the word "employee" to include unpaid ritualistic officers
was erroneous.
Fortunately, a test case was already being prosecuted by Pacific Lodge
No. 136, through its attorney, Brother Henry B. Nathan, and the committee
made use of that test case in raising these objections.
The Grand Masters' Committee on Social Security, headed by Brother
Joseph Earl Perry, Grand Master of the Massachusetts jurisdiction, presented the objections raised by your committee in Washington, with the
result that th.e federal department issued a ruling upholding our contention
that the term "employee" in the law did not contemplate including unpaid

516

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ritualistic officers and therefore that each Lodge was only liable if it had
eight or more paid employees. As has already been set forth in our preliminary reports, the California commission finally followed the federal
ruling, with the result that nearly all Lodges in California have been exempted from payment of unemployment taxes because they do not have
four pa id employees, and are entitled to refunds of any taxes paid.
The case pioneered •by Pacific Lodge was favorably decided. But no
decision was made upon the issue that the Lodges should have been ex.empted because they come within the basic exception to coverage of the act.
Your committee has not had an opportunity to present another test case
involving that issue.
The Tax Problem of 1939
In the meantime, both the federal and state acts have been amended
to effect an exclusion not only for all religious, charitable and educational
institutions, 'but also "for a fraternal, beneficiary society, order or association." It is the opinion of your committee that this amendment fortifies the
previous exemption from the act and shows clearly an intent to exempt atl
fraternal organizations. No departmental rulings have yet passed squarely
upon any case raising the issue since this amendment to the act. If the
opinion of your committee that the Masonic Fraternity is entirely excluded
from the coverage of the Security Tax Act is sustained, then there would
be no tax to pay either for unemployment reserves or for old age pensions.
In view of the fact that further amendments may possibly be made to
the act during the coming year and the desirability of keeping constantly
in touch with departmental rulings on the question of the coverage of the
taxation statutes, we recommend that this Grand Lodge continue a special
committee on taxation during the next Masonic year. In making this
recommendation the committee does not have in mind that the Fraternity
should align itself as being adverse to such legislation, but merely to
protect the Lodges under such legislation. If the Lodges are properiy
within the coverage of the act, then it is obvious that the Lodges should
pay the tax, but if the Lodges are not under the act, then the tax should
not be paid because no benefits will ever be paid to the supposed beneficiaries. Furthermore, · the Fraternity should lbe advised at this time
whether or not its employees are properly within the coverage of the act
so that if found not to be within the coverage of the act, adequate provision
may be made for them by the Fraternity itself if it is so desired. Similar
action is being taken by many other fraternal organizations.
Public Relations
It is probable that in the future some factual presentations may be
necessary before legislative committees or taxing authorities on behalf of
our interests. To this end, the committee, if continued, would serve as a
central agency for coordinating presentations. Along this line it is the
judgment of ·your committee that Masonry has a right to be heard ·on all
matters affecting its interests, and if necessary, should openly fight for
its rights.
To this end and for the purpose of showing that we are within the
exceptions embraced lby the Act, much good could be done by declaring
and defining the basic principles of Masonry, namely, that Freemasonry
is a charitable, benevolent, educational and religious society.
The unknowing sometimes have a false fear of Masonry because they
think anything with which it is connected is cloaked in secrecy. We should
make clear that we are essentially the type of organization which is normally excluded from the taxing statutes. Many organizations have been ex-
