PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC EDUCATION
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
At the annual communication of Grand Lodge held two years ago,
your committee submitted a Lodge system of Masonic education. Grand
Lodge approved the system and directed the committee to prepare and
publish a manual to be used as a source of material for the instruction
of candidates for degrees.
During the ensuing Masonic year, the manual was prepared and
published. It contains 147 pages covering many aspects of Masonry,
including its history, symbolism and interpretation of the ritual, as well
as an explanation of the functioning of Grand Lodge and of the constituent Lodges of this jurisdiction. To date over 50-0-0 copies of the manual
have been distributed.
One year ago we reported to Grand Lodge that the next task was
to put the Lodge system of Masonic education into practical operation.
Grand Lodge directed us fu go ahead and appropriated money for incidental expenses.
During the past year your committee has not engaged in an aggressive campaign or put on a " drive" to get the several Lodges to use the
system. We wanted the 1System to sell itself on its merits. We did no'
want to try to sell the system to the Lodges. If the system would sell
itself upon its merits, we believed that it would last longer than if we
tried to force it.
·
Your committee recently condm;ted a survey by mail to ascertain
the extent to w.h ich the system was being used in this jurisdiction. To
our letter of inquiry the Masters of about half of the Lodges replied.
We are happy to state that the Masters of 180 Lodges of this jurisdiction
have reported, in writing, that they are using the system, in whole or
in part. Of the Lodges which did not use the SY'Stem, 46 Lodges had a
legitimate reason therefore, such as no candidates, etc. The Masters of
34 Lodges have written to us that they inrtend to use the system in· the
near future while 31 other Lodges have requested further details concerning the system and the manual.
A careful study of the survey returns as well as outside information,
leads the committee to believe that about 300 Lodges of this jurisdiction
are using the system, in whole or in part.
Amortg the letters and postal cards received in the survey, the Masters of 63 :Lipdges voluntarily praised the system. Permit us to quote a
few Masters. One Master writes: "Best thing Grand Lodge has done
for Lodges in a long time . . . Would take years of searching for average
member to locate information found in manual." Another Master states,
"An excellent program which should be encouraged." Another, "Should
have been used years ago ." Another, " We are very enthusiastic about
this system." The Master of a new Lodge writes: "A great help in our
work with new members. Indispensable." Another Master states: "It
is doing the officers as much good as the candidates." One Master admits,
"I have a better understanding of Masonry myself because of it."
From a Lodge on the islands, by clipper airmail, comes this message:
"We are using the system in whole and find it an excellent piece of
work . .. We have a definite need here for more of this type of information."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

523

The problem of how a program of Masonic education can best be
carried on has, for a , number of years, puzzled the leaders of at least
40 Grand Lodges. No one has yet found the "perfect" answer. We have
not done so in this jurisdiction but we have made progress. With your
co-operation we believe that we can make still .further progress. We beg
that co-operadbn, not for .the sake of the members of our committee; not
for the sake of you older men in Masonry; but for the sak'e of those
young men who stand on the threshold of Masonry, with their eyes to
the East and who "seek further light in Masonry."
Based upon the foregloing, your committee makes the following
recommendation:
1. That the Committee on Masonic Education be continued next
year; its members to be appointed by the incoming Grand Master.

2. That the use of the Lodge system of Masonk education be aontinued.
3. That the sum of $300 be appropriated from the funds of Grand
Lodge for the incidental expenses of the Committee.
Respectfully submitted,
A. HEBER WINDER, Chairman

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History is pleased to report a year of
significant discoveries and satisfactory progress. Our previous search
for California material has been centered in this State. During the first
part of this year we began to seek eastern sources, particularly the libraries
of older Grand Lodges. This proved to be successful in Ohio, New
Hampshire, Iowa and New Jersey, where we found seve!al important
documents and publications. Several of these related specifically to the
first five years of our Grand Lodge proceedings. During these years, from
1850 to 1854, there were nine meetings of iour Grand Lodge, including
that o.f the Constitutional Convention of 185C>. There are now known
to have been ten different original printings of the proceedings of those
nine meetings in addition to the reprinted ones which we now recognize
to be official. The additional original is a previously u'n known semiofficial account of the Called Meeting of Grand Lodge which was held in
August, 1852 and to which is appended Grand Master Hyam's explanation
of the causes of that meeting.
Through the kindness of the Grand Lodges who loaned those rare
originals to us we were gi~en permission to have · photostatic copies made
for our own historical files. With the co-operation of the Bancroft Library
at Berkeley we now have domplete photographic copies of all of those
proceedings exce,pt for the semi-annual . communication of May, 1851.
Arrangements are being made to secure this. We believe that several of
these items were not even owned by Grand Lodge prior to the destructive
fire of 1906. They are distinct additions to our files.
, . We were also fortunate in the discovery of a number of early docume.nts in Lodge archives, and in accounts in old newspapers which have
added materially to our records of early California Masonry. Where originals· were not obtainable we usually have been able to secure· photographic
copies. In this manner more than ~o.ur hundred prints have been added
to our sources of authentic historical material during the year.
The most colorful story was found in the so-called "Narrative" which
was printed by Grand Master Hyam in 1852, and which referred to
troubles w\hich arose in Grand Lodge during that year. Accounts of the
difficulty were then deleted from the proceedings, and there has been
much erroneous speculation in the matter since that time. We can now
correct many mistaken ideas. A complete review of fac'ts of the controversy was prepared by the chairman of our committee in a hooklet
which was distributed recently to the Lodges by <irder of the Grand
Master. The original supply is exhausted. Because of the requests for
additional copies a second prin'ting was ordered and extra copies will be
supplied through the Grand Secretary at a price which will cover the
liowered cost of re-printing.
During the year various members of the committee have responded
to the requests of one hundred and three Lodges to participate in programs and speak on our early hiStory. In several instances there were
group or district meetings where more than one Lodge was represented.
Entertainment which featured the showing of our historical lantern slides
was given before thirty-six Lodges.
The inquiries for information on historical subjects which we receive
from officers and members indicate a growing interest in this phase of

GRAND. LODGE ~F CALIFORNIA

525

our activities. Our files and indexes are being improved steadily so that
we are better organized eac:h year to give attention to such requests. The
yrork of in~exing and cataloguing the mass of material which we possess
is necessarily slow because of the magni'tude of the job and because it
has .to be done by volunteer workers. To them we are deeply grateful.
Their research brings to light some interesting stories.
The records of San Jose Lodge No. 10 show that Br'o ther William
H. Howard was elected Master by acclamation in December 1853. He
was presiding Master four months later when his own 'application
for membership was received. T~-u~re is no indication that Brother Howard
vacated the East. The committee of investigation mad'e a prompt and
favorable report, and recommended that the ballot be taken the same
evening. The ballot being clear, Bro ther Howard declared himself
elected to membership "subject to the approval of Grand L odge." We
offer no explanation of this strange procedure. If the matter was referred
tio Grand Lodge it is ndt shown by our records, but one m onth later on
May 8, 1854, William H. Howard was elected from the floor to bec~me
the fift~ Grand Master of Masons of t:he State of California. He held
that office for three years with distinction to himself and with honor to
the fraternity. The Qriginal Grand L odge record for 1854 which came
into our possession recently shows that Brother Howard and the five
other elective officers were chosen "unanimously." It is further disclosed
that the balloting began at 10 o'clock at night and ended at 4 o'clock
the following morning. Since less than forty Lodges were represented
and six hours. were required to arrive at the unanimous results we suspect
that much time was spent in oratorical nominations and acceptance
speeches.
An interesting account came from the Hawaiian Islands, where members of one of the Lodges attended church services in a body. The officers
w_ere dre~sed in full regalia. The fact that the Worshipful Master wore
his hat disturbed the clergyman, but he was sufficiently aware of Masonic
usage to soon mention 'the name of God. The desired result was only
momentary, whereupon the pastor uttered the name anew and the hat
was again removed. The clergyman's reiteration of the holy name and
the Master's gesture of respect assumed a fast tempo. Then the minister
began to ".ary his expressions by references tto The Lord, Th~ Omnipotent,
The Almighty, The Creator, Jehovah, and names of Diety of other
religious faiths. The frequently repeated gestures of the Master became
~ono!ono~s. Finally, he bared his head in a mark of respect which contmued until the conclusion of the services.
In 1927, America Llodge No. 475 elected a candidate who was an
~ccomplis,'hed linguis~ and arranged so that he received his first degree
m French by the officers of Vallee de France Lodge No. 329; his second
degree in German by officers of Acacia Lodge No. 428 · a nd his third
degre.e i~ Ei:tglish by the officers of America Lodge. He can pass an
ex~mmat10n.. m any one of seven t ongues, and is described by his Lodge
officers as a good Mason in any language."
We ~r.e pleased to note that a steadily increasing number of Lodges
are prov1dmg adequate safes or vaults to protect the records and relics
from JQss by fire or accident. Summit L odge No. 112, located at Knights
Ferry, ai:id consisting of only forty-one members, recently completed a
vault which would be a credit to any Lodge of the jurisdiction. Again
we urge the ne~d of sue~ protective measures to all Lodges where they
do not now exist. Horrutos Lodge No. 98, under the leadership of its
Master, Walter A. McCollum, loc.a ted the neglected grave of William B.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws has carefully considered the amendments
submitted by thirty-nine Lodges during the past year. All amendments
• were corr~ ct as to form and in accordance with present Masonic law. They
have all been approved by the Grand Master and we recommend their
approval by Grand Lodge.
Two Lodges increased their fees, two increased their dues, seven reduced their fees, one reduced its dues, and five reduced their affiliation fees.
Amendments providing for excepting holidays as to stated meetings were
submitted by six Lodges.
Eighteen Lodges considered and adopted amendments as to change of
time of meetings or place of meetings. We note that those amendments
changing time of meetings do not provide for possible conflicts with holidays; this matter however, rests entirely within the discretion of the Lodge.
We move the adoption of this report approving all amendments submitted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
Organ Solo: "Adagietto" from "l'Arlesienne" ................................ Bizet
Invocation: Grand Chaplain.

To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
It has been a laudable custom for our Grand Lodge' to devote this
hour to the memory of our brethren whom God in His wisdom has seen
fit to remove from our midst, and also for those of us who survive to
reflect and meditate on the duties which man owes his Creator and also
the duties which we owe each other.
The Greeks held that death was the greatest gift to man from the
gods, and the naturalness of death was expressed by the great Buddha
when he said, "As all earthen vessels made by the potter end in being
broken, so is the life of mortals."
All Masons profess to believe in God and a future existence. Our great
Fraternity has wisely decreed that each of us must seek God after his own
conscience.
Mas-0nry declines to be called a religion, but rather prefers to be
classified as a great moral system. However, do not all religions have but

We are also taught the advantage of faith. But faith to be strong
must be adequately founded. During these turbulent times human values
and concepts have suffered change and confusion along other phases of
our lives. Let us, as Masons, survey our environment that we may not be
weakened in our faith, but on the contrary become strengthened by the
knowledge that our faith rests upon a sound foundation.
The rapid strides of science have disclosed a universe of vast complexity, the ·enormity of which our minds can not evaluate. As Mohammed
put it, "He causeth the night to succeed the day, and he causeth the day
to succeed the night; and he obligeth the sun and the moon to perform
their services: each of them run an appointed course. This is God, your
Lord: He is the Kingdom." (Koran Sayle, p. 340.)
We must, therefore, acknowledge that there is an Infinite Being who
is responsible for the creation of man and all other things contained in our
universe.
T.he great teachers of the past have taught that the principle of a great
Creator is inconsistent without justic\!. This was affirmed by the Emperor
Marcus Aurelius, who clearly enunciated the four cardinal virtues which
as such have been adopted by Masons as their .g uiding principles, and
chiefly among them is justice. To quote Marcus Aurelius, "As a means of
living conformably to nature he (man) must study the four chief virtues,
each of which has its own sphere: Wisdom, or knowledge of good and
evil; justice, or the giving to every man his due; fortitude, or the enduring
of labor or pain; and temperance, which is moderation in all things." (p. 86,
Long.)
Since we know that our concept of God endowed with infinite wisdom
and justice is well founded, our faith is therefore strong.
In the book of Job the question is asked, "If a man die, shall he live
again?" The question was answered by the Rev. Dr. Schaff as follows:
"We can not conceive that a wise creator should make man in his own
image and endow him with highest faculties, without ordaining him for
endless existence."
Our faith then, robs death of fear, and as we think of our brethren
who have gone on to that great experience ahead of all of us, let us not
forget that they did their part well and that they have received the happy
reward to which they are justly entitled. May their good example cause us
to continue to carry on in their admirable ways, and may we remember
the words of Coltar who aptly said, "Life is the jailer of the soul, and its
only deliverer is death."
Our Grand Lodge has suffered the loss of one hundred and sixty-four
members, the list of which is included at the end of this report.
Most of them were leaders in the community in which they resided, and
we know that they have left permanent marks of achievement behind them.
Among the most widely known, whom we will now miss, are Past Grand
Masters Benjamin F. Bledsoe and James William Foley, and Inspectors

542

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

DeRoy Gates, Charles ·K. Tuttle and Frank M . Wise. Appropriate
eulogies will be delivered at the conclusion of the reading of this report.
Brother Foley was Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of North Dakota
in 1904 ·a nd was a member of Corona Lodge No. 324 in Pasadena. In his
boyhood and earlier years, he was engaged in newspaper work. Brother
Foley was the recipient of many literary honors, among which was that
-0f poet laureate of North Dakota. He was a member of the Scottish Rite and
also a member of Rotary, Kiwanis, Cauldron and other societies. He was a
contributor to the Saturday E.vening Post, Century, Colliers and other
well known publications. He took active part in the political affairs of
North Dakota, serving as secretary to the State Senate and secretary of the
State Railroad Commission. Among his multitude of friends was Theodore
Roosevelt, who wrote a foreword in one of Foley's .books. The passing of
Brother Foley is a great loss to Corona Lodge and his host of friends.
Thus one rb y one we answer that call when it pleases Him who spoke
us into existence. In honor of those who have served so faithfully and
whose lives are an example to those who survive, let us carry on honorably
seeking to make our short sojourn in this earthly existence a credit to ourselves and an honor to our great Institution which has contributed so much
to our moral and spiritual welfare.
Let us conclude with Bryant's Thanatopsis :
"So live, that when thy summons comes to join
The innumerable caravan that moves
To that mysterious realm, where each·shall take
His chamber in the silent halls of death,
Thou go not, like the quarry slave at night,
Scourged to his dungeon, but sustained and soothed
By an unfaltering trust, approach thy grave
Like one who wraps the draperies of his couch
About him, and lies down to pleasant dreams."
Respectfully submitted,
ROY H. p ARKIN SON
HERBERT GEORGE POLHILL
DAVID M. BIVENS
ROBERT W . WATSON
WALTER D. ADRIANCE

In Memoriam

BENJAMIN FRANKLIN BLEDSOE
by WALTER W. ROBINSON,
Junior Past Master San Bernardino Lodge No. 348
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:

In searching for a great truth which might in some degree portray the
character of our 'beloved Past Grand Master, Benjamin Franklin Bledsoe,
we must turn to the poet who said,
"And when a good man dies, for years beyond our ken,
The light he leaves behind him lies upon the paths of men."
Benjamin Franklin Bledsoe was born at San Bernardino, California,
February 8, 1874. He came from a long line of distinguished ancestors who
had been pioneers since their arrival in early colonial America. Each
gen.eration add~d fame and distinguished credit to the family, and this
native son remained true to the tradition of the name of B1edsoe.
A great-grandfather, James Bledsoe, was the first United States
Senator from Kentucky, and his father, Robert Emmet Bledsoe was a
·
'
distinguished lawyer and judge in San Bernardino.
Few men have attained the many high honors which were bestowed
upon Judge Bledsoe. He had a brilliant judicial mind with vision and
perspective; a deep understanding toward the opinions of others· a
personality that drew men of all stations in life toward him· kind sinc~re
upright in hi.s ~very a<;t, and a ~reat moral strength that adhered only t~
right and prmc1ple regardless of personal gain.
.

I

'

After graduating from San Bernardino High School he entered Stanford University graduating in the class of 1896. There he excelled in many
scholastic achievements. He evidenced his outstanding ability as an executive, organizer, orator and was awarded honorary membership in Phi
Beta Kappa. It was at Stanford University he met and in 1899 married
Katherine Shepler, a classmate, who was to ·be his constant c~mpanion
and inspiration throughout his colorful career.
Two daughters were born to this union, Barbara S., now Mrs. Glenn
Pollard, and Frances P. Bledsoe.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

551

covered two years time, and when Judge Bledsoe ruled in favor of the
Southern Pacific, the Government was so impressed by his clear, comprehensive decision that they did not appeal.
He was awarded the degree of doctor of laws from the University of
Southern California for his articles on Constitutional Law.
During his busy career he found time to serve in many capacities outside his legal work. He was president of the Stanford University National
Board, the Stanford University Alumni Association~ and maintained his
college fraternities, Delta Upsilon and Phi Delta Phi.
He was the first president of the Y. M. C. A. of San Bernardino. In
Los Angeles he assisted in organizing the Welfare Federation, operating
the Community Chest. From 1924 to 1926 he was president of the Los
Angeles Grand Opera Association, and in 1932 he became president of the
Los Angeles Oratorio Association.
Judge Bledsoe became a member of the California Society, Sons of the
Revolution in 1915 by right of descent from Co). Nathaniel Gist of Maryland. He served on the board of directors from 1925 until he became
president in 1931 and 1932.
At the last election of the Triennial Convention of the General Society,
he was honored ·by election to the General President. Illness, however,
prevented him from carrying out the plans which he had formulated.
His Masonic career was even more colorful. His devotion to the cause
of Masonry was the outstanding characteristic of his entire life. He received
his third degree in San Bernardino Lodge No. 348 on August 29, 1902 and
served as Master during 1908. His leadership was soon recognized by
Grand Lodge. He was Junior Grand Warden in 1911, Senior Grand Warden
in 1912, Deputy Grand Master in 1913, and Grand Master in 1914. His
services did not cease, however, as he served as a member of the Grand
Lodge Committee on Jurisprudence from 1920 until his death.
He was Grand Commander of Knights Templar in 1919 and served on
Committee on Templar Jurisprudence Grand Encampment Knights Templar
from 1922 to 1928.
Benjamin Franklin Bledsoe was a member of Keystone Chapter No.
56, Valley Council No. 27 and St. Bernard Commandery No. 23 of San
Bernardino. He ·belonged to the Scottish Rite bodies of Los Angeles from
1912.

In 1906 at the early age of twenty-six, he was elected Judge of the
Superior Court of San Bernardino County on the Democratic ticket. He
was reelected in 1912 and so popular was this young judge that the
Republican Party did not contest his election with another candidate for
the office.

We sometimes wonder why a great man such as Benjamin Franklin
Bledsoe should be so untimely taken from the useful life he was serving to
his fellowmen. The only consolation comes from Him who said, "His
Infinite plan is just and in Him we must place our trust."

. President Wilson appointed him United States District Judge in 1914
which office he served until March 1925. He resigned during 1925 to run
for Mayor of Los Angeles for which office he was defeated. Judge Bledsoe
then returned to private practice.

Past Grand Master Bledsoe's unexpected summons came at the close
of day Sunday, October 30, in his mountain home at Crestline in the San
Bernardino mountains. He had withdrawn from daily work a short time
previous to his death to his mountain retreat to regain the sapped strength
he had so unselfishly given to his fellowmen, his country and his community.

As District Judge he gained nation-wide prominence. It is said that
his outstanding case was the suit of the United States Government relative
to ~he patent rights of the Southern Pacific Railway to California oil lands
estimated to exceed five hundred million · dollars. The hearing of this case

For twelve consecutive years previous to his passing he had annually
installed the officers of his own Blue Lodge, San Bernardino Lodge No.
348. Regardless of how occupied he was he held this loyalty to Masonry
and his mother Lodge paramount above all things. The memory of this

devotion will ever be cherished by his brothers and the officers who were
inspired by his sincerity and kindliness.
He was a devoted husband and father and the void left in his family
circle is beyond comprehension. I quote from the recent pen of his widow
Katherine S. Bledsoe. "I know how much the Masonic Order meant i~
Ben's life, and above all how much the fine friendships he made there have
meant in his life. They all grew more precious as the years went by."
Benjamin Franklin Bledsoe so lived that he went out into the sunset
amid the evergreen hills of his Native State that he loved so well fearless
and unafraid, with head erect to meet the Supreme Grand Master.' He had
fulfilled the pledge which his pen had once recorded:
"I am determined in any way I can, to contribute something helpful to
civilization, of which I am a part,. that my children and those coming after
them shall perhaps find the world just a little better in virtue of my
having been here."

In Memoriam

DeROY H. GATES
by ARTHUR P. CRIM, Past Master Redlands Lodge No. 300

To the M.' .. W.' . Grand Lodge of California :
In the mid-summer of 1927, after several preliminary meetings and
conferences, the Masonic brethren of Banning decided they would organize
a Masonic Lodge. As the result of this decision twenty-five Master Masons
met and in the preliminary meeting held October 3, 1927, DeRoy .H. Gates
was elected Master of the new Lodge. The name chosen was San Gorgonio.
Prior to this time I had only a slight acquaintance with Brother Gates,
having met him in the Scottish Rite. In the organization of this new Lodge,
at that time being Inspector of the 105th Masonic District, it became my
duty to coach and qualify the officers . . This duty soon became a privilege
for here I had the opportunity of forming friendships as indelible as time
itself.
After Brother Gates served his Lodge as Master under Dispensation,
he was elected and gain served another year in that capacity. He and I
became bosom companions and friends and this mutual fe eling was
augmented when in 1932 he received his first appointment as Inspector.
Our late Brother Tom Baker gave his credentials to me to give to our
Brother when fully qualified. After some weeks of reviewing and coaching
I gave Brother Gates his appointment and since then we have been nearer
than blood brothers. He was Inspector of the 107th District from this time
until his death.
·
DeRoy H. Gates was born in Selins Grove, Pennsylvania, December
14, 1872 of English parentage. He spent his boyhood in his native State,
coming to Los Angeles a mere youth of sixteen years. October 23, 1895
he married Rose J. Roth and came to Banning the following year. There
were no children and this seems to have been a wise provision for it left
him with time and opportunity to minister to the needs of others. He was
a devoted husband and he and Mrs. Gates were inseparable in their devotion
to each other. Their lovely home, built just after their coming to Banning,
was the center of very many social activities. He had a summer home at
Hermosa Beach where they spent most of their weekends. They had gone
to their beach home for the weekend May 19, and on Saturday evening,
May 20 they visited friends in Manhattan. Starting home at 10 :30 they had
only gone a half a block when he received his summons to enter the
Supreme Grand Lodge for all eternity.
Masonically he was initiated March 3, 1898, passed March 24, 1898 and
raised April 21, 1898, in Ashlar Lodge, Colton. · He was a member of Riverside Royal Arch Chapter No. 67, Riverside Commandery K. T. No. 28. He
was a member of all the Scottish Rite Bodies in Long Beach, A. & A. S. R.
He was also a life member of Al Malaikah Temple, A . A. 0. N. M. S.
The highest testimonial of the love and esteem in which he was held
by his many friends and brethren was exemplified at his funeral services
held May 24. There were hundreds of beautiful floral emblems from every
section of California and the friends could not all be seated in the Methodist
Church from which the services were held.
Brother Gates had not been in good health for some time and he talked
with Mrs. Gates about the probability of his passing and requested that I

554

PROCEEDINGS Oi' THE

should conduct his funeral service. This I did with the assistance of the
Master of San Gorgonio Lodge.
As a tribute to the high regard in which he was held by his brother
Inspectors, every Inspector in the five adjoining districts was present,
Brother Carl Mikesell coming all the way from Needles, a distance of
over 250 miles.
Every life to be worth while must be motivated 1by a high ideal. Such
a life was lived by our departed Brother. Service was the zenith of his
aspirations. A resume of his work in the City of Banning, where he lived
for 43 years, is most interesting. He served Banning as Mayor for 17 years
and to any one familiar with the responsibility of this office, it suggests
almost unlimited time. A lasting monument to his prodigious and unceasing
effort is the new Banning City Hall, built while he was yet in office. He
had a very real interest in schools, grammar and high, serving as President
of the Board of Trustees for eight years. The schools closed on the day of
the funeral and the flag on the City Hall was flown at half-mast for nearly
four days, a fine civic tribute.
He loved his fellow citizens and their interest was his. In the words of
Newton, " No voice of distress ever reached his ears in vain and no hand
ever sought his aid without response." Like the Master of old, "He went
about doing good." No man ever gave more freely of his time to his
fellow-citizens. No man ever gave more liberally of his means and his
sympathy to the needy of his home city. No Mason ever gave more
willingly of his strength and his talents to his Masonic brethren than our
departed brother. Sick or well he attended faithfully to his Masonic
responsibilities.
In the death of Brother Gates, his dear wife lost a faithful companion,
Masonry lost a real true Mason and his community lost a sincere friend
for his friendship as Coleridge once said, "Was like a sheltering tree." No
loss of friend or brother has ever been so great to me personally, but with
the poet may I say,
"I cannot always know
And understand the Master's rule.
I cannot always do the tasks
He gives in life's hard school.
But I am learning with his help
To solve them one by one,
And when I cannot understand
To say 'Thy will be done'."

Gustave Durschang, Jewel Lodge No. 374

In Memoriam
CHARLES KIRKHAM ·TUTTLE
by E. WILEY REEVES, Master of Salinas Lodge No. 204

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Brother Charles Kirkham Tuttle was born at Benicia Arsenal, California, December 29th, 1859. He was educated in San Francisco, California,
graduating from High School in 1874. The following year he entered the
employ of Coffin and Mayhew, prominent drug.g ists of San Francisco,
where he remained for five years. In 1880 he moved to Salinas, California,
where he opened and managed a drug store for J. B. Scott, which he
successfully operated for three years, when he returned to San Francisco,
to conduct a dispensary for Dr. James Murphy. In 1887 he moved to
Pacific Grove, and opened a drug store in that city which he operated
until his death, fifty-two years later.
Brother Tuttle was initiated in Salinas Lodge No. 204 F. & A. M.
July 6th, 1882. Passed July 27th, 1882, and raised to the sublime degree
of Master Mason on August 10th, 1882.
He became a life member of Islam Temple A. A. 0. N. M. S., April 25th,
1903, and a 32nd degree Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite Freemason,
San Jose Consistory No. 9, Valley of San Jose, March 10th 1925.
He helped institute Pacific Grove Lodge No. 331 at Pacific Grove,
California, in 1897, serving as its first Senior Warden. He served Pacific
Grove Lodge as Master in 1899, 1900 and part 1901, 1902, 1903.
In 1907 he was appointed Inspector of the 56th Masonic District
serving in this capacity for thirty years, and while the administration of
his drug store, which he operated personally, made constant and heavy
demand upon his time and energy, yet throughout those thirty long years,
he gave most generously both of his time and energy toward furthering
Masonry in his district, and never was he too busy or too tired to assist
in any and every way the officers and men of the Lodges under his
jurisdiction. He was always, and at all times kind, agreea•ble, and most
considerate-living Masonry as he taught it. His daily life, in and out of
the Lodge room was an example and an inspiration to men and Masons
everywhere. He was honored and respected lby all, and loved by those
who knew him ·b est.
Brother Tuttle obeyed the summons of the Kind Messenger to the
Supreme Grand Lodge above, on August 2nd, 1939, waiting and well
prepared.
Funeral services were conducted in Del Monte Chapel, the Rev. Theodore Bell officiating, and the remains were accompanied to Cypress Lawn
cemetery by the family, and the officers of Pacific Grove Lodge No. 331,
where Masonic services were conducted. The Most Worshipful Leon 0.
Whitsell, Grand Master, acted as Master, and the Right Worshipful Lloyd
Wilson, Jr., Grand Warden acted as Chaplain.
His day is done; his sun has set.
The battle's fought and won, and yet,
The life he lived we so admire
His memory will our lives inspire. .

In Memoriam
FRANK MARVIN WISE
by IRA D. WHEELER, Senior Past Master of Palisades Lodge No. 637
To the M.".

w:. Gra11d Lodge of California:

· During the first week of last August Frank drove to San Francisco
with his son, Robert, to meet Mrs. Wise on her return from a visit in
Oregon. The family saw the Fair, visited several of their many friends in
the Bay District and returned to their home in Santa Monica on Sunday.
The next day Frank went to his office in fine spirits and collapsed at his
desk Word of his passing came as a distinct shock to his host of friends,
who had been hopeful that his health was improving.
Brother Wise was a zealous member of our Fraternity for twenty-two
years, having been raised in Santa 'Monica Lodge in 1917. He served as its
Master in 1921, was appointed Inspector of our District toward the end of
that year and continued in that capacity until the beginning of this year,
when he asked to be relieved because of ill health. During those seventeen
years he cemented the six Lodges of the Santa Monica Bay District into an
energetic, harmonious and efficient group. His executive ability, pleasing
personality and sincere interest in the affairs of the Fraternity won him
the ~espect and affection of the officers and members of our Lodges.
· Brother Wise attended every annual communication of this Grand
Lodge since 1921, and it was my good fortune to have been his companion
at most of them. His work in Grand Lodge was centered in the annual
meetings of the Board of Control, of which he became a member in 1927,
soon after its formation. The resulting contacts with officers of Lodges
and Boards of Retie.£ throughout the State extended his acquaintance to alt
sections. In every community some one knew him as "Frank" and met
him with a smile and a hearty hand-clasp. Last spririg we made a tour of
the Lodges in the Mother Lode District and seldom was an introduction
necessary.
Frank's influence in Santa Monica was profound. In c1v1c, business,
service and social circles he had the respect and admiration of all who
knew him. He was sincere, of kindly disposition, cheerful and friendly,
devoted to his family and to his home; a good citizen and a good Mason.
I am proud to say that he was my friend, for friends are surely our most
comforting possession. It is hard enough to have them go to far away
places, but much harder when they are taken away entirely. .
In 1935, from this platform, Brother Wise presented a eulogy in
memory of Past Grand Master David J. Reese. Perhaps our feelings for
Frank are expressed best by the words he used then. He said:-"It was a
privilege and an honor to have known him. Masonry in California is richer
for his life, devoted as it was to the practice of Masonic ideas and ideals.
He loved Masonry. It was ever in his thought and a vital part of his life.
He was never happier than when rendering some service to the Craft or
to a needy brother. He was truly a Craft Mason, a man among men."

. Frank's name will not be on the rolls of Grand Lodge this year, but
his character and example as a faithful member of the Masonic Fraternity
will serve as an inspiration to those who are here today and to those who
may be here during the years to come.

MASONIC DAY AT TREASURE ISLAND

u:.

To the
w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Special Committee on Masonic Day at the Golden Gate International Exposition begs leave to report as follows:
The original date set for Masonic Day was April 19, 1939 but was
postponed by order of the Grand Master to October 11, 1939, so that the
brethren who attend the annual communication might be able to be present.
Your committee endeavored to arrange a program that was in keeping
with the dignity of our Fraternity and at the same time make the day outstanding at the Exposition. It was also thought advisable to leave the
brethren and their families as much time as possible to view the wonderful
attractions of the Fair.
The high light of the day was the reception to the Grand Master, by
the Mayor of San Francisco, at which the Mayor officially presented the
San Francisco Building to the Masons for the day. Thereafter addresses
were given by the Grand Master and the Grand Orator, Brother Ellsworth
Meyer.
Following the official reception, a concert was rendered by the San
Francisco municipal orchestra, interspersed by solos by Elsa Behlow
Trautner, after which refreshments were served on the balcony, all through
the courtesy of the City and County of San Francisco.
Later, Flag retreat ceremony by the 30th U. S. Infantry was most
impressive, and was witnessed •by many brethren and the general public.
A number of Lodges in the San Francisco bay area held anniversary
dinners on Treasure Island in connection with Masonic Day and many
informal dinners were held at the official restaurants.
In the evening a grand ball was held in the California Building,
attended by several thousand brethren and ladies.
Fifteen thousand souvenir courtesy books were distributed to members of the Craft and their families, entitling them to reduced admissions to
many of the better class concessions.
We were favored by perfect California weather, and while we cannot
state exactly the number of Masons who attended, we are informed by the
Exposition management that "Masonic Day" contributed between 20,000
to 25,000 of the total attendance of 43,000 for the day.
We are indebted to the Trustees of the Masonic Homes, who very
kindly changed the date of the customary visit to the Decoto Home from
Wednesday to Monday.
The committee expresses its thanks to the many brethren who
volunteered their services in making the day a success. Thanks are especially due to Brother Otto Hansen, Military Service Lodge No. 570, and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

559

Brother Andrew Burke, Justice Lodge No. 549, who although not members
of the committee, met with it for months and aided greatly in formulating plans.
A full accounting of the costs has lbeen made to the Finance Committee.
Copies of the souvenir courtesy book which contained the program for
the day and other literature are attached herewith.
We sincerely trust that all who attended enjoyed the day and the Committee consider it a pleasure to have served the Fraternity.
Respectfully submitted,
JOEL H. SPRINGER, Chairman

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
To the Committee on Appeals and Grievances there have been referred
a total of nineteen records. Three of these involve petitions for restoration
and will be separately reported to you. In two trials, both of which resulted
in expulsions; appeals have been taken by the accused and, consequently,
these likewise will be the subject of separate reports.

In the cases covered by the remaining fourteen records there were
twelve expulsions and two acquittals. 'N ine of these expulsions resulted
from proceedings under Section 192 of the Constitution following conviction
of crimes classified as felonies under the law and imprisonment pursuant
thereto. The proceedure prescribed <b y the Constitution was correctly followed by the several Lodges. None of the accused demanded a trial and
automatic expulsion resulted.
In three of the remaining cases covered by this report in which expulsions resulted and the two cases which resulted in acquittals, trials were
held before properly constituted and elected trial commissions. No appeals
were taken by either the accusers or the accused. A careful review of these
records demonstrates compliance with the necessary requirements as to
procedure and proof. Your committee feels that in each of these five
matters the records are free from error and that substantial justice has been
accomplished.
Your committee therefore recommends that the judgments be ratified,
approved and affirmed in each of the fourteen cases covered by the following trial records:

REPORT OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF
U. C. L.A. CLUBHOUSE
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
We have just concluded the tenth and most successful year in the
history of our Clubhouse. · Many of the brethren present will not remember
when the plans to create this property were first presented.
This undertaking, fron:i its beginning to completion, ran through the
administrations of five of our Grand Masters. The Masonic Club U. C. L. A.
was incorporated January 24, 1924, the same year the Berkeley Clubhouse
was built. Most Worshipful Albert E. Boynton, as Grand Master, approved
the project, and the following year, Most Worshipful George L. Jones
gave his approval. Some formative work was done during those years,
but it was not until early in 1928, under the direction of Most Worshipful
Will H. Fischer, that the campaign to secure the funds was aggressively
promoted. This effort was continued under the guidance of Most Worshipful Gustav A. Hutaff, and the ground was purchased on March 1, 1929.
Plans were approved and the contract to erect the building was let on
March 28, 1929. The corner stone was laid on April 6, 1929, Most Worshipful Brother Hutaff officiating. The 'building was furnished and opened on
September 1, 192_9 for the benefit and service of young men and young
women from Masonic families attending the University of California at
Los Angeles. It was dedicated on March 'l'l, 1930, Most Worshipful Charles
L. Wollenberg, Grand Master, officiating.
The property-land, building and furnishings-was turned over to
Grand Lodge free of indebtedness and has been one of its important contributions to the building of character and citizenship in this great State
of ours.
During all of this time, and until his death, our beloved Brother Ira
F . Thompson served as Chairman of the Board of Directors and was the
motivating spirit of the enterprise.
Ours was the only building of similar kind near or on the campus to
serve the students when the University opened in September, 1929. This
past year students made 29,365 visits to the Clubhouse, an average of 150
each college day.
Each year the University enrollment increases-this year it exceeds
8,000, and naturally the proportion from Masonic families follows the same
trend.
The Masonic Affiliate Council, the body governing the activities of the
Clubhouse, is well organized and a well thought out program is under
way. We have every reason to believe that we will render a finer and
better service than ever before.
Again we had the pleasure of having our Most Worshipful Grand
Master and several of his officers with us, and his presence and inspiring
message were deeply appreciated.
The financial condition is refiected by the report of Brot her Reynold
E. Blight, certified public accountant, which is attached hereto and made a
part hereof.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Control is pleased to submit once more a report of its
activities during the past Masonic year.
The hearty co-operation of the Grand Officers, and particularly the
information and assistance given to us by Grand Secretary Whicher and his
assistant, Frank Hobbs, is highly appreciated. As always hearty co-operation
and assistance have been given by Boards of Relief and individual Lodges.
. Every case that has come before the· Board has received caref~l
analysis, the Board keeping ever in mind that justified relief should be m
no way curtailed.
The Board deeply deplored the passing of one of its most earnest and
valued members Brother Frank Marvin Wise, who had ever been untiring
in · the interest of Freemasonry and the Board of Control In particular. The
Board feels that this report would not be complete without proper recognition; being made of one who had •been so earnest in his work and so beloved
by the Fraternity.
·
The strict a<lherence to the standardized procedure adopted by the
Board of Control and the Boards of Relief and the care and watchfulness
exercised by said Boards of Relief, is reflected in the small amount of
reimbursements shown in this report.
·
Meetings
' We held one business meeting of the Board during the year, February
4 1939 in Los Angeles; also a special all day meeting October 9, 1939
i~ San' Francisco, at which the problems of employment service were
thoroughly discussed including a standardization of employment methods
and reports.
Recoveries
There was recovered for this Grand Lodge for relief advanced the sum
of $147.35. The detail of this recovery follows: .
Dixon Lodge No. 7, Dixon, Illinois................................- ............$ 76.85
Lodge Cumberland Kilwinning No. 217, Port Glasgow,
Scotland .......................................................................................... 70.50
Total ............................................•.......................................................$147.35
Reimbursements
It is significant to note that the Secretaries of the various Boards of
Relief have exercised the usual vigor in attempting to secure reimbursement · for relief advanced, which will be noted in the following.
. After carefully examining the requests for reimbursements we have
recommended to the Finance Committee that the following requests be
granted.
East Bay Board of Relief...........................·-·······-·······················$ 345.00
Pajaro Lodge No. 110, Watsonville.....·-···································· 100.00
Sacramento Board of Relief........................................................ 167.50
San Diego Board of Relief.............·-····························--·-·-····· 20.00
San Francisco Board of Relief.....................................•...·-·········· 26.95
Total ················-··········-················································-················-$ 659.45
Employment Service
There is no disputing the fact that the greatest help that can be given
any person is to help him to help himself. We well know that our brethren
are not willingly seeking relief; we well know that what they as men and as
Masons want is gainful employment. Our seven Employment Services

GRAND LODGE OF CAX.IFORNIA

565 .

have been doing just that thing to a remarkable degre~and under very
difficult economic circumstances.
10,657 jobs were found for our Brethren during the year just dosedthe greatest number in the history of the service. This is of itself encouraging, but when we realize that the number of applicants is constantly increasing, we realize that this work demands the utmost we are ·able to put into it.
You will ·be astonished to learn that the number of applicants during
this past year was 18,264-an 11%% increase over the previous year-and
1938 was a 29% increase over 1937. . Comparing 1937 and 1939, the latter
shows a 44% increase in the number of men, women, boys and girls who
sought our assistance in thefr struggle to live.
This Grand Lodge appropriated $13,850.00 for this · work last year.
Other monies used brought the total expense to $27,916.79, or an average
·
cost of $2.62 per job secured.
Had these jobs been secured through a private fee charging agency,
our distressed brethren would have paid out more than $130,000.00. Masonic
Employment Service saved them that amount.
Brethren-get behind your Masonic Employment Service-talk itsing it-shout it.:.._help a brother to help himself.
.
The Board of Control has had under consideration a suggested plan
for. circularizing all Lodges of the jurisdiction. with information and advice
concerning employment as well as a further plan for the clearance of
requests for employes to fill positions in any place where local applicants
are not available. From information obtained by our investigation and
after due consideration, our .unanimous conclusion is we can not recommend
the plans as presented.
· Appropriations
It has ·bec:n . the· practke of Grand Lodge during the past year to
appropriate various sums of money to the support of the several Employment
Services. In addition to this appropriation, the local Boards of Relief expend as much of their own funds as they can spare without crippling their
own work. After careful examination and hearings we recommended to
the Finance Committee the following appropriations for 1939-40:

. GENERAL REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE.

Your committee tlhis year is in accord with the recommendations of
last year, that is, that the expense for these purposes should not extend
$2,500.00 and also that the amount allocated should not be exceeded.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
·adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $2,500.0Q, or so much thereof, as may .be
· necessary to pay, the expenses incurred by the Grand Lodge Week Achvi ties Committee be, and the same is, hereby appropriated out of the funds
of Grand Lodge and the same be allocated to the payment of ~he expenses
incurred in the entertainment of officers and memb~rs attendmg the next
annual communication ·of Grand Lodge.

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Finance begs leave to submit the following report:
Audit of Accounts
Your committee has again employed Brother Floyd F. Webb of the
firm of Ruckstell, Burrows and Webb, certified public accountants, to
examine the books and records of the Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary, tihe Masonic Homes of California and the Endowment Fund. The
reports of Brother Webb's examination of these records have been filed
with your committee · and have had its consideration. These reports are
now on file with the records of Grand Lodge. They indicate that all records
are correct and in pr<Jper shape and all receipts properly accounted for and
all expenditures properly made.
Your committee is again mindful of the debt it owes Brother Webb
for the personal interest he has shown in making the various audits. He
has devoted considerable time to the affairs of Grand Lodge, for which
he is asking no remuneration and for which your committee is duly
appreciative.
The amount asked for the complete audit is the same as it was for
last year, that is the sum of $700.00. Of this sum $550.00 is paid by the
trustees of the homes and only $150.00 paid out of Grand Lodge funds.
Grand Lodge Week Activities
The Committee on Grand Lodge Week Activities has furnished your
committee with an estimate of the cost of the entertainment which it has
provided for the members who are attending this session of Grand Lodge.
Necessarily the best that the committee can do at this time is to furnish
this committee with an estimate, as it is very difficult to determine the
actual amount of expenditure until all activities are over and bills are
actually presented.
For tlhe purpose of the entertainment of the members, the Finance
Committee last year allocated to the committee $2,500.00. In its report it
particularly called the committee's attention to its wish to have the cost of
this entertainment not to exceed the amount allowed. It would seem that
the committee has kept within the amount, with the exception of the cost
of the Inspector's luncheon, $90.00, and of the visit to Treasure Island, of
approximately $750.00. These two items of expense were worked out in
collaboration with the Grand Master and we approve of them.
'As stated in previous reports, the Finance Committee is in entire
accord with the plan of providing the representatives some entertainment
while in attendance of Grand Lodge. It is also to be noted that of the
amount expended, $440.00 was for transportation of the representatives
to Decoto for the purpose of better acquainting them with our homes and
their adhievements. With this we are particularly in accord.
The Committee on Grand Lodge Week Activities has a difficult duty
to perform. We feel they have performed their duties in a most gratifying
manner. You, who are listening to this report, are best able to judge
of the excellence of the entertainment provided.
It would seem that the authorization of the Finance Committee of
last year of $2,500.00 is ample to pay all expenses incurred. It is therefore
unnecessary to present a further resolution to care for any excess expenses.

Adopted.
Masonic History
The chairman of your Committee on Masonic History has appeared
.before this committee·and discussed the w~rk .the committee has done this
. past year and is planning on doing this. coming year,
It appears to your Finance Committee that for th.e past year this
committee has done work of real excellence and that 1t has been .ver!
modest in the amount expended in compiling and printing the material 1t
has prepared. It also seems to your committee that the work it. has outlined
for this coming year should be of real benefit to the Fratermty, and that
the amount asked for to assist it in this work is most reasonable. We are
in accord with the request and therefore offer the following resolution and
recommend its adoption:
Resolved that the sum of $250.00 be appropriated from the funds of
Grand Lod~e and be paid to the chairman of the .histo~y com~~ttee to
defray expenses which may be incurred by the comm.1ttee m comp1lmg a~d
preparing additional information gathered on the history on Masonry m
. California.

Masonic Homes
Your Committee on Finance to which was referred that portion of the
report of the Board of Trustees of Masonic Homes relating to the finances
of our homes, begs leave to report as follows:
We have reviewed the report of the certified public accountants and
are of the opinion that the financial affairs of our homes are fully and
correctly reported by the trustees.
The report submitted by your Board of Trustees and the review of
the accountants is, of course, submitted in printed form and we do not
believe it necessary to refer in detail to facts and figures. We do, however,
note that the trustees have, during the past year, paid the balance of
$25,000.00 on the loan made by the Endowment Fund.
A careful survey of the report of your trustees indicates clearly that
they have at all times endeavored to manage the financial affairs o.f your
two institutions not only to the best interest of those housed therein, but
also to the interest of this Grand Lodge. The trustees are to be congratulated upon the efficient manner in which they have at all times managed
our two institutions.
We have discussed the needs of the homes for the coming year with
the chairman of the Board of Trustees. The Board of Trustees recommends
the continuance of the per capita tax of 40 cents for the coming year in
which recommendation we concur. We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, that the special per capita tax for the maintenance of the
Masonic Homes be set at 40 cents.

Adopted.
Masonic Homes Endowment Board
Your Committee on Finance has studied with interest the report of
the Masonic Homes Endowment Board and the audited report of receipts
and disbursements for the year 1938-39.
Again this very efficient board reports that a very substantial sum
has been added to our Endowment Fund by the efforts and interest of a
comparatively small percentage of our membership. It is interesting to
note that while that percentage is still small yet the number of individual
donors is growing from year to year.
The Endowment Fund was increased from $1,097,493.71 in 1938 to
$1,170,181.88 in 1939, an increase of $72,688.17. Of this increase $58,295.70
came from donations and bequests and $14,392.47 from profit on sales of
securities. While we all wish that this increase might have been larger,
we must remember that this is just the known increase and that we do
not know the number of wills made during the last year in which bequests
were made to the homes, but which may not become available for many
years.

Adopted.

We must not forget that this is a long range program, the ultimate
success of which depends upon the continued efforts of all of us.

Rearrangement of the Constitudon
Our good Brother, Past Grand Master John Ross, has just completed
a rearrangement of the Constitution, which will be presented at this session
of Grand Lodge for your consideration. It has come to our attention that
in rewriting the Constitution, Brother Ross was put to considerable
expense in addition to the many hours of his time devoted to the work.
Brother Ross has not presented a bill. In fact, he did not care to
inform · the committee of the amount of his expenditures, but expressed a
desire to donate the completed book to the Grand Lodge. However, we
feel that Brother Ross in doing this splendid work should not find it
necessary to assume any financial burden, and we therefore, offer the
following resolution:

In seven years the work of our Endowment Board has almost doubled
our Endowment Fund and with continued interest and redoubled efforts
another seven years surely will give us far greater results. Already our
Endowment Fund stands very high in comparison with those of other
Grand Lodges, some of which have been in operation for many years.
At our last annual communication Grand Lodge appropriated $6,000
for the use of the Endowment Board. We have reviewed very carefully
the details of the expenditure of that $6,000. We believe that these expenditures have been very carefully worked out and that the board has had in
mind not only the education of the entire membership, but also the arousing

Reports of Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary
The reports of these two officers again display the care and elliciency
exercised by both in conducting the affairs of their offices and handling the
records and finances of Grand Lodge. We again want to commend these
officers for the ever watchful care given and express the appreciation of
this committee for the work they have done for Grand Lodge and the
assistance given this committee.
As already recorded in our repor.t on the "Audit of Accounts," the
items of receipts and disbursements have been properly accounted for,
and that their records are in perfect shape; Your committee has nothing
but words of commendation for their reports and their work.
It is worthy of note that we have had the services of both these
officers for many years, the Grand Treasurer having served in that capacity
for twenty-five years, and the Grand Secretary as such for thirty-two years
and that the latter has been a Mason for si:ict:y years. ·
That Masonry in California, and particularly Grand Lodge, is benefiting
from these years of service, there can be no question.
We again feel that it is mete to call to Grand Lodge's attention the
very grea.t responsibility that the Grand Treasurer has in properly investing the funds of Grand Lodge and, more particularly, the moneys of the
Endowment Fund. These investments require much study and great care
as well as extensive knowledge of securities and investments. The Grand
Treasurer has met and fulfilled all his responsibilities in a manner that
should bring genuine appreciation from every member of the Fraternity.

Adopted.
Unpaid Grand Lodge Dues
For a number of years it has been necessary for this committee to
report the inability of some of the constituent Lodges to pay their Grand
Lodge dues. This condition has gradually improved until last year we were
able to report the dues of every Lodge in the jurisdiction, with one
exception, settled in full and up-to-date. This one exception, being Yorba
Linda Lodge No. 469 in the sum of $239.60, was paid during the year.

It is particularly pleasing to your committee to be able to report that
R. E. Dolley Lodge No. 616 has paid the amount it owed in full, and that
Chowchilla Lodge No. 485 has reduced its indebtedness in the sum of
$350.00. Your committee wishes to extend the thanks of Grand Lodge. as
well as of this committee for these repayments and for the efforts which
we know these Lodges must have made in caring for their obligations.

This Lodge has presented a request to Grand Lodge for reimbursement in the sum of $50.00 for the Homes fee of $25.00 each on two applicants for membership and which memberships were not completed due to
inability to secure demits from the original Lodge of membership. These
two applicants, therefore, did not eventually become members of Pajaro
Lodge and the Homes fee was paid in error. The Grand Secretary confirms
the report. It would therefore seem that Pajaro Lodge had paid to Grand
Lodge $50.00 more for the Homes fee than was required and in equity
should be entitled to a refund of this amount.
Your committee therefore offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $50.00 be appropriated from the funds of
Masonic Homes and be paid to Pajaro Lodge No. 110 to reimburse it for
the amount it had previously paid in excess of the amount required for
the Homes fee.

Adopted.

Correspondence Committee Report

Your committee is sure that this communication of Grand Lodge will
wish to continue this pleasing policy and to have the portrait of their
present retiring Grand Master included in this gallery. Your committee
therefore recommends that our retiring Grand Master, the M. W. Leon 0.
Whitsell, have his portrait painted and present the bill to the Grand Secretary, in an amount not to exceed $250.00, who is authorized ·t o pay same,
and when the portrait is finished to be hung in the gallery of Past Grand
Masters.

The chairman of your Committee on Correspondence has prepared his
report for the past year and it will be printed in the Grand Lodge
Proceedings.
This committee reviews all the reports of the proceedings of all Grand
Lodges of the world, which have been received by the committee. The
report indicates the great amoun<t of work necessary to prop~rly revie~
what is being done in Masonry elsewhere in the world. This report 1s
valuable and, in the opinion of your committee, should be much more
extensively read than it ordinarily is. We suggest to the Masters that,
upon receipt of the proceedings, they not only call the attention of their
Lodges to the fact that this report on correspondence will be made available to any member of the Lodge desirous of reading it, but that they
recommend such reading, and, also, review this report themselves.
It had been the policy of Grand Lodge in the past to appropriate for
the purpose of preparing and compiling this report the sum of $500.00.
Your committee this year is fully cognizant of the amount of work necessary to properly review the proceedings and prepare the report and is
fully in accord that the chairman of the committee should be reimbursed
for his expenses in doing this work for Grand Lodge. It therefore offers
the following resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $500.00 be and is hereby appropriated from
the funds of Grand Lodge and be paid to the chairman of the Committee
on Correspondence for the purpose of defraying expenses for reviewing
and preparing their report for that committee.

Adopted.
Traveling Expenses of Grand Master
Your committee has discussed with our present Grand Master what
he considers would be an appropriate amount to allow for the traveling
expenses of our incoming Grand Master in caring for the duties of · his
office for this coming year. We learned from him and from other sources
that our incoming Grand Master proposes to devote much of his time
during the year to attending to the duties of his office and in extensive
travel throughout the entire jurisdiction. ·
The committee is thoroughly in favor of the Grand Master meeting
just as many of the members of the Craft and in every part of the State
as his time and endurance and other responsibilities permit, and that the
Grand Master should not be expected to pay any part of the costs of his
travels from his own personal funds:
Your committee has concluded there should be appropriated for these
expenses a sum not less than $4,500.00, and, therefore, offers the following
resolution and recommends its adoption :
Resoroed, th.at the sum of $4,500.00 be appropriated from the funds of
Grand Lodge for the traveling expenses of the Grand Master.

Adopted.

Reimbursement of Expenses of Inspectors
The resolution presented by the committee representing the Inspectors
of Grand Lodge and which resolution provides for a change in that provision of the Constitution providing for the method of payment of expense

590

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of Inspectors in performing their various official duties, and which resolution has been referred by the Grand Master jointly to the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes, and this committee, has had the full consideration of your Finance Committee.
In consultation with the chairman of the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes we are advised that the report of that committee will
be favorable to the adoption of such a policy.
While your Finance Committee is favorable to a plan whereby the
Inspectors will receive repayment of necessary expense from Grand Lodge,
rather than as now provided for by the Constitution, and yet it is unwilling
to recommend the adoption of the resolution as presented for several
reasons; the main one being that the provisions of the resolution are too
broad and therefore the intent of the resolution could be abused. There is
also the further objection that the cost by such a method of payment is
difficult to determine without more information than this committee now
has, and therefore it is not possible for your Finance Committee to
determine, within reasonable bounds, the cost to Grand Lodge. We feel
unwilling to recommend the approval of the resolution until these objections are removed.
It would seem to this committee that the Grand Lecturer should be
instructed to study the cost to Grand Lodge of the reimbursements of
Inspectors' expenses under such a plan, and also to frame a resolution
which would prevent abuses of the plan, and be prepared to present the
facts and the resolution at the next annual communication.
It would seem further to your committee that the proposed reimbursement of the expenses of the Inspectors by Grand Lodge need not be
deferred until such study and rcommendations are made by the Grand
Lecturer. With that in mind this committee has decided to recommend
an expenditure for this purpose of $2,000.00, with the recommendation that
the Grand Lecturer adopt certain regulations providing for reimbursement
of expenses of Inspectors, such regulations to be approved by the Grand
Master, and all reimbursements to be made in accordance with such regulations. In our opinion such regulations should provide that no Inspector
should be reimbursed for expenses incurred for more than two visitations
to each Lodge, such visits to be for the purpose of instruction, except
that the Grand Lecturer should have the right to require such additional
visitation as, in his judgment, any Lodge might require; further, that the
Inspectors be allowed expenses incurred in attending not more than two
schools of instruction, whether district or general; and further, that the
regulation provide that for any reimbursement for use of automobile it be
at a rate not to exceed five cents per mile.
In consultation with the committee of Inspectors we are advised it is
not the intent to reimburse those Inspectors who are serving in metropolitan areas; we are in accord with this idea.
Your committee might further say, that in consultation with the committee appointed by the Inspectors, the plan above outlined has been fully
agreed to by them. Your Finance Committee therefore offers the following
resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, that the resolution presented by the committee representing
the Inspectors of Grand Lodge be not adopted and be it further,
Resolved, that the sum of $2,000.00 be appropriated from the funds of
Grand Lodge for the purpose of defraying expenses of Inspectors in performing their official duties, such repayment to be made upon bills duly

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

presented to the Grand Secretary and which said bills shall be approved
first by the Grand Lecturer.

Adopted.

This income is not sufficient to pay the operating expenses of Grand
Lodge during this coming year and to care for the various appropriations
that are being recommended in this report.
For a number of years prior to the year just closing, deficits occurred
-such deficits being cared for out of surpluses accumulated a number of
years ago. Two years ago your Finance Committee took the position that
these deficits should not continue. While a deficit has not occurred for this
year yet the amount added to surplus was very meager, amounting to
approximately $3,000.00.
This committee has always been mindful of the financial burden the
Lodges are carrying and, therefore, is disposed to provide for only sufficient
funds to be sure that no additional calls shall be made upon the previously
accumulated surplus.
It is to be noted that the total appropriations being recommended in
this report are somewhat less than last year. While small, yet this downward trend is gratifying, and the more so when it is borne in mind that
the anticipated revenue for this coming year will probably be less than
that of last year. We are, therefore·, recommending the same additional
per capita levy for the purpose of caring for the expenses of Grand Lodge
and the appropriations being made in this report as we did last year, that
is, an additional per capita levy above that provided for in the Constitution
of twenty-five cents.
The report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes asked for, in addition to the Constitutional requirement, a per capita levy of forty cents.
This committee concurs in the recommendation and in that part of its
report dealing with the report of the trustees of the homes, presented a
resolution providing for this levy of forty cents, which resolution has
already been approved by you, and, therefore no additional resolution at
this time is necessary.

Compulsory Proficiency in the Lecture of the Third Degree
The resolution of Brother J. Hall Hearne, Master of Ocean Park
Lodge No. 369, printed in the advance information sheet of August 16,
1939, reading as follows, was referred to the Ritual Committee :
To amend Section 3 of Article IV of the Uniform Code of By-Laws
to read as follows:
Sec. 3. Every person raised to the degree of Master Mason in
this Lodge, and proving his proficiency by passing a satisfactory
examination in the candidate's lecture of the third degree (except
when such degree shall have been conferred at the request of another Lodge), or elected to be a member thereof, shall sign its
By-Laws.
Alse>Resolved, that membership in a Lodge for newly raised Master
Masons shall commence with the passing of a satisfactory examination, in open Lodge, on the candidate's lecture of the third
degree. ·
Resolved, that the application of the ritual be modified by
having the delivery of the Master's congratulation and the candi-.
date's signing of the By-Laws postponed until immediately after
the candidate passed said examination.
That Sections 136, 137 and 139 of the Constitution be amended
·to include the provision that no 'Master-elect, Senior or Junior
Warden-elect, nor Senior Deacon appointed, shall be installed until
he shall have produced to the installing officer a diploma of proficiency in the candidate's lectu.r e of the third degree.
And that Section 154 of the Constitution, subd. 1st, be
amended by adding thereto: "And proving his proficiency by
passing a satisfactory examination in the candidate's lecture of
the third degree."
After consideration, the committee reports that they agree with the
purposes and objects sought to be accomplished and commend them as
laudable and worthy objectives for the Fraternity to work toward in
principle, but that the present condition of the Craft, particularly in some

595

We do recommend that it be the policy of the Grand Lodge of California that Masters of Lodges shall continue to encourage all newly made
Masons to immediately learn the candidate's lecture of the third degree as
a concrete expression of their real appreciation for the honor conferred
upon them by the officers and brethren of the Lodge; and that an emphasis
of this policy in the respective Lodges will in season ultimately permit the
adoption of a compulsory regulation of similar character which will accomplish the purposes sought.
We recommend that the resolution be not adopted.

Report adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CLANDESTINE
MASONRY
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as
follows:
The members of the committee have been in close observation of the
activities of the many irregular bodies previously reported as being active
in California, as well as several new organizations. Generally speaking the
old bodies are maintaining their existence with some slight changes. A new
Grand Organization from New York State has chartered a Lodge in Los
Angeles and certain other alleged organizations from Mexico have invaded
our jurisdiction and organized subordinate Lodges here. These will be
specifically referred to later.
Negro Masonry
The M. W. Prince Hall Grand Lodge. Your committee has previously
reported that this Grand Lodge was known as "The Most Worshipful
Sovereign Grand Lodge of A. F. & A. M." but in deference to our Grand
Lodge changed its name to "The Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand
Lodge." It held its annual 1939 communication July 17-23 in the City of
Oakland. A well attended session is reported. The financial difficulties

596

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

which had involved their property near Tulare as a prospective home for
aged members, appear to have been straightened out, and they have
apparently recovered full control of t_his property and propose to proceed
with the development of it.
This year they advanced their grand officers. Theodore Moss of San
Jose, who had been Grand Master for a number of years, retired, and
Roscoe H. Broyles of Santa Monica, was elected Grand Master; George
Vaughins of Oakland, Deputy Grand Master; Ray Hunter of Fresno,
Senior Grand Warden; J.C. Simms of Los Angeles, Junior Grand Warden;
and Nathan Hardy of 845 Brockhurst Street, Oakland, Grand Secretary.
Roscoe H. Broyles is an old resident of Santa Monica, very well
known and highly respected in that city, and has served the Masonic
bodies of his rite for many years. Apparently it has not been the practice
of the negro grand Lodges to advance their grand officers each year.
M. W. Hiram of Tyre Grand Lodge. This Grand Lodge held .its
annual communication in Los Angeles on June 19, and all grand officers
were present. At this meeting their Master, Brother J. P . Lea, of 1378 East
108th Street, Los Angeles, who had served for many years, retired, and
the Rev. C. B. Terrance of 1358 East 42nd Place, Los Angeles, was elected
Grand Master; F. W. Jingles of 1011 East 43rd Place, Los Angeles,
Deputy Grand Master; John Cannon of 1961 "E" Street, Fresno, Grand
Treasurer; S. C. Hannibal of 1651 "E" Street, Fresno, was appointed
DistriCt Deputy Grand Master of San Joaquin Valley and Stockton. This
Grand Lodge is recovering from its internal difficulties terminating in a
law suit in 1935, and many indications now point to developing interest
and growth. The two Lodges in the San Joaquin valley, to-wit, Raisin
Center Lodge No. 5, and Ezra Lodge No. 11 of Stockton, are meeting
steadily and regularly, and we are informed initiating new members.
We are informed that a new Lodge under this negro rite is to be
instituted on Wednesday of this week in Santa Monica.
A movement appears to be on foot for the harmonizing of the differences which has for many years divided these two negro Grand Lodges.
Filipino Masonry
The Grand Lodge Caballieros de Dimas-Alang. As previously reported,
the Lodges of this organization represent twenty-five ·individual subordinate
bodies. They are said to constitute the Masonic aristocracy among the
Filipinos. Their name, "Dimas Alang," which is neither Spanish nor
Tagalog, but is an idiomatic phrase meaning "Touch Me Not." It was
first used as a pen name by Dr. Jose Rizal, a very distinguished Mason in
Philippine history.
We are informed that the next tri-annual communication will be held
in Sacramento in January of 1940. They issue a quarterly publication

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Pay of Members submit the following report
covering the 90th annual communication of Grand Lodge:
Those entitled to compensation are the duly accredited representatives
of each Lodge, Inspectors, Past Grand Masters, officers of Grand Lodge,
chairmen and members of committees enumerated in Section 27 of the
Cons ti tu tion.
Compensation of members is fixed in Section 71 of the Constitution
as being twice the single first-class one-way railway fare, plus Pullman
sleeper where necessary. As has been the custom for many years, no compensation is allowed to members from San Francisco or the immediate
vicinity, nor where the prescribed compensation does not exceed $1.00.
We have carefully checked and computed the transportation rates from

with the pay-roll the registration records as submitted to us by the Committee on Credentials. The amount required to meet transportation costs
