REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE
Life Memberships
Resoli•ed, that the second paragraph of Sec. 129 of the Constitution be
amended to read as follows:
"All amounts paid for life membership shall be deposited in
some reputable bank or invested in securities legal for savings
banks under either the laws of the State of California or the laws
of the Territory of Hawaii, and only the income thereof shall be
used by the Lodge, the original amounts to be kept and maintained
· as and for a permanent life membership fund. PROVIDED: that
on the death of a member holding a life membership the amount
standing against h~ name in the life membership fund shall revert to
the general funds of the Lodge, notwithstanding the wording of the
sentence immediately preceding thu proviso."
OTTO F. HANSEN,
Military Service No. 570.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The foregoing resolution was continued from last year as unfinished
business:
This is an amendment to the section providing for the form of a
resolution to be adopted by a Lodge creating life membership.
It is in effect, an attempt. on the part of Grand Lodge, to change the
terms of a solemn binding contract between the Lodge and its members
that cannot be abrogated except by the unanimous consent of all parties
interested therein. It does not give to the Lodge any discretion, but says
that on the death of a life member his contribution to the life membership
fund shall revert to the general funds of the Lodge. Thus, the contract
between the Lodge and its life members is set as nought without the
consent of either of the contracting parties. In view of these fa.cts, it is
evident that the purposed amendment could not affect life membership
funds now existing, nor could it operate on future contracts of life membership, unless and until the Lodge has adopted an amendment to its life
membership resolution incorporating the provision, after the same notice as
was required for the adoption of the original resolution.
As the suggested amendment would not accomplish the purpose for
which it was apparently intended, and if it is intended to act retroactively,
it is in our opinion illegal. We recommend that it be not adopted.

The report of the Committee was adopted.

While your committee appreciates the motive of the Grand Master
and while it believes, as do we all, that Masons should extend every
courtesy and consideration to the dependents of deceased brethren, it does
not concur in the suggestion made. The giving of advice on financial
matters involves serious responsibilities. Those really competent to assume
such responsibilities are relatively few in number, and it would appear that
they undertake such responsibilities with considerable reluctance. The
widows and orphans of deceased Masons have recourse to attorneys,
bankers, and experienced business men and women. We do not believe that
Masonic Lodges, as represented by committees, can practically and satisfactorily undertake this type of service.

The Grand Master in his Message directed our attention to the

adv1sab1bty of recommending to the constituent Lodges of this grand

The Ross Digest
The Grand Master in his address directed the attention of Grand
Lodge to the monumental work that has been done by Past Grand Master
John Stewart Ross in compiling the Constitution and R egulations of Grand
Lodge and in making a logical arrangement of the sections of our law.
An examination of the work done by Brother Ross discloses that no
liberties have been taken with the substance of our law, but such changes
made in the compilation are merely of verbiage to make the provisions of
the Constitution and Regulations more easily found and more understandable.
In the opinion of your committee this Grand Lodge owes Brother Ross
a debt of gratitude for his long and painstaking work. Y>our committee
also is of the opinion that the compilation so made should be adopted as
w ill be recommended by the Committee on Jurisprudence.
The Grand Master's recommendation that the Constitution and Regulations, as prepared, be published under the name and be known as "Ross'
Digest" has been considered by your committee and this matter has been
discussed with Brother Ross. Your committee recommends that the title
of the work be "Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge, Annotated and Compiled by John Stewart Ross, Past Grand Master," and that
the title of the Masonic Digest prepared by Brother Ross be entitled and
referred to as " Ross' Digest."

Adopted.
Expenses of Inspectors
Lawrence C. Kelley, Harold W. Conklin and Rudolph Mohr hl\ve introduced a resolution that section 56 of the Constitution be amended by
eliminating therefp~m the following words:
"Each Lodge shall pay such necessary expenses of the Inspector as may be incurred in performing the duties of visitation
herein required."
They, also recommend that Section 57 of the Constitution be amended
to read as follows:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

606

"It shall also be the duty of each Inspector of this jurisdiction
to attend the Lodge of Instruction to be held by the Grand
Lecturer immediately before, during, or immediately following each
annual communication of the Grand Lodge and he shall be allowed
transportation from the Representative Fund in the same manner
as is allowed the officers or the representatives of the Lodges;
provided that he shall produce the certificate of the Grand Lecturer that he has attended the Lodge of Instruction; and in addition thereto shall be entitled to receive payment out of funds of
Grand Lodge of the amount of his necessary traveling expenses
in attending school of instruction held by the Assistant Grand
Lecturer of his district and in performing his other duties as Inspector. Claim for such expense must be approved by the Grand
Lecturer and presented for payment at the following annual communication of the Grand Lodge. No Inspector receiving payment
of expenses as herein provided for attendance on Grand Lodge in
any capacity as a member or otherwise shall receive any such
payment as Inspector."
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has received the
approval of the Ritual Committee to the foregoing proposals and has had
the assurance of the Committee on Finance that it would appropriate the
sum of $2,000.00, or such part thereof as may be necessary, to pay the
necessary expenses of Inspectors, as contemplated by the proposed amendment to Section 57 of the Constitution.
·
Your committee, however, is of the opinion that a survey should be
made to ascertain the amount of expenses incurred by' Inspectors in the
performance of their duties, the inspectorial districts where distance is
great, and the duties unusually burdensome and other pertintent facts,
to determine whether or not it is a sound policy for Grand Lodge to
continue the payment of such expenses.
During the period elapsing between this annual communication and
the next annual communication of Grand Lodge, such a survey can be
made and pertinent facts can be collected and then this committee can
make some definite recommendation.
We are not disposed to open a door of expenditures which now may
seem small but which may grow larger and larger with the demands of
the coming years. Sometimes it is difficult to stop a pay-roll.
That hardships may not be worked on individual Lodges, yo'ur committee is of the opinion that a temporary experiment in this matter would
be justified and, therefore, recommends that no amendment be made at
this time to $aid Section 57; but that the Grand Treasurer be authorized
to reimburse Inspectors for their actual expenses when such reimbursement
is approved by the Grand Lecturer, and that such reimbursement shall not
exceed the aggregate sum of $2,000.00 for the year commencing with the
closing of this annual communication and the beginning of the next annual
communication. We further recommend that the Grand Lecturer cause a
survey to be made respecting the expenses of Inspectors and the travel
requirements of the inspectorial districts, and submit the same together
with his recommendation to the next annual communication of this Grand
Lodge. We also recommend that no inspector be reimbursed for any
expenses if he receives money from any Lodge in his inspectorial district.

Adopted.

607

Forfeiture of Fees
The representative of Russian River Lodge No. 181 proposes Section
2 of Article IV of the Uniform Code of By-Laws be amended to read as
follows:
"Sec. 2. If an applicant, elected to receive the degrees in this
Lodge does not come forward to be initiated within three months
thereafter, or having been initiated fails to come forward for
advancement within one year thereafter, the fee shall be forfeited,
unless the Lodge shall otherwise direct."
Your committee is of the opinion that such amendment should not be
adopted and that the present provision on this subject is just and amp!~.
The reason for our opinion in this matter is that a candidate has paid his
fees been elected to receive the degree, and has been initiated or passed.
He bas become a Mason and is entitled to brotherly Masonic consideration.
By a delay in appearing for advancement he has not ha~med the Lod~e
which has received the fee here now proposed to be forfeited. The loss 1s
sustained by the Apprentice or Fellow Craft, and not by the Lodge.
Moreover the candidate has placed himself, by being initiated, under the
exclusive Jurisdiction of his Lodge and his rights and expectation of future
advancement depend upon the action of his Lodge. It would not seem
quite fair for the Lodge to have power and authority over the candidate's
advancement and, at the same time, deprive him of his equity in the fee
he had paid for such advancement. It is true that some inconvenience .might
be suffered by the secretary of the Lodge, but the aggravation would not
justify exacting a forfeiture of money paid by a Mason as fees for the
degrees.
Your committee therefore recommends that the proposed amendment
be not adopted.

Adopted.
Stated Meetings on Holidays
Various persons have proposed that section 1 of Article III of the
Uniform Code of By-Laws be amended to provide that when a meeting
date shall fall on a legal holiday, the stated meeting shall be held on some
definite succeeding day not a legal holiday.
We are of the opinion that the present Section 1 of Article III is
ample. There are certain holidays that are not generally observed, and
many Lodges might prefer to hold their stated meetings on Lincoln's
birthday, or Columbus day, or Armistice day, or some other holiday that
is not generally observed and which does not seriously interfere with
secular activities. The present form permits a Lodge to select a time for
. stated meeting when the usual time thereof falls on a holiday which is
generally observed and which the members of the Lodge think should
not be an appropriate time for Masonic meeting. The proposed amendment
covers all holidays and does not take into consideration the fact that many
Lodges do not have the exclusive use of the hall in which they meet, and
that a uniform rule of postponements would work an undue hardship.
Your committee respectfully recommends that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

Adopted.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

608

The Lecture of the Third Degree
]. Hall Hearne, Master of Ocean Park Lodge No. 369, proposes an
amendment to the Uniform Code of By-Laws and to certain sections of
the Constitution to require that a candidate shall, after receiving the degree
of Master Mason, be required to pass a satisfactory examination, in open
Lodge, in the candidate's lecture of the third degree before he can be
congratulated or sign the By-Laws, or become a member of the Lodge.
Your committee is of the opinion that the proposed amendment should
not be adopted. If the amendment were adopted, after a man had received
the third degree he would be without any of the rights of a Master Mason
for some indefinite period of time. During this period of time he might
die, in which event he would not be entitled to Masonic burial nor would
his family have the rights or benefits to which the ritual of the third
degree indicates to be their due. There might be reasons which' would
prevent a Mason from making an immediate study of the lecture, or might
deter either himself or the Lodge from an examination in open Lodge
for a period of time. During this time he would be in the position of a
Master Mason unaffiliated and unrecognized because he had been denied
by circumstances perhaps not under his control which have prevented his
complying with the requiremi;nts for signing the By-Laws of his Lodge.
We found our objection also upon the belief that those Masons who
memorize the lecture of the third degree and secure a diploma of proficiency take a pride in making themselves proficient in this duty of
Masonic work which is voluntarily undertaken and done, and that such
pride and zeal would not be evinced if this matter was one of compulsion
exacted by the Masonic law. The present law gives a stimulus to the
voluntary doing of a useful thing, while the proposed amendments would
diminish or destroy such stimulus.
Your committee respectfully recommends that the resolution be not
adopted.

Adopted.
InvestmC'llts of Masonic Funds
Charles R. Cooper of Presidio Lodge No. 354 proposes amendments
to Sections 87 and 129 of the Constitution by adding thereto the following
language:

"* * * and certificates and/or shares in State chartered institutions to the extent of said institutions' insurance for its depositors in the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance corporation."
At the present time the investment of funds by a Lodge shall be in
securities prescribed as legal by the law of California or Hawaii for investments by savings banks. The only test in this State for the investment of
trust funds is the law specifying the securities which are legal investments
for savings banks. The funds of the Masonic Lodge! are in the nature of ·
trust funds.
Your committee is of the opinion that until a better standard has been
devised than that now in use, the Lodges in this grand jurisdiction should
follow the present standard of investments.
It is true that at a recent session of the legislature an act was passed
making shares of an insured federal building and loan association legal
investments for savings banks. The shares or certificates of building and
loan associations organized under the laws of the State of California are

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

609

not legal investments for savings banks, although some of such associations
have the same insurance that federal associations enjoy. There is no reason
why an insured state institution should not be qualified by the legislature
to the same extent as a federal buildingt and loan association. But the fact
remains that the state associations failed to have the legislature give their
certificates the same investment status as that given to federal associations.
It appears to us that instead of expanding our tests for investment to cover
this case, it would be better to let the state associations, if they wish us
to invest our money with them, go to the legislature and have the act
amended.
It would be a bad precedent for us to begin expanding our investment
field beyond the limitations prescribed by the rules which we use as a
measure of our right.
For the foregoing reasons we respectfully recommend that the resolution be not adopted.

Adopted.
The Six-Months' Rule
William Penn Humphreys of Occidental Lodge No. 22 proposes the
abrogation of the rule that a Master Mason shall not, within six months
after receiving the degree of Master Mason, apply for or receive any degree,
or be initiated in any body, order, or organization, the prerequisite of
membership therein is that the person be a Master Mason. This rule was
adopted in 1922 for the purpose of correcting practices which Grand Lodge
believed to be improper. It was then thought and we now believe that a
Master Mason should not be hurried away from his Lodge to join some
other order. Six months' attention to the duties of his Lodge is not too long
for a Mason unmolested to gain information and to become familiar with
the atmosphere and spirit of the Lodge with which he has allied himself as
a member and a Mason.
We are of the opinion that during the past seventeen years the wisdom
of our present rule has be.e n justified by its salutary effect in this grand
jurisdiction.
Your committee respectfully recommends that the proposal to eliminate
question 13 of Form 246 be not adopted.

Adopted.
Restoration to Membership
Carl Leue of Huntington Beach Lodge No. 380 proposes amendments
to Section 3, Article IX of the By-Laws, to provide that should any one or
more members in the Lodge protest to the Master against the restoration
of any member suspended over two years, and such protes t is upheld by a
majority of the living members of the delinquent committee of the year of
suspension, the applicant for restoration shall be required to pay in full all
arrearages to date of suspension, plus not less than 50% of accrued dues
payable since suspension.
It appears to the committee that the present Section 3 of Article IX of
the Uniform Code of By-Laws, and by Section 119 of the Constitution, is
sufficiently explicit to cover the case of the restoration of a suspended
member, and leavel' with the Lodge the right and authority to deal with
each case on its merits in accordance with the wishes of a substantial
number of the members of the Lodge. We therefore recommend that the
resolution be not adopted.

Adopted.

610

The American Flag
Brothers R. B. Hood, W. J. Lembke, and M. P. Roberts, Jr., of
Arcata Lodge No. 106, propose .a resolution relative to the procedure of
presenting the flag in the Lodge room. In such resolution they propose
that the Master demand a pledge of allegiance to the flag from each
member present.
This is a proper subject matter for the Ritual Committee and, in addition thereto, it appears to us that in view of the fact that many Freemasons
owe allegiance to the governments of lands other than the United States,
that a requirement that every person present in a Lodge room should
signify affirmatively his allegiance to the national emblem of the United
States-be he a citizen of the United States or of any other countryis unfair. The implication of such a requirement would deny the universality
of Masonry and would imply it to be a national institution.
Your committee respectfully recommends that the subject matter of
the resolution be referred to the Ritual Committee, and as to that part
thereof which requires a pledge of allegiance, be not adopted.

Adopted.
Fee for Courtesy Degrees
Paul R. Queen, Master of Glendale Lodge No. 544, proposes that the
Grand Lodge or the constituent Lodges demand fees for any degrees
conferred at the request of a Lodge in another jurisdiction, such fees to
be the same as those now required for each degree conferred upon a
candidate in this jurisdiction, but that no contribution shall be required for
the Masonic Homes of California.
The conferring of degrees by courtesy to a sister jurisdiction is
intended to be and is a fraternal courtesy extended without obligation and
without price to another grand jurisdiction. When degrees are conferred
at our request by other jurisdictions, we accept the performance of such
Masonic courtesy to be untainted by any demand for money or other
material consideration. That abuses may not spring from a willingness to
be kind, Section 155 requires that requests for the conferring of courtesy
degrees shall be transmitted through the Grand Master or Grand Secretary.
It appears to us that this is a sufficient safeguard. Your committee
recommends that the proposal be not adopted.

Adopted.
Masonic Home Fee
Brother C. E. Mallachowitz, Past Master of Caledonia Lodge No. 486,
proposes that the Masonic Home fee for out-of-state affiliates be not
charged.
Your committee is of the opinion that no persuasive reasons appear
for the abrogation of the Masonic Home fee, charged either for the degrees
or for affiliation. It is possible that there are cases where the Masonic
Home fee deters a Mason from affiliating with a California Lodge, but
such cases cannot be numerous. Our homes are so important and the
Masonic work we do there is so beneficial to our elderly people and to our
orphan children that there would be few indeed who would hesitate to
make a contribution to the noble cause of the homes upon becoming a
member in this jurisdiction and, as such member, having rights as well as
duties with respect to the homes.
Your committee recommends that the resolution be not adopted.

Adopted.

Refreshment Fund
Brother F. W . Dobbel of Temple Lodge No. 14 p~oposes that the
cumulative clause in Section 89 of the Constitution be stricken out.
Section 89 places limitation on the amount of the total revenue~ of a

It seems to your committee that all power should not be taken from

refreshment funds of the Lodge when it has placed a hm1tatton on the total
amount thereof which can be expended. The right of the cumulative use of
the fund may or may not be exercised in the sound discretion of the Lodge
itself.
We recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

Personnel of Standing Committee
Carl 0 . Olsen of Fremont Lodge No. 497 and R. C. Strehlow, Jr., of
Oak Grove Lodge No. 215, have introduced a resolution proposing an
amendment to Section 27 of the Constitution, to provide that the membership of the Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and General
Purposes shall be composed of four Past Grand Masters, two Past Masters,
two Masters, and one warden. The section now provides that a Master
and warden be appointed on each of the standing committees.
No reasons for the proposed change in Section 27 appear in the resolution or have been presented to your committee, and your committee is
unaware of any reason why the time-honored rule that the Grand Master
is the proper appointing power of Grand Lodge committees and that all
members of Grand Lodge, regardless of rank, are eligible to appointment
to any committee should be abrogated. Your committee is of the opinion
that the selection of committee members should be left in the sound discretion of the Grand Master, with no further limitation than that now
expressed in Section 27 and recommend that the proposed amendment to
Section 27 be not adopted.

Grand Lodge did not concur in the report of 1he committee
and the resolution proposing to amend Section 27 was referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence. Subsequently the Committee on Jurisprudence reported that the resolution was in
proper form. A vote being had thereon, the resolution failed
of a majority vote and was declared lost.

REVISED CONSTITUTION

Petition for Change of Name
Your committee has had under consideration an application requesting
your approval of a resolution heretofore adopted by Veteran Lodge, located
in West Los Angeles. In the resolution thus adopted it is proposed to
change the name of Veteran Lodge No. 373 to West Los Angeles Lodge
No. 373.
Y°;ur committee is unanimously of the opinion that the reasons urged
for the purposed change are so meritorious as to be deserving of every
consideration. Likewise, your committee believes that the reasons advanced
in opposition thereto, namely, partial duplication and similarity in name
are entitled to equal consideration.
However, aside from the merits of the question, there is to be considered the purpose of a tesolution adopted by this Grand Lodge in 1924,
concerning which I quote from the 1924 Proceedings as follows, at page 92 :
"The Committee on Charters submit the following resolution."
"Resolved, that hereafter no dispensation shall be granted on a
petition for a new Lodge with a name similar to a Lodge already
existing; which name shall have as its purpose the memorializing
of a particular person, place, or event."
This resolution was referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes, which committee reported as follows: page 219, 1924 Proceedings:
"The purposes of this resolution undoubtedly is to prevent a
confusion in the names of Lodges borne upon the Roster of Grand
Lodge, and to avoid duplications and similarities in the matter of
Lodge names. It is desirable that a rule be adopted to govern this
subject and we therefore recommend that said resolution be
adopted."
The recommendation of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
was adopted.
Inasmuch as the evident purpose of the standing resolution, as
adopted in 1924, is to eliminate duplications and similar names of Lodges,
and inasmuch as the purposed name, West Los Angeles is similar to and
a partial duplication of Los Angeles No. 42, your committee feels that it
has no choice but to recommend to Grand Lodge that the resolution of
Veteran Lodge No. 373, wherein it is purposed to change the name of said
Lodge to West Los Angeles Lodge No. 323, be not approved.
LEE T. MULLEN,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
For the sixteenth annual period in a service of eighteen years as Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence, herewith is presented its Report.
As in former years, the same is the work of the Chairman and the views
expressed under the various topics are, of course, his own.
In compiling the same the Proceedings of over 60 Grand Lodges have
been summarized, with a view of giving the reader briefly the thought and
action of the various jurisdictions. There is no dearth of material and the
problem is to select and confine within the pages allotted interest and instructive information.
During the preparation of the report for the last sixteen years the trend
of Masonic activities, discussions, or legislation have generally featured a
particular subject and pertinent to all the various Proceedings. These included such matters as "Dual and Plural Membership, Masonic Education,
Reformation of Procedure in Masonic Trials, The Regulation of Co-ordinate Masonic Bodies, Liquor or Gambling."
Next year, as the Chairman of the Correspondence Committee of North
Carolina says, it may probably be a uniform "Declaration of Principles" by
Masonic Grand Lodges. England, Massachusetts and some other jurisdictions have started the consideration of this problem.
Grand Master Steuart of the District of Colwnbia, when called upon to
respond to the toast of the " GRAND LODGES OF THE UNITED
STATES" at Nova Scotia, perhaps outlined the problem that confronts the
Chairman of a Correspondence Committee when endeavoring to select from
the Proceedings that which would interest the readCt" of a Correspondence
Report.
"To respond to this toast and speak for forty-nine Grand Lodges, seems.
to require the combined talents of a Solon, a Tallyrand and a Demosthenes.
"The task is the greater since the members of our far-flung Masonic
family of Grand Lodges have such diverse sizes, ages, customs, ideas.
United in every fundamental, every one of us in fraternal relations with all
the rest. Our largest Grand Lodge with more than a thousand Lodges and
more than a quarter million Masons-our smallest Grand Lodge with 26
Lodges and a few more than 3,000 Masons, and all those in between, live
together in peace and harmony-but we disagree violently if in the most
friendly manner, over many a question of law and custom, practice and idea.
"Thirty-six of our forty-nine Grand jurisdictions have Masonic homes,
hospitals, orphanages, asylums or other institutions to make practical the
brotherly idea of relict · Grand Lodges which have found it wiser in their
jurisdictions not to provide institutions, have charity foundations or funds
from which liberal contributions are made to the support of the helpless.
The united funds held for charitable purposes top ten millions of dollarsone Grand Lodge alone has two and a half millions in its charity account.
An average of one hundred and forty guests inhabit each of these thirty-six
homes, including also seventeen hospitals, valued at over twenty millions
of dollars.
"Remarkable though it seems, the average yearly contribution made by
each Master Mason to his Grand Lodge is only $1.92 (ninety cents the
smallest, four dollars and a half the largest) and nearly four-fifths of this
is spent in charity.

· PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"A few customs we hold in common-we elect a Grand Master every
year, for instance, in all forty-nine Grand jurisdictions. But in twelve we
customarily sentence the incumbent to a second term, and in Massachusetts
they are so loathe to let a good man go that they condemn him to a threeyear sentence I
"Curiously enough, in only three states is the old custom of appointing
a Deputy Grand Master followed-elsewhere, he, too, is elected, as are
Grand Wardens and the Grand Secretaries and Grand Treasurers. But in
two jurisdictions there are no such animals as Grand Treasurers, either in
captivity or at large. In two of our Grand jurisdictions the Grand Master
is elected from the ftoor of Grand Lodge, without any necessary previous
service as a Grand Lodge officer, a custom which must seem delightful to
those patient brethren who in four jurisdictions climb station by station
through twelve offices before they may sit in the Grand East.
"Grand Masters are Most Worshipful in forty-eight states, Right Worshipful in one. When we retire from our labors, we are Most Worshipful
in forty-seven Grand Lodges, Right Worshipful in two. Senior and Junior
Grand Wardens sit in forty-one states, and Grand Senior and Junior Wardens in eight, a matter of almost as much importance as is the fact that on
the Volume of the Sacred Law rest the Square and Compasses in fortythree jurisdictions, but the Square and Compass in six. And if you want a
right little, tight little argument, just try to change either custom, even
though the brethren who refuse to change quite willingly admit that they
are wrong!
"Every Grand Lodge in the union meets once a year. Three meet twice
and one meets three times yearly. Then there are those gluttons for punishment, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, which hold quarterly meetings,
with one extra thrown in for good measure on St. John's Day in winter!"
Without referring to the "UNUSUAL" weather that has ·prevailed in
the ENTIRE State of California for the past two weeks, we are reminded
of a story of a certain Moslem preacher ·w ho was very very lazy and yet enjoyed his work very much. One hot Moslem Sunday, it being very warm, in
developing his discourse he didn't want to make it too long; and coming
forward he said, "Do you know what I am going to speak to you about
this morning?"--and his hearers said "No." "Well, then," he said, "what's
the use of my talking to you about it?"; so he closed the Koran and left.
The next Moslem Sabbath he asked them the same question, and they
were ready for him this time, they thought. When he asked, "Do you know
what I am going to speak to you about?" they said "Yes." "Well," he
said, "you know, so what's the use of my talking to you about it?"-and
then he again closed the Koran and left.
Well, on the third Sunday they were ready for him, and when he asked
the usual question, they said, "Well, some of us do and some of us don't."
"Oh," he said, "that's fine; those that do know tell those who don't."

A MAN'S OWN COUNTRY
"Americanism" has been an over-worked term for a number of years.
There is a patriotism of War and a patriotism of Peace. Under existing conditions the latter is one that may be the most difficult. We believe that the
,Grand Master of Vermont sounded the keynote when he said: "If any one
does not like the Constitution under which our country has prospered for
one hundred and fifty years, then let him migrate to Italy, Germany, rebellious Spain or Russia, as suits his taste, and there remain."
Experience in the World War demol18trated that victory depends as
much on the home front as on the battlefield-the formation of the spiritual
strength and unity of the people will be decisive; without it no National
defense is adequate. Those who divide our country by stirring up racial
and religious animosities, or as citizens of this country take part in the
internal affairs of other Nations, either directly or indirectly, by propaganda
or financial support, weaken our National Defense as effectively as though
they sabotaged the industries that produce the implements of war.
We commend to our readers a statement made over the radio a few
days ago by Colonel Chas. A. Lindbergh:
"We must keep foreign propaganda from pushing our country blindly
into another war. We must not permit our sentiment, our pity, or our personal feelings of sympathy to obscure the issue, to effect our children's
lives. Our safety does not lie in fighting European wars. It lies in our
own internal strength, in the character of Amedcan people and Am.erican
institutions."

Perhaps what is contained in this report can be considered along the
same lines.
Yours sincerely and fraternally,
JESSE M. WHITED, Chairman.

Canada (1937):
(Grand Master): Activities subversive of freedom and democracy, such
as communism, fascism, nazism, do not accord with our ideas of liberty and
security. A large part of the world is now ruled by dictators under one form or
another of autocracy. On every side, even in democratic countries, it looks as if
Masonry and civilization itself are being challenged by these issues and are
facing a crisis. Unrest and uprisings, against law and order are showing themselves in too many places and too frequently to justify us in being in any degree
complacent or feeling secure. We do not know what can or will happen here
or elsewhere, so long as we find disrespect for law, order and authority, as
shown in various parts of the world to~ay. The present seems to be the
winter-time of liberty. Restriction of the freedom of the individual, and concentration of authority and power autocratically in the state are taking place.
District of Columbia (1938):
(Chairman Committee on Correspondencr) : In one of the opening paragraphs of his address the Vermont Grand Master said: "The fundamental
cause of the ills of our country today is our forgetting God, not honoring Him
nor obeying His commandments as we ought to. His word is little read in
our homes, is untaught in our public schools, and instead of prayer to Him,
petitions are sent to Washington, D. C." (Well, maybe they think He really
lives here.) Concerning the meddling of foreigners in our domestic affairs,
he says : "* * * If anyone does not like the Constitution under which our
country has prospered for 150 years, then let him migrate to Italy, Germany,
rebellious Spain, or Russia, as suits his taste, and there remain and enjoy what
he wants." There would seem to be a note of dissatisfaction with some men
now in public office in the following expression: "Also, let those who swear
to support the Constitution of the United States on taking public office, either
mean what they say or stop swearing." (Amen, Brother.)

Iowa (1937):
(Grand Master): Only on the soil of a democratic form of government
can Freemasonry grow and flourish. The Masons of war-ridden Europe no
longer are privileged to meet as we do in America. A distinct challenge to
democracy was made in Central Europe within the last quarter of a century
and, as a result of this challenge, democracy has become almost extinct. And
the sad part of it all, my brethren, is the fact that the democratic form of government of these United States is being challenged at this very hour by insidious
forces, at work among our own people which would destroy this government
of laws which was bought at so great a price by the blood of patriotic men and
the tears of sacrificing women.

The immortal hero of the American Revolution used Masonry as a weapon
of offense and defense against tyranny and oppression and made possible the
birth and present heritage of Americans.
Theory alone is not sufficient when not put into actual practice.
Masonry and our nation are "beset with dangers of many kinds and may
even meet with death" unless defended at every outpost and properly garrisoned
by men who believe in our Order and in our nation's _institutions.
Let us not be afraid to show our colors and rout the enemies; we cannot
do it by mere theory of goodness and morality, but by strong, active, united,
shoulder-to-shoulder front and the Cherubims' wings touching from north to
south and yea ! from east to west, in guarding the forts of our national and
Masonic life, and leave no loopholes for our enemies to breach our battlements.

Maine (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Grand Master Fairchild (Nevada) verges a little too near the line of politics in his only recommendation,
and while this writer cordially agrees with him in his conviction relative to
dictatorships and totalitarian states, we question if such recommendations are
advisable or warrantable. Here are his words:
In order to accomplish their purpose and feel more secure in the furtherance and maintenance of their despotic power, one of the first acts of each of
those dictators was to abolish freedom of religion, freedom of the press, the
right of assemblage and the right of free speech, all liberties guaranteed by the
Constitutfon of the United States and espoused by our Order.
Masonry, the champion of those rights of the people, was peremptorily and
immediately outlawed and banished from those respective countries. Our
Order has no rights there and their revolutionary doctrines have no rights here.
I recommend that, as a patriotic measure and as a proper appreciation of the
sacrifices and struggles of our forefathers, which secured for us the freedom
and privileges we have enjoyed in the past, that this Grand Lodge go on record
as being opposed to communism, fascism and nazism.
The Jurisprudence Committee approved this recommendation, however.

Vermont (1938):
(Grand Master): Furthermore, as in the days of Ethan Allen, Vermont's

When the craftsmen of Vermont put their heads into a noose, it is advisable

There are too many people in the United States today from countries

Washington (1938):
(Committee on Jurisprndence): Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to
whom was referred the resolution, relating to certain evil tendencies in governmental matters, recommend that such resolution be adopted in the following form, to-wit :

698

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Whereas, Freemasonry has from time immemorial believed in and fought
for -liberty, justice, equality, and individual responsibility, which qualities are
the distinguishing and essential features of a democratic government, and
Whereas, propaganda emanating from countries which have never known
true liberty, justice, equality or individual responsibility, is being spread throughout our country in an endeavor to persuade our people to adopt some form of
government which will inevitably result in dictatorship, and thereby deny to our
people all liberty, equality and even-handed justice;
Now Therefore, the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Washington reaffirms it~ faith in the' fundamental principles and forms of democratic government, and firm in that belief, condemns all tendency toward dictatorship,
whether as the result of fascism, nazism, communism, totalitarian state, or under
whatsoever guise, or looking to whatsoever professed ends. Firm in the belief
in the virtue and value of democratic government, this Grand Lodge encourages the brethren of the Craft to study and discuss the evils'resulting from these
efforts to destroy our form of government.
However, no discussion shall be permitted within the tiled recesses of the
L<xlge that shall violate the time-honored principle of Masonry in prohibiting
the discussions within the Lodge room of any political subject.
GOLD IS WHE,RE YOU FIND IT
We are told that Masonry is both operative and speculative. While
the Blue Lodge is speculative perhaps some of its operations are best carried on through the co-ordinate Bodies. At times they may have, intentionally or otherwise, transgressed some of the Landmarks, but we believe
. their efforts have been to put into practical operation what they were
taught in the symbolic degrees.
In previous reports we have advanced the idea that the Masonic Fraternity is similar to our Public School System, the kindergarten, grammar
school, the high school and university.
After a person becomes a Master Mason, if he is interested in the aims
of the Fraternity, he naturally deserves to assist in carrying them out.
Unfortunately Blue Lodges, as generally conducted do not furnish such an
outlet. He, therefore, associates himself with the activity that interests
him most. If he transgresses the rules of the parent organization perhaps
it is due more to its failure to furnish a firm foundation upon which Masons,
both individually and collectively, must erect the superstructure of all
activities.

Florida (1938):

(Grand Master): During the year I approved the organization of luncheon clubs at Tampa and Key West after reviewing their by-laws and suggesting some minor changes. I also advised them that their membership must be
composed of all Master Masons in good standing regardless of ~ffiliation, and
that all who wished to participate be allowed and that no exclusiveness should
exist whatever; that if any good benf'fit was to be derived from the formation
of such clubs it would be in the encouragement of some brethren to participate
in active Masonic affairs.
I fully realize that there is a probability that the extensions of Masonic
affairs are becoming enlarged to a point where it should be discouraged. I have
information which leads me to believe that there is something like 300 organizations that derive membership from Masonic affiliates and to some it is believed that these hang-on organizations are endeavoring to predominate the
field and are a detriment to Masonry in general. The only real disappointment
I have had during the past year with these organizations is that some of them
are getting very near the area that would be termed units ~f gamb~ing, and to
those organizations I would like to issue a word of warnmg statmg that we
do not control their operations but still have something to say about the behavior of our Masonic brethren and can demand that they discontinue participating in such schemes.
Michigan (1938):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): This "Edict" is in direct keeping

"No Mason within the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge shall promote or

Considering this petition, the Committee on Jurisprudence says in part:
"No one can doubt that these are laudable purposes. But the worth of a
purpose does not necessarily entitle an organization to the official approval of
the Grand Lodge. There are many laudable movements which Masons, as
individuals, shouid foster. We, individually, may · approve churches, the Red
Cross the Boy Scout movement, and innumerable others. But Masonry has
alwa;s taken the position that it should concern itself with purely Masonic
matters, leaving to the brethren complete freedom as individuals in all nonMa~onic movements.
"Your committee feels that because the State Association of High . Twelve
Clubs does not confine its acti~ities to those of social dinner clubs, but is an
organization having among its purposes non-Masonic activities, and such Masonic
work as it uoaertakes to do by way of 'co-operating' with, rather than in com-

plete subordination to and as an agency of a regular Lodge, it should not have
the formal approval of the Grand Lodge.
"Your Committee on Jurisprudence therefore recommends that . the petition
of the State Association of High Twelve Clubs of Michigan be not approved."

Tennessee (1939)
(Grand Lodge) : Any club, association, organization, or society, composed

and the Lodge officers are then requested to permit the officers of the club to
initiate such candidates for the Lodge. * * ,. . But these clubs, in some instances,
have virtually taken over the Lodge itself. The club officers insist upon the
· right to exemplify the degrees on every candidate who is employed by the
company, and in many Lodges this comprises practically all of its candidates.
· As a consequence, the regular Lodge officers are required to step aside and do
nothing."

(Grand Master) : Our Masonic Clubs have proved to be a wonderful help

work, and causes a lodge to stand out as a good lodge.

HIGH, LOW AND WIDE OPEN
What constitutes Masonic Education is a debatable question. Some
jurisdictions seem to think that by having frequent mass meetings featuring lecturers and the distribution of literature is sufficient. Others think
that proficiency in the ritualistic work with attendance is all that is necessary or that by learning a few set questions the candidate or a new member
will be properly educated. Some believe that a course of lectures or readings will be sufficient. The chairman of the Committee on Correspondence
of the District of Columbia offers the following suggestion.
We have been waiting, however, for somebody to put forth the idea
that a valuable phase of Masonic education would be to teach the brethren
that what goes on in the Lodge room is nobody's business outside. That
they should be careful about discussing Masonic topics in mixed company,
in the home, on the street corner or street cars or railway trains, for, as
the old saying goes, "even the walls have ears."
Colorado (1938):

(Grand Master): I am impressed with one situation relative to newly
initiated brethren, which I take to be of paramount importance. The observation is not new, and yet very little has ever been done about it, and I am not
sure that my own suggestion will solve the problem. However, I wish to present it for your consideration. All of us will agree, I think, that the newly
initiated candidate is more enthusiastic and interested, and more athirst for
Masonic information, than he is likely ever again to be during the course of his
Masonic life. But he is often very much at sea and does not know where to
turn or what to do. After his initiation is completed and he is a full fledged
member, he is likely to be turned adrift to shift for himself and to find his way
through uncharted waters. Unless more than ordinarily equipped with the
unusual qualities of persistence and self-assertiveness, he is likely to drop into
the background and to feel somewhat out of it, until his enthusiasm cools and
his interest lags, with sometimes· disastrous results.
As a remedy for this situation, I suggest a system of Masonic Preceptorship. This may sound formidable, but it means only that an older Brother shall
take a personal interest in the younger's Masonic career-to guide and instruct
him for a period of one year. For example, the Preceptor could see to it that
the younger man made ready promptly for his Third Degree examination-or,
for that matter, he could take on his duties earlier, even before initiation, and
guide him through all three degrees. He could call for him and personally see
that he attended communications. He could introduce him to the other members of his lodge. He could suggest a proper course of Masonic reading. He
could familiarize the new member with Masonic precedent and procedure and
make him feel at home and at ease in the lodge room. And he could attempt
to answer many natural questions regarding the new things and the new life
which Masonry opens up. In addition to these few ideas, there are innumerable
other services that individual ingenuity and initiative will suggest to the interested, intelligent and enthusiastic preceptor. Thus the initiate will not be lost
to the Craft, as many so frequently are who become only nominal members
after their raising.
Such a Masonic Preceptorship would delegate to some worthy Brother in
each instance a pleasant duty, and here again would a constructive thing be
done for the Fraternity. For if we wish to enlist the interest and renew the
loyalties of our older members, the best way we can accomplish that object is

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

703

to give them something constructive to do. And what more coiistructive and
congenial duty could devolve upon any Mason than that. of guiding and instructing a younger Brother?
Hoping that these few ideas may be made to bear practical fruit, I recommend, when feasible, that the Worshipful Master of each lodge appoint, for
each newly elected candidate, a Masonic Preceptor, to serve for a period of one
year, thus giving this suggested method a trial in those lodges where no such
procedure has been adopted.

New York (1938):
(Grand Masti1): We have not promoted the organization of these clubs
and classes as extensively, nor as effectively, as the benefits to be derived from
them give promise.
This is to be regretted.
Both of these agencies of culture are capable of making a real contribution
to the enjoyment of lodge communications. Through the Study Club our
members learn to trace the history of Masonry, to follow its philosophical
development, appraise the value of its professions, its charities, the many elements of its humanitarian service-there are no limits to the field of such study
and research.
Knowledge acquired in the Study Club, then comes the turn of the Speaking Club. Here is learned the ability to present to an audience, big qr little,
the things one has mastered in the Study Club.
No one can speak who has nothing to say; and no one wants to listen to
a person with nothing to say. Pleasure or profit follows a clear presentation
of any subject. Our ritual, well spoken, excells in beauty. In the Speaking
Club all can learn to do the ritual justice. The Board of General Activities
will explain how to go about it to organize these clubs, and head them on the
path to a career of usefulness.

BROOD OF DUCKLINGS
The establishment of "Public Schools Week" by the Grand Lodge
of California has been followed by other jurisdictions, notably Montana
and Georgia.
While it has been termed "politics," George Washington, Benjamin
Franklin and DeWitt Clinton were in a large measure responsible for the
foundation of our free public educational system. Some of the critics of
this present day interest and activity of the Masonic Fraternity in _our
Public Schools do not hesitate to assume credit on behalf of Masonry for
the work that these men did in establishing our government.
Perhaps in the far distant future those who have "f ostered the work of
Masonry in our Public Schools in this era may receive . the same recognition.

TRAVEL IN FOREIGN COUNTRIES
Under this heading we are printing an address of Past Grand Master
Melvin M. Johnson of Massachusetts before the Grand Lodge of Virginia
(1938). Brother Johnson is one of the most noted ·Masonic writers. He is
also a historian and a traveler. His outline of the situation abroad can
therefore be accepted as both authentic and instructive.
"There was a mother entertaining some guests one evening, and she said
to her guests, 'Do you know, I think some of the most beautiful things I have
ever heard in the world have come from the lips of my children, after they have
knelt by their bed with me, said their prayers, and I have turned out the light.
They seem to reach over into the other world and bring back messages.' And
as she was expatiating at length upon that subject one of her children ~tuck
her head over the railing. 'Now,' said the mother, 'we shall prepare to hear
something of that kind.'
"'Mother, Willie found a bedbug.'
"Now the point of that is, that if you expect anything like oratory on the
'pillar of liberty', paens of praise, and all that, you are going to be very much
mistaken.
"After all, I think it is worth while for us to know what is going on in
our fraternity elsewhere, and I hope when I am through I shall have been able
to give you some idea of what Masonry is facing in other countries, where it is
successful and where it is not. Maybe you can see why it is not successful in
some of the countries, and why it is in others. I hope I may be more successful
than the teacher was, in teaching philosophy in the grammar school. At the
end of the year, instead of having her pupils answer ten questions, she told
them to write a composition on the human body. One of the little girls wrote :
'The human body is split halfway up and they walk on the split ends. It is
held by the spinal column, which is not a column. The head sets on one end
and you set on the other. The body itself is divided into three parts, the head,
thorax and abdomen. Inside of the head are brains, when there are any. In
the thorax is the stomach and liver. In the abdomen is the bowels, which are
five in number, A, E. I, 0 and U.'
. "Canadian Masonry is very much like ours.
"When we get down into Central and South America we run across Masonry
in every country except Brazil. Just what the situation is in Brazil I did not
find out definitely from anybody. The newspapers tell us that since Brazil has

708

!'ROCEEDINGS OF THE

been taken over by a dictator, Masonry has been banned. Yet it was only about
ten days ago we received a letter from the Director General of Brazil, suggesting that our representative near the Supreme Council had resigned his position and we should elect another.
"In every other 'country in South America there is Masonry. In almost
all the countries of South America, Masonry was founded, not by Grand Lodges,
but by the Scottish Rite. It is not generally known around this country that
the Scottish Rite system of 33 degrees-a rite which, by the way, being called
Scottish, did not originate in Scotland any more than the York Rite originated
in York-but the system of Scottish Rite contains the first three degrees just
as much as any of the others. In every country, however, where there exists
a Grand Lodge, the Scottish Rite abandons the first three degrees to the lodges
because it does not wish to conflict with them. Nevertheless, the Supreme
Council has given Masons their first three degrees as well as the others.
"They have a hard struggle in those countries, if you remember. One of
our Supreme Southern Commanders, of Ecuador, said to me, 'You may realize
the position we have when I tell you that there is not one single protestant
church in our whole country.' Yet the leader who produced revolution in
Ecuador is very strong there today. How is it that there is only one religion
prevailing in that country, unless the brethren down there very largely keep
their religion as some of us do here, in their wives' names?
"Masonry has very largely influenced the recent developments in South
America. Let me give you a little instance. ,Jn Panama, when they broke off
from Colombia, Panama was 96 per cent illiterate. Today it is almost the
other way round, because the first president of the Republic of Panama established a Department of Education in the Panama government. He put at the
head of it a Minister of Education, and at the present time, for the fourth or
fifth time, the Grand Master of Masons, but now the Southern Grand Commander. They had a great struggle, because Arosema was determined Panama
should have an educational system. He had succeeded in establishing the system from the kindergarten to the normal school inclusive; but they had a great
struggle getting it through the Panama parliament. Foreseeing the establishment of the school system in Panama, it met with great opposition from the
Roman Church, because they maintained !he only schools that were in Panama,
and no one could go to those schools unless a member of a wealthy family who
could afford the very high tuition . . On fin;µ passage he needed three or more
votes, ;i,nd the only way he could 'see was to make a compromise. They made a
promise that on Thursday afternoons the Roman . Church should send priests
into the schools and give the pupils instn1ction in the Catholic religion . . After
he hai:I established the school system; he issued an executive order that atten-.
dance upon · ~chool Thursd,ay afternoon should not be compulsory. That is just
an example, of .many that I might give you, of how the spirit of Masonry,
seeking to put education into the hearts and minds of men, has had its great
influence in South America.
·
"Let's take ship across the Pacific.
"In China and Japan there is some Masonry. In Japan the government
absolutely prohibits secret societies, and has always done so; but it has a gentlemen's agreement with the Masonic fraternity that so long as they will not
make any Japanese Masons, they may continue to function; and so the Masonic
fraternity continues to function, not only blue lodges but the Scottish Rite.
The only Japanese who are Masons are those who have been to this country
for educational purposes or diplomatic work. None are admitted to Japanese
lodges.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

.709

"In China it is not the kind of Masonry we know at all. For three generations it has been there, established in the early days by the Grand Lodge of
England, the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, and there have since come in the
Grand Lodge of Ireland, the Grand Lodge of Scotland, the Grand Lodge of
Vienna and the Grand Lodge of the Philippines. The Grand Lodge of Massachusetts has ten lodges in China. Just what condition they are in, we do not
know.
"In most of the British Possessions and in most of the countries of Africa
you will not find any Grand Lodges, but you will find provisional lodges, established by the Grand Lodges of England, Scotland and Ireland, still operating
under charters issued by them, so that their influence extends very widely
throughout the whole world.
"In Russia, Masonry has existed sporadically from time to time. Of
course, under the Bolshevist regime it is absolutely wiped out.

"In Germany, Masonry was very strong until the present regime came in.
They had eleven lodges, nine or ten of which were recognized by nearly all the
Grand Lodges of the world as re~ular. They were of the highest type of
citizens in Germany. The finest hospital in Germany was built by one of these
~rand Lodges; and yet by that one decree of that dictator who now rules, all
the Masonry in Germany was wiped out. If members appeared-he allowed
one or two to meet-they had no chance to function as a chivalric fraternity;
and having no obligation to be true to Hitler and the Reich, he has since broken
those up; so that there is no Freemasonry whatever in Germany today.
"It has also been wiped out in Italy by Mussolini. There were two Grand
Lodges in Italy prior to his time, but the persecution of Masons in Italy was
almost equal to that which is now being carried on in Spain.
"I am going to tell you something you will read in no newspaper anywhere.
No newspaper will publish it, In Spain, most of the correspondents call the
Loyalist government forces 'Reds.' The fact is that the Spanish government
was elected in the only fair election that ever was held in that country, and
only thirteen per cent of the votes cast in that election were cast by those
whom we would class as Reds. And today only sixteen per cent of the Spanish
Cortes of five hundred members would be classed by us as Reds. It is not true
that the dominant factors in Spanish government are Communists or Bolshevists,
or otherwise Reds. ft is true that they are liberal in their views; it is true
that they stand for freedom of conscience, that they stand for the liberty of
man, that they stand for the principles of democracy. Now if you turn to the
other side, we shall find a vastly different picture. We shall find among the
rebels in the Spanish government today all the forces which exactly resemble
Hitler and Mussolini in their country, in the governments they are conducting
in their countries. It is the type with which they are more closely allied. This
is true, and no newspaper in this country, apparently, dares print it.
"When a part of Franco's troops captures any part of Spain, they immediately take all those in that town known to be members of the Masonic fraternity, and put them to death, instantly, without trial and without any opportunity to defend themselves, for no other reason but that they are members of
the Masonic fraternity.
"I am not giving you testimony on hearsay, but on information from the
Gr;nd Secretary of the Supreme Council of Spain, a man I have known for
many years, in whom I place every confidence. He dared not send it by mail,
but it came by diplomatic sources. We have an official at Washington who is
as loyal a friend as we can need or use.

"There is a man in this country today who was a Mason, a member of a
lodge containing thirty-eight members. He was in his home town, the town
where he was born, when it was captured by Franco's hordes. He showed his
naturalization papers as a naturalized American citizen, and they did not dare
do anything with him. One of the other thirty-seven members of the lodge
succeeded in getting hold of an English officer's old uniform, and putting it on,
he escaped. The other thirty-six were marched out at night to a field on the
outskirt~ of. town, compelled to dig their own graves, and immediately shot,
and buried m those graves. That is the type of government which Spain will
?ave, and the attitude which that government will have towards Freemasonry,
1f those opposed to the government forces in Spain win in the bitter war which
is now raging in that country.

"In Czecho-Slovakia and Bulgaria they are few in numbers, but the Masonry there is strong in the character of its membership.
"In Roumania, during the great war, there was a man by the name of
Pango, who got an appointment in Paris as some sort of attache to the Roumanian delegation there, for the service of Roumanian soldiers or visitors who
happened to be in France. He heard of Masonry while in France, and after
the war went back to his native country. He thought Masonry would be a kind
of nice thing to have in his country; so he proceeded to initiate himself and
conferred the principle degrees upon himself, and elected himself Grand Master
and Sove.reign Gra~d Commander of the Supreme Council, and started Freemasonry m ~oumama. He succeeded, through some schemes of his, in getting
some people m, and finally even Prince Robesco, and when he came in he got
a good deal of recognition all over the world, because he was related to the
Duke of . Connaught. But last February, about a year ago today, Prince
Robesco lifted Freemasonry out of Roumania as irregularly as he brought it in
for he issued a decree ousting Freemasonry. I saw in a Roumanian newspape;
a photograph taken of Pango, and in the group were the Apostolic Delegate
of the Roman Catholic Church and the Roumanian head of the Roumanian
Orthodox Church, both in the regalia of their offices.
"In Switzerland Freemasonry has been through trial. Switzerland is a
free country, and they cherish the idea of Freemasonry as we do but under
the constitution if 50,000 voters ask for an amendment to the constitution, it must
go before the people. Fifty-six thousand voters pleaded for an amendment to
the constitution, forbidding Freemasons, Odd Fellows and even Rotarian$ 1 to
exist in Switzerland. There was a long campaign, which went to ballot last
November, and I am glad to say that, three to one, the Swiss people voted against
the amendment, so as to preserve Freemasonry in Switzerland. It is the •Jne
place where they have held against the tide against Freemasonry which is sweeping over Europe. It is rather strange, though, that they have succeeded, because
they are surrounded with Nazis and Fascists. It stands good wherever a dictator exists, that there can be no Freemasonry. If we ever let a dictator take
control of this country, Freemasonry will go here just as it has gone elsewhere,
because Freemasonry in addition to charity teaches freedom, religious, social
and intellectual, and no dictator can permit liberty, either social, political or
intellectual. That is the peril which Masonry faces all over Europe today.
...In France there are three Grand Lodges, the Grand Orient, the Grand
Lodge of France and the National Grand Lodge. The Grand Orient is the
oldest historical unit. After many yea:rs it abolished the Bible from the altars

"The Grand Lodge of France, in my opinion (and I am speaking as a
Grand Master that recognizes the same Grand Lodges you do)-1 believe the
Grand Lodge of France is worthy of recognition. The National Grand Lodge
of France is largely composed of English-speaking people. It is almost a provincial Grand Lodge of the Grand Lodge of England. It was founded by English, run by English, supervised by English; but the Americans join the Grand
Lodge of France. What do they do when they come back? They are just as
good Masons as we are, but they cannot take a demit to our Grand Lodge.
So they take their demits to New Jersey, which recognizes the Grand Lodge of
France, and they affiliate with the Grand Lodge of New Jersey ; and when they
move to Virginia they get a demit from New Jersey and come into your lodge.
As far as I am personally concerned, I would be very glad indeed to see the
Grand Lodge of France come into the fold if it could, because it is historically
sound and, I believe, a legitimate organization.

"In the smaller states, as we work north from France, Holland and Belgium, we usually fin.d Masonry strong in the character of its membership, but
not strong in numbers.
"Now I want to say a little something to you about three states which
practice a very different system of Masonry from that which we practice here.
They are Sweden, Norway and Denmark. In these countries they do not have
-nor in any of the countries of which I have spoken-the organizations we
have here. They do not have the Scottish Rite of 33 degrees, Chapter, Council,
Commandery, and all that. They have a unified system of 18 degrees. The
Duke of Soderman found throughout Europe the peculiar condition which resulted in the Scottish Rite in this country. There were at that time not only
Blue Lodges throughout the countries of Europe, but between 900 and 1,000
degrees floating around Europe. If you had devised a degree, worked it up
and called it by a high-sounding title, you sold it to anybody you could sell it
to. Then, in order to be as distinguished as yourself, I would swap my degree
for yours. The Duke of Soderman was interested in Freemasonry, but not
·that kind of Freemasonry. He wanted to consolidate it all into one system, and
with his own hand, after he became Charles XIII, he revised it into eleven
degrees, and that is all the degrees they have in the Swedish system. He cr•n. densed all the legitimate Freemasonry there was in that day, forty years before
our predecessors in the United States consolidated all their degrees into the
33-degree system known as the Scottish Rite. Now, they have just as much
right to establish their system as we have ours. In fact, their system is forty
years older than ours. If they want a Masonic system of eleven degrees when
ours is thirty-three, they are entitled to it, just as they are as much entitled
to have a king as we are to have a president. As they run their civil government, they have a right to run their Masonry.
"Their system is older than ours. Since 1737 their system has been practiced in Sweden. Ever since the day of King Charles XIII, because their

713

King of Sweden has been their Grand Master or Protector. They are not split
up into controlling bodies, and the king comes pretty near controlling the whole.
He has so much power that if a lodge rejects a candidate and the king thinks he
ought to be initiated, the lodge has to initiate him. Vice versa, the king can
order any lodge he sees fit, not to take in anybody that has been elected.
"That system from Sweden has swung over into Norway, and has come
into Denmark. The King of Denmark is Grand Master there, and a most cordial gentleman.
"I am glad that you recognize in Virginia those three great Grand Lodges
of Sweden, Norway and Denmark, because there are no truer Freemasons in
the world than the Freemasons in those Grand Lodges. And they do not advance up through their degrees in a hurry. Any man there gets along with a
year's wait between the degrees, to the eighth, ninth and tenth degrees. They
work along very slowly. A man cannot apply for a degree beyond the sixth.
He is chosen. and before he can advance even to the sixth degree, between the
degrees he has to write a thesis as one has to do in college for a doctor's degree,
after studying, and that thesis had to be passed upon by a committee, and he
has to show himself as a worthy Mason, to go ahead ; and no man ever gets
up to the eighth degree until he is well along in years, and when he reaches the
tenth arid eleventh degrees he is practically a patriarch.
"I suppose there are only two men in the world who have never taken the
tenth and eleventh degrees there and yet have seen them. I was at a banquet
one afternoon in Oslo. The brother sitting at my left wanted to know when I
was going to leave. He said that the next afternoon at 5 o'clock they were
going to work in the tenth and eleventh degrees. He said, 'I would like to
invite you to these degrees, but we have a rule in the Swedish system that nobody can witness these degrees unless he has received them; but I suppose the
Grand Master has the power of granting a dispensation, so I will see if I can
get you in.' The Grand Master issued a dispensation to me and my companion
to visit the lodge, and we saw that night the tenth and eleventh degrees, and
were informed by the Grand Master that night that, so far as he knew, nobody
outside of the Swedish system had 'ever before witnessed these degrees.
"We crossed over from Sweden for the event which I have no doubt you
have been told all about, the 200th Anniversary of the Grand Lodge of Scotland,
with the installation of His Royal Highness the Duke of York, now King of
England, as Grand Master · Mason, as they call it, of Scotland, the first time
that a ruler had ever become Grand Master in Scotland. A ruler has frequently
been Grand Master in England, but not in Scotland.
"The grand hall was filled to the limit; an assembly of men from all over
the world were there to witness it. They have an officer in that lodge we do
not have, the Grand Piper. He went out and piped in the Duke of York, who
came in and was received as any one would be received, knelt at the altar and
took his obligation as Grand Master Mason in just the form any commoner
would have taken it, and went through the ceremonies any one would have
taken. You say it is aristocratic to have these royal people in the Grand Lodge.
I was very proud of it; but it is democratic, at the same time.
"In order that His Royal Highness might be Grand Master Mason in
Scotland, he had to belong to a Scottish lodge, and so he joined a little local
lodge at Glamis Castle, where his wife was born. They have a ceremony of
affiliation, and when he was affiliated, the Master of that lodge, who happened
to be the R. F. D. postman, with His Royal Highness now coming and kneeling
before him. Such is the aristocratic Freemason.
"About this young man who is now king: he has not been played up, like
some other people have. A great deal of propaganda played his brother up, over

the world. But the present king, who was Grand Master-installed Grand
Master only twelve days before he became king, is a fine; upstanding man of
the highest character, and a man who will always have the affection and respect
of the countries over which he rules. Make no mistake about that. That is a
man you can look up to and respect in character.

"His brother would have been Grand Master of Masons in England if it
had not been for the fact that the Duke of Connaught has remained, according
to their custom, Grand Master for many years ; for when the Duke of Connaught' s brother, the former King Edward, became king, he ceased to be Gra?d
Master as he had been before that, and the Duke of Connaught succeeded him
as Gra~d Master. He is well along in his eighties, but still retains his position
as Grand Master of Masons of England.
"Some of you may think there is no Freemasonry in Ireland. There is one
of the justices-in fact, the senior justice of the Supreme Court of Ireland,
who is Sovereign Grand Commander of the Council of Ireland, who came over
to visit us here last year. The Masons of Scandinavia and of the British Isles
are the kind of Masons that you and I want to tie to. They are the kind of
Masons that represent the highest type of citizenship in their communities.
They are the kind of Masons who think as we think, and predicate it upon belief
in GOD and the development of a morality as taught us in God's Holy Word.
They ar~ the type of men we should be proud of, and although in some of the
countries Sweden and Denmark, they are more or less select in their membership, yet' they are democratic in spirit, and the type of men upon whom this
civilization of ours must rest, if liberty, civil, religious and intellectual, is to
be preserved in the world; and if liberty is not to be preserved in the world,
not only will Freemasonry cease to exist, but that civilization which has built
up and made this land of ours a great land to live in, will also cease to exist ;
for it rests on liberty of conscience of the individual, his right to think for
himself, his right to vote as he thinks is right, and worship GOD as his conscience shall dictate.
"My brethren, Freemasonry has an important attitude and opportunity
today. It is not merely a society to get together and enjoy and taste the friendships which it promotes, which are dear to the human heart; it is a society
whose duty it is to teach, not only ourselves but the world with which we come
into contact that there are landmarks of civilization which cannot be changed
if it is to endure. People readily recognize the laws of mathematics, and realize
that two and two make four. People readily recognize it as a law of science,
that if one stands before a great locomotive that is moving toward him, with
that momentum the human body may be ground to pieces, because it cannot
stand that great force. But men in the world do not seem to realize that God
not only established the laws of science and established the laws of mathematics.
but established the laws of morality, and they are just as firm and just as true
and just as unbreakable as the laws of science or any of the laws of mathematics. If a man sees fit to break them, if a man thinks, with this puny form
of his that he can stand in the way of God's laws, man will be crushed, whether
he st;nds individually against them or stands collectively against them.
"Here in Freemasonry we are taught to reverence the landmarks, the
things that most.endure. It is my duty, as I look at it, as part of the red blood
of this nation, that is put here to bless the rest of the world, to see that our
belief in God stands at the basis of this land . of ours, that the red flag of 'No
God and No Master' shall not be raised with authority in this broad land. It
is our duty as Masons to see that here and now, in this day, we preserve these
great prinriples which our forebears in Masonry, like Washington and Marshall

and Franklin and others, had when they built this land of ours, upon that
proper foundation on which they erected if.
"It is our duty as Masons to see that these things stand, as we hand on to

liberty and worship of God which Masonry teaches, and which it is for us to
preserve ip the land in which we live, for the days which are to come."
