THE END OF THE TRAIL
Any funeral ritual that has yet been adopted seems to be generally
unsatisfactory, even to the jurisdiction adopting it. Like all Masonic ceremonies, it has been influenced by the evolution apparent in all walks of life
during the past decade.
Regardless of the ceremony itself, the chief criticism of Masonic funerals at the present time seems to be inability of the Master or those assisting
him to render the same in such a manner as to produce a favorable impression upon the general public.
Undoubtedly when the custom of Masonic funerals was first established
it was believed that it was a ceremony which every Mason should attend.
Now it has become more of a personal proposition than a public event.
With this changing view the attendance of the general membership has of
course decreased.

Two or three day later I received a letter from our mutual friend, from
which I quote:
"That was the first Masonic funeral service I ever attended. I think it is
splendid to have a member's friends rally 'round and join in this fine expression
of fraternal interest and friendship.

Florida (1939):
(Gra11d Master): In the conduct of a Masonic funeral, of late years, I
have observed profanes among the pallbearers. I have also observed other
organizations in the procession. On one occasion, at least, it has come to my
knowledge that the ceremony over the remains of a deceased Brother was performed in its entirety by another organization, even including the actual committal, before the service was turned over to the Masons.
It may be well to say here for the benefit of those who may not have a
full knowledge of these matters, that when Masonry is to have charge of a
burial ceremony no one but Masons, including pallbearers, can participate, and
there must not be any other ceremony, other than the religious ceremony, nor
should there be any organization or profanes in the Masonic procession. Other
organizations and profanes may follow the procession and gather around the'
grave, but taking no part in the ceremony.
The same procedure should obtain in the ceremony of laying a cornerstone by Masons ; the burial ceremony and the cornerstone ceremony being the
only outside work that Masons do as a Lodge.
These are our most bindinl!' traditions, called by some "Landmarks," but
os Masonic students and scholars disagree on what is and what is not a Landmark, I shall not so name it but merely say that a Landmark is something that
cannot be changed.
Maine (1939):
(Chairman Corresponde11ce Committee): In harmony with many Grand
Lodges there is felt the need of a new funeral service, and Grand Master
Erskine (Kansas) recommends that a committee be appointed to formulate
such a service, which is so important in time of bereavement. It is a rather
large order which the Grand Master places on the committee in these words,
"it should be appropriate, comforting and helpful to the family and friends and
given with such dignity and decorum as will best serve its purpose and do credit'
to our Institution."

"I don't know how you feel about it yourself, nor do I know whether it
would be futile for you to try to do anything about it-even if you agreed with
me. I do feel that the ritual ought to be rewritten by someone who, without
changing the ideas at all, could put it in much simpler and more effective language. There were at least half a dozen words in the ritual which the W orshipful Master stumbled over; in fact, some of them he apparently had never
seen, as he was quite at sea in the pronunciation, and one of them he mispronounced so that it had an entirely different meaning."
Regretting it as I did, I could but acknowledge the truth of this letter.
Here was ample evidence of the impression left upon a non-member by a poor
rendition of the service, and this, I fear, is all too frequently the case.
The Masonic funeral service, as now in use, is one of feeling and sympathy,
and dignified and impressive when properly rendered. It is not a question of
rephrasing it, but entirely a matter of enunciation, pronunciation, emphasis and
delivery.
The great trouble with the average officer is that he rarely" makes a real
study of his job. He does not get beneath the surface, and utterly fails to grasp
the vision, thought and intent contained within the compass of our service.
Usually, his uppermost thought is to "get it over with," and thereby, oft-times,
as in this instance, ensues a sorry spectacle, to the detriment of the group in
particular and the Craft in general. A Masonic funeral service, although a
part of our ritual, is open to the public, and the public judges as it sees and hears.
I but emphasize what other Grand Masters have recommended, that a
Masonic service should be in charge of a brother who is best qualified, in every
way, to conduct this most important ceremony.

New York (1938):
(Grand Master): It is a mistaken notion that it is the duty of the Worshipful Master personally to conduct the Masonic funeral service when the
lodge is requested to officiate. Rather it is his duty to see to it that the brother
best qualified to discharge this sacred duty is assigned the task.
The scriptural quotations, the prayers, the committal, and the benediction
are properly the part of the clergy, and should be entrusted to the chaplain, if
he be a clergyman; if he be not, in many cases it will be best to obtain for the
part a brother of the cloth because of his experience in officiating on such
occasions.
The "profession of faith," the "word of sympathy," the "deposit of the
lamb skin," and the "sprig of acacia," are portions ('f the service which the
Master may take if he feels he is qualified to render them.
The occasions are not many when Freemasonry is on public view, when it
is exposed to the critical eye of the nonunderstanding or unsympathetic, and it
behooves us to guard against giving cause for wrong impressions of our fraternity; it behooves us to reveal it in its true light 'lS the reverent, serious,
dignified, sympathetic, understanding, and comforting institution which it is.
Our funeral rites, well rendered, bring comfort and hope to grieving hearts;
they will make for better understanding of what we are by those ignorant of
Freemasonry's purposes and ideals. Let it not be overlooked that while Freemasonry's performance of these sad rites is both duty and obligation, it is also
a solemn opportunity coupled with very real responsibility: the world's verdict.

indicating that this has been done."
We are of much the same mind about this. No one loves flowers more than
we; but the present tendency is toward overdoing the matter to a rather
regrettable degree. We attended a funeral the other day, at which so much
attention was given to fussing around flowers that everything else was almost
forgotten. They had to put them all in the home of the deceased; they had to
put them all in the church for the church funeral; and they had to take enough
time to make a ceremony of moving them all out of the church, and they had
to line up a whole company and flock of associates to hold those funeral designs
in a sort of march at the graveside. There must have been several thousand
dollars' worth of flowers on display there, and it seemed as if every item had to
be displayed individually. It made us feel that we wanted to make a request
against that last day when the "earth to earth" committal should be said for
us, that no flowers be sent except by organizations of cur connection, and that
in lieu of flowers, all individuals give books to a good library, doing service to
our people. We sent a book a few days ago, and not a few others in our
vicinity have done it, too, recently.

West Virginia (1939):
(Grand Master): Ordinarily there are only two occasions when the public
can witness Masonry openly and in the performance of any part of its ritual,
namely, at the laying of cornerstones, and at the performance of a Masonic
funeral. I have found the brethren thinking much about Masonic funerals.
The good taste of modern times requires that the intF-rment of the dead be
performed with the utmost simplicity, dignity and orderliness. It frequently
happens that the Master of a lodge lacks all the qualifications for performing
this ceremony, with the result that it is not well done, not pleasing to the
family of the deceased, and not admirable to the bystander. It seems to me
that a funeral should normally be conducted, not by the lodge, but by the
church, and that when it is conducted by the lodge it should be performed by
one of sufficient culture and skill at the difficult task that it will at least not
be a sacrilege. That member of the lodge, or of some neighboring lodge, who
can perform this ceremony well, should be called upon to perform this service.
LADY LUCK
If the space in the various Proceedings reviewed is an index, the attempt to curb gambling not only in Blue Lodges but also in the co-ordinate
Bodies still continues.
Perhaps the best rule that could be established is to pass an enforceable
law based upon the advice of Mark Twain, who said:
"There are two times in a man's life when he should not speculate;
when he can't afford it and when he can."
You may pass laws upon the subject but enforcement is another matter, particularly as all of us "want to take a chance."

New Mexico (1938):

New York (1938):
{Grand Master): In times of financial stress man is prone to take a chance
in the hope, so often vain, that "Dame Fortune" will smile upon him, bring him
good luck, rescue him from the abyss he visualizes all to really. He yields
to the temptations of the gambling table, the game of chance, the winning
number, the lucky point where the wheel stops-to any of the alluring devices
tempting to the financially distressed. Insofar as these things are forbidden by
the law of the land, Masons, obligated to obey that law, cannot indulge in them.
Insofar as they are on the borderline between what is lawful and what is unlawful, Masons should scrupulously avoid them, and thereby avoid the risk of
bringing shame upon the fraternity; in other words, we should abstain from
"gambling" with the decisions of the law courts, lest we guess wrong and
bring dishonor to Freemasonry.
North Carolina (1938):
(Grand Master): We recommend that the Grand Lodge adopt the resolution presented by the Grand Master, as follows:
Resolved, That it is inconsistent with the professions and purposes of Freemasonry for any Masonic body to promote, participate in, or profit by any
lottery, game of chance, door prize, or other device or activity whereby the
individual participant may be able, through the element of luck or chance, to
win a greater value than he pays, and each Masonic body within the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge is hereby enjoined to observe the letter and spirit of
this resolution.
Be it further Resolved, That all so-called collateral bodies, clubs or other
organizations in North Carolina whose membership is related to or dependent
on Masonic membership, or which in the public mind are likely to be regarded
as Masonic organizations, are requested, and all individual Masons owing allegiance to this Grand Lodge are enjoined to respect the purpose of this resolution.

Ohio (1937):
(Grand Master): We cannot permit raffles, punch boards, the selling of
chances, or any form of lottery or pernicious gambling held under Masonic
auspices, nor can we permit these things to be done by organizations which base
their membership upon Masonry.
I realize clearly that the spirit of gambling pervades many of our institutions today, including some of our churches, but until the laws against gambling
are repealed, Masons, I am sure, will cheerfully obey those laws. Let us not
cheapen Masonry by sanctioning those things which the laws expressly forbid.

conventions so acute, that they convinced themselves it was an honorable way
for Masons to raise money even though the government did deny them the use
of the mails to distribute their materials.

"Open to others than members of such organization"-and they are Masons ! It is said that the sting of a scorpion lies in its tail. That seems to

Wisconsin (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Gambling came in for a few words
of comment by the Grand Master (Connecticut, 1937), particularly that form

playing to once a month instead of once a week, if he was powerless to stop

to stop gambling is the form of intestinal fortitude displayed by a recent Grand
Master in Illinois who caused several prominent Masons to be tried for this
offense. A few such trials and there will be no more gambling.

West Australia (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Having, figuratively, disposed
of the liquor, Brother Mortimer (South Dakota) then ran his gidji (spear)
through lodge gambling for lodge financial improvement. Whether by lodges
or related bodies; it was, he said, unmasonic and rendered the offender liable
to discipline. In fact, his observations suggest that speculative varieties of
competitive undertakings are, or should be tabu. Way down in "Californy,''
as in many other states, the state public laws are "agin" gambling ; and one
is proudly told in the Golden State that lotteries are not possible within its
limits. Quite correct. At Tia Juana, a Mexican place across the border,
there is horse racing, coupled with sinful speculation, most Saturdays, and
then both pride and sin largely (and profitably to some) congregate. Yes, it is
quite easy to become strictly moral by legislation.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Any action, either by lodges or
individual Masons, that would imperil the high standard of Masonic principles
may justly be considered ground for Masonic legislation. But such action is
not without danger. Before gambling is made an offense against either Masonic or
public law, care should be taken to correctly define gambling. I know of euchre
and whist parties conducted in connection with United States Masonry, and sponsored by the "angels" as an American Grand Master styled the members of the
Order of the Eastern Star. Would those parties be called "gambling." American stock exchanges are notorious for the wild "speculation," it is called, in
shares of stock, when fortunes are made or lost, the latter not infrequently
followed by suicide. Does gambling enter there? If it does, would a lodge
holding such shares as part of its finances be justified in utilizing the services
of a broker to sell on a rise? The whole question is fraught with too many
considerations for hasty legislation, however laudable its object.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee:) Many years ago we had in use
in England the word "ballybash." What it signified no one seemed to knowwhether it was good, bad or indifferent. Like Lord Dundreary's whiskers,
ballybash" was of such social importance that "it moved in the highest circles"
and was even "patronized by royalty" as though it was a special brand of
pickles, but its meaning was one of those things, I suppose, "no fella can find
out," to use Dundreary's favorite declaration. It seems that Connecticut during the year under review also had a word-"a word highly prized among
Freemasons," and it was quite the proper thing to make allusion to it: it was
"bingo." That is how it was spelled in Grand Lodge. Now "bingo" forms the
caption to a number of consecutive sentences in the address apparently relating to the greatly and rightly. frowned at association of gambling with Masonry. Whether "bingo," or anything of or belonging to or in any way related to or associated with gambling or anti-gambling, "this affiant knoweth
not," but as already said, "bingo" is at the head of a series of paragraphs in
the Grand Master's address.

PATHS OF GLORY
The privilege of serving for a brief time as head of the Craft, and the
hope of perhaps performing some service, is the chief reward which the
occupant of this high office receives as compensation for the mental, physical
and financial outlay required of him.
The result of the administration of a Grand Master is largely reflected
in the character or ability of the officer himself. There is an old saying
that, "Advice is mighty easy to give but mighty hard to take."
We believe that a Grand Master who does not take himself too seriously, who shifts some of the duties of his office to subordinate Grand
Lodge officers, with a view of carrying on a continuous program for a
Grand Lodge, and omits from his annual message a large amount of detail,
correspondence, visitations and dispensations is the one that finds favor
with all the Chairmen of Correspondence Committees who are obliged to
read the same in order to form an opinion of his work and ability.
District of Columbia (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): To some Grand Masters requests
for decisions are vexing questions, while for others they seem to be very simple.
Where the law is adequate decisions are a simple matter; otherwise sometimes
complex. Some Grand Masters, however, seem to have all the answers.
One Grand Master ruled that the application of a man who had lost the
first joint of his index finger (did not say whether left or right), and whose
right leg was five-eighths of an inch shorter than the left, could not be received
for lack of jurisdiction. This same Grand Master also decided that at a joint
installation of a lodge and a chapter of the Eastern Star, the Master should
wear his hat, the brethren should wear their aprons, and that the public grand
honors should be given. Another decision was that a salesman for a candy
company which had added wholesale liquor and beer to its line could not apply
for the degrees, and he would not permit a lodge to sponsor a bowling team
and provide them with shirts. He would not permit a lodge to conduct a trial
of its Worshipful Master for un-Masonic conduct, nor ~ould he permit a lodge
to make a contribution to the Salvation Army, the Red Cross, nor any similar
organization. He also ruled that a brother who was a bartender in a tavern
was in good standing provided he had committed no Masonic offense.
A decision from another Grand Master was that a man born without a right
hand could not apply. (We wonder who could have been silly enough to ask
the question.)
The Grand Master of New York reported increased interest on the part of
the Craft in the observance of "Masonic Sunday," (which always seemed to
this writer more or less of a publicity gesture. A Mason is either a churchgoer or he is not. We see no reason why Masons should "gang up" on
the churches.)

Iowa (1937):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master (New Jersey) had been bothered during the year by the great amount of time used in

no value until the Grand Secretary had affixed his signature, and there was nothing in the code, he wondered if it would not serve as well for the Grand Master
to have his signature placed on the voucher by a rubber stamp, to be done by

to help the new Grand Master. The Committee on Grand Master's Address,

Lodge, as such action might impair the validity of the fiduciary bond protecting
the Grand Lodge against loss."

West Virginia (1938):
{Grand Master): The high discretion immemorially vested in a Grand
Master to di~pense with the laws, rules and regulations in special cases, undoubtedly exists. But I have declined to exercise this power in many cases.
In my judgment Masonic laws and rules and regulations are made to be observed, not to be dispensed with. I am very strongly of opinion that this
dispensing power in the Grand Master is not to be a mere convenience to cover
the carelessness, negligence and indifference on the part of lodges and lodge
officers. I have, therefore, refused in all cases to correct the carelessness of
subordinate lodges by the issuing of special dispensations.

•

•

•

(Grand Master): I have issued no proxies. My conception of the Grand
Master's ?ffice is such that I believe it to be his business to perform personally
the functions .thereof, and not to call upon others to do that which he should
do himself. Moreover, I have been a somewhat jealous Grand Master. I have
not desired that another wear my mantle while I occupy the Grand East. Therefore, no man has worn my jewel or wielded my gavel. Often at great inconvenience I have done that which a proxy could have done with ease. I have
felt that since mine is the duty, mine also should be the labor, and that I should
not have accepted this elevation if I was not prepared to make the sacrifice.
I have literally gone wherever I was called, and where the duties of the Grand
Master needed to be performed. I feel justified in repeating the boast that I
have issued no proxies.

West Australia ( 1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee}: Most American Grand Masters
cultivate the persuasive art of recommendation. More than one of those distinguished brethren muster a perfect drove of them. Brother Fairchild had
only one and it had reference to political dictatorship in Russia, Italy and
Germany. The Grand Master (Nevada) recommended that "as a patriotic
measure and as a proper appreciation of the sacrifices and struggles of our
forefathers, which secured for us the freedom and privileges we have enjoyed
in the past, that this Grand Lodge go on record as being opposed to communism,
fascism and nazism." This won the approval of the Jurisprudence Committee
and, on report, of Grand Lodge. Now this, so far as Nevada is concerned is
Nevada's own affair; but the utility of "going on record" over such a matter
seems to the writer to be as useful, in a practical sense, as "going on record"
against original sin, nasal warts and ingrowing toenails. Moreover, it seems
to the same critic to add to the already too numerous instances of official
Masonry inserting its proboscis into the Landmark which forbids the intrusion
of politics into Masonic lodges. Likewise, it does not, nor can it prevent the
various "isms" from menacing the Plan of Masonry owing to the weakness of
lodges allowing propagandists of the "isms" brand to become successful candidates for our degrees. It is just that brand which must be kept out of
Masonry, and can be kept out if lodges are admonished by Grand Lodges to
do their duty and how to do it. Going on record! It is more than probable
that had Abraham Lincoln merely "gone on record" against slavery the United
States would have still had a fine crop of Legrees to torture the Uncle Toms
of today. But the great man didn't; he moved. To meet today's problems
requires Masonic statesmansJi.ip; not going on record.

Wisconsin (1938):
(("hairman Correspondence Committee) : The Grand Master of Iowa also

BIOGRAPHY OF A FAMILY
The printed Proceedings of a Grand Lodge in most cases refl.ects the
capabilities of its various Grand Lodge officers as well as the conduct and
activities of the Grand Lodge itself. They are of all sorts and conditions.
As to some of them we believe with Chairman Louis L. Silverman that,
"Thei:e is less reading matter on a dollar bill than in the Congressional
Record, yet, many of us will lay aside the labored Record any day to peruse
the briefer, yet sweeter, message on the one dollar bill."

THE LIFE OF THE PARTY
Various Proceedings are enlivened with stories, anecdotes and other
forms of humor. Some one said: "Society pays for its sins. It once made
Willie speak pieces on Friday afternoon and now I must listen to his after
dinner speeches."
We have endeavored to include only those that did not fall under the
opinion given by Ambassador Walter Hines Page, editor of the World's
Work and, like all editors, obliged to refuse a great many stories. A lady
once wrote him:
"Sir: You sent back last week a story of mine. I know that you did
not read the story, for as a test I had pasted together pages 18, 19, and 20,
and the story came back with those pages still pasted; and so I know you
are a fraud and turn down stories without reading same."
Mr. Page wrote back:
"Madame: At breakfast when I open an egg I don't have to eat the
whole egg to discover it is bad."

It seems that out in Minnesota there was a Swede farmer . He was out in
the country, and along came one of those tornadoes which picked him up and
carried him for a mile and dropped him down on a haystack of a neighbor about
a mile off ; and this neighbor coming out and finding the old fellow there, and
being of a pious turn of mind, said, "Well, Brother, the Lord was with you."
"Well, if he were, he were going some."
However, I confess that coming down I felt a good deal like the old lady
years back who was having her first ride on a train. She looked out the
window and she couldn't see. When they came to a bridge she looked down
and couldn't see anything below at all to support them, and she just held her
breath, and presently the train ran onto the abutment on the other side, and she
said, "Well, thank God, we have lit."

Honorable Frederic W. Cook, secretary of the Commonwealth, in his address said :
Whenever a proclamation is issued in this Commonwealth it is the duty of
the secretary to affix the great seal, and to add that time-honored prayer, "God
save the Commonwealth of Massachusetts," but I confess there have been times

This presiding officer said he had recently attended services in a certain
church. The preacher, when he had finished his sermon, said, "I wish the members of the board present to meet me over here in this corner of the church
immediately after the benediction."
The benediction was pronounced and the brethren met over there, and in
the group was a man who did not belong to the board of the church. Of course
that was what the preacher was referring to, but the preacher, upon recognizing this stranger, said, "Brother, is there anything we can do for you?" He
said, "No, no, nothing at all."
Well, the preacher was ready to start the meeting of the board, because he
had called it to attend to some important business, and he saw that man edging
in a little closer and closer. Finally he said the second time, "My friend, is
there anything we can do for you?" The man said, "No, except you made the
announcement that you wanted all of the bored to meet you over here," and he
said, "I am the worst bored man in your congregation this morning."
"I was born in a Methodist parsonage, and I was brought up in a hardshell Baptist Sunday School; I later joined the Congregationalist Church. Then
I married a Presbyterian girl in a Unitarian home, the service being performed
by a Universalist minister. I went to a Universalist college and a Methodist
law school. Now I attend the Episcopal church and for fourteen years have
lived in a hotel inhabited mostly by Christian Scientists."
If a fellow could get his religion as easily as a Methodist, keep it as
eternally as a Baptist, practice it with the same dignity as a Presbyterian, the
ritualistic perfection of an Episcopalian, the devoutness of a Catholic and of a
] ew, and then enjoy it like a negro, he really would have the ideal religion.

Brothers and Sisters, I have come here now to pastor this. congregation,
and I am going to do my best to heal the dead, cast out the sick and raise
the devil."

OLD WINES AND NEW
In the various discussions, opinions, regulations and laws finding a
place in Grand Lodge Proceedings, the Masonic Fraternity seems to be
up against the same proposition that the United States was during the era
of prohibition.
The attempt to pass a general regulation, and then allowing exemptions to fit a particular class of candidates or those already members of
the Fraternity, is producing the same results as the "Noble Experiment."
In a few Jurisdictions they leave the matter entirely with the subordinate Lodge. The conduct of a Mason perhaps could perhaps be better
served by first inculcating in him the practice of "TEMPERANCE" in all
walks of life, rather than attempting to regulate it by sumptuary laws.
Alberta (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Lodge, by the investigating
committee and the ballot can exclude those who, by their use of or traffic in
intoxicating drinks, are offenders against the moral law.

Colorado (1938):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): In many cases, as in Colorado,
the question both of initiation and of retention of membership of those engaged
in any way in the liquor trade is left largely to the good judgment of the
members of subordinate lodges. A two-thirds majority can discipline any member and one only can prevent any one from being initiated. We really, as in
cas~s of crime and other offenses against common decency, need no specific
legislation upon the question. Any member who so conducts his business as
to bring discredit upon the Craft is and always has been subject to charges of
unmasonic conduct, whether that business is the sale of liquor, the handling
of securities, or even the practice of law.
Florida (1938):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A resolution was introduced by
the Jurisprudence Committee (Wisconsin) making it a Masonic offense for
one personally and actively engaged in the operation of saloon, tavern, bar
room or resort of any kind, principally for the sale of intoxicating liquor, and
no Lodge can receive a petition from one engaged in this business, and "Every
Lodge shall exclude intoxicating liquors from its Lodge room, anterooms,
recreation and dining rooms." Upon vote of the Grand Lodge the above resolution was NOT ADOPTED. Appears out of order to this reviewer for intoxicating liquor to be served in a room dedicated to GOD. Too bad that the
majority believed in the stuff "That made Milwaukee Famous."

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Then there was the case from
Scotia, Nebraska. The lodge has a hall, beneath which is a store. They asked
whether they might rent the store to a man who as a part of his mercantile
business sold beer. It is ruled that this cannot be done. This is a good ruling.
If things are in Nebraska as they are in North Carolina, this wine and beer
business is quite bad. In Eastern North Carolina the ABC stores sell liquor
and there is not so much wine business; but in central and western North
Carolina every place is full of restaurants and other places which can afford
to pay the wine license, which is pretty high, and the wine that they sell is of
the fortified variety, running about 21 per .cent alcohol. Of course, it is well
known that 21 per cent goods are almost as useful in alcoholic contents as the
whiskey customarily sold, showing 86 per cent proof, or 43 per cent alcohol.
One can get drunk about as easily on one as on the other ; the difference is
that one contains the chaser and the other gets it separately.

West Australia (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Nearly everywhere there has
been a growing indication that Masonry and the liquor traffic do not mix. Perhaps that is true when regard is had to the United States which business men
in that country often assured me a few years ago was "the only part of the
world that counts." There still seems to exist in the land of the Stars and
Stripes that exalted opinion that caused a Jewish poet to write that "in six
days the Lord created heaven and earth, the sea and all that in them is, and the:
United States." The fact is that outside the sphere of American assertion,
Masonry and liquor do mix, and as a lifelong total abstainer I am glad to record that Masonry in those realms on which the sun never sets, is upheld by
men whose attitude toward liquor is worthy of those principles which have
made Britain and her Dominions the most respected empire in the world.

(Cliairman Correspondence Committee): That several of the Grand Master's decisions related to the United States Masonic triangle, alcohol, legislation, in~erpretation, goes without saying. This triangle appears to be one of

had not been voted upon. He, too, was rated ineligible, aspirations and derrink being an unholy combination. And then we come to the cook. A good

. (Chairman Correspondence Committee) : A special committee on intoxicating liquors (Montana, 1937) which was referred by the Grand Master in his

MY FELLOW CITIZENS
It has been said that the practical politician is a man who shakes your

hand before election and your acquaintance afterward. This is all too true
of the member who uses Masonry for his personal advantage.
In practical operation members of this class can probably best be described in the words of Artemus Ward:
"Ez to my princerples, I glory
In hevin' nothin' o' the sort;
I aint a Whig, I aint a Tory,
I'm jest a canderdate, in short."
Florida (1939):
(Grand Master): It is a standing joke in many parts of this Grand Jurisdiction .that you can al_ways tell when a political campaign year is approaching
by the mflux of would-be political officers into Masonic meetings and the very
sudden interest they acquire in Masonic affairs. If they are elected they are
rarely seen in lodge until the next campaign. If defeated they are not .seen in
lodge, and unless they are going to make a retry for some political office thev
want, th~ chances are that they will drop out for non-payment of dues, only
to rush m and pay up back dues and get themselves reinstated if the political
office fever rises again.
Political office-seekers have been heard to declaim from the platform before
a public audience that they were "High Masons," even as high as the 33rd
degree.
These Masonic misfits d~ not know, as the Masons know, and the public
knows, that they a re really domg themselves an injury as well as bringing more
or less shame on the Masonic fraternity.

Oregon (1937):
(Grand Master): Masonry takes no part in politics. It is right that it
should not. Neither should it permit discussions of poiltical matters concerning
which there can be an honest difference of opinion among Masons. Such discussions would only lead to dissension. But as to those forms of government or
political systems concerning which there is no room for difference of opinion
among Masons, a different situation exists. We have a right to discµss them
within the lodge. I refer to those forms of government or political systems
which do not permit or tolerate Masonry. During the year I have talked in
the lodges throughout this jurisdiction against those subversive influences which,
if permitted to go unchallenged, might eventually gain control in this country
and destroy our liberties, our free institutions, and our Masonry. If to talk
against these sinister influences which are gradually boring into our government, our educational institutions, our patriotic organizations, and our fraternities constitutes the talking of politics, then let us to that extent get into
politics. If Masonry is worth maintaining, worth having, it is worth fighting
for, even if we have to go into politics for that purpose. If we have any
stamina, any vitality, we ought to fight those things which are trying to destroy
Masonry. If we do not, we may awake too late to find Masonry in this
country in the same condition that it is in Russia, Germany, and Italy today.

THEY ALSO SERVE
The Chinese have a proverb that one picture is worth a thousand
words. The following wisdom can apply in connection with the membership of the Fraternity.
"Simple devices properly used or applied may have a beneficent effect,
but in the hands of the unskilled or inexperienced may often result in
serious and unforeseen injury. Take, for example, that little gadget that

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

has played such a part in our young lives-the safety pin. What could be
simpler? When utilized by mothers or nurses trained in its use, it undoubtedly exerted a comforting and, indeed, supporting influence, but in the
hands of the innocent babe it became an instrument of danger, if not of
torture."
In the initial instance it is a question of the selection of the individual
and afterwards his betterment by the Fraternity. This must be not only by
precept and example but by maintaining his continued interest.

"There never has been any doubt, that a Mason, being in good standing,
has a right to demit from one lodge for the purpose of immediately joining
another...•
This, then, appears to me to be the state of the law on this subject; a
Mason, being in good standing, has a right to claim a demit from his · lodge,
and the lodge cannot withhold it. But a demit from a lodge, as it severs the
relation of the demitting member to his lodge, and releases hi~ from the
obligation to pay dues, deprives him also of certain privileges with which his
membership had invested him . •..
"Although, as I have already said, there is no law in any of the ancient
constitutions which forbids the granting of demits to individual Masons, yet
the whole spirit of the institution is opposed to such a system. To ask for a
demit, without the intention to unite with another lodge is an act which no
Mason can commit without violating the obligations which he owes to the Order.
It is an abandonment of his colors, and although we have no power to prevent
his desertion, yet we can visit his unfaithfulness with moral condemnation. . . .

736

New Jersey (1938):
{Chairman Correspondence Committee): In considering an application for
restoration of a member under suspension for N. P. D., accompanied with the
amount that had accrued against him to the date of his suspension, plus the
dues for the current year, it was decided by the Arizona committee that the
application was fatally defective, in that he had not also sent an amount "covering the dues that would have accrued aganist him between the date of his ~us­
pension and the date of his application for reinstatement" (in this case amounting to two years), in accordance with the require~ents of the constitution.
To require a suspended member to pay dues for the period of his suspension,
in addition to those charged against him when suspended, before his application
for reinstatement can be received and acted upon by a lodge, is most unusual.
Suspension for N. P. D. has a two-fold purpose. In the first place, it is
imposed as a punishment upon the delinquent, by denying him all the rights,
privileges and charities of the Order for the time being, and in the second
place, it is a protection to the suspended member from forther accumulation of
arrears during the period of suspension.
The latter is clearly implied in the report of Committee on General Policy,
in which the practice of granting further time for payment of arrears is condemned because as they said, "the amount may become so great that the obligation
cannot be met, and then when a brother is suspended he will feel, and the feeling will not be without foundation, that he has been unjustly treated by being
suspended when his debt to his lodge has been permitted to become so large ·
that he cannot satisfy it." Suspension would, however, have no effect upon the
accumulation of dues if the applicant is required to pay also for the time he
was under suspension. It is not only un-Masonic, but very unjust, to require
him to pay for privileges that were denied him and would certainly tend to
discourage petitions for restoration.
New Mexico (1938):
(Grand Master) : I feel that Masonry is a voluntary association and a
man should be entitled to withdraw from it at any time, but I carniot see why
such a man should remain on a more or less equal status with contributing
members. I admit that any Mason has the right to transfer his membership
to another lodge at any time that he sees fit, provided he is in. good standing.
In this I am supported by the opinion of the eminent Masonic scholar, Albert
G. Mackey, who in his "Masonic Jurisprudence" has this to say regarding
the right of demission:
"The word 'demit' is peculiarly and technically Masonic . . . .It is, in fact,
the act which in any other society would be called resignation ... .
"The right of demission is, then, an important right in its reference not
only to the Mason who applies for it, but also to the lodge which grants it,
since its operation is to dissolve all Masonic connection between the two parties.

'(Grand Master): This is a vital question. It challenges our most careful

b~other Masons. Our actions betray us. You are Masonry-I am Masonry, to
him. And what you are and what I am must determine his attitude-his decision. In a very real sense, then, the future of Masonry is determined by the
quality of life Masons are exhibiting today before those young men. So it behooves us to take heed to our vows and obligations.

Utah (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : The question of perpetual jurisdiction is not of particular interest to us. But the matter of lodges of this
jurisdiction protecting themselves and Masonry from the effects of the misdoings
of sojourning Masons is a matter of a good deal of importance, as we see it.
To us it seems neither fair nor Masonic virtually to tie the hands of a local
lodge while a sojourning Mason is guilty of acts which would not be permitted
to go unpunished if committed by one of its own members.
It may be urged, let the aggrieved lodge prefer charges, and with supporting evidence send them to the lodge of the accused for trial ! "Yeah"? and
again "Yeah" !
The present writer recalls two instances among others, in which .this was
done. In one case the accused went to his home lodge, taking with him a
shrewd lawyer; the lodge was not represented, it did not have funds to send
witnesses and some one to speak for it; the outcome was foregone from the
start. In the second case the papers were sent to the Grand Secretary of a
distant state by the Grand Secretary of this jurisdiction. Nothing ever came
of this action beyond acknowledgment of receipt of documents !
Theory sometimes is a mighty fine thing, and plausible, but many theories
when put to the test of the sensible and the practical are seen to be, if not
absurd, at least nonworkable.
If the jurisdictions which insist on disciplining their own members, wherever
dispersed, would insure other jurisdictions against the effects of the wrongdoing of those absent members, well and good-we would have nothing to say
concerning the injustice of the practice under consideration.
Victoria (1938):
(Grand L odge): The Grand Lodge of England has for some time had as
one of its subordinate lodges a lodge known as "Lux in Tenebris," the name
meaning "light in darkness." That lodge is composed entirely of blind brethren.
In the ranks of the lodges under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Victoria there are two blinded brethren who are fully accredited members o.f Free. masonry. There is a lodge in Victoria under the English constitution to which
three blinded candidates applied at various times for initiation. In each case
the matter was referred to the Grand Master of England under whose jurisdiction that lodge-Lodge Combermere-exists, and each application was approved.
Any such brother, having been initiated, passed and raised in Lodge Combermere, may as of right become a joining member of a lodge under the Grand
Lodge of Victoria. Furthermore, a candidate who had been initiated in any
lodge in Victoria under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge might meet with
some accident, and as a result lose the sight of both eyes. He would still be
eligible to be passed and raised. The question is should Grand Lodge continue
to usurp what should be the function of the Grand Master and deal, in the
Book of Constitutions, with three particular kinds of physical disability, leaving
the whole gamut of other disabilities to be decided on by the Grand Master
himself? There is what is known in the medical profession as "commercial
blindness." If a person cannot see more than a certain number of metres he
is classed as "blinded commercially." There are also numbers of cases of
persons who are just able to distinguish between light ;;md darkness, but cannot

740

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

be classed as totally blind, yet in a lodge room they would be in exactly the
same position as a totally blind person so far as the effect of their disabilities
was concerned. What logical explanation is there for allowing the Grand
Master to give a dispensation to a candidate who can only distinguish light
from darkness, and take it away in the case of a candidate who is totally blind?
We believe that, so far as concerns blinded candidates, they should only be
refused admission into Freemasonry if they are likely to be a charge upon any
of the funds of Grand Lodge or if they are the recipients of charity or are
living on the benevolence of others.

ANYTHING BUT THE TRUTH
Publicity given to Masonic affairs has developed to such an extent that
there is practically little secrecy regarding our institution or its activities.
Secrecy, we believe, was at one time the source of our strength. Publicity
has developed into a real evil, which is found to a greater or less degree in
all jurisdictions. This concerns not only organizations predicating their
membership on the Masonic Fraternity, but also members who use it for
personal ends.
The same objection is also found in some publications which carry the
word "Mason" or "Masonic" in their titles and use their advertising columns for political or business members who endeavor to sell their personalities or commodities through their connection with the Fraternity.
Some of the Grand Lodges publish the entire list of their membership, which furnishes an excellent "Sucker List" for all sorts of propositions.
A few that followed this practice have discontinued it, which we believe
can only work for the good of the Fraternity.

Rhode Island (1937):
(Grand Master): What the Craft needs today is that which it has always
needed-leadership. We need men, who by their patience will enthuse, uplift
and enthrall, until others sha!I catch the spirit and become enthusiasts of such
a program. As ari institution, we again need to recall the fact that Freemasonry
does not find its greatest value by counting members, but rather by the careful
development of men into Craftsmen-men who, to begin with, are the very
soul of honor and who, reinforced with the principles of Freemasonry, will
develop into Masons whom we shall delight to honor. Mediocre leadership is
quite apt to develop a like kind of Craftsmanship-mediocre. A better leadership will be an improvement, but the best kind of leaders obtainable are _not
only necessary, but will bring us nearer and surely more quickly to our Masonic
goal. Anything less than that is neither desirable nor expedient, if the fraternity is going to be able to cope with the problems of the oncoming years.

District of Columbia (1937):
(Grand Master): I have always held that after a man has assumed the
title of Mason he should be a Mason first, last and all the time. Anything
which places a stigma on the Craft or alienates the respect of men of Masonic
dignity and character will not be tolerated, and I pledge myself to this Grand
Lodge that I shall not be unmindful of my duties should any occasion of this
kind arise; There is no place in the entire structure of Masonry that admits
of anything which is unclean. Masonry is a dignified organization, and it has an
ethical code that should never be violated. During the years I have been a
member of this Grand Lodge line I have had occasion to visit many Masonic
organizations, and I am sorry to say that the entertainment features at times
have been a discredit to the Craft."
Indiana (1938):
(Grand Master): I would like to see the Masonic Lodge a center of wholesome activity for both young and old. Why may we not develop more entertainment of a social, instructive and interesting nature? Possibly some like to
dance or play cards; that could be done in the social or dining rooms. My
thought is that if we do not offer those things, should we feel a real need for
them, to men and women, old and young, in a decent way and in wholesome
surroundings, they will be had somewhere and someway, in night clubs, pool
halls or dance halls, with all attendant evils.
Missouri (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Many of us have read the book
"It Can~t Happen Here," yet if you are a student of government and foreign
relations and have been keeping in touch with the daily press, you will find
that it is happening here, and happening now. At the present time it is a subtle
thing, too subtle indeed for many of our people to perceive. On the outside it
appears a sheep, but in reality the skin covers the body of the wolf. We rave
about communism, socialism, fascism and the like without knowing even what
they are. All the laws in Christendom are of no avail unless backed by the
forces of decency and law and order. Today is the day of the demagogue;
graft runs riot. Punchboards, gambling machines, crime, murder, political protection, scandal are too common. Men in high places, many of them entitled to
wear the square and compass, emblem of moral honesty, are failing to measure
up to the principles taught them at the Masonic altar.

Rhode Island (1938):
(Grand Master): After a study of the institution of Freemasonry one
marvels at the farsightedness of our forefathers in framing its constitution and
by-laws, and the beauty of its ritual. There should be no difficulty in the
practice of its principles in our daily life, but its success depends entirely on
the type of its membership, and I strongly advise exercising great care in the
consideration of all applicants. The strength of the fraternity lies in the quality
of its membership rather than in numbers.
A Masonic lodge can and should be a factor in the life of its community,
not through any concerted action on the part of the lodge itself, but rather
through the exemplary conduct of its members. The institution as a whole is
often judged by the actions of an individual, and when we assume the obligations of a Mason we are responsible 11ot tc ourselves alone, but to those brethren
with whom we are associated and bound by the ties of fidelity and honor.
West Australia (1938):
(Grand Master): The other day we read in the daily press that a referendum is to be taken in Switzerland on next Sunday to determine whether
Freemasonry should be banned. There is a curious Swiss law, under which a
certain number of citizens, if dissatisfied with any church or organization, can
ask for a referendum on the question of its abolition, and evidently this law has
been invoked either .by political or ecclesiastical zealots. It is not the only instance i~ recent times of ungrounded and biased opposition to the Craft, and I
may be pardoned perhaps for repeating some few words spoken in connection
with another branch of our Order.
We all know something of Masonry, and know how far short we each
of us fall from its ideals, but we do know this, and there is no man and no
institution that can contradict us, there are no finer ideals for an individual
to strive to follow than the tenets and principles of Freemasonry. When we
are told that Freemasonry is subversive of good government, and that the evils
from which countries suffer at the present time are due to the fact that the
Masonic Craft has intervened for evil, and when we are told that it is destructive to the beliefs of any ecclesiastical organization, we know it is not true. Masonry stands in all its branches for a firm belief in God and the Brotherhood
of Man, and that ultimate Brotherhood of Man can never be achieved except by
supporting, helping and furthering every good movement, no matter what it
may be. We have all seen within the last two or three weeks letters and press
reports pointing out how deeply the Masonic influence has ingrained itself into

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

countries of the world, and how bad that influence is. The man or organization
that can think evil of Masonry has that evil in himself to start with.
We are not afraid to stand before the world, and we are not afraid that
the world may know the tenets and principles upon which we rest. We are
not afraid of anything that we may do in furtherance of those tenets and
principles, and apart from our ritualistic ceremonies we have nothing to hide
from the world. I question very much whether some of the organization1
which criticise Masonry can with any degree of truthfulness make the same
statement. It is all very well for us to think that as Freemasons we may
go on our way rejoicing and there is none to say nay, but there are many force1
striving to say nay, and all those forces are destructive, not only to Masonry
but of everything that is good and free and just. If we have to choose between the two, there is no doubt that we who live in a British community under
laws of enlightenment, and with the history of a thousand years of democratic
freedom behind us, would prefer to be Freemasons rather than subscribe to
any autocratic fiat, whether it be fascist, communist, or ecclesiastical.

Many lodges have undertaken to interpolate sketches, write in parts explanatory of the work, using pantomime in exemplifying the work. This is
particularly the case with the second section of the Third Degree, Grand Lodge
officers are sometimes invited to attend to witness these performances.
No Master nor officer of any lodge shall consider that any such work is
approved contrary to the ritual, nor that it is anything but a Masonic offense
for a lodge to put on such work, except as an illustration or interpretation
rather than as an actual rendition of the work itself.

EARLY CANDLE LIGHT
The Ritual has been developed or changed from time to time as the
original ideals and aims of the Fraternity have progressed. In some
cases the dotting of "i's" and the crossing of "t's" has become the sum and
substance of the work of the average Lodge. Members in time become
surfeited with this and the dwindling of attendance at Lodge meetings can
be directly traced to this practice. "Mouth to Ear" served its purpose at
one time, but it is now in competition with the newspapers, magazines,
radios, automobiles and movies. They offer a larger field of entertainment and instruction to the individual than the customary Lodge meeting.

Missouri (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Lecturer of California finds :
"For many years it has been customary to wear the apron outside the coat
while attending the communications of the Grand Lodge and when on processions
at other times. Many of the brethren choose to wear it under the coat. I have
learned that in some jurisdictions the apron is worn outside the coat on :ill
occasions, but so far this ruling has never been made in California. To clarify
the situation, let me say that the Grand Lodge communications and processions
of lodges are looked upon as formal in nature and at such times the apron
should be worn outside the coat. No harm is done in wearing it beneath the coat
at lodge meetings if the brethren care to do so."
·
Thus California provides two ways of wearing the Masonic apron. We
had hoped the Grand Lecturer would stop before he reached the situation in
subordinate lodges. In our opinion the apron should be worn one way, and one
way only. If the apron is to be worn under the coat then the brother had just
as well enter the lodge room without any apron whatsoever. There shoulcl be
uniformity of use on all occasions.

expressed a desire that these services be made an annual affair. Whether this
becomes the order or not, lodges which so desire can make these services traditional and a part of their yearly schedule.

749

From time immemorial Masonic Ritual has received the attention of the
greatest scholars of their day. History tells us that in A. D. 926 King Atholstan applied to his brother, Prince Edwin, to formulate or put in order the
ritual of that day. A history of ritual would fill many volumes. Countless
books and manuscripts have been written about it. However, we are not going
to detain you by reciting what you can read at home, other than to give you a
brief summary of the origin of the ritual as we now have it.
About the greatest activity in ritualistic literature began with William
Preston (1742-1818), an eminent scholar of his day. In 1772 he submitted a
course of lectures and ritual for the first three degrees to the Craft of England. This course was a revision of that which had been practiced since the
revival of 1717, and was intended to confer a higher literary character on
Masonic Ritual. These were adopted by the English Masons and practiced
until the union of 1813, when, for the sake of securing uniformity, they were
substituted, to some extent, by the inferior system of Dr. Hemming, However, the Prestonian Lectures and Ritual are still used by many lodges in
England.
Leaving England and coming to America, we find Thomas Smith Webb
(1771-1819) who, among other· prominent offices, was Grand Master at Rhode
Island in 1813 and considered the greatest ritualist of his day. Being little
acquainted with_philosophical symbolism, he revised the Prestonian Lectureswhich he considered too long and deep for the average man-putting them in
the form of a Monitor, his only publication. Webb, later, greatly altered the
Prestonian work, although the fundamentals remained the same. Other learned
Masons edited rituals from time to time, although all appear to be based upon
the Prestonian work. Such men as Sickles, Mackie, Simons and many others,
published various Monitors. Then there was the influence of the ritualistic
work of the various lodges working the Grand Lodge of Scotland and the
Grand Lodge of England-to such an extent that hardly two jurisdictions of
North America have what you would. call exactly uniform work.
South Australia (1937):

(Grand Master) : It would seem that many brethren become worried because they do not render our ritual word for word. I would point out that
obvious sincerities, although it may be delivered without true elocutionary effect,
is far more likely to impress the candidate with our moral teachings. Word
memory is far from being the summum bonum of Freemasonry. First impressions have a vital bearing on the outlook of the initiate, he is not aware whether
the ritual has been given absolutely correct or not, yet he is undoubtedly able to
feel, and therefore appreciate that the brethren who have rendered it have
really felt it themselves.

Washington (1937):
(Grand L ecturer): It is my opinion. that if the books are used merely to
check up the memory or settle a controversy, great good will accrue in promoting accuracy and uniformity in the work. But if the books are used for
original study and as a substitute for mouth to ear instruction, the brethren so
attempting to learn their Masonry will lose the benefit of those lasting friendships which are formed between teacher and student, and they will fail, from
the printed page, to catch the spirit of the institution, which a Mason apprehends
only little by little as he receives explanation of the work and lectures from his
teacher. These matters have never been written, and can be passed down only
from mouth to ear. The young Mason who does not get these traditions and
oral teachings is unknowingly cheating himself out of the best that Masonry
has to offer him; and I apprehend that a long continued use of books for original study may result in the ultimate loss of many of these traditions and
teachings. As the old members pass away there will come a time when no one
i~ left in the lodge who can answer the questions which arise in the mind of
the novitiate, and explain the hidden meanings of our ritual to the seeker after
light. Should such a result attend the use of these books, the loss might well
be deemed to more than offset any benefit accruing from ritualistic accuracy.

West Australia (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A German friend domiciled in
the United States in the pre-nazi days told me that he was glad to leave Berlin
and escape the word "Verboten," which everywhere stared him in the face.
There are signs that in the United States (including Texas) the question may
arise among folks harassed by the word "improper," as it arose in the mind
of a schoolboy regimented from morn till dewy eve by that identical word.
Here is the latest Texan contribution: It is improper to rent the lower floor
of a Masonic building to a beer agency for the storage of beer, It is improper
even though it is represented that no package will be opened in the place of
business. It is improper to have beer stored in and sold from any portion of a
Masonic building. This last seems to me so comprehensive that to store the
beer up the chimney of a Masonic building, and sell it from the chimney pot
would come within the decision. It is improper to permit a group of ladies to
hold a domino tournament in the dining room of a lodge and charge money
therefor, even for a praiseworthy object. It is improper for a Masonic lodge
as such, to join with civic organizations in the sale of tickets for a cha~ity ball.
It is improper for a lodge or body of Masons to give attendance prizes, the
winner thereof to be decided. Evidently, as charity covers . a multitude of sins,
"attendances" covers a multitude of improprieties. Why the need for such
"verbotens" should exist passes comprehension. "I was fed up with 'verboten,'"
said my German friend. American jurisdictions seem to be faced with the
task of manufacturing similar pabulum.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : After labor comes refreshment
and invariably such is within the bounds of propriety. Unfortunately, however,
there is a tendency for many lodges to continue proceedings long after the singing of the National Anthem, and frequently well past midnight. Instances are
not unknown where an adjournment is made elsewhere and festivities continued indefinitely. Most members of the Craft are married, and such practices
are scarcely fair to their wives or families. Conduct of this nature is not in
the best interests of the Craft and cannot help being viewed by outsiders with
the gravest disapproval. The festive board must be closed after the singing
of the National Anthem. On the question of harmony, at times the items given
are scarcely in keeping with the dignity of a Freemason. The responsibility
for decorum, whilst a lodge is in session and at the festive board, falls solely
on the Worshipful Master, and he has ample powers to curb any unseemliness.
There is no excuse for failure to keep the festive board within due bounds.
GONE WITH THE WIND
In this Jurisdiction we have a number of examples that the building
of Masonic Temples should be governed by the same rules that apply to
any business proposition:. Perhaps three illustrations that enthusiasm and
interest at the beginning of a project evaporate when faced with stern
realities are-the New Orleans Masonic Temple, the United Masonic Temple project of the District of Columbia and the George Washington Memorial.
A number of Jurisdictions have established the rule that before erecting edifices a practical financial program must be adopted and approved by
the Grand Lodge. However, in cases of large projects it has developed they
"locked the stable door after the horses had been stolen."

North Carolina (1939):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The New Orleans Masonic Temple sticks up like a sore thumb. Three years ago there was a refinancing, and
the Grand Master is not satisfied that things are in an entirely satisfactory
condition even now. The building cost nearly two and one-third million dollars
with furnishings, and the present indebtedness on it is one million one hundred
thousand dollars, or a little less than half of its cost. These do not include the
ground, so that the present equity of the Grand Lodge in it is a millio~ and a
half. The Grand Master sees that something must be done. One thmg that
suggests itself is to get the membership in the fraternity in Lousiana back to
where it used to be-from 21,000 men to 35,000. Another is to levy a fivedollar Temple assessment, instead of the present two-dollar assessment for it.
Then voluntary pledges from ten thousand Masons would save it, if the assessment on the entire body should fail. It would, he says, be a severe blow to
Louisiana Freemasonry to have to lose the Temple. But that is not all. Other
office buildings in New Orleans are being air-conditioned, and if the Temple
is not, tenants are going to be increasingly difficult to find. "We have already
lost one important tenant because of the desire for this comfort,'' says the
Grand Master. And he adds that "the probable cost of the air-conditioning
would be $1,58,000.00, and there are no funds available for this desired or necessary improvement." New Orleans Masons pay rent for the places in which they
meet, the cost being some $25.00 per meeting.

• • • •
The sore thumb which sticks up in front of the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia is the United Masonic Temple project and that parcel of real
estate appertaining thereunto known as Temple Heights. It was a noble ideal
which inspired the beginning of Temple Heights-an ideal quite in common
with the boom days of Freemasonry which gave it birth. They wanted to
build a Masonic Temple in the city of Washington which would be a monument
to the fraternity in the nation's capital. Only great hill left in the city which
could be bought to fittingly show forth such a monumental structure was this
one, and so they bought it. There were rumors that other groups were trying
to get it-and these persisted. The price was nine hundred thousand dollars.
Of this the Grand Lodge has paid $554,000.00, plus interest in the total amount
of $397,059.26, and taxes to date of $192,637.75. So the total payments to date
run over eleven hundred thousand dollars and a third of a million still to pay
before they even own the bare real estate, plus interest until liquidated and
taxes thereafter. A year ago it was resolved to sell the property; but no bidders
can be found. Those interests which had been rumored to be after it some
years ago just vanished. It was stated that the surrounding property is going
into the hands of negroes-so we heard at Washington. The government has
not been interested in the place. But they still have hopes. It is a good thing
that the depression hit them before they went further in debt by contracting
to have a great structure placed on the property; H this had been done, doubtlessly the whole thing would have been ignominiously lost to them.

The proposed $1.70 per capita was not presented as a possible goal for
more than a decade after the date given. The first goal designated was $1.00
per capita. Characteristic of the position taken by the officers of the association in the early days of this movement, is the plan adopted at a Conference
held in Denver, August 22nd, and 23rd, 1919. Eight States were represented at
that meeting. The "following' plan of operation was finally adopted."
"That the quota for each state should not be fixed, but that in the drive,
the equivalent of $1.00 per capita on the membership should be the goal in each
Lodge and that subscriptions in any amount be accepted, * * * ."
At a regional Conference held in Boston, almost exactly ten years later
(May 18, 1929), composed of representatives of the Six New England States
and New York and New Jersey, it was recorded as the sense of that group
that its members would :
" * * * consider favorably recommending to their Grand Jurisdictions the
pledging of an equivalent of sixty cents per member (in addition to the original
$1.00 per capita; which all the Jurisdictions present had exceeded) to be paid
during a period of not exceeding three years * * *."
At the February meeting of the Association, following this conference,
Grand Master Dutton of New York, agreed to " * * * undertake to raise
at least $200,000.00 more." As there appeared to be some misunderstanding
concerning the sixty cents referred to, Past Grand Master Johnson of
Massachusetts, made clear the matter, that "the goal is that every Grand Lodge
should come up to $1.75 per capita."

Ohio (1938):
(Grand Master): These latter years there has grown up a widespread
custom of exchanging visits with lodges belonging to other jurisdictions. Properly controlled and regulated, this is a most desirable activity. For your information I will say that the general procedure is for the lodge desiring to make
such a visit to call the matter to the attention of their Grand Master, who
thereupon issues a dispensation for the meeting, subject only to the granting
of a similar consent by the Grand Master of the other grand jurisdiction. The
actual proceedings are then as follows :
The hGst lodge opens in the work of its own jurisdiction and calls from
labor to · refreshment. The visiting lodge then opens in accordance with the
~egular work of its jurisdiction, confers the degree on its own candidate according to the work of its jurisdiction, and closes. Whereupon the host lodge
recalls from refreshment to labor and closes.

Virginian and half foreign, along our border lines, without deliberately creating
more. The Masonic ritual is not an entertainment or a show. The work of
the lodge is not vaudeville. It behooves the lodges along the border line to
recognize that they are strictly and absolutely West Virginia lodges, and to be
such in spirit and letter.
Wisconsin (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Dispensations were issued by
the Connecticut Grand Master to seven lodges to open lodge in another Grand
jurisdiction, the consent of the Grand Master of such other grand jurisdict~on
having first been obtained. There can be no doubt about. the value of meeting
with lodges in another jurisdiction, the good fellowship and the exchange of
fraternal greetings doing much to cement friendly relations between the respective jurisdiction, but as a matter of Masonic jurisprudence we cannot see how
it can be done.

MASONIC CALENDAR
Ancient Craft Masons-Commence their era with the creation of the
world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L.), "in the year of light."
Add 4000 years to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 4000-5923.
· · Scottish Rite--Same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology
is · ~sed. Anno Mundi (A. M.), "in the year of the world."
!.dd 3760 to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 3760-5683. After
September add another year.
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple was commenced by Zerubbabel, Anno Inventionis. (A. Inv.), "in the year of discovery."
.
Add 530 years to the vulgar era. Thus: 1923 and 530-2453.
Royal and Select Masters-Date from the year in which the temple of
Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.), "in the year of the
deposit."
Add 1000 to the common time. Thus: 1923 and 1000-2923.
Knights Templar-Commence their era with the organization of their
Order. Anno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the Order."
From the Christian era take 1118. Thus: 1118 from 1923-805.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Order of High Priesthood-Dates from the year of the blessing of
Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benedictionis (A. B.).
"in the year of the blessing."
To the Christian era add 1913, the year of blessing. Thus: 1923 and
1913-3836.

The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly speaking,
they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish Rite, for the
one called York is peculiar in its organized proceedings only to the United
States.

The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the Cryptic
and the Templar Degrees.
The Symbolic Degrees are conferred in a Lodge and are the Entered
Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They are called
Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is by symbols.
The Capitular Degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the Mark
Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent Master and the Royal Arch.
The supplemental and honorary degree of High Priesthood is conferred
in a Council of High Priests upon thos·e who have been regularly elected
to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They are called Capitular
because they are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning
"done. in a Chapter."
The Cryptic Degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the Royal
Master, the Select Master . and the Super-Excellent Master.. They are
called "Cryptic" because the word "crypt" means a secret vau.l t or. underground passage.
The Templar Degrees are conferred in a C~mmandery and are t~
Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta.· The name Knight Templar comes
from the efforts of the Christian Knights to .take the temple at Jerusalem
from the Mohammedans.
